Medinan by unanimous agreement.

This passage contains five issues.

**First: its names.** Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, about Surah Bara'ah (al-Tawbah), and he said: "That is al-Fadihah (the Exposing). It kept descending, 'and among them, and among them,' until we feared it would leave no one out." Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr 'Abd al-Rahim said: This surah was revealed during the Battle of Tabuk, and it was revealed after the others. At its beginning is the repudiation of the covenants of the disbelievers toward them. The surah exposes the secrets of the hypocrites, so it is called al-Fadihah and al-Bahuth, because it searches out (yabhathu) the secrets of the hypocrites. It is also called al-Muba'thirah, and al-Ba'thirah means al-bahth (searching).

**Second: the reason the basmalah is absent from the beginning of this surah.** The scholars differed over this, giving five opinions.

The first: It is said that it was the custom of the Arabs in the Jahiliyyah, when there was a covenant between them and a people and they wished to break it, to write them a letter without a basmalah in it. When Surah Bara'ah was revealed, annulling the covenant that had existed between the Prophet ﷺ and the polytheists, the Prophet ﷺ sent it with 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, who recited it to them at the season of pilgrimage, and he did not begin it with the basmalah, following their established practice of omitting the basmalah when annulling a covenant.

The second opinion: al-Nasa'i narrated, saying: Ahmad told us, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna told us, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, who said: 'Awf told us, who said: Yazid al-Raqashi [[In manuscripts B, J, K, Z and H: "al-Rawasi." The text in Sahih al-Tirmidhi reads "al-Farisi." Al-Tirmidhi commented on it: "... a hasan sahih hadith; we know it only from the hadith of 'Awf, from Yazid al-Farisi, from Ibn 'Abbas. Yazid al-Farisi narrated more than one hadith from Ibn 'Abbas. It is said he is Yazid ibn Hurmuz. Yazid al-Raqashi is Yazid ibn Aban al-Raqashi, who did not meet Ibn 'Abbas; he narrated only from Anas ibn Malik, and both are from Basra. Yazid al-Farisi is earlier than Yazid al-Raqashi."]] told us, [who] said: Ibn 'Abbas said to us: I said to 'Uthman: What led you to combine al-Anfal, which is of the al-mathani (the oft-repeated, under one hundred verses), and Bara'ah, which is of the mi'in (the hundred-verse surahs), placing them together without writing the line "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy" between them, and placed them among the al-sab' al-tiwal (the seven long surahs) [[The seven long surahs are: al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, and al-A'raf, which are six consecutive surahs. The scholars differed about the seventh. Some said the seventh is al-Anfal together with Bara'ah, counting them as one surah. Others made the seventh Surah Yunus.]]? What led you to do that? 'Uthman said: When something was revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he would call some of those who wrote for him and say: "Place this in the surah in which such-and-such is mentioned." And when verses were revealed to him, he would say: "Place these verses in the surah in which such-and-such is mentioned." Al-Anfal was among the first to be revealed [[i.e., after the Hijrah]], and Bara'ah was among the last of the Qur'an, and its story resembled that of al-Anfal. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed away without making clear to us that it was part of it, so I assumed it was part of it. For this reason I combined them and did not write the line "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful" between them. Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi also narrated it and said: This is a hasan hadith.

The third opinion: It was also narrated from 'Uthman. Malik said, in what Ibn Wahb, Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam narrated: When its beginning fell away, the basmalah fell away with it. It was also narrated from Ibn 'Ajlan that it reached him that the surah of Bara'ah was equal to al-Baqarah or close to it, and part of it was lost; therefore the basmalah was not written between them. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: It was like Surah al-Baqarah.

The fourth opinion: This was stated by Kharijah, Abu 'Ismah and others. They said: When they compiled the Mushaf (codex) during the caliphate of 'Uthman, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ differed. Some said: Bara'ah and al-Anfal are one surah. Others said: They are two surahs. So a gap was left between them to accommodate the view of those who said they are two surahs, and the basmalah was omitted to accommodate the view of those who said they are one surah. Both groups were satisfied, and the proofs of both were preserved in the Mushaf.

The fifth opinion: 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas said: I asked 'Ali ibn Abi Talib: Why was "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy" not written at the beginning of Bara'ah? He said: Because the basmalah is security (aman), and Bara'ah was revealed with the sword, with no security in it. Its meaning is also narrated from al-Mubarrad, who said: For this reason they were not joined. The basmalah is mercy, and Bara'ah was revealed in wrath [[In al-Jamal's citation from al-Qurtubi: "with His wrath."]]. The same is narrated from Sufyan. Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: It was only not written at the beginning of this surah because the tasmiyah (saying the basmalah) is mercy, mercy is security, and this surah was revealed about the hypocrites and with the sword, and there is no security for the hypocrites.

The correct view is that the tasmiyah was not written because Jibril, peace be upon him, did not bring it down with this surah. This was stated by al-Qushayri.

In 'Uthman's words, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed away without making clear to us that it was part of it," there is evidence that all the surahs were arranged by his word and his clarification, and that Bara'ah alone was joined to al-Anfal without a command from the Prophet ﷺ, because death overtook him before he clarified that. The two were called al-Qarinatayn (the two companions), so it was necessary that they be joined and one added to the other, because of the attribute that came with their being paired, while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was still alive.

**Third:** Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is evidence that analogy (qiyas, reasoning by comparison) is a foundation of the religion. Do you not see that 'Uthman and the eminent Companions resorted to analogy by resemblance when there was no explicit text, and they saw that the story of Bara'ah resembled the story of al-Anfal, so they attached it to it? If Allah the Exalted has shown the admission of analogy in the composition of the Qur'an, what then do you suppose about the rest of the rulings?

**Fourth:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Bara'ah (a declaration of freedom)﴾. You say: "I was freed (bari'tu) from the thing, I am freed (abra'u) with freedom (bara'ah), so I am free of it (bari'un minhu)," when you remove it from yourself and cut the tie between you and it. "Bara'ah" is in the nominative as the predicate of an implied subject, its implied form being: "This is a bara'ah." It is also permissible for it to be nominative as the subject, with the predicate being in His words: ﴿to those﴾. The beginning with an indefinite noun is permissible because it is qualified, so it becomes definite in a certain sense, and it is permissible to make a predicate of it. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "Bara'atan" (in the accusative), with an implied sense of: "Commit yourselves to a bara'ah," so it carries the meaning of urging (ighra'). It is a verbal noun on the pattern fa'alah, like al-shana'ah and al-dana'ah.

**Fifth:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿to those with whom you made a covenant among the polytheists﴾, meaning: to those with whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made a covenant. This is because he was the one who concluded the agreements, and all his Companions were content with that, so it is as though they themselves contracted and covenanted, and the contract is attributed to them. Likewise, what the leaders of disbelief contracted on behalf of their people is attributed to those people and counted against them, and they are held accountable for it, since nothing else is possible, because obtaining the consent of everyone is impossible. So when the imam (ruler) contracts a matter that he sees as in the public interest, it binds all of the subjects.

There are three issues in this verse.

The first concerns God's words ﴿So travel freely﴾, where the address shifts from the third person to the second person. The meaning is: say to them, "Travel (sihu) freely in the land," that is, go about in the land coming and going, secure and unafraid of any Muslim, whether by war, plunder, killing, or capture. It is said: Fulan sāḥa fī al-ard, yasīhu siyāḥatan, wa-suyūḥan, wa-sayaḥānan. From this comes al-sayḥ, meaning water flowing and spreading out. From the same root is the verse of Tarafah ibn al-'Abd:

*"If I feared this from you, you would not have reached me,*
*until you see, before me, the flowing (of the water)."*

The second issue is that the scholars differed over how this respite was to be applied and over who the people are from whom God and His Messenger declared themselves free. Muhammad ibn Ishaq and others said: they are two categories of polytheists. One of them had a treaty whose term was less than four months, so he was given the full four months. The other had a treaty with no fixed term, so it was limited to four months so that he could make his arrangements. After that, he is an enemy of God, His Messenger, and the believers, to be killed wherever he is found and taken captive, unless he repents. The beginning of this term is the Day of the Greater Hajj, and its end is the tenth of Rabi' al-Akhir. As for the one who had no treaty, his term ends with the expiry of the four sacred months. That amounts to fifty days: twenty days of Dhu al-Hijjah and the month of Muharram.

Al-Kalbi said: the four months applied only to those who had a treaty with the Messenger of God ﷺ of less than four months. Whoever had a treaty of more than four months, God commanded that his treaty be fulfilled to its term, by His words ﴿So fulfil for them their treaty until their term﴾ [al-Tawbah: 4]. This is the view chosen by al-Tabari and others.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq, Mujahid and others mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning the people of Makkah. The Messenger of God ﷺ made a treaty with the Quraysh in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, that they would lay down war for ten years, during which people would be secure and would refrain from attacking one another. The tribe of Khuza'ah entered into the covenant of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and the tribe of Bakr entered into the covenant of the Quraysh. Then Bakr attacked Khuza'ah and broke their covenant. The cause of this was a blood-debt that Bakr owed to Khuza'ah from a time before Islam. When the truce concluded at al-Hudaybiyah was in force and people were secure from one another, the clan of al-Dil from Bakr, who were the ones owing the blood-debt, seized that opportunity, and Khuza'ah were heedless. They wished to take revenge for the sons of al-Aswad ibn Razn [[In the margin of the European edition of Tarikh al-Tabari, vol. 1, p. 1619: (Razin).]], whom Khuza'ah had killed. Nawfal ibn Mu'awiyah al-Dili went out with those of Bakr ibn 'Abd Manat who obeyed him, until they launched a night attack [[To attack a people or enemy by surprise at night.]] upon Khuza'ah and fought them. The Quraysh aided Bakr with weapons, and some of the Quraysh aided them in person. Khuza'ah were routed to the sanctuary, as is well known and recorded [[See Tarikh al-Tabari and the Sirah of Ibn Hisham, the chapter on the conquest of Makkah.]]. That was a breach of the truce concluded at al-Hudaybiyah.

Then 'Amr ibn Salim al-Khuza'i, Budayl ibn Warqa' al-Khuza'i and a group of Khuza'ah set out and came to the Messenger of God ﷺ, seeking his help against what Bakr and the Quraysh had done to them. 'Amr ibn Salim recited:

*"O Lord, I appeal to Muhammad*
*by the covenant of our father and his father, the ancient one.*
*You were a father to us, and we were children.*
*Then we became Muslims and did not withdraw a hand.*
*So, may God guide you, give us a mighty victory,*
*and call the servants of God, that they may come to help.*
*Among them is the Messenger of God, who has come out,*
*fair like the sun, rising to the heights.*
*If he is struck with disgrace, his face darkens,*
*in an army like a sea flowing with foam.*
*Indeed, the Quraysh broke their promise to you*
*and violated your firm covenant.*
*They claimed that you would call no one,*
*while they are the most humiliated and fewest in number.*
*They attacked us by night at al-Watir [[In the originals: (al-Hatim). The correction is from the Sirah of Ibn Hisham, the Tarikh al-Tabari, the Mu'jam of Yaqut, and the books of the Companions under the entry 'Amr ibn Salim al-Khuza'i. Al-Watir: the name of a water-place in lower Makkah belonging to Khuza'ah.]] while we were sleeping,*
*and they killed us while we were bowing and prostrating."*

The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Let me not be helped if I do not help the tribe of Ka'b." Then he looked at a cloud and said: "Indeed, it is pouring rain for the victory of the tribe of Ka'b," meaning Khuza'ah. The Messenger of God ﷺ said to Budayl ibn Warqa' and those with him: "Abu Sufyan will come to strengthen the treaty and extend the truce, and he will depart without achieving his aim." The Quraysh regretted what they had done, so Abu Sufyan went out to Madinah to renew the treaty and extend the truce. He returned without achieving his aim, just as the Messenger of God ﷺ had told them, as is well known from his account.

The Messenger of God ﷺ prepared to go to Makkah, and God granted its conquest, and that was in the eighth year of the Hijrah [[The migration from Makkah to Madinah.]]. When news of the conquest of Makkah reached Hawazin, Malik ibn 'Awf al-Nasri gathered them, as is well known from the expedition of Hunayn, some of which will come later. Victory and triumph were for the Muslims over the unbelievers. The battle of Hawazin on the Day of Hunayn took place in early Shawwal of the eighth year of the Hijrah.

The Messenger of God ﷺ left the division of the spoils, of wealth and women, and did not divide them until he reached al-Ta'if. The Messenger of God ﷺ besieged them for about twenty nights. It was also said otherwise. He set up the catapult against them and bombarded them with it, as is well known from that campaign. Then the Messenger of God ﷺ returned to al-Ji'ranah and divided the spoils of Hunayn, as is well known from that matter and its account.

Then the Messenger of God ﷺ departed, and the people dispersed. In that year 'Attab ibn Usayd led the Hajj for the people; he was the first commander to lead the Hajj in Islam. The polytheists performed the Hajj according to their own rites. 'Attab ibn Usayd was good, virtuous and pious.

Ka'b ibn Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma came to the Messenger of God ﷺ, praised him, and stood before him reciting his qasidah whose opening is:

*"Su'ad has departed, and my heart today is enslaved."*

He recited it to its end. In it he mentioned the Muhajirun and praised them. Before that he had been recorded as having lampooned the Prophet ﷺ. The Ansar criticised him because he had not mentioned them. So he came to the Prophet ﷺ the next morning with a qasidah praising the Ansar, saying:

*"Whoever is pleased with the nobility of life, let him remain*
*in a company of the righteous Ansar [[Al-Miqnab: a band of horsemen.]].*
*They inherited nobility, generation from generation.*
*Indeed, the best are the sons of the good."*

*"Those who force the spear of al-Samhari [[Al-Samhari: the spear. The sāfilah (lower part) of the spear is its thickest part and its shortest in joints. Al-Hindi: the lances.]] with their arms,*
*like the lower shafts of Indian lances, not short."*

*"And those who look with eyes reddened*
*like embers, their sight unweakened."*

*"And those who sell their souls to their Prophet*
*for death, on the day of embrace and charging."*

*"They purify themselves, seeing it as a rite for them,*
*with the blood of those among the unbelievers they have struck."*

*"They were trained as the lions of the thicket of Khafiyyah*
*were trained, the thick-necked, fierce lions [[Dariba: they became accustomed. Khafiyyah: a place abounding in lions. Al-Ghulb: thick-necked. Al-Dawari: those which have become accustomed to eating human flesh; singular dari.]].*"

*"And when you alight to have them protect you, you are*
*in the fortresses of the wild goats [[Al-Ma'aqil: fortresses. Al-Aghfar: the young of the mountain goat (al-Wa'l), singular ghafr.]]."*

*"They struck 'Ali on the Day of Badr with a blow*
*by whose impact the whole of Nizar submitted."*

[[ 'Ali: 'Ali ibn Bakr ibn Wa'il. It is said that he is 'Ali, brother of 'Abd Manat ibn Khuzaymah through his mother. And it was said: he is 'Ali ibn Mas'ud ibn Mazin.]]

*"If the peoples knew all my knowledge of them,*
*those whom I dispute with would confirm me."*

*"A people who, when the stars are barren [[Khawat: when there is no rain.]], are*
*for the visitors and those who alight, hosts [[Al-Maqari: plural of muqri, one who hosts the guest.]]."*

Then the Messenger of God ﷺ remained in Madinah after his return from al-Ta'if: Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram, Safar, Rabi' al-Awwal, Rabi' al-Akhir, Jumada al-Ula and Jumada al-Akhirah. In Rajab of the ninth year he went out with the Muslims to fight the Romans, the expedition of Tabuk, which was the last expedition he undertook.

Ibn Jurayj said, on the authority of Mujahid: When the Messenger of God ﷺ returned from Tabuk, he intended to perform Hajj, then he said: "Naked polytheists come to the House and circumambulate it. I do not like to perform Hajj until this no longer happens." So he sent Abu Bakr as commander of the Hajj, and sent with him forty verses from the beginning of "Bara'ah" [al-Tawbah] to recite to the people at the gathering. When Abu Bakr set out, the Prophet ﷺ called 'Ali and said: "Go out with this portion from the beginning of Bara'ah, and proclaim it to the people when they gather." So 'Ali went out on the Prophet's ﷺ she-camel al-'Adba' until he overtook Abu Bakr al-Siddiq at Dhu al-Hulayfah, may God be pleased with them both. When Abu Bakr saw him, he said: "Are you a commander or one commanded?" He said: "Rather, one commanded." Then the two went on together. Abu Bakr led the people in the Hajj according to the stations they had observed in the Jahiliyyah.

In the Sunan of al-Nasa'i, on the authority of Jabir: 'Ali recited "Bara'ah" to the people until he finished it, before the Day of Tarwiyah by one day. And on the Day of 'Arafah and on the Day of Nahr, at the conclusion of Abu Bakr's sermon, during the three days. When the first day of departure came, Abu Bakr stood and preached to the people, informing them how to depart and how to throw the pebbles, teaching them their rites. When he finished, 'Ali stood and recited "Bara'ah" to the people until he completed it.

Sulayman ibn Musa said: When Abu Bakr preached at 'Arafah, he said: "Stand up, O 'Ali, and deliver the message of the Messenger of God ﷺ." 'Ali stood and did so. He said: Then it occurred to me that not all the people had witnessed Abu Bakr's sermon, so I began to follow the tents on the Day of Nahr.

Al-Tirmidhi related on the authority of Zayd ibn Yuthay' who said: I asked 'Ali: "With what were you sent in regard to the Hajj?" He said: "I was sent with four things: that no naked person circumambulate the House; whoever had a treaty with the Prophet ﷺ, it remains until its term; whoever had no treaty, his term is four months; no one enters Paradise except a believing soul; and the Muslims and the polytheists shall not gather after this year of theirs." He said: "This is a good, sound hadith." Al-Nasa'i also related it, and said: "So I was proclaiming until my voice became hoarse [[Al-Sahl: harshness of voice with hoarseness.]]."

Abu 'Umar said: 'Ali was sent to return to every party with a treaty its treaty, and to make a covenant with them that no polytheist should perform Hajj after that year, and no naked person should circumambulate the House. Abu Bakr led the Hajj that year, the ninth year. Then the Messenger of God ﷺ performed his Hajj the following year, the Hajj he did not perform other than that, from Madinah, and his Hajj fell in Dhu al-Hijjah. He said: "Indeed time has come round..." — the hadith — as will be explained in the verse of al-Nasi' [[See vol. 13, p. 136, p. ??? (page reference left unfinished in the source).]]. The Hajj became fixed in Dhu al-Hijjah until the Day of Resurrection. Mujahid mentioned that Abu Bakr performed Hajj in Dhu al-Qa'dah of the ninth year.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: The wisdom in giving "Bara'ah" to 'Ali was that "Bara'ah" contained the annulment of the covenant which the Prophet ﷺ had made. The custom of the Arabs was that a covenant could be dissolved only by the one who had concluded it or by a man from his own household. So the Prophet ﷺ wished to silence the tongues of the Arabs with proof, and to send his cousin, the Hashimite from his own house, to annul the covenant, so that no one would remain to argue. Al-Zajjaj said the same meaning.

Third issue: The scholars said: this verse includes permission to terminate a covenant between us and the polytheists. There are two situations to this. The first is when the term between us and them expires, and we then notify them of war. The notification is a matter of choice.

The second is when we fear treachery from them, so we cast their covenant back to them, as has already been explained.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The verse is abrogated (mansukhah, i.e. superseded by a later ruling), for the Prophet ﷺ made a covenant, then annulled the covenant when he was commanded to fight.

Three issues (masa'il):

The first: God's words, ﴿And a proclamation﴾. Al-adhan (the proclamation, meaning notification) is, linguistically, notification, with no disagreement about this. It is conjoined to "Bara'ah" (Immunity). "To the people": here "the people" means all of creation. "On the day of the greater Hajj" is a time adverb, and the word governing it is "proclamation." Although it is described by the phrase "from God," the sense of the verb remains in it, and it governs the adverbs of time. It was also said that the governing word is "disgracing" (mukhzi), and that "proclamation" cannot govern it, because it has been qualified and has thereby left the rule of the verb.

The second: The scholars differed about "the greater Hajj." It was said to be the Day of 'Arafah. This is related from 'Umar, 'Uthman, Ibn 'Abbas, Tawus and Mujahid. It is the position of Abu Hanifah, and al-Shafi'i also said so. It is also related from 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas (again), Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abi Awfa and al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah that it is the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). Al-Tabari chose this view. Ibn 'Umar related that the Messenger of God ﷺ stood on the Day of Sacrifice during the Farewell Hajj, and said: "What day is this?" They said: "The Day of Sacrifice." He said: "This is the Day of the Greater Hajj." This was narrated by Abu Dawud. Al-Bukhari related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, sent me among those who proclaimed on the Day of Sacrifice at Mina: 'No polytheist shall perform Hajj after this year, and no naked person shall circumambulate the House.' The Day of the Greater Hajj is the Day of Sacrifice. It was called 'the greater' because of people's saying 'the lesser Hajj.'" Abu Bakr then announced this to the people that year, so that no polytheist performed Hajj in the year of the Farewell Hajj in which the Prophet ﷺ performed Hajj. Ibn Abi Awfa said: "The Day of Sacrifice is the Day of the Greater Hajj, on which blood is shed, hair is shortened, the unkempt state (tafath) is removed, and the states of ihram are lifted." This is the position of Malik, because the Day of Sacrifice contains the whole of Hajj: the standing (wuquf) is only its night, while the stoning, sacrifice, shaving and circumambulation take place in its morning.

Those who held the first view argued with the hadith of Makhramah that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The Day of the Greater Hajj is the Day of 'Arafah." This was transmitted by Isma'il al-Qadi. Al-Thawri and Ibn Jurayj said: "The greater Hajj is all the days of Mina." This is like the saying: "the Day of Siffin, the Day of the Camel, and the Day of Bu'ath," where what is meant is a period of time and an era, not the day itself.[[Siffin (with two kasras and a doubled fa'): a place near al-Raqqah on the bank of the Euphrates. There was a battle there between 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, and Mu'awiyah in the year 37 AH. The Day of the Camel was a battle between 'Ali and 'A'ishah, Mother of the Believers, may God be pleased with them both, in which a number of Companions and others were killed. It was in the year 36 AH. Bu'ath (with the first letter vowelled and the 'ain unpointed; some have reported it with an unpointed ghayn): a place in Madinah two nights' distance away, where there were battles between the Aws and the Khazraj in the pre-Islamic period.]]

It is related from Mujahid that "the greater Hajj" is qiran (combining Hajj and 'Umrah in one ihram),[[Qiran (with kasra): combining Hajj and 'Umrah. Ifrad: to enter ihram for Hajj alone.]] and "the lesser" is ifrad. But this has nothing to do with the verse. It is also related from him and from 'Ata' that "the greater Hajj" is the one in which standing at 'Arafah occurs, and "the lesser" is 'Umrah. Also from Mujahid: all the days of Hajj. Al-Hasan and 'Abdullah ibn al-Harith ibn Nawfal said: "It was only called the Day of the Greater Hajj because in that year the Muslims and the polytheists performed Hajj together, and on that day the festivals of the religions coincided: the Jews, the Christians and the Magians." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is weak, that God, Mighty and Majestic, would describe it in His Book as 'the greatest' for this reason." Also from al-Hasan: "It was only called 'the greatest' because Abu Bakr performed Hajj in it and covenants were annulled in it." This is what resembles al-Hasan's view. Ibn Sirin said: "The Day of the Greater Hajj is the year in which the Prophet ﷺ performed the Farewell Hajj, and the nations performed Hajj with him in it."

The third: God's words, ﴿That God is free of obligation to the polytheists, and so is His Messenger﴾. "Anna" with a fatha is in the accusative position, and the estimate is "that God." Whoever reads it with a kasra takes it as if it were in the sense of "saying," so that it means "saying: indeed God." "Bari'" (free of obligation) is the predicate of "anna." "Wa-rasulihi" is conjoined to the position (of the subject of anna), and if you wish, to the pronoun in "bari'." Both are good, because the speech has been long. If you wish, it may be a new sentence (mubtada'), with the predicate omitted, the estimate being: "and His Messenger is free of obligation toward them." Whoever reads "wa-rasulahu" with a fatha, as al-Hasan and others did, conjoins it to the name of God, Mighty and Majestic, according to the wording. Among the irregular readings (shawadh) is "wa-rasulihi" with a kasra, as an oath, meaning "by the right of His Messenger," and it was related from al-Hasan. The story of 'Umar concerning this has already been mentioned at the beginning of the book.[[See vol. 1, p. 24.]]

(فَإِنْ تُبْتُمْ) i.e. from polytheism.

(فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ) i.e. it is more beneficial for you.

(وَإِنْ تَوَلَّيْتُمْ) i.e. turned away from faith.

(فَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّكُمْ غَيْرُ مُعْجِزِي اللَّهِ) i.e. you will not escape Him, for He encompasses you and will bring His punishment down upon you.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 4:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except those with whom you made a covenant among the polytheists﴾ is in the accusative case as an exception of the connected type (istithna' muttasil). The meaning: Allah is free of obligation toward the polytheists, except toward those who were covenanted, for the duration of their covenant.

It has been said: the exception is disconnected (istithna' munqati'), meaning: Allah is free of them, but as for those with whom you made a covenant, who remained steadfast in the covenant, then fulfil their covenant to them.

His saying: (﴿then they have not fallen short of you﴾) indicates that among the people of the covenant there were those who broke (khasa) their covenant, and among them were those who remained steadfast in fidelity. So Allah, glorified is He, permitted His Prophet (ﷺ) to annul the covenant of whoever broke it, and commanded fidelity toward whoever remained upon his covenant until its term. The meaning of "they have not fallen short of you" is: they did not diminish anything of the conditions of the covenant.

(﴿and have not supported anyone against you﴾) means: they have not helped anyone (against you). Ikrimah and Ata' ibn Yasar read ﴿then they have not violated (yanquduukum) you﴾ with a dotted ḍād, on the basis of an elided noun, the implied meaning being: "then they have not violated their covenant." It is said that this ruling is specific, and that it refers to the Banu Damrah in particular. Then he said: (﴿so fulfil their covenant to them until their term﴾), meaning: even if it exceeds four months.

**Sixth-Part Translation: Al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*, Surah 9, Verse 5**

There are six issues in this verse.

**First issue:** God's words ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed (insalakha al-ashhur al-hurum)﴾ mean "have gone out." One says *salakhtu al-shahr* (I have "stripped" the month) when one has reached its final days; the verb is *salkhan* and *sulukhan*, meaning "you have come out of it." A poet said:

*When I have stripped the month and begun the next one before it,*
*My stripping of the months and my beginning them suffice to kill me.*

[The Lisan and al-Bahr al-Muhit have "*ahlaltu mithlahu*" (I began its like) in place of "*ahlaltu qablahu*."]

One also says *insalakha al-shahr* and *insalakha al-nahar min al-layl al-muqbil* (the day has gone out of the coming night). A woman *salakhat dir'aha* (took off her shift). In the revelation God says: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip the day from it﴾ [Ya-Sin: 37]. A *nakhla maslakh* is a palm whose unripe dates fall off while green. [See vol. 15, p. 26.]

As for "the sacred months" (al-ashhur al-hurum), scholars have two opinions. It is said they are the well-known months: three in succession (Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram) and one single month (Rajab). Al-Asamm said: it refers to those among the polytheists who had no covenant. Thus God obliged that they be left alone until the sacred months had passed, which, according to Ibn Abbas, is a period of fifty days, because the proclamation was made on the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). This has already been mentioned.

It is also said that the months of the covenant were four. This was said by Mujahid, Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Zayd and Amr ibn Shu'ayb.

It is said they are called *hurum* (sacred) because God made it forbidden for the believers, during them, to shed the blood of the polytheists or to attack them, except in a way that is good.

**Second issue:** God's words ﴿then kill the polytheists﴾ are general concerning every polytheist. But the Sunnah (the prophetic practice and tradition) made exceptions to this, as was explained earlier in Surah al-Baqarah [vol. 2, p. 348], such as a woman, a monk, a child and others. God said concerning the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab): "until they give the jizya (poll tax)" [see below, p. 109 and following in this part].

However, it is possible that the word "polytheists" does not include the People of the Book, and this would require prohibiting the taking of the jizya from idol-worshippers and others, as will be explained later. [In manuscripts B, J, Z, K and H: "for the two books" (lil-kitabayn).]

Know that the unrestricted wording of "then kill the polytheists" requires that they may be killed in any manner. However, reports have come forbidding mutilation (al-muthla). Nevertheless, it is possible that when Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) killed the apostates (ahl al-riddah) by burning with fire, by stoning, by throwing them from the tops of mountains and by pushing them head-first into wells, he was relying on the general wording of the verse. Likewise, the burning by Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) of a group of apostates may be an inclination toward this view and a reliance on the generality of the expression. And Allah knows best.

**Third issue:** God's words ﴿wherever you find them﴾ are general in every place. Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) made an exception for the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram), as was mentioned earlier in Surah al-Baqarah [vol. 2, p. 351].

Then they differed. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: this verse abrogated (nasakha; *naskh* means abrogation, the cancelling of one ruling by a later one) every verse in the Qur'an that mentions turning away and patience over the harm of enemies. Al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and Ata said: it is abrogated by God's words ﴿Then either grace afterward or ransom﴾ [Muhammad: 4] and that a captive may not be killed in cold blood; he is either to be granted grace or to be ransomed.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: rather, it abrogates God's words "Then either grace afterward or ransom," and that concerning captives from among the polytheists nothing is permitted except killing.

Ibn Zayd said: both verses are muhkam (clear and unabrogated). This is the correct view, because grace, killing and ransom have never ceased to be the rulings the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) applied to them from the first battle he fought against them, which was the Day of Badr, as has already been mentioned. God's words "and seize them" (wa khudhuhum) point to this. Seizing (al-akhdh) is taking captive (al-asr). Taking captive is only for killing, or ransom, or grace, as the imam sees fit.

The meaning of "confine them" (ihsuruhum) is: prevent them from moving freely into your lands and from entering among you, except that you permit them to enter among you under safe-conduct (bi-aman).

**Fourth issue:** God's words ﴿and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush﴾. *Al-marsad* is the place where the enemy is watched. One says *rasadtu fulanan arsuduhu*, meaning I watched him. The meaning is: lie in wait for them at the places of heedlessness where they are observed.

'Amir ibn al-Tufayl said:

*I know, and I do not think you are forgetful,*
*that death for a young man is at the ambush.*

'Adi (in the originals "al-Nabigha," corrected from the Lisan) said:

*O censurer, the ignorant man [distracts] from the pleasure of the youth,*
*and death for souls is at an ambush.*

In this is evidence for the permissibility of assassinating them before the call (to Islam, al-da'wah).

"Kull" (every) is in the accusative as an adverbial of place (zarf), and this is the choice of al-Zajjaj. One says *dhahabtu tariqan* and *dhahabtu kulla tariqin* (I went a way / every way). Or the preposition is dropped, the sense being "at every ambush" and "upon every ambush," so that *al-marsad* is treated as a name for the road.

Abu Ali al-Zajjaj (in the original, al-Zajjaj is named as Abu Ali) erred in making the road an adverbial of place, and said: the road is a specific place like the house and the mosque, so it is not permissible to omit the preposition from it except in what is heard (as transmitted) with omission, as Sibawayh reported: *dakhaltu al-Sham* (I entered Syria) and *dakhaltu al-bayt* (I entered the house), and as it is said:

*As the fox treads the path (ka-ma 'assala al-tharlab)*

[The speaker is Sa'idah ibn Juwayyah. Its completion, as in the Lisan and Sibawayh's Kitab, is: "Like the swaying of its back under the striking of the hand, as the fox treads the path."]

**Fifth issue:** God's words ﴿But if they repent﴾ mean: from polytheism.

(﴿and establish prayer and give zakat, then let them go their way﴾.) This verse requires reflection. God made killing dependent on polytheism, then said "if they repent." The principle is that killing exists whenever polytheism exists, and it ceases when polytheism ceases. That requires the cessation of killing by repentance alone, without considering the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakat. For this reason, killing ceased by repentance alone before the time of prayer and zakat. This is clear in this sense. However, God mentioned repentance and mentioned with it two other conditions, so there is no way to disregard them.

A parallel is the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I have been commanded to fight the people until they say: there is no god but Allah, and establish prayer and give zakat. When they do that, they are protected from me in their blood and their property, except by their rights, and their reckoning is with Allah." Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "By Allah, I will fight whoever separates between prayer and zakat, for zakat is the right of property." Ibn Abbas said: "May Allah have mercy on Abu Bakr; how deep in understanding he was." Ibn al-Arabi said: thus the Qur'an and the Sunnah agree and are consistent.

There is no disagreement among Muslims that whoever abandons prayer and the other obligations (fara'id) while regarding them as lawful has disbelieved. Whoever abandons the sunan (recommended practices) out of carelessness has committed sin. Whoever abandons the supererogatory acts (nawafil) is not blameworthy, unless he denies their merit, in which case he disbelieves, because he becomes one who rejects what the Messenger (peace be upon him) brought and reported.

They differed concerning one who abandons prayer without denying it or regarding it as lawful. Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la reported: I heard Ibn Wahb say, Malik said: whoever believes in Allah and accepts the messengers but refuses to pray is to be killed. Abu Thawr and all the companions of al-Shafi'i said the same. This is also the view of Hammad ibn Zayd, Makhul and Waki'.

Abu Hanifa said: he is imprisoned and beaten, and not killed. This is also the view of Ibn Shihab, and Dawud ibn Ali says the same.

Among their evidence is the Prophet's statement (ﷺ): "I have been commanded to fight the people until they say there is no god but Allah. When they say that, they are protected from me in their blood and property, except by their right."

They said: its right is the three that the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except by one of three: disbelief after belief, or fornication after marriage (ihsan), or killing a soul without a soul."

A group of Companions and Successors (tabi'un) held that whoever deliberately abandons one prayer until its time has passed, without an excuse, and refuses to perform it or make it up, and says "I will not pray," is a disbeliever. His blood and property are lawful, his Muslim heirs do not inherit from him, and he is asked to repent. If he repents, well; otherwise he is killed. The ruling on his property is the ruling on the property of an apostate (murtadd). This is the view of Ishaq. Ishaq said: this has been the view of the people of knowledge from the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) until our own time.

Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: our companions (the Malikis) differed as to when one who abandons prayer is to be killed. Some said at the end of the preferred time (al-waqt al-mukhtar), and some said at the end of the time of necessity (waqt al-darurah), which is the sounder view. This is when there remain, from the time of 'Asr, four rak'ahs until sunset; from the night, four rak'ahs for the 'Isha' time; and from the dawn, two rak'ahs before sunrise. Ishaq said: the passing of the time is when one delays Zuhr until sunset, and Maghrib until dawn.

**Sixth issue:** This verse indicates that whoever says "I have repented" is not accepted by his words alone, unless his actions that confirm repentance are added to that. This is because God, Mighty and Majestic, here made, together with repentance, the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakat, so as to confirm repentance through them.

He also said concerning interest (riba): ﴿But if you repent, you shall have your principal﴾ [al-Baqarah: 279]. And He said: ﴿except those who repent, amend and make clear﴾ [al-Baqarah: 160]. The meaning of this has already been explained in Surah al-Baqarah [vol. 2, p. 187].

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 9, verse 6:

There are four issues in this verse.

The first concerns God's words: ﴿And if any one of the polytheists﴾, meaning: of those whom I have commanded you to fight. "Asked you for protection (istajarak)" means he sought your protection (jiwar), that is, your security (aman) and guarantee (dhimam). So give it to him, "so that he may hear the Qur'an", that is, understand its rulings, commands and prohibitions. If he accepts, that is good; if he refuses, return him to his place of safety. This is something on which there is no disagreement. And God knows best.[[In J, W, K, H and Y: "And all praise is due to God."]]

Malik said: if an enemy combatant (harbi) is found on the road within the lands of the Muslims and says, "I came seeking safe-conduct (aman)," Malik said: these are ambiguous matters, and I think he should be returned to his place of safety. Ibn al-Qasim said: likewise the one who is found having landed as a merchant on our coast and says, "I assumed you would not confront one who came as a merchant until he has sold his goods." The apparent meaning of the verse concerns only one who wishes to hear the Qur'an and consider Islam. As for granting protection for other purposes, it is only for the benefit of the Muslims and considering what benefit they gain from it.

The second issue: there is no disagreement among all the scholars that the safe-conduct granted by the ruler (sultan) is valid, because he is charged with considering what is good and beneficial, and he acts on behalf of everyone in bringing benefits and averting harms. They differed regarding the safe-conduct granted by someone other than the caliph. A free person's safe-conduct is valid according to all the scholars, except that Ibn Habib said: the imam should consider it. As for a slave, he may grant safe-conduct according to the well-known position of the school (madhhab), and this is the view of al-Shafi'i and his companions, Ahmad, Ishaq, al-Awza'i, al-Thawri, Abu Thawr, Dawud and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan. Abu Hanifa said: he has no safe-conduct, and this is the second opinion of our scholars (the Malikis). The first is more correct, because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "The Muslims' blood is equal, and the least of them may extend protection on their behalf." They said: since he said "the least of them," the safe-conduct of a slave is valid, and the free woman is more deserving of this. There is no weight given to the reason "he is not given a share (of the booty)." Abd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun said: the safe-conduct of a woman is not valid unless the imam permits it, but with this statement he departed from the majority (jumhur). As for a child, if he is able to fight, his safe-conduct is valid, because he is among those who fight and is part of the protecting group (fi'a hamiya).

Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi held that this verse was abrogated (mansukha) by His words: "Then kill the polytheists." Al-Hasan said: it is muhkam (firm, not abrogated), a sunnah, until the Day of Resurrection, and Mujahid said the same.[[Thus in the original sources and in Ibn Atiyya's Tafsir. Only in B is it "muhkama muthbita" (firm and established). This word does not appear in al-Hasan's statement in the references.]] It was also said: the ruling of this verse remained in effect only for the duration of the four months that were set as a term for them, but this is nothing (of substance). Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: a man from the polytheists came to Ali ibn Abi Talib and said: if one of us wants to come to Muhammad after the four months have ended, to hear the speech of God, or to come to him with a need, he will be killed! Ali ibn Abi Talib said: No, because God, blessed and exalted, says: "And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection until he hears the speech of God." And this is the correct view, and the verse is muhkam.

The third issue concerns God's words: ﴿And if any one﴾. "Ahad" (any one) is in the nominative case, governed by an implied verb like the one that follows it. This is acceptable with "in" (conditional particle) but is ungrammatical with its sister particles. Sibawayh's view on distinguishing "in" from its sisters is that, since it is the mother of conditional particles, it is specially treated this way, and because it does not occur in any other context. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: his statement "because it does not occur in any other context" is an error, because it can have the meaning of "ma" (negation) and can be a lightened form of the heavy "inna," but it is ambiguous, and the others are not like this. Sibawayh recited:

Do not grieve if I have destroyed a precious wealth,
And if I die, then grieve at that time.[[The verse is by al-Nimr ibn Tawlab. He describes his wife blaming him for squandering his wealth out of fear of poverty, and he tells her: do not grieve over my destruction of precious property, for I guarantee its replacement after it is lost; but if I die, then grieve, for you will have no replacement from me.

(From the commentary on the shawahid [Sharh al-Shawahid].)]]

The fourth issue: the scholars said: God's words "until he hears the speech of God" are evidence that the speech of God, exalted and majestic, is heard when the reciter recites it. This was stated by Shaykh Abu al-Hasan, al-Qadi Abu Bakr, Abu al-Abbas al-Qalanisi, Ibn Mujahid, Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini and others, based on God's words: "until he hears the speech of God." He explicitly stated that His speech is heard when the reciter recites His speech. This is also supported by the consensus of the Muslims that when a reciter recites the Opening Chapter of the Book or a surah, they say: "We heard the speech of God." They distinguished between reciting the speech of God, exalted be He, and reciting the poetry of Imru' al-Qays. The meaning of God's speech, exalted be He, and that it is neither a letter nor a sound, has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqara,[[See vol. 2, p. 1.]] and all praise is due to God.

How can there be a covenant with God and His Messenger for the polytheists, except for those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque? (Q 9:7)

"Kayfa" here is used for wonder (al-ta'ajjub), as you say, "Kayfa yasbiquni fulan," meaning: it is not fitting that so-and-so should outdo me. "'Ahd" is the subject of "yakun" (its noun).

There is an ellipsis in the verse, meaning: how can there be a covenant for the polytheists while treachery is concealed (in them)? As the poet said:

"You two informed me that death is in the villages, so how (can it be)? And here is a hill [[As it stands in the originals and al-Bahr. What is in the shawahid of Sibawayh and Jamharat ash'ar al-'Arab is: (wa-qalib). Al-Shantamari said: (He meant by the qalib the grave, and its origin is a well. It seems he was wary of the plague of the cities, which are the villages, so he went out to the desert, saw a grave, and knew that death cannot be escaped, so he said this, denouncing those who warned him against residing in the villages.)]] and a sand dune..."

The estimate is: "fa-kayfa mata" (so how did he die), according to al-Zajjaj.

It has also been said: the meaning is, how can there be for the polytheists a covenant with God by which they feel secure from His punishment tomorrow, and how can there be for them with His Messenger a covenant by which they feel secure from the punishment of this world? Then He made an exception, saying: "except those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque." Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: they are the Banu Bakr, meaning the covenant is only for those who did not break it and did not violate it.

His words, exalted is He: "So as long as they remain true to you, remain true to them" (Q 9:7), meaning: as long as they keep to the fulfilment of your covenant, then you keep to the same toward them. Ibn Zayd said: since they did not remain true, He set for them a term of four months. As for those who have no covenant, fight them wherever you find them, unless they repent.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 9, verse 8:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿How (can they have a covenant), when if they gain the upper hand over you...﴾ He repeats the expression of wonder at how they could have a covenant, given the wickedness of their deeds. That is, how could they have a covenant, when if they gain the upper hand over you, they will not observe any kinship (*illan*) or pact (*dhimmah*) regarding you. It is said: *zahartu ʿala fulanin*, meaning I overcame him, and *zahartu al-bayt*, meaning I climbed onto the house. From this comes ﴿So they were not able to scale it﴾ [al-Kahf 18:97], meaning they could not climb over it. (See vol. 11, p. 62.)

His saying, Exalted is He: (*la yarqubu fikum illan wa la dhimmah*). *Yarqubu* means *yuhafizu*, they observe or guard. *Al-raqib* is the guardian. This has already been discussed (see vol. 5, p. 8).

*Illan* (covenant): this is the view of Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. Also from Mujahid: it is one of the names of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak said it means kinship. al-Hasan said it means protection by neighbourhood. Qatadah said it means alliance. *Dhimmah* means covenant. Abu ʿUbayda said it means oath. He also said: *illan* means the covenant, and *dhimmah* means obligation (*al-tadhammum*). Al-Azhari said: it is the name of Allah in Hebrew, and its root is from *al-alil*, which is brightness. It is said *alla lawnuhu yallu allan*, meaning his colour became clear and shining. It is also said that its root is from sharpness, and from this comes *al-allah* for a spearhead, and from this comes *udhun mu'allalah*, meaning a sharpened ear. From this is the verse of Tarafah ibn al-ʿAbd describing the ears of his she-camel as sharp and erect:

*Two sharpened ears, in which nobility is recognised,*
*like the two ears of a lone wild ox at Hawmal.*

[Note: *al-sam'atan* means the two ears. The *shah* here means the wild ox. Hawmal is the name of a sandy tract. He likened her ears to the ears of a wild ox, because they are sharp and their hearing is accurate. The ear of the wild ox is more reliable than its eyes, and he described it as *mufrad* (lone) because this makes its hearing more acute and its alarm stronger. (From the commentary on the Diwan.)]

When *illan* is applied to covenant, protection by neighbourhood, or kinship, its meaning is that the ear is turned towards that direction, that is, it is made sharp for it. A covenant is called *illan* because of its clarity and prominence. In the plural of fewness it is *ala'il*, and in the plural of abundance it is *ilal*. Al-Jawhari and others said: *al-illu* with a kasra is Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. *Al-illu* also means covenant and kinship. Hassan said:

*By your life, your kinship with Quraysh*
*is like the kinship of the young camel with the ostrich chick.*

[Note: *al-saqb* is the young of a she-camel. *Al-ra'l* is the young of the ostrich.]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and not a pact﴾, that is, a covenant. *Dhimmah* is every sacred obligation which, if you neglect it, becomes a sin for you. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: *dhimmah* is covenant. Whoever takes *illan* to mean covenant, then the repetition is due to the difference in the two words. Abu ʿUbayda Ma'mar said: *dhimmah* means *al-tadhammum*. Abu ʿUbayd said: *dhimmah* means security or safe-conduct, in the words of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "and the least of them may extend protection on their behalf" (*wa yasʿa bi-dhimmatihim adnahum*). The plural of *dhimmah* is *dhimam*. A *bi'r dhammah* (with fatha on the dhal) is a well with little water, and its plural is *dhimam*. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*Upon Himyari camels, whose eyes are like*
*the wells of the watering-places, drained by the buckets.*

[Note: *al-Himyariyyat* are camels attributed to Himyar, which is a tribe of Yemen. *Al-dhimam* means having little water. *Al-rakaya* is the plural of *rakiyyah*, which is a well. *Ankazathā* (with the letter zay) means: *nakazat al-rakiyyah*, the well's water became little. *Al-mawatih* is the plural of *matih*, who draws water from the well. He described camels whose eyes had sunk from exhaustion.]

*Ankazatha* means it removed its water. *Ahl al-dhimmah* means the people of the contract.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They satisfy you with their mouths﴾, that is, they say with their tongues what pleases you outwardly.

(﴿while their hearts refuse, and most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾), that is, breakers of the covenant. Every disbeliever is defiantly disobedient, but here He intended those who openly commit abominations and break covenants.

The commentary refers to the polytheists in their breaking of covenants for a meal that Abu Sufyan fed them; this is said by Mujahid. It was also said: they exchanged the Qur'an for the goods of this world.

(﴿فَصَدُّوا عَنْ سَبِيلِهِ﴾) meaning they turned away, from ṣudūd (turning away). Or they barred [others] from the path of Allah, from ṣadd (barring).

Al-Nahhas said: This is not a repetition; rather, the first (reference) is to all the polytheists, and the second is specifically to the Jews. The evidence for this is ﴿They have sold the signs of Allah for a small price﴾, meaning the Jews, who sold the proofs of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and their clarification, for the pursuit of leadership and greed for something.

(﴿And it is those who are the transgressors﴾) i.e., those who go beyond what is lawful to what is unlawful by breaking the covenant.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 11:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But if they repent﴾, meaning: from polytheism, and they adhere to the rulings of Islam.

(Then they are your brothers) meaning: then they are your brothers (in religion). Ibn 'Abbas said: this verse made the blood of the People of the Qiblah (ahl al-qibla, those who face the Ka'bah in prayer, i.e., Muslims) inviolable. This meaning has already been mentioned earlier. Ibn Zayd said: God made the prayer and the zakat obligatory, and He refused to separate them, and He refused to accept the prayer without the zakat. Ibn Mas'ud said: You were commanded to perform the prayer and to pay zakat, so whoever does not pay zakat, there is no prayer for him. And in a hadith that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever separates between three things, God will separate between him and His mercy on the Day of Resurrection: whoever says, 'I obey God and I do not obey the Messenger,' while God, the Exalted, says: ﴿Obey God and obey the Messenger﴾ [an-Nisa': 59]; and whoever says, 'I establish the prayer and I do not give zakat,' while God, the Exalted, says: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakat﴾ [al-Baqarah: 43]; and whoever separates between thanking God and thanking his parents, while God, the Exalted, says: ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents﴾ [Luqman: 14]."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We detail the verses﴾, meaning: We explain them.

(for a people who know) He specified them because they are the ones who benefit from them. And God knows best.

**First issue:** The verse's words ﴿wa-in nakathu﴾ (and if they break [their oaths]) use *al-naks*, which means undoing or breaking. Its original sense is untwisting something that was twisted. It is used figuratively for oaths and covenants. The poet says:

*"Even if she swears that the passage of time will not break her covenant, there is no oath for one whose fingertips are dyed."*

That is, "covenant."

The words "and they slandered your religion" mean by undermining it, by war, and by other things that the polytheist does. One says *ṭaʿanahu bi-l-rumḥ* (he stabbed him with the spear), and *ṭaʿana bi-l-qawl al-sayyiʾ fīhi yaṭʿanu* (he slandered him with a bad word), both with a *ḍamma* on the ʿayn. It is also said: *yaṭʿunu* with the spear (with *ḍamma*) and *yaṭʿanu* with words (with *fatḥa*). Here the usage is figurative. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) when he appointed Usama: "If you slander his leadership, you have already slandered the leadership of his father before him. By Allah, he was indeed fit for leadership." This is related in the *Ṣaḥīḥ* (Sahih Muslim, Book of Virtues).

**Second issue:** Some scholars cited this verse as proof that every person who slanders the religion must be killed, since he is an unbeliever. Slander means attributing to it what does not befit it, or attacking what belongs to the religion with contempt, because the decisive evidence for the soundness of its foundations and the correctness of its branches has been established. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "The majority of the people of knowledge agree that whoever insults the Prophet (ﷺ) must be killed." Among those who said this were Malik, al-Layth, Ahmad and Ishaq, and it is the position of al-Shafiʿi. It has been reported from al-Nuʿman (Abu Hanifa) that he said: "One who insults the Prophet (ﷺ) from among the People of the Covenant (ahl al-dhimma) is not to be killed," as will come later.

It is related that a man said in the gathering of ʿAli: "Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf was killed only by treachery." ʿAli ordered that his neck be struck. Another said it in the gathering of Muʿawiya, and Muhammad ibn Maslama stood up and said: "Is this said in your gathering while you remain silent? By Allah, I will not share a roof with you ever again, and if I find him alone I will kill him." Our scholars said: "This man is to be killed and not given the chance to repent, if he attributes treachery to the Prophet (ﷺ)." This is what ʿAli and Muhammad ibn Maslama, may Allah be pleased with them both, understood from the one who said it, because that is heresy (zandaqa).

As for if he attributes it to those who directly killed him, saying that they gave him safe conduct and then betrayed him, this attribution would be pure falsehood. There is nothing in their words with him that indicates they gave him safe conduct, nor did they declare it to him. Even if they had done so, it would not have been a valid guarantee, because the Prophet (ﷺ) had only directed them to kill him, not to grant him protection. He (ﷺ) permitted Muhammad ibn Maslama to say what he said. On this basis, there is room for doubt and hesitation about killing one who attributes that treachery to them. The question is: does attributing treachery to them necessarily entail attributing it to the Prophet (ﷺ), since he approved their act and was pleased with it, so that whoever states this openly is killed? Or does attributing treachery to them not necessarily entail attributing it to the Prophet (ﷺ), so that he is not killed? If we say he is not killed, then he must be disciplined and punished, by imprisonment, severe beating and great humiliation.

**Third issue:** As for the dhimmi, if he slanders the religion his covenant is broken according to the well-known position of the Maliki school, because of the words ﴿and if they break their oaths﴾. Thus He commanded their killing and fighting. This is also the position of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him. Abu Hanifa said regarding this that he is to be asked to repent, and that mere slander does not break the covenant unless breaking of the covenant occurs with it. This is because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, only commanded their killing under two conditions: first, that they break the covenant, and second, that they slander the religion. We reply: if they act contrary to the covenant, their covenant is broken. Mentioning the two matters does not require that the fighting against them depends on both being present, since breaking the covenant alone permits this, both by reason and by law. Our understanding of the verse is: if they break their covenant, fighting them is lawful, and if they do not break it but slander the religion while keeping the covenant, fighting them is also lawful.

It has been reported that ʿUmar was informed about a dhimmi who prodded a riding animal on which a Muslim woman was seated, so that it bucked and threw her off, uncovering part of her private parts. He ordered that he be crucified on the spot.

**Fourth issue:** If the dhimmi wages war, his covenant is broken, and his property and children become spoils of war along with him. Muhammad ibn Maslama said: "His child is not held responsible for it, because he alone broke the covenant." He also said: "As for his property, it is seized." This is a contradiction that does not befit the standing of Muhammad ibn Maslama, because it was his covenant that protected his property and his child. So when his property is lost, his child is lost too. Ashhab said: "If the dhimmi breaks the covenant, he remains under his covenant and never returns to slavery." This is strange, as though he regarded the covenant as a tangible thing. The covenant is only a ruling required by reasoned judgment, which the Muslims have committed to, so when it is broken, it is broken like all other contracts.

**Fifth issue:** Most scholars hold that whoever insults the Prophet (ﷺ) from among the People of the Covenant, or alludes to him, or belittles his rank, or describes him in a way other than that by which he disbelieved, must be killed, because we did not give him the protection or covenant on these terms. The exception is Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri and their followers from the people of Kufa, who said: "He is not killed, because the polytheism he is upon is greater, but he is disciplined and punished." The proof against them is His words: ﴿and if they break their oaths﴾, and some of them used as evidence the Prophet's (ﷺ) command to kill Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, who was under a covenant. Abu Bakr became angry at a man among his companions, and Abu Barza said: "Shall I not strike his neck?" He replied: "That was not permitted for anyone after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

Al-Daraqutni related from Ibn ʿAbbas that a blind man had a slave-mother (umm walad) by whom he had two sons like two pearls. She used to abuse the Prophet (ﷺ) and speak ill of him. He forbade her, but she did not stop, and he rebuked her, but she did not desist. Then one night she mentioned the Prophet (ﷺ), and her master could not endure it. He took a hatchet, placed it on her belly, leaned on her until it pierced her. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Bear witness that her blood is void (hadar)." In another report from Ibn ʿAbbas: he killed her, and in the morning this was told to the Prophet (ﷺ). The blind man stood up and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am her master. She used to abuse you and speak ill of you. I forbade her but she did not stop, I rebuked her but she did not desist. I have two sons by her like two pearls, and she was kind to me. But last night she began to abuse you and speak ill of you, so I killed her." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Bear witness that her blood is void."

**Sixth issue:** They differed about one who insulted the Prophet (ﷺ) and then embraced Islam to escape being killed. It is said that his Islam drops the killing from him, and this is the well-known position of the school, because Islam erases what came before it. This is unlike a Muslim who insults him and then repents. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has passed will be forgiven for them﴾ [al-Anfal: 38]. It is also said that embracing Islam does not drop his killing. This was stated in al-Utbiyya, because it is a right of the Prophet (ﷺ) that became due through violating his sanctity and intending to inflict defamation and disgrace upon him. So his return to Islam does not drop it, and he is not in a better position than a Muslim.

**Seventh issue:** The words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿fa-qatilu a'immata al-kufr﴾ (then fight the leaders of disbelief). "A'imma" is the plural of *imam*. According to some scholars, the intended meaning is the chieftains of Quraysh, such as Abu Jahl, ʿUtba, Shayba and Umayya ibn Khalaf. This is far-fetched, because the verse is in Surat Bara'a, and when it was revealed and recited to the people, Allah had already uprooted Quraysh so that none remained except a Muslim or one at peace. So it is possible that the intended meaning of "fa-qatilu a'immata al-kufr" is: whoever undertakes to break the covenant and slander the religion is a root and chief in disbelief, and thus is among the leaders of disbelief in this sense. It is also possible that it refers to the foremost and chiefs among them, and that fighting them is fighting their followers, and that they have no sanctity.

The original form is *a'immah*, like *mithal* and *amthila*. Then the *mim* was assimilated into the *mim*, and the vowel was transferred onto the hamza, so two hamzas came together, and the second was changed into a *ya*. Al-Akhfash claimed that one says *hadha ayamm min hadha* with a *ya*. Al-Mazini said *awamm min hadha* with a *waw*. Hamza read "a'immah." Most grammarians hold that this is a mistake (laḥn), because it joins two hamzas in one word.

[[Al-Zamakhshari said in his Kashshaf: "If you ask, how is the word a'imma pronounced? I say: a hamza followed by a hamza, between-between, i.e., between the articulation of the hamza and the ya. Pronouncing both hamzas is a well-known reading, though it is not accepted by the Basrans. As for pronouncing the ya explicitly, it is not a reading, and it is not permissible to be a reading; whoever pronounces it that way is a solecist and distorter." Abu Hayyan commented on this in al-Bahr: "That is his habit of calling the reciters solecists. How can it be a solecism when Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ, the leading grammarian of the Basrans, read it so, and so did Ibn Kathir, the reciter of Mecca, and Nafiʿ, the reciter of Medina, may Allah bless him?" Al-Alusi said in Ruh al-Maʿani: "Nafiʿ, Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read a'imma with two hamzas, the second between-between, i.e., between the articulation of the hamza and the ya, with an alif between them. The Kufans and Ibn Dhakwan from Ibn ʿAmir read them as two fully articulated hamzas without inserting an alif, and Hisham likewise except that he inserted an alif between them. This is the well-known position of the seven readers..."]]

**"Innahum la aymana lahum"** means: they have no covenants; that is, their covenants are not truthful, so that they keep them. Ibn ʿAmir read *la īmāna lahum* with a kasra on the hamza, from *al-īmān* (faith), meaning they have no Islam. It may also be the verbal noun of *āmantuhu īmānan*, from *al-amn* (security), whose opposite is fear, meaning they do not believe. From *amantuhu īmānan*, meaning I granted him protection (ajartuhu). For this reason He said: "fa-qatilu a'immata al-kufr."

**"La'allahum yantahun"** means: that they may desist from polytheism. Al-Kalbi said: The Prophet (ﷺ) had made a truce with the people of Mecca for a year while he was at al-Hudaybiya. They prevented him from the House, then they made peace with him on condition that he return. They remained as long as Allah willed. Then the allies of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from Khuzaʿa were attacked by the allies of Banu Umayya from Kinana. Banu Umayya aided their allies with weapons and food, so Khuzaʿa sought help from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to help his allies, as had been established before.

In al-Bukhari, from Zayd ibn Wahb who said: "We were with Hudhayfa, and he said: 'Of those who were the companions of this verse,' meaning 'fa-qatilu a'immata al-kufr innahum la aymana lahum,' only three remain, and of the hypocrites only four remain.' A Bedouin said: 'You are the companions of Muhammad, you report reports that we do not know! You claim there are only four hypocrites, so what about these people who split open our houses and steal our precious goods?' He said: 'Those are the wicked. Indeed, only four of them remain, one of whom is an old man who, if he drank cold water, would not feel its coolness.'" [[Al-Qastalani said: "Because his desire has gone and his stomach has deteriorated as a punishment from Allah in this world, so he does not distinguish between things."]]

**The words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿la'allahum yantahun﴾** means: that they may desist from their disbelief, their falsehood, and their harm to the Muslims. This implies that the purpose of fighting them is to repel their harm, so that they may cease fighting us and enter our religion.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 13:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths﴾ is a rebuke, and it carries the meaning of tahdid (urging and incitement). It was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Makkah, as we mentioned just above.

(And they resolved to expel the Messenger) meaning that they were the cause of the departure, so the expulsion was attributed to them. It was also said: they expelled the Messenger, peace be upon him, from Madinah in order to fight the people of Makkah because of the breach of oath that had come from them. This is reported from al-Hasan.

(And they began with you) meaning they began the fighting.

(For the first time) meaning they broke the covenant and aided Banu Bakr against Khuza'ah. It was also said: they began the fighting with you on the day of Badr, because the Prophet ﷺ went out for the caravan, and when they had secured their caravan it was possible for them to turn back, but they refused except to reach Badr and to drink wine there, as has already been mentioned.

(Then Allah has more right that you fear Him) meaning that you should fear His punishment for abandoning the fighting against them, rather than fearing that some harm might befall you in fighting them. It was also said: their expelling the Messenger was their prevention of him from the Hajj, the 'Umrah and the Tawaf, and that was their initiation of hostility. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 14–15:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Fight them﴾ is a command. "Allah will punish them" is its answer (jawab). It is in the jussive mood, with the meaning of conditional reward (mujazah). The implied sense is: if you fight them, Allah will punish them at your hands, and disgrace them, and give you victory over them, and heal the breasts of a people who are believers.

(And remove the rage of their hearts) is evidence that their rage had become intense. Mujahid said: it refers to Khuza'ah, the allies of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). All of it is coordinated (ʿatf), and all of it may be read in the nominative (raf') by way of resumption (qat') from the first. It may also be read in the accusative (nasb) by implying "an" (an), which is the sarf according to the Kufans, as the poet said:

"If Abu Qabus dies, the spring of the people will die, and the sacred month,
and after him we will take up the tail of a life, its back shorn, with no hump on it."
[The dhanab (with a kasra on the dhal): the end and rear of anything. Al-ajabb: a camel whose hump has been cut off. The two verses are by al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani. He describes the illness of al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir and that if he dies, people will be in the worst condition after him, with the narrowest life, clinging to him like the tail of a humpless camel. There is another witness in the verse. See Khizanat al-Adab by al-Baghdadi, under the 756th witness, and Sibawayh's witnesses, vol. 1, p. 100, Bulaq edition.]

If you wish, you may read "and we will take" in the nominative, and if you wish, you may read it in the accusative. By his saying: (and heal the breasts of a people who are believers), what is meant is the Banu Khuza'ah, as we have mentioned from Mujahid. For Quraysh aided the Banu Bakr against them, while Khuza'ah were allies of the Prophet (ﷺ). A man from the Banu Bakr recited a satire (hija') of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so one of Khuza'ah said to him: "If you repeat it, I will break your mouth." He repeated it, and he broke his mouth. Fighting broke out between them, and they killed some people from Khuza'ah. So 'Amr ibn Salim al-Khuza'i went out with a group to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of it. He entered the house of Maymunah and said: "Pour water over me," and he began to wash, saying: "I would not be victorious if I did not support the Banu Ka'b." [Banu Ka'b are within Khuza'ah, and they are the people of 'Amr.] Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered preparation and departure to Makkah, and the conquest came.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah turns in forgiveness to whom He wills﴾ The reading with the nominative (raf') is by way of resumption (isti'naf), because it is not of the same kind as the first. For this reason he did not say "wa-yatub" in the jussive, because fighting does not necessitate repentance for them from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, whereas it necessitates for them punishment, disgrace, the healing of the breasts of the believers, and the removal of the rage of their hearts. Its parallel is: ﴿If Allah wills, He would seal upon your heart﴾ [al-Shura: 24], the sentence is complete. Then He said: ﴿And Allah will erase falsehood﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 24 onward.]] [al-Shura: 24]. Those whom Allah turned to in forgiveness include Abu Sufyan, 'Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, and Suhayl ibn Abi 'Amr, for they embraced Islam. Ibn Abi Ishaq read "wa-yatuba" in the accusative, and it is similarly reported from 'Isa al-Thaqafi and al-A'raj. According to this reading, repentance falls within the answer of the condition, because the meaning is: if you fight them, Allah will punish them.

Likewise is what is conjoined to it. Then he said: "and Allah turns in forgiveness," meaning, if you fight them. Thus he combined their punishment at your hands, the healing of your breasts, the removal of the rage of your hearts, and His turning in forgiveness toward you. The nominative is better, because repentance is not caused by fighting, since it may occur without fighting for whomever Allah wills to turn to in every state.
