Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do you think﴾ is a shift from one thing to another.

(An tutraku) is in the position of the two objects according to the view of Sibawayh (the founder of Arabic grammar). According to al-Mubarrad, the second object has been omitted. The meaning of the statement is: "Or do you think that you will be left alone without being tested by that through which the believer and the hypocrite become manifest, the manifestation that merits reward and punishment?" This meaning has been mentioned earlier in more than one place.

"﴿And Allah has not yet known﴾": the verb is jussive because of lamma, even though ma is extra (za'ida). According to Sibawayh, it serves as an answer to your saying "qad fa'ala" (he has done), as mentioned earlier (see vol. 4, pp. 220 and 178). The letter mim is given a kasra because of the meeting of two sukun letters.

"Walijah" (intimate confidant) means an inner circle and intimate association, from al-wulujh (wulul), which is entering; from it the hiding place of wild animals is called "tawlaj," the place into which they enter. Walaja yalij wulujan means he entered. The meaning is: an intimate friend of affection apart from Allah and His Messenger.

Abu Ubayda said: Everything you insert into something that is not part of it is a walijah, and a man who is among a people without being one of them is a walijah.

Ibn Zayd said: The walijah is the intruder, and the walija'a are the intruders. So the walijah of a man is the one who is specially close to the secrets of his affairs, apart from people. You say: "He is my walijah," and "They are my walijah," the singular and plural being the same in this usage. Aban ibn Taghlib, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"Then how wretched is the confidant of fugitives ... and of transgressors and people of doubt."

It is also said: walijah means bitanah (inner confidant), and the meaning is the same; its parallel is ﴿Do not take as bitanah (confidants) other than yourselves﴾ [Al 'Imran: 118]. Al-Farra' said: walijah is a bitanah from among the polytheists, whom they take as confidants and to whom they reveal their secrets and inform of their affairs.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah﴾. The clause beginning with "an ya'muru" (that they maintain) is in the position of the subject (raf') of kana (is). "Shahidin" (testifying) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal).

The scholars differed in interpreting this verse. It has been said: it means that they have no right to perform the Hajj after it was proclaimed concerning them that they are barred from the Sacred Mosque, and that the affairs of the House, such as al-sidana (keeping the keys), al-siqaya (providing water for pilgrims) and al-rifada (providing food for pilgrims), were in the hands of the polytheists; so He made clear that they are not fit for that, rather its people are the believers. It has also been said: when al-Abbas was taken captive and was reproached for his disbelief and for severing ties of kinship, he said: "You mention our bad deeds but you do not mention our good deeds." Ali said: "Do you have good deeds?" He said: "Yes, indeed we maintain the Sacred Mosque, we serve the Ka'bah, we give water to the pilgrims and we free the captives." So this verse was revealed in reply to him. It is therefore obligatory upon the Muslims to take charge of the affairs of the mosques and to prevent the polytheists from entering them.

The common reading is "ya'muru" with a fathah on the ya' and a dammah on the mim, from 'amara ya'muru. Ibn al-Sumayqa read it with a dammah on the ya' and a kasrah on the mim, meaning they make it populated or help in its maintenance. It is also read "masjid Allah" in the singular, meaning the Sacred Mosque. This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Mujahid, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Muhaysin and Ya'qub. The rest read "masajid" in the plural, to indicate generality. This is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd, because it is more general and the specific falls under the general. It is possible that the plural reading is intended to refer to the Sacred Mosque alone. This is permissible in nouns of genus, as one says: "So-and-so rides horses," even if he rides only one horse. The reading "masajid" is more correct, because it admits both meanings. The scholars have agreed on the reading of His saying: "Innama ya'muru masajid Allah" in the plural, as stated by al-Nahhas.

Al-Hasan said: He said "masajid" while meaning the Sacred Mosque, because it is the qiblah of all mosques and their leader.

His saying, may He be exalted: (testifying). It has been said: He meant "wa hum shahidun" (while they are witnesses), and when the "hum" was dropped, it became accusative. Ibn 'Abbas said: their testimony against themselves of disbelief is their prostration to their idols, and their acknowledgement that they are created.

Al-Suddi said: their testimony of disbelief is that when a Christian is asked, "What is your religion?", he says, "Christian"; the Jew says, "Jew"; the Sabian says, "Sabian"; and the polytheist is asked, "What is your religion?", and he says, "Polytheist."

(Those—their deeds have become void, and in the Fire they will abide forever.) Its meaning has already been mentioned.

There are three issues in this verse.

The first concerns His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who maintain the mosques of Allah are only those who believe in Allah⦆. This is evidence that testifying to the faith of those who frequent the mosques is valid, because Allah, glory be to Him, linked it to them and informed that they are characterized by their constant attendance. Some of the early scholars (al-salaf) said: "When you see a man who maintains the mosque, then think well of him." Al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you see a man who is constant in attending the mosque, then bear witness to his faith." Allah the Exalted says: "Indeed, those who maintain the mosques of Allah are those who believe in Allah and the Last Day." In another narration: "who is diligent in (yata'ahhad) the mosque." He said: it is a hasan gharib hadith. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This applies to outward righteousness, not to the final determinations of testimony, for testimonies have states according to those who know them. Among them is the intelligent, perceptive person who correctly grasps what he knows, both in belief and in reporting, and among them is the heedless one. Each is placed in his own rank and assessed according to his description.

The second concerns His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and fears none but Allah⦆. If it is said: there is no believer who has not feared other than Allah, and believers and prophets [[In K: the friends of Allah.]] have always feared enemies from others. It is answered: the meaning is "and fears none but Allah" concerning what is worshipped, for the polytheists used to worship idols, fear them and hope in them. A second answer: that is, he did not fear anyone in matters of religion except Allah.

The third concerns: if it is said: the verse has affirmed faith for one who maintains the mosques by praying in them, cleaning them, and repairing what has decayed of them, and who believes in Allah, yet it did not mention belief in the Messenger in it, and there is no faith for one who does not believe in the Messenger. It is answered: what is mentioned of establishing prayer and other acts indicates the Messenger, because these are among what he brought. Establishing the prayer and giving zakat are valid only from one who believes in the Messenger, so he did not single him out for mention. And "perhaps" (ʿasā) from Allah is obligatory, according to Ibn 'Abbas and others. It is also said: ʿasā here means "worthy of" (khalīq), i.e., it is worthy that "they be among the guided."

There are two issues here.

The first is His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿Do you consider the providing of water for the pilgrims and the maintaining of the Sacred Mosque﴾. The grammatical construction (taqdir) in Arabic is: "Do you consider [the people of] the providing of water for the pilgrims [equal to] those who believe in God and strive in His way?" It is also permissible to supply an ellipsis in "those who believe," meaning: "Do you consider the work of watering the pilgrims like the work of those who believe?" It has also been said that the construction is: "like the faith of those who believe." The word siqaya (providing water) is a verbal noun (masdar), like si'aya (striving) and himaya (protection). The noun has been placed in the position of the verbal noun since its meaning is known, as in "generosity is Hatim" and "poetry is Zuhayr." The phrase "maintaining of the Sacred Mosque" is like ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82].

Abu Wajza recited "Do you consider the watering-men (suqat) of the pilgrims and the caretakers (amarat) of the Sacred Mosque." Suqat is the plural of saqin, and the original form is suqyah on the pattern fu'lah; this is how the defective (mu'tall) form of this word is pluralized, as in qadin / qudat and nasin / nusat. If the word is not defective, it is pluralized on the pattern fu'alah, as in nasi' / nusa'ah, referring to those who would postpone (yunsi'un) the months. Likewise, Ibn al-Zubayr and Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited "suqat(a) and 'amarat(a)," except that Ibn Jubayr put "the Mosque" in the accusative, by intending the tanwin on "'amarah."

Al-Dahhak said: siqayah with a damma on the sin, and this is a dialectal form. Al-hajj is a collective noun (ism jins) for al-hujjaj (pilgrims). The maintaining (imarah) of the Sacred Mosque means attending to it and carrying out its affairs.

The apparent meaning of this verse is that it refutes the claim of those among the polytheists who boasted of providing water for the pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque, as al-Suddi mentioned. He said: Abbas boasted of the watering, Shayba boasted of the maintenance, and Ali boasted of Islam and jihad. God confirmed Ali and rejected the other two, and informed that maintaining (the mosque) does not occur with disbelief, but only with faith, worship and performing obedience. This is clear and beyond dispute.

It is said that the polytheists asked the Jews, saying: "We are the watering-men of the pilgrims and the caretakers of the Sacred Mosque; are we better, or Muhammad and his companions?" The Jews said to them, out of obstinacy toward the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "You are better."

A problem has arisen here, which is what came in Sahih Muslim from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, who said: "I was by the pulpit of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when a man said: 'I do not care if I do no deed after Islam except that I give water to the pilgrims.' Another said: 'I do not care if I do no deed after Islam except that I maintain the Sacred Mosque.' Another said: 'Jihad in the way of God is better than what you have said.' Umar rebuked them and said: 'Do not raise your voices at the pulpit of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)—and it was Friday—but when the Friday prayer has been performed I will go in and ask him about what you have disagreed upon.' Then God, may He be exalted, sent down: ﴿Do you consider the providing of water for the pilgrims and the maintaining of the Sacred Mosque as [equal to] one who believes in God and the Last Day﴾ to the end of the verse."

This context requires that it was revealed when the Muslims differed about which of these deeds is most excellent. In that case, it is not fitting that it be said to them at the end of the verse: ﴿and God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, so the problem is established. Its resolution is to say: some narrators were lax in their statement, and "God sent down the verse." Rather, the Prophet (ﷺ) recited the verse to Umar when he asked him, and the narrator assumed it was revealed at that time. The Prophet (ﷺ) used it as evidence that jihad is more excellent than what those whom Umar heard had said; so he sought a ruling on their behalf, and recited to him what had been revealed to him, not that it was revealed concerning these people. And God knows best.

If it is said: then on this basis it would be permissible to derive evidence against Muslims from what was revealed concerning disbelievers, though their rulings are known to differ. It is said in reply: it is not unlikely that rulings suited to Muslims may be extracted from what God revealed about the polytheists. Umar said: "If we wished, we would have made for ourselves sala'ik (grilled meats) and roasts, with one dish placed and another removed; but we have heard the word of God, may He be exalted: ﴿You expended your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 20]." This verse is explicit about disbelievers, yet Umar understood from it a rebuke fitting their conditions to some degree, and none of the Companions disagreed with him. So it is possible that this verse is of this type. This is precious, and by it the problem is removed and the ambiguity lifted. And God knows best.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Those who believe﴾ is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada', "the inchoative subject") of the sentence. Its predicate (khabar) is ﴿are greater in rank with Allah﴾. The word "دَرَجَةً" (darajatan, "in rank") is in the accusative as a specification (bayan, "explicative specification"), meaning: of those who boasted of giving water and maintaining the Sacred House. There is no rank for the disbelievers with Allah, so it cannot be said, "the believer is greater in rank." The meaning is that they assigned rank to themselves through maintaining the Sacred House and giving water, so He addressed them according to what they assumed about themselves, even though the assumption was mistaken. This is like Allah's saying: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day will have the better abode and the finer resting place﴾ [Al-Furqan: 24] [See vol. 13, p. 21 onward.]. It has also been said that "أَعْظَمُ دَرَجَةً" means greater in rank than every possessor of rank, that is, they have the distinction and the lofty station. ﴿And those are the triumphant﴾ by that.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 21–22:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Their Lord gives them good tidings﴾, meaning: He informs them in this world of what they will have in the Hereafter of abundant reward and enduring bliss. And al-Na'im (bliss) is the ease and abundance of life.

(Khalidin) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). And al-Khulud (eternal abiding) means remaining.

(Inna Allah 'indahu ajrun 'azim) meaning: He has prepared that reward for them in the abode of His honour.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 21–22:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Their Lord gives them good tidings﴾, meaning: He informs them in this world of what they will have in the Hereafter of abundant reward and enduring bliss. And al-Na'im (bliss) is the ease and abundance of life.

(Khalidin) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). And al-Khulud (eternal abiding) means remaining.

(Inna Allah 'indahu ajrun 'azim) meaning: He has prepared that reward for them in the abode of His honour.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 23:

The apparent meaning of this verse is that it is addressed to all believers without exception, and its ruling remains in force until the Day of Resurrection, in cutting off loyalty (wilayah) between believers and disbelievers. But a group has narrated that this verse was revealed only to urge emigration (hijrah) and to abandon the lands of the disbelievers. On this view, the address is to the believers who were in Makkah and other lands of the Arabs, who were addressed with the instruction not to take as allies their fathers and brothers, lest they follow them in dwelling in the lands of disbelief. "In-istahabbu" means: if they love, as one says istajaba meaning ajaba. That is, do not obey them and do not give them preference.

Allah, glory be to Him, singled out fathers and brothers because there is no closer kinship than these. He thereby negated loyalty between them, just as He negated it among people in His words, ﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51], to make clear that nearness is nearness of religions, not nearness of bodies. Something similar is recited by the Sufis:

They say to me, "The abode of the beloved has drawn near," while you are grieved. Indeed, this is strange.

I said, "What good are nearby dwellings when there is no nearness between hearts?

How many a one far in abode has attained his desire, while another, a neighbor beside you, has died in grief."

He did not mention sons in this verse, because it is most common among people that sons follow their fathers. Goodness and gifts are excepted from loyalty. Asma' said: "O Messenger of Allah, my mother has come to me desiring, and she is a polytheist; should I maintain ties with her?" He said: (ﷺ) "Maintain ties with your mother." Recorded by al-Bukhari. As for His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And whoever among you takes them as allies, then those are the wrongdoers﴾, Ibn 'Abbas said: he is a polytheist like them, because whoever is pleased with polytheism is a polytheist.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 24:

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded the emigration (hijrah) from Makkah to al-Madinah, a man would say to his father, a father to his son, a brother to his brother, and a man to his wife: "Indeed we have been commanded to emigrate." Some of them hastened to do so, and some refused to emigrate. The one who refused would say: "By Allah, if you do not go out to the abode of emigration, I will not benefit you, and I will never spend anything on you." Others were held back by their wives and children, who would say to them: "We implore you by Allah, do not leave, lest we be lost after you." Some of them would relent, abandon emigration, and remain with them. Then the verse was revealed: "O you who believe, do not take your fathers and your brothers as allies if they prefer disbelief over faith." He says: [if they choose] to remain in disbelief in Makkah over faith in Allah and emigration to al-Madinah. "And whoever among you takes them as allies" after the revelation of the verse, "then it is those who are the wrongdoers." Then there was revealed concerning those who stayed behind and did not emigrate: "Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your wives, and your kinsfolk..." The "'ashirah" is the group that is bound to one contract, like the contract of ten or more, and from it comes "mu'ashirah," which is gathering around a thing.

(And wealth you have acquired) he says: that you have earned in Makkah. The root of iqtiraf is detaching a thing from its place to another.

(And commerce, whose slackness you fear) Ibn al-Mubarak said: these are the daughters and sisters when they become unmarried (kasadna) in the house, finding no suitor for them. The poet said:

They have become unmarried from poverty among their people... and my remaining has increased their unmarried state.

(And dwellings with which you are pleased) he says: homes in which you find delight to dwell.

(are more beloved to you) than that you emigrate to Allah and His Messenger in al-Madinah. "Ahabba" is the predicate of "kana." Outside the Qur'an it is permissible to put "ahabba" in the nominative as the subject and predicate, with the noun of "kana" being a hidden pronoun within it. Sibawayh cited:

When I die, people will be of two kinds: one who gloats, and another who praises what I used to do.

And he cited:

She is the cure for my ailment, if I were to attain her, but the cure for the ailment is not available.

(From the book of Sibawayh.)

In the verse there is evidence of the obligation of love for Allah and His Messenger, and there is no disagreement among the Muslim community on this, and that this takes precedence over every other beloved. The meaning of the love of Allah the Exalted and the love of His Messenger has already been discussed in Al 'Imran.

(And jihad in His cause, then wait) its form is the form of a command, but its meaning is a threat. He says: wait.

(until Allah brings His command) meaning: by fighting and the conquest of Makkah, according to Mujahid. Al-Hasan said: by a punishment, either delayed or immediate. In His saying "and jihad in His cause" there is evidence of the virtue of jihad and of preferring it over the comfort of the self and its attachments to family and wealth. The virtue of jihad will come in the end of the surah. The rulings on emigration have already been mentioned in al-Nisa' sufficiently, and praise be to Allah. In the authentic hadith: "Indeed, Satan sat in wait for the son of Adam at three stations. He sat in wait for him on the path of Islam and said: 'Will you abandon your religion and the religion of your fathers?' He disobeyed him, embraced Islam, and then sat in wait for him on the path of emigration and said: 'Will you abandon your wealth and your family?' He disobeyed him and emigrated. Then he sat in wait for him on the path of jihad and said: 'You will fight and be killed, so your wife will be married off and your wealth will be divided.' He disobeyed him and fought, and it is incumbent upon Allah to admit him into Paradise." Al-Nasa'i narrated it from the hadith of Sabarah ibn Abi Fakih, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed, Satan..." and he mentioned it. Al-Bukhari said: (Ibn al-Fakih), and he did not mention any difference in it. Ibn Abi 'Adi said: it is said Ibn al-Fakih and Ibn Abi al-Fakih. End.

**Part 1 of 2: Commentary on Surah 9, verses 25–27**

This contains eight issues. The first concerns the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah has given you victory on many battlefields﴾. When news of the conquest of Makkah reached Hawazin, Malik ibn Awf al-Nasri from the clan of Nasr ibn Malik gathered them. Leadership of the whole army was given to him. He brought with the disbelievers their wealth, their livestock, their women and their children, and he claimed that this would protect their souls and that their resolve in battle would be strengthened by it. They numbered eight thousand according to al-Hasan and Mujahid. It was also said that they were four thousand, from Hawazin and Thaqif. Malik ibn Awf commanded Hawazin, and Kinanah ibn Abd commanded Thaqif. They camped at Awtas [[Awtas: a valley in the lands of Hawazin, where the battle of Hunayn took place.]]. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Abdullah ibn Abi Hadrad al-Aslami as a scout. He came back and informed him of what he had seen of them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then resolved to march against them, and he borrowed armour from Safwan ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi. It was said that this was one hundred coats of mail, and it was also said four hundred. He also borrowed thirty thousand, or forty thousand, from Rabi'ah al-Makhzumi, and when he came back he repaid it to him. The Prophet (ﷺ) then said to him: "May Allah bless you in your family and your wealth. The reward of a loan is only repayment and gratitude." Ibn Majah recorded this in his Sunan.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out with twelve thousand Muslims. Among them were ten thousand who had accompanied him from Madinah, and two thousand from the Muslims of the conquest, namely the Tulaqa', together with those Bedouins who joined him from Sulaym, Banu Kilab, Abs and Dhubyan. He appointed Attab ibn Usayd over Makkah. On this march, some ignorant Bedouins saw a green tree. In the Jahiliyyah there had been a well-known tree called Dhat Anwat, to which the disbelievers would go out on a set day of the year and venerate it. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, make for us a Dhat Anwat as they have a Dhat Anwat." He (peace be upon him) said: "Allahu Akbar! You have spoken, by Him in whose hand my soul is, as the people of Musa said: 'Make for us a god as they have gods.' He said: 'Indeed you are a people who are ignorant.' You will certainly follow the ways of those before you, step by step, so that even if they entered a lizard's burrow you would enter it too." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then moved on until he reached the valley of Hunayn, which is one of the valleys of Tihamah. Hawazin had lain in ambush on both sides of the valley, at the dim light of dawn. They charged the Muslims as one man, and most of the Muslims fled. No one turned back [[i.e., did not turn or look back.]] for anyone. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood firm, and with him stood Abu Bakr and Umar, and from his family Ali, al-Abbas, Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib and his son Ja'far, Usamah ibn Zayd, Ayman ibn Ubayd, who was Ayman ibn Umm Ayman and was killed that day at Hunayn, Rabi'ah ibn al-Harith, and al-Fadl ibn Abbas. It was said that in place of Ja'far ibn Abi Sufyan it was Qutham ibn al-Abbas. These were ten men, and this is why al-Abbas said:

"We helped the Messenger of Allah in battle, nine of us,
while those who fled had fled from him and scattered.
And the tenth of us met death with his own soul,
with what touched him for the sake of Allah, without complaint."

Umm Sulaym also stood firm among those who stood, girded up, holding the camel of Abu Talhah, and in her hand was a dagger. Neither the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) nor any of these men fled. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was on his grey mule, whose name was Duldul. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Anas, al-Abbas said: "I was holding the bridle of the mule of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), restraining it so that it would not hasten, while Abu Sufyan was holding the stirrup of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Abbas, call the companions of the Samurah [tree]." [[i.e., the companions of the tree called al-Samurah, which was the tree under which the Pledge of Ridwan was made in the year of Hudaybiyyah.]] Al-Abbas, who had a loud voice, called out. It is related that because of the intensity of his voice, once when he raided Makkah and cried "Waa sabahah!" every pregnant woman who heard his voice miscarried her child. I cried out at the top of my voice: "Where are the companions of the Samurah?" He said: "By Allah, it was as though their turning back, when they heard my voice, was like the turning of cows toward their calves." They said: "Here we are, here we are!" He said: "Then they fought, while the disbelievers..." [The hadith continues, and in it:] He said: "Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took some pebbles and threw them into the faces of the disbelievers," and then said: "They are defeated, by the Lord of Muhammad!" He said: "I went to look, and the fighting was in its former state, as it appeared to me. By Allah, it was only that he threw them his pebbles, and I continued to see their edge blunted and their affair turned back."

Abu Umar said: We have related from several routes, from some of those among the polytheists who had embraced Islam and who had witnessed Hunayn, that he said, when asked about the day of Hunayn: "We met the Muslims, and we had not waited long before we defeated them and pursued them, until we reached a man riding a white mule. When he saw us he rebuked us with a rebuke and scolded us, and he took in his hand pebbles [[in another version: dust.]] and dust, threw them and said: 'May the faces be disfigured.' No eye remained without being struck by it. We could not control ourselves, and we turned back on our heels." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: A man from the polytheists told me on the day of Hunayn: "When we met the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they did not stand against us for the length of a milking of a sheep, until we came to the owner of the grey mule, meaning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Men with bright faces and handsome appearance met us and said to us: 'May the faces be disfigured! Turn back!' So we turned back, and they rode upon our shoulders, and they were them." He meant the angels. I say: there is no contradiction, for it is possible that "May the faces be disfigured" came both from the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) and from the words of the angels together, and this indicates that the angels fought on the day of Hunayn. And Allah knows best.

Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) killed forty men with his own hand on the day of Hunayn. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took four thousand captives. It was also said six thousand, and twelve thousand camels, besides spoils whose number is unknown.

The second issue: The scholars said regarding this campaign that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever kills an enemy for whom he has evidence, his spoils belong to him." Its explanation has already passed in Surat al-Anfal [[See vol. 7, p. 363.]]. Ibn al-Arabi said: For this point and others, the jurists of rulings included this verse in the books of legal rulings. I say: In this there is also the permissibility of borrowing weapons, the permissibility of making use of what has been borrowed when it is used in the customary manner for which the like of it is borrowed, and the permissibility of the ruler borrowing money when there is need for that and returning it to its owner. The hadith of Safwan is a foundation for this topic. In this campaign the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) also ordered: "A pregnant woman shall not be had sexually until she gives birth, nor a non-pregnant woman until she has menstruated once." This indicates that captivity cancels the sanctity of a woman's marriage. Its explanation has already passed fully in Surat al-Nisa' [[See vol. 5, p. 121.]]. In the hadith of Malik it is related that Safwan went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was still a disbeliever, and he witnessed Hunayn and al-Ta'if, while his wife was a Muslim. The hadith continues. Malik said: This was not by the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I do not think that one should seek help from polytheists against polytheists, except if they are servants or sailors. Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i, al-Thawri and al-Awza'i said: There is no harm in this when the rule of Islam is dominant, and seeking their help is only disliked when the rule of polytheism is apparent. The discussion of giving them a share in the spoils has already passed in Surat al-Anfal [[See the twentieth issue, p. 18 of this part.]].

The third issue: The words of the Exalted ﴿and the day of Hunayn﴾. Hunayn is a valley between Makkah and al-Ta'if. It is declined (with tanwin), because it is a masculine noun, and this is the dialect of the Qur'an. Some Arabs do not decline it, treating it as the name of a place. Someone recited:

"They helped their Prophet and strengthened his back
at Hunayn, on the day when the champions were tested [[The verse is by Hassan ibn Thabit.]]."

"Yawm" [day] is an adverb of time, and here it is in the accusative in the sense of: "And He gave you victory on the day of Hunayn." Al-Farra' said: "Mawatin" is not declined, because it has no singular counterpart and no collective form, except that a poet may sometimes be compelled and pluralise it, though not everything permitted in poetry is permitted in ordinary speech. He recited:

"So they chew their iron bits."

Al-Nahhas said: I saw Abu Ishaq wondering at this. He said: He took the statement of al-Khalil and erred in it, because al-Khalil says regarding it: it is not declined because it is a plural with no singular counterpart, and it is not formed as a broken plural. But with the suffix of alif and ta' there is no prohibition.

The fourth issue: The words of the Exalted ﴿when your great number impressed you﴾. It was said that they were twelve thousand. It was said eleven thousand and five hundred. It was said sixteen thousand. Some of them said: "We will not be overcome today for lack of numbers." So they were left to this statement, and what we have mentioned of the defeat at the beginning happened until they regrouped, and then victory and triumph belonged to the Muslims by the blessing of the Master of the Messengers (ﷺ). So in this verse Allah, Mighty and Majestic, explained that victory comes only by the help of Allah, not by numbers. He has also said: ﴿And if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 160] [[See vol. 4, p. 253 onward.]].

The fifth issue: The words of the Exalted ﴿and the earth, despite its vastness, was confining for you﴾. That is, because of fear, as he said:

"As if the lands of Allah, though wide,
were to the fearful one who is hunted like the snare of the fowler [[al-kifah (with kasra): the snare of a hunter. al-habil: the one who sets the snare.]]."

Al-ruhb (with a damma on the ra') means breadth. One says of it: So-and-so is broad-chested. Al-rahb (with a fatha) means wide. One says of it: a wide country, and a wide land. And it has become wide: taruhbu, ruhban and rahabah. It was also said that the ba' has the meaning of ma'a, "with," that is, along with its breadth. It was said it means 'ala, "upon," that is, upon its breadth. It was also said that the meaning is "with its breadth," in which case "ma" is verbal (masdariyyah).

The sixth issue: The words of the Exalted ﴿then you turned back, retreating﴾. Muslim related on the authority of Abu Ishaq who said: A man came to al-Bara' and said: "Did you turn back on the day of Hunayn, O Abu Umarah?" He said: "I bear witness upon the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) that he did not turn back, but some people hastened away from him, and the unarmed ones [[akhfa': plural of khafif, like tabib and atibba'. They meant those who were hasty. **Part 1 of 2: Commentary on Surah 9, verses 25–27**

This contains eight issues. The first concerns the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah has given you victory on many battlefields﴾. When news of the conquest of Makkah reached Hawazin, Malik ibn Awf al-Nasri from the clan of Nasr ibn Malik gathered them. Leadership of the whole army was given to him. He brought with the disbelievers their wealth, their livestock, their women and their children, and he claimed that this would protect their souls and that their resolve in battle would be strengthened by it. They numbered eight thousand according to al-Hasan and Mujahid. It was also said that they were four thousand, from Hawazin and Thaqif. Malik ibn Awf commanded Hawazin, and Kinanah ibn Abd commanded Thaqif. They camped at Awtas [[Awtas: a valley in the lands of Hawazin, where the battle of Hunayn took place.]]. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Abdullah ibn Abi Hadrad al-Aslami as a scout. He came back and informed him of what he had seen of them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then resolved to march against them, and he borrowed armour from Safwan ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi. It was said that this was one hundred coats of mail, and it was also said four hundred. He also borrowed thirty thousand, or forty thousand, from Rabi'ah al-Makhzumi, and when he came back he repaid it to him. The Prophet (ﷺ) then said to him: "May Allah bless you in your family and your wealth. The reward of a loan is only repayment and gratitude." Ibn Majah recorded this in his Sunan.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out with twelve thousand Muslims. Among them were ten thousand who had accompanied him from Madinah, and two thousand from the Muslims of the conquest, namely the Tulaqa', together with those Bedouins who joined him from Sulaym, Banu Kilab, Abs and Dhubyan. He appointed Attab ibn Usayd over Makkah. On this march, some ignorant Bedouins saw a green tree. In the Jahiliyyah there had been a well-known tree called Dhat Anwat, to which the disbelievers would go out on a set day of the year and venerate it. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, make for us a Dhat Anwat as they have a Dhat Anwat." He (peace be upon him) said: "Allahu Akbar! You have spoken, by Him in whose hand my soul is, as the people of Musa said: 'Make for us a god as they have gods.' He said: 'Indeed you are a people who are ignorant.' You will certainly follow the ways of those before you, step by step, so that even if they entered a lizard's burrow you would enter it too." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then moved on until he reached the valley of Hunayn, which is one of the valleys of Tihamah. Hawazin had lain in ambush on both sides of the valley, at the dim light of dawn. They charged the Muslims as one man, and most of the Muslims fled. No one turned back [[i.e., did not turn or look back.]] for anyone. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood firm, and with him stood Abu Bakr and Umar, and from his family Ali, al-Abbas, Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib and his son Ja'far, Usamah ibn Zayd, Ayman ibn Ubayd, who was Ayman ibn Umm Ayman and was killed that day at Hunayn, Rabi'ah ibn al-Harith, and al-Fadl ibn Abbas. It was said that in place of Ja'far ibn Abi Sufyan it was Qutham ibn al-Abbas. These were ten men, and this is why al-Abbas said:

"We helped the Messenger of Allah in battle, nine of us,
while those who fled had fled from him and scattered.
And the tenth of us met death with his own soul,
with what touched him for the sake of Allah, without complaint."

Umm Sulaym also stood firm among those who stood, girded up, holding the camel of Abu Talhah, and in her hand was a dagger. Neither the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) nor any of these men fled. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was on his grey mule, whose name was Duldul. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Anas, al-Abbas said: "I was holding the bridle of the mule of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), restraining it so that it would not hasten, while Abu Sufyan was holding the stirrup of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Abbas, call the companions of the Samurah [tree]." [[i.e., the companions of the tree called al-Samurah, which was the tree under which the Pledge of Ridwan was made in the year of Hudaybiyyah.]] Al-Abbas, who had a loud voice, called out. It is related that because of the intensity of his voice, once when he raided Makkah and cried "Waa sabahah!" every pregnant woman who heard his voice miscarried her child. I cried out at the top of my voice: "Where are the companions of the Samurah?" He said: "By Allah, it was as though their turning back, when they heard my voice, was like the turning of cows toward their calves." They said: "Here we are, here we are!" He said: "Then they fought, while the disbelievers..." [The hadith continues, and in it:] He said: "Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took some pebbles and threw them into the faces of the disbelievers," and then said: "They are defeated, by the Lord of Muhammad!" He said: "I went to look, and the fighting was in its former state, as it appeared to me. By Allah, it was only that he threw them his pebbles, and I continued to see their edge blunted and their affair turned back."

Abu Umar said: We have related from several routes, from some of those among the polytheists who had embraced Islam and who had witnessed Hunayn, that he said, when asked about the day of Hunayn: "We met the Muslims, and we had not waited long before we defeated them and pursued them, until we reached a man riding a white mule. When he saw us he rebuked us with a rebuke and scolded us, and he took in his hand pebbles [[in another version: dust.]] and dust, threw them and said: 'May the faces be disfigured.' No eye remained without being struck by it. We could not control ourselves, and we turned back on our heels." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: A man from the polytheists told me on the day of Hunayn: "When we met the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they did not stand against us for the length of a milking of a sheep, until we came to the owner of the grey mule, meaning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Men with bright faces and handsome appearance met us and said to us: 'May the faces be disfigured! Turn back!' So we turned back, and they rode upon our shoulders, and they were them." He meant the angels. I say: there is no contradiction, for it is possible that "May the faces be disfigured" came both from the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) and from the words of the angels together, and this indicates that the angels fought on the day of Hunayn. And Allah knows best.

Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) killed forty men with his own hand on the day of Hunayn. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took four thousand captives. It was also said six thousand, and twelve thousand camels, besides spoils whose number is unknown.

The second issue: The scholars said regarding this campaign that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever kills an enemy for whom he has evidence, his spoils belong to him." Its explanation has already passed in Surat al-Anfal [[See vol. 7, p. 363.]]. Ibn al-Arabi said: For this point and others, the jurists of rulings included this verse in the books of legal rulings. I say: In this there is also the permissibility of borrowing weapons, the permissibility of making use of what has been borrowed when it is used in the customary manner for which the like of it is borrowed, and the permissibility of the ruler borrowing money when there is need for that and returning it to its owner. The hadith of Safwan is a foundation for this topic. In this campaign the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) also ordered: "A pregnant woman shall not be had sexually until she gives birth, nor a non-pregnant woman until she has menstruated once." This indicates that captivity cancels the sanctity of a woman's marriage. Its explanation has already passed fully in Surat al-Nisa' [[See vol. 5, p. 121.]]. In the hadith of Malik it is related that Safwan went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was still a disbeliever, and he witnessed Hunayn and al-Ta'if, while his wife was a Muslim. The hadith continues. Malik said: This was not by the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I do not think that one should seek help from polytheists against polytheists, except if they are servants or sailors. Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i, al-Thawri and al-Awza'i said: There is no harm in this when the rule of Islam is dominant, and seeking their help is only disliked when the rule of polytheism is apparent. The discussion of giving them a share in the spoils has already passed in Surat al-Anfal [[See the twentieth issue, p. 18 of this part.]].

The third issue: The words of the Exalted ﴿and the day of Hunayn﴾. Hunayn is a valley between Makkah and al-Ta'if. It is declined (with tanwin), because it is a masculine noun, and this is the dialect of the Qur'an. Some Arabs do not decline it, treating it as the name of a place. Someone recited:

"They helped their Prophet and strengthened his back
at Hunayn, on the day when the champions were tested [[The verse is by Hassan ibn Thabit.]]."

"Yawm" [day] is an adverb of time, and here it is in the accusative in the sense of: "And He gave you victory on the day of Hunayn." Al-Farra' said: "Mawatin" is not declined, because it has no singular counterpart and no collective form, except that a poet may sometimes be compelled and pluralise it, though not everything permitted in poetry is permitted in ordinary speech. He recited:

"So they chew their iron bits."

Al-Nahhas said: I saw Abu Ishaq wondering at this. He said: He took the statement of al-Khalil and erred in it, because al-Khalil says regarding it: it is not declined because it is a plural with no singular counterpart, and it is not formed as a broken plural. But with the suffix of alif and ta' there is no prohibition.

The fourth issue: The words of the Exalted ﴿when your great number impressed you﴾. It was said that they were twelve thousand. It was said eleven thousand and five hundred. It was said sixteen thousand. Some of them said: "We will not be overcome today for lack of numbers." So they were left to this statement, and what we have mentioned of the defeat at the beginning happened until they regrouped, and then victory and triumph belonged to the Muslims by the blessing of the Master of the Messengers (ﷺ). So in this verse Allah, Mighty and Majestic, explained that victory comes only by the help of Allah, not by numbers. He has also said: ﴿And if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 160] [[See vol. 4, p. 253 onward.]].

The fifth issue: The words of the Exalted ﴿and the earth, despite its vastness, was confining for you﴾. That is, because of fear, as he said:

"As if the lands of Allah, though wide,
were to the fearful one who is hunted like the snare of the fowler [[al-kifah (with kasra): the snare of a hunter. al-habil: the one who sets the snare.]]."

Al-ruhb (with a damma on the ra') means breadth. One says of it: So-and-so is broad-chested. Al-rahb (with a fatha) means wide. One says of it: a wide country, and a wide land. And it has become wide: taruhbu, ruhban and rahabah. It was also said that the ba' has the meaning of ma'a, "with," that is, along with its breadth. It was said it means 'ala, "upon," that is, upon its breadth. It was also said that the meaning is "with its breadth," in which case "ma" is verbal (masdariyyah).

The sixth issue: The words of the Exalted ﴿then you turned back, retreating﴾. Muslim related on the authority of Abu Ishaq who said: A man came to al-Bara' and said: "Did you turn back on the day of Hunayn, O Abu Umarah?" He said: "I bear witness upon the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) that he did not turn back, but some people hastened away from him, and the unarmed ones [[akhfa': plural of khafif, like tabib and atibba'. They meant those who were hasty. His words "ahmar al-ba's" mean the fighting intensified. (See al-Nawawi's commentary on Sahih Muslim, Book of Military Expeditions.)]] went toward this tribe of Hawazin. They were archers, so they shot at them with a volley of arrows, as if it were a swarm of locusts, and they were routed. So the people went back toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while Abu Sufyan was leading his mule. He dismounted, called upon Allah, sought victory, and was saying: 'I am the Prophet, there is no lie. I am the son of Abd al-Muttalib. O Allah, send down Your victory.'" Al-Bara' said: "By Allah, when the fighting became fierce, we would take refuge with him, and the bravest among us was the one who stood close to him," meaning the Prophet (ﷺ).

The seventh issue: The words of the Exalted ﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and upon the believers﴾. That is, He sent down upon them what calmed them and removed their fear, until they became bold enough to fight the polytheists after they had turned away.

(And He punished those who disbelieved) — that is, by your swords.

The second issue: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ divided the spoils of Hunayn at al-Ji'ranah [[al-Ji'ranah: a place seven miles from Makkah on the way to al-Ta'if.]], a delegation of Hawazin came to him as Muslims, desiring his kindness and benevolence toward them, and they said: "O Messenger of Allah, you are the best of people and the most righteous of people, and you have taken our sons, our women, and our property." When he saw us he rebuked us with a rebuke and scolded us, and he took in his hand pebbles [[in another version: dust.]] and dust, threw them and said: 'May the faces be disfigured.' No eye remained without being struck by it. We could not control ourselves, and we turned back on our heels." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: A man from the polytheists told me on the day of Hunayn: "When we met the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they did not stand against us for the length of a milking of a sheep, until we came to the owner of the grey mule, meaning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Men with bright faces and handsome appearance met us and said to us: 'May the faces be disfigured! Turn back!' So we turned back, and they rode upon our shoulders, and they were them." He meant the angels. I say: there is no contradiction, for it is possible that "May the faces be disfigured" came both from the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) and from the words of the angels together, and this indicates that the angels fought on the day of Hunayn. And Allah knows best.

Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) killed forty men with his own hand on the day of Hunayn. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took four thousand captives. It was also said six thousand, and twelve thousand camels, besides spoils whose number is unknown.

The second issue: The scholars said regarding this campaign that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever kills an enemy for whom he has evidence, his spoils belong to him." Its explanation has already passed in Surat al-Anfal [[See vol. 7, p. 363.]]. Ibn al-Arabi said: For this point and others, the jurists of rulings included this verse in the books of legal rulings. I say: In this there is also the permissibility of borrowing weapons, the permissibility of making use of what has been borrowed when it is used in the customary manner for which the like of it is borrowed, and the permissibility of the ruler borrowing money when there is need for that and returning it to its owner. The hadith of Safwan is a foundation for this topic. In this campaign the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) also ordered: "A pregnant woman shall not be had sexually until she gives birth, nor a non-pregnant woman until she has menstruated once." This indicates that captivity cancels the sanctity of a woman's marriage. Its explanation has already passed fully in Surat al-Nisa' [[See vol. 5, p. 121.]]. In the hadith of Malik it is related that Safwan went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was still a disbeliever, and he witnessed Hunayn and al-Ta'if, while his wife was a Muslim. The hadith continues. Malik said: This was not by the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I do not think that one should seek help from polytheists against polytheists, except if they are servants or sailors. Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i, al-Thawri and al-Awza'i said: There is no harm in this when the rule of Islam is dominant, and seeking their help is only disliked when the rule of polytheism is apparent. The discussion of giving them a share in the spoils has already passed in Surat al-Anfal [[See the twentieth issue, p. 18 of this part.]].

The third issue: The words of the Exalted ﴿and the day of Hunayn﴾. Hunayn is a valley between Makkah and al-Ta'if. It is declined (with tanwin), because it is a masculine noun, and this is the dialect of the Qur'an. Some Arabs do not decline it, treating it as the name of a place. Someone recited:

"They helped their Prophet and strengthened his back
at Hunayn, on the day when the champions were tested [[The verse is by Hassan ibn Thabit.]]."

"Yawm" [day] is an adverb of time, and here it is in the accusative in the sense of: "And He gave you victory on the day of Hunayn." Al-Farra' said: "Mawatin" is not declined, because it has no singular counterpart and no collective form, except that a poet may sometimes be compelled and pluralise it, though not everything permitted in poetry is permitted in ordinary speech. He recited:

"So they chew their iron bits."

Al-Nahhas said: I saw Abu Ishaq wondering at this. He said: He took the statement of al-Khalil and erred in it, because al-Khalil says regarding it: it is not declined because it is a plural with no singular counterpart, and it is not formed as a broken plural. But with the suffix of alif and ta' there is no prohibition.

The fourth issue: The words of the Exalted ﴿when your great number impressed you﴾. It was said that they were twelve thousand. It was said eleven thousand and five hundred. It was said sixteen thousand. Some of them said: "We will not be overcome today for lack of numbers." So they were left to this statement, and what we have mentioned of the defeat at the beginning happened until they regrouped, and then victory and triumph belonged to the Muslims by the blessing of the Master of the Messengers (ﷺ). So in this verse Allah, Mighty and Majestic, explained that victory comes only by the help of Allah, not by numbers. He has also said: ﴿And if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 160] [[See vol. 4, p. 253 onward.]].

The fifth issue: The words of the Exalted ﴿and the earth, despite its vastness, was confining for you﴾. That is, because of fear, as he said:

"As if the lands of Allah, though wide,
were to the fearful one who is hunted like the snare of the fowler [[al-kifah (with kasra): the snare of a hunter. al-habil: the one who sets the snare.]]."

Al-ruhb (with a damma on the ra') means breadth. One says of it: So-and-so is broad-chested. Al-rahb (with a fatha) means wide. One says of it: a wide country, and a wide land. And it has become wide: taruhbu, ruhban and rahabah. It was also said that the ba' has the meaning of ma'a, "with," that is, along with its breadth. It was said it means 'ala, "upon," that is, upon its breadth. It was also said that the meaning is "with its breadth," in which case "ma" is verbal (masdariyyah).

The sixth issue: The words of the Exalted ﴿then you turned back, retreating﴾. Muslim related on the authority of Abu Ishaq who said: A man came to al-Bara' and said: "Did you turn back on the day of Hunayn, O Abu Umarah?" He said: "I bear witness upon the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) that he did not turn back, but some people hastened away from him, and the unarmed ones [[akhfa': plural of khafif, like tabib and atibba'. They meant those who were hasty. Al-husr: plural of hasir, like sajid and sujud, referring to one who has no coat of mail and no helmet, that is, who has no weapon. al-Rashq (with kasra): the name for the arrows that a group shoots at once. al-Rijl (with kasra): a piece. His words "ahmar al-ba's" mean the fighting intensified. (See al-Nawawi's commentary on Sahih Muslim, Book of Military Expeditions.)]] went toward this tribe of Hawazin. They were archers, so they shot at them with a volley of arrows, as if it were a swarm of locusts, and they were routed. So the people went back toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while Abu Sufyan was leading his mule. He dismounted, called upon Allah, sought victory, and was saying: 'I am the Prophet, there is no lie. I am the son of Abd al-Muttalib. O Allah, send down Your victory.'" Al-Bara' said: "By Allah, when the fighting became fierce, we would take refuge with him, and the bravest among us was the one who stood close to him," meaning the Prophet (ﷺ).

The seventh issue: The words of the Exalted ﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and upon the believers﴾. That is, He sent down upon them what calmed them and removed their fear, until they became bold enough to fight the polytheists after they had turned away.

(And He sent down hosts you did not see) — and they were the angels, who strengthened the believers by what they cast into their hearts of thoughts and steadfastness, and weakened the disbelievers by striking terror into them from a place where they could not see them, and without fighting, for the angels did not fight except on the day of Badr. It is related that a man from the Banu Nasr said to the believers after the battle: "Where are the piebald horses, and the men who were upon them, white? We were among them only like the mark of a mole, and our killing was only at their hands." They informed the Prophet ﷺ of that, and he said: "Those were the angels."

(And He punished those who disbelieved) — that is, by your swords.

(And that is the recompense of the disbelievers. Then Allah turns, after that, to whom He wills) — that is, to whoever fled and then Allah guides him to Islam, such as Malik ibn Awf al-Nasri, the chief of Hunayn, and those of his people who embraced Islam with him.

The second issue: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ divided the spoils of Hunayn at al-Ji'ranah [[al-Ji'ranah: a place seven miles from Makkah on the way to al-Ta'if.]], a delegation of Hawazin came to him as Muslims, desiring his kindness and benevolence toward them, and they said: "O Messenger of Allah, you are the best of people and the most righteous of people, and you have taken our sons, our women, and our property." He said to them: "I had delayed with you, and the distributions have already taken place, and what you see is with me. The best speech is the most truthful, so choose either your offspring or your property." They said: "We do not equate the lineages with anything." He stood up to address them and said: "These people came to us as Muslims, and we gave them the choice, and they did not equate the lineages with anything. So they are content with the return of their offspring. What belongs to me and to the sons of Abd al-Muttalib and the sons of Hashim is theirs." The Muhajirun and the Ansar said: "As for what belongs to us, it is for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." Al-Aqra' ibn Habis and Uyaynah ibn Hisn, among their people, refused to return anything of what had fallen to their shares. Al-Abbas ibn Mirdas al-Sulami likewise refused, hoping that his people would support him as the people of al-Aqra' and Uyaynah had supported them. But the Banu Sulaym refused and said: "Rather, what belonged to us is for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever among you is stingy with what is in his hands, we will compensate him for it." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to them their women and children, and he compensated those whose hearts were not willing to give up their share with compensations with which they were content.

Qatadah said: It was mentioned to us that the wet-nurse of the Prophet ﷺ who had nursed him, from the Banu Sa'd, came to him on the day of Hunayn and asked him for the captives of Hunayn. He ﷺ said: "I do not own anything except what falls to me from them, but come to me tomorrow and ask me, while the people are with me. When I give you my share, the people will give you theirs." She came the next day, and he spread his garment for her and seated her upon it. Then she asked him, and he gave her his share. When the people saw that, they gave her their shares.

The number of the captives of Hawazin, according to the statement of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, was six thousand heads. It was also said: four thousand. Abu Umar said: among them was al-Shaymaa', the sister of the Prophet ﷺ through nursing, who was the daughter of al-Harith ibn Abd al-Uzza from the Banu Sa'd ibn Bakr, and the daughter of Halimah al-Sa'diyyah. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ honored her, gave her, and treated her well, and she returned joyfully to her land with her religion and with what Allah had granted her as booty.

Ibn Abbas said: On the day of Awtas, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw a woman running and crying out, not settling in one place. He asked about her, and it was said: She had lost a little child of hers. Then he saw her having found her son, kissing him and drawing him close. He called her and said to his companions: "Do you think this woman would throw her child into the fire?" They said: "No." He said: "Why not?" They said: "Out of her compassion." He said: "Allah is more merciful to you than she is to it." Muslim related it in meaning, and praise be to Allah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 28 (part 1 of 2):

It contains seven issues.

The first: the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿O you who believe, the polytheists are only unclean﴾. It is a subject and predicate construction (mubtada' wa khabar). The scholars differed over the meaning of describing the polytheist as "unclean" (najas). Qatadah, Ma'mar ibn Rashid and others said: it is because he is in a state of major ritual impurity (junub), since his washing from major impurity is not a valid washing. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: rather, the meaning is that it is polytheism itself that made him unclean. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: whoever shakes hands with a polytheist should perform ablution (wudu').

The whole school (madhhab) holds that washing is obligatory upon the disbeliever when he embraces Islam, except Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, who said: it is not obligatory, because Islam wipes out what came before it. Abu Thawr and Ahmad held that washing is obligatory for him. Al-Shafi'i dropped it and said: it is more beloved to me that he wash. Ibn al-Qasim held a similar view. There is also a saying of Malik that he does not know washing (la ya'rifu al-ghusl), related from him by Ibn Wahb and Ibn Abi Uways. The hadith of Thumamah and Qays ibn 'Asim refutes these sayings. Abu Hatim al-Busti related both in his Sahih Musnad. The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by Thumamah one day, and he embraced Islam. He sent him to the orchard (ha'it) of Abu Talhah, and ordered him to wash. He washed and prayed two rak'ahs. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, your companion's Islam has become good." Muslim related it with a similar meaning. In it: when the Prophet (ﷺ) freed Thumamah, he went to a palm grove near the mosque and washed. And Qays ibn 'Asim was ordered to wash with water and lote-leaves (sidr). If his Islam came shortly before reaching puberty (ihtilam), then his washing is recommended (mustahabb). Whenever he embraces Islam after reaching puberty, he is obliged to intend by his washing the major impurity (janabah). This is the saying of our scholars, and it is the established position of the school. Ibn al-Qasim permitted the disbeliever to wash before pronouncing the testimony with his tongue, when he believes in Islam in his heart; this is a weak view in reasoning, contrary to the report, because no one becomes a Muslim by intention alone without speech. This is the saying of the community of the People of the Sunnah regarding faith: it is speech with the tongue and assent in the heart, and it grows through action. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿To Him ascend the good words, and righteous deed raises them﴾ [Fatir: 10].

The second: the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿So let them not approach the Sacred Mosque﴾. "So let them not approach" is a prohibition, and for this reason the nun was dropped from it. "The Sacred Mosque": this expression is applied to the entire Haram, and this is the view of 'Ata'. Accordingly, it is forbidden to allow a polytheist to enter the whole Haram. If a messenger of theirs comes to us, the imam goes out to the outskirts (al-hill) to hear what he says. If a polytheist enters the Haram secretly and dies, his grave is dug up and his bones are removed. They have no right to settle in it or to pass through it. As for the Arabian Peninsula, which comprises Makkah, Madinah, al-Yamamah, Yemen and its mikhalif, Malik said: everyone who is not upon Islam is to be removed from these places, and they are not prevented from passing through them as travellers. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said the same, except that he excepted Yemen from this. A period of three days is set for them, as 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, set it for them when he expelled them. They are not to be buried in it, and they are to be driven to the outskirts (al-hill).

The third: the scholars differed over the entry of disbelievers into mosques, and into the Sacred Mosque in particular, in five opinions. The people of Madinah said: the verse is general, covering all polytheists and all mosques. Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz wrote to his governors accordingly and cited this verse in his letter. The words of Allah the Exalted support this: ﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned﴾ [al-Nur: 36]. The entry of disbelievers into them contradicts their being raised. In Sahih Muslim and others: "Indeed these mosques are not suitable for any of the urine and filth" — the hadith. And the disbeliever is not free of that. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I do not make the mosque lawful for a menstruating woman or for one in major impurity," and the disbeliever is in major impurity. The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Only the polytheists are unclean﴾, so Allah named him unclean. Either this means he is unclean in substance, or he is kept at a distance by way of ruling. Whichever it is, prohibiting him from the mosque is obligatory, because the cause, which is uncleanness, exists in them, and the sanctity exists in the mosque. It is said: "a man is najas, a woman is najas, two men are najas, two women are najas, men are najas, women are najas," not declined in the dual or plural because it is a verbal noun (masdar). As for al-najis (with a kasra on the nun and a sukun on the jim), it is used only when it is said together with rijs. When used alone, it is said najis (with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the jim) and najus (with a damma on the jim).

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the verse is general concerning all polytheists, but specific to the Sacred Mosque, and they are not prevented from entering other places. He therefore permitted the Jew and the Christian to enter all mosques. Ibn al-'Arabi said: this is rigid literalism on his part, because the words of the Mighty and Majestic: "Only the polytheists are unclean" point to the cause as polytheism and uncleanness. If it is said: the Prophet (ﷺ) tied Thumamah in the mosque while he was a polytheist. It is answered: our scholars have responded to this hadith, though it is sound, with several answers. The first: that it came before the revelation of the verse. The second: that the Prophet (ﷺ) already knew of his Islam, and that is why he tied him. The third: that it is a particular case, and it should not be used to override the evidences we have mentioned, since it restricts the ruling of the general principle. It may also be said: he tied him in the mosque so that he might see the good prayer of the Muslims and their gathering for it, and the good manners of their sitting in the mosque, so that he would feel at ease with that and become Muslim, and so it happened. It may also be said: they had no place to tie him except the mosque, and Allah knows best.

Abu Hanifah and his companions said: the Jews and Christians are not prevented from entering the Sacred Mosque or any other mosque, and only the polytheists and the idol-worshippers are prevented from entering the Sacred Mosque. This is a view that all that we have mentioned from the verse and other evidence refutes. Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: according to Abu Hanifah, it is permissible for a dhimmi to enter all mosques without any need. Al-Shafi'i said: need is taken into account, and with need it is not permissible to enter the Sacred Mosque. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: the whole Haram is a qiblah and a mosque, so they should be prevented from entering the Haram, based on the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. The journey was from the house of Umm Hani'. Qatadah said: no polytheist may approach the Sacred Mosque except one who is a jizyah-payer or a disbelieving slave of a Muslim. Isma'il ibn Ishaq related: Yahya ibn 'Abd al-Hamid narrated to us, saying: Sharik narrated to us from Ash'ath, from al-Hasan, from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "No polytheist may approach the mosque except one who is a slave or a bondmaid, who enters it for a need." Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah said likewise, for he said: the generality prevents the polytheist from approaching the Sacred Mosque, and it is specified in the case of the male slave and the female slave.

The fourth: the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿after this year of theirs﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions. One: that it is the year nine, in which Abu Bakr performed the pilgrimage. The second: the year ten, said by Qatadah. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "And this is the correct view, which the implication of the wording gives. It is strange to say that it is the year nine, which is the year in which the call (adhan) took place. If a man's slave entered his house one day, and his master said to him: do not enter this house after today, it would not mean the day on which he entered."

The fifth: the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if you fear poverty﴾. 'Amr ibn Fa'id said: the meaning is "and if you fear" (wa idh khiftum). This is a non-Arabic usage, and the meaning is sound with "in" (in). When the Muslims prevented the polytheists from the seasonal gathering, while they used to bring food and trade goods, Satan cast into their hearts the fear of poverty, and they said: from where will we live? So Allah promised them that He would enrich them from His bounty. Al-Dahhak said: Allah opened for them the door of jizyah from the people of the dhimmah, by His words the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or the Last Day﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29], to the end of the verse. 'Ikrimah said: Allah enriched them with abundant rain, plant growth and fertile land. Tabalah and Jurash, a town in Yemen of fertile land, and Jurash, a district of the Yemeni regions (makhalif), became fertile, and they carried food and fat (wadak) to Makkah, and goodness increased. The Arabs embraced Islam, the people of Najd and Sana'a and others, so their pilgrimage and trade flourished. Allah enriched them from His bounty through jihad and through victory over the nations. Al-'Ayla means poverty. It is said: "al-rajul ya'ilu" when he became poor. The poet said:

"The poor man does not know when his wealth will come, and the rich man does not know when he will become poor."

Ali ibn Qalqam (A'mash?) and others from the companions of Ibn Mas'ud read "ʿāʾilatan" (poverty)... 

Wait, I need to render the passage faithfully. Here is the translation:

Alqama and others among the companions of Ibn Mas'ud read ʿāʾilatan (عَائِلَةً), which is a verbal noun like al-qāʾilah (الْقَائِلَة), from qāla yaqīlu, and like al-ʿāfiyah (الْعَافِيَة). It is possible that it is an adjective (naʿt) for an omitted noun, its implied sense being ḥālan ʿāʾilatan, and its meaning is a burdensome circumstance. From it one says: ʿālanī al-amr yaʿūluhunī, i.e. it was hard and severe upon me. Al-Ṭabarī related that one says: ʿāla yaʿūlu when one becomes poor.

The sixth issue: In this verse is evidence that attachment of the heart to means (asbāb) in seeking provision is permissible, and that this does not contradict tawakkul (trust in God), even though provision is predetermined and God's decree and distribution are carried out. Rather, He has tied it to means for wisdom, so that He may distinguish the hearts that attach themselves to means from the hearts that place their trust in the Lord of lords. It has already been mentioned that means do not contradict tawakkul. The Prophet ﷺ said: (If you were to place your trust in God as He deserves, He would provide for you as He provides for the birds: they go out hungry in the morning and return full in the evening). Narrated by al-Bukhari. He informed that true tawakkul is not opposed by going out and returning in pursuit of provision.

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: But the shaykhs of the Sufis said: it is only by going out and returning in acts of obedience that one [the means] is what brings provision. They said: the evidence for this is two matters. The first: the words of the Exalted: ﴿And enjoin your family to prayer and be steadfast in it. We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you﴾ [Taha: 132]. The second: the words of the Exalted: ﴿To Him ascend good words, and righteous deeds raise them﴾ [Fatir: 10]. So provision descends from its place, the heaven, only in return for what ascends, which is good remembrance and righteous deeds, and not by striving on the earth, for there is no provision in it. The correct view is what the Sunnah has established according to the jurists of the literal (Ẓāhirī) school: acting upon worldly means, such as tilling, trading in markets, developing wealth, and planting fruit trees. The Companions did this while the Prophet ﷺ was among them.

Abu al-Hasan ibn Battal said: God the Glorified commanded His servants to spend from the good things they earn, and other verses to that effect. He also said: ﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173]. So He permitted for the compelled person what had been forbidden to him when he lacked food, since He commanded him to earn food and nourish himself with it, and did not command him to wait for food to descend upon him from heaven. Had he abandoned striving to obtain what he eats, he would have been a killer of himself. The Messenger of God ﷺ would writhe from hunger when he found nothing to eat, and no food came down to him from heaven; he would store for his household the provision of a whole year, until God granted him conquests.

Anas ibn Malik related that a man came to the Prophet ﷺ with a camel and said: "O Messenger of God, shall I tie it and trust (in God), or release it and trust?" He said: (Tie it and trust). I say: The people of the Suffah have no proof in their favour, for they were poor people who sat in the mosque, neither farming nor trading, having no earnings or wealth; they were merely guests of Islam when the lands were straitened. Nevertheless, they would gather firewood by day, carry water to the house of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and recite the Qur'an and pray by night. Thus al-Bukhari and others described them. So they did engage in means. When a gift came to the Prophet ﷺ he would eat it with them, and if it was charity he would give it specifically to them. When conquests multiplied and Islam spread, they went out and took up governorships, like Abu Hurayrah and others, and did not remain sitting.

Then it was said: the means by which provision is sought are of six kinds. The highest is the earnings of our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. He said: (My provision has been placed under the shade of my spear, and humiliation and abasement have been placed upon whoever opposes my command). Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, who graded it authentic. God made the provision of His Prophet ﷺ to be in his earnings, because of his excellence, and specified for him the most excellent kind of earning, which is seizing by conquest and dominance, because of his nobility. Second: a man eating from the work of his hands. He ﷺ said: (The best a man eats is from the work of his hands, and the Prophet of God Dawud used to eat from the work of his hands). Narrated by al-Bukhari. In the revelation: ﴿And We taught him the crafting of armour for you﴾ [al-Anbiya: 80]. It is also related that ʿIsa, peace be upon him, used to eat from the spinning of his mother. Third: trade, which was the occupation of most of the Companions, may God be pleased with them, especially the Emigrants, and the revelation indicates it in more than one place. Fourth: tilling and planting, which we explained in Surat al-Baqarah. Fifth: teaching and reciting the Qur'an and ruqyah, which has passed in al-Fatihah. Sixth: one takes with the intention of repayment when in need. He ﷺ said: (Whoever takes people's wealth intending to repay it, God will repay on his behalf; and whoever takes it intending to destroy it, God will destroy him). Narrated by al-Bukhari, related by Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him.

The seventh issue: the words of the Exalted: "if He wills" (in ﴿if He wills﴾) indicate that provision is not by striving alone, but is from the bounty of God, who has taken charge of its distribution among His servants. This is clear in the words of the Exalted: ﴿We have distributed among them their livelihood in the life of this world﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32], and so on.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 29 (part 1 of 2):

There are five issues in this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day﴾. When Allah, exalted is He, forbade the disbelievers to approach the Sacred Mosque, the Muslims felt in themselves a loss of the trade that the polytheists used to bring to them. Allah, mighty and majestic is He, said: ﴿And if you fear poverty﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28], the verse, as preceded. Then in this verse He made the jizyah (poll-tax) lawful, and it had not been taken before that. He made it a substitute for what He had prevented them from, namely bringing their trade to the polytheists. So Allah, mighty and majestic is He, said: "Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day", the verse. He, glorified and exalted is He, commanded the fighting of all the disbelievers, since they were united (li-ishfāqihim [[asfaqa al-qawm 'ala amr wahid: ajma'u 'alayhi, "the people agreed upon one matter: they unanimously agreed on it."]]) upon this description. He singled out the People of the Book for mention, out of honour for their Book, and because they were knowledgeable of the Tawhid (Oneness of God), the Messengers, the sharia laws and the religions, and especially because of the mention of Muhammad ﷺ, his religion and his community. When they denied him, the proof was firmly established against them and their offence became grave, so He drew attention to their status, then made for the fighting a limit, which is the giving of the jizyah in place of killing. This is the correct view. Ibn al-'Arabi said: I heard Abu al-Wafa' 'Ali ibn 'Aqil in a session of disputation reciting it and arguing with it. He said: "Fight" is an order to punish. Then he said: "those who do not believe", and that is an explanation of the sin which necessitates the punishment. His saying "nor in the Last Day" is an emphasis of the sin on the side of belief. Then he said: "nor do they forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden", an increase of the sin in opposing the acts. Then he said: "nor do they follow the religion of truth", an indication of the emphasis of the disobedience through deviation, obstinacy and refusal to submit. Then he said: "from among those who were given the Book", an emphasis of the proof, because they used to find it written with them in the Torah and the Gospel. Then he said: "until they pay the jizyah willingly, while they are humbled", so He explained the limit to which the punishment extends and specified the substitute by which it is lifted.

The second: The scholars have differed concerning from whom the jizyah is taken. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the jizyah is not accepted except from the People of the Book specifically, whether Arabs or non-Arabs, because of this verse, for they are the ones singled out for mention, so the ruling is directed to them and not to others, due to His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [[See p. 72 of this part.]] [al-Tawbah: 5]. And He did not say "until they pay the jizyah" as He said concerning the People of the Book. And he said: it is accepted from the Magians by the Sunnah [[Due to his, peace be upon him, saying: "Treat them as you treat the People of the Book."]]. This is also the view of Ahmad and Abu Thawr, and it is the school of al-Thawri and Abu Hanifa and his companions. Al-Awza'i said: the jizyah is taken from every worshipper of idols, or fire, or denier, or one who denies. Likewise is the school of Malik, for he held that the jizyah is taken from all kinds of polytheism and denial, Arab or non-Arab, Taghlibi or Qurashi, whoever he might be, except the apostate. Ibn al-Qasim, Ashhab and Sahnun said: the jizyah is taken from the Magians of the Arabs and from all nations. As for the idol-worshippers among the Arabs, Allah did not establish a jizyah for them, and none of them remains upon the earth; for them there is only fighting or Islam. It is found from Ibn al-Qasim that the jizyah is taken from them, as Malik says; and that is in the Tafri' of Ibn al-Jallab, and it is a possibility, not an explicit text.
