Ibn Wahb said: the jizyah is not accepted from the Magians of the Arabs, and it is accepted from others. He said: because there are no Magians among the Arabs except that they have all embraced Islam; so whoever is found among them in opposition to Islam is an apostate, who is to be killed in every case if he does not embrace Islam, and no jizyah is accepted from them. Ibn al-Jahm said: the jizyah is accepted from everyone who follows a religion other than Islam, except those upon whom the consensus of the disbelieving Quraysh was reached. He mentioned as its reasoning that it is an honour for them, to keep them from humiliation and abasement, because of their position with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Others said: that is only because all of them embraced Islam on the day of the conquest of Makkah. And Allah knows best.

The third: As for the Magians, Ibn al-Mundhir said: I know of no disagreement that the jizyah is taken from them. In the Muwatta': Malik, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab mentioned the matter of the Magians and said: "I do not know how to act regarding their affair." 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf said: "I bear witness that I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: '(Treat them as you treat the People of the Book).'" Abu 'Umar said: he means concerning the jizyah specifically. In the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, "Treat them as you treat the People of the Book", there is evidence that they are not People of the Book. This is the view of the majority of jurists. It has been narrated from al-Shafi'i that they were People of the Book who altered (their scripture). I think he went in this direction on the basis of something narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, through a chain that is weak, revolving around Abu Sa'id al-Baqqal, mentioned by 'Abd al-Razzaq and others. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is narrated that a prophet named Zaradusht was sent to the Magians. And Allah knows best.

The fourth: Allah, glorified and exalted is He, did not mention in His Book the amount of the jizyah taken from them. The scholars have differed concerning the amount of the jizyah taken from them. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: there is no fixed limit for it; it is according to what they have agreed upon. Likewise said Yahya ibn Adam, Abu 'Ubayd and al-Tabari, except that al-Tabari said: its minimum is a dinar and its maximum has no limit. They argued with what the people of the Sahih narrated from 'Amr ibn 'Awf: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made a treaty with the people of Bahrain concerning the jizyah. Al-Shafi'i said: a dinar upon the rich and the poor among the free adult males, none of it to be reduced. He argued with what Abu Dawud and others narrated from Mu'adh: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent him to Yemen and ordered him to take from every adult male a dinar as jizyah. Al-Shafi'i said: this is what explains the intent of Allah, exalted is He. This is also the view of Abu Thawr. Al-Shafi'i said: if they are reconciled upon more than a dinar, it is permissible; and if they increase and their souls are content with that, it is accepted from them. If they are reconciled upon hosting for three days, it is permissible, provided the hospitality is specified in bread, barley, straw and condiments, and he mentioned what is required of the average person and what is required of the wealthy, and mentioned the place of lodging and shelter from cold and heat. Malik said, in what Ibn al-Qasim, Ashhab and Muhammad ibn al-Harith ibn Zanjawayh narrated from him: it is four dinars upon the people of gold and forty dirhams upon the people of silver; the rich and the poor are equal, even if he is a Magian. It is not increased or decreased from what 'Umar prescribed; nothing else is taken from them. It has been said that the weak is lightened by the amount the imam sees fit. Ibn al-Qasim said: it is not decreased from 'Umar's prescription because of poverty, nor increased upon it because of wealth. Abu 'Umar said: it is taken from their poor according to what they can bear, even if it is a single dirham. And Malik returned to this view. Abu Hanifa and his companions, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: twelve, twenty-four, and forty (dirhams). Al-Thawri said: various rates have come from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab concerning this, so the governor may take whichever of them he wishes, when they are dhimmis. As for the people of treaty, what they have been reconciled upon, and nothing more.

The fifth: Our scholars, may Allah have mercy upon them, said: what the Qur'an indicates is that the jizyah is taken from the fighting men, because He, exalted is He, said: "Fight those who..." up to His saying: "until they pay the jizyah", so this requires its obligation upon those who fight. And it indicates that it is not upon the slave, even if he is a fighter, because he has no property, and because He, exalted is He, said: "until they give". It is not said of one who does not possess that he gives. This is a consensus of the scholars that the jizyah is only imposed upon the heads of free adult men, who are those who fight, excluding women, offspring, slaves, the insane who are overcome in their minds, and the aged decrepit. And there was disagreement concerning monks. Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik that it is not taken from them. Mutarrif and Ibn al-Majishun said: this is if he has not become a monk after it was imposed...

Sixth: When the people of the jizya (poll tax, levied on protected non-Muslims) pay the jizya, nothing is to be taken from their fruits, their trade goods, or their crops, unless they trade in lands other than the lands in which they were allowed to remain and with which they made their agreement. If they go out as merchants from the lands in which they were allowed to remain to other lands, a tenth ('ushr) is taken from them whenever they sell, once the price of those goods comes into their hands as cash (nadda al-mal: money became coin after having been goods), even if this happens several times in one year. The exception is when they carry food, namely wheat and olive oil, specifically to Madina and Makka. In that case, half a tenth is taken from them, following what 'Umar did. Some of the people of Madina hold that a tenth should be taken from the dhimmis for their trade only once in a year, just as it is taken from Muslims. This is the view of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and a group of leading jurists. The first view is the view of Malik and his companions.

Seventh: When the people of the jizya pay the jizya that was imposed on them or agreed upon, they are left free to hold all their property, and their vineyards and presses, so long as they keep their wine hidden and do not openly sell it to a Muslim. They are forbidden to display wine and pork in the markets of the Muslims. If they display any of that, the wine is poured out over them, and whoever displays pork is disciplined. If a Muslim pours out their wine without its having been displayed, he has transgressed and must compensate. It is also said that compensation is not required. If he seized it by force, he must return it. They are not to be interfered with in their legal judgments or in their dealings among themselves involving usury (riba). If they bring their disputes to us, the judge has the choice: if he wishes, he may judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and if he wishes, he may turn away. It is also said that he should judge between them in cases of injustice in every circumstance, and that the strong among them should be made to give to the weak, because this is part of defending them. It is the duty of the Imam to fight their enemy on their behalf, and to seek their help in fighting them. They have no share in the fay' (revenue taken from the enemy without battle). As for the churches over which they reached agreement, they may not add to them, but they are not prevented from repairing what has fallen into disrepair, and they have no way to build new ones. They take on the clothing and appearance by which they are distinguished from Muslims, and they are prevented from imitating the people of Islam. There is no harm in buying the children of the enemy from them when those children have no dhimma. Whoever is contentious in paying his jizya is disciplined for his contentiousness (laddad: fierce hostility), and the jizya is taken from him while he is humiliated.

Eighth: The scholars differed about the reason for which the jizya became obligatory. The scholars of the Malikis said: it was made obligatory as a substitute for being killed because of disbelief. Al-Shafi'i said: it was made obligatory as a substitute for their blood and for residing in the land. The practical result of the disagreement is that if we say it was obligatory as a substitute for being killed, then if he becomes Muslim, the jizya is dropped from him for the past, whether he became Muslim a day before the year was complete or after it, according to Malik. According to al-Shafi'i, it is a debt fixed upon the dhimma (the liability of the person), so Islam does not cancel it, like the rent of a house. Some of the Hanafis agree with our view. Some of them said: it was only made obligatory as a substitute for support and jihad. This was chosen by al-Qadi Abu Zayd, who claimed it was the secret of Allah in this matter. The view of Malik is more correct, because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "There is no jizya upon a Muslim." Sufyan said: its meaning is that if the dhimmi becomes Muslim after the jizya has become due upon him, it is cancelled for him. Al-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud transmitted it. Our scholars said: the words of Allah the Exalted indicate this: ﴿until they pay the jizya willingly while they are humbled﴾, because with Islam this meaning ceases. There is no disagreement that when they become Muslim, they do not pay the jizya "willingly while they are humbled." Al-Shafi'i does not take it after Islam in the manner which Allah the Exalted described. He only says that the jizya is a debt which became due upon him because of a prior cause, namely residing in the land or avoiding the harm of being killed, so it became like all other debts.

Ninth: If the Imam makes a treaty with the people of a town or a fortress and then they break their covenant, refuse to pay what is required of them of the jizya and other obligations, and refuse to submit to the rule of Islam, without having been wronged, and the Imam is not oppressing them, then it is obligatory upon the Muslims to raid them and fight them alongside their Imam. If they fight and are defeated, they are to be treated according to the ruling for the abode of war (dar al-harb) in the same way. It has been said: they and their women are to be enslaved, and there is no one-fifth (khums) due on them, and this is one view.

Tenth: If they go out as robbers cutting off the road, they are in the position of Muslim fighters (muharibin) when they do not withhold the jizya. If they go out seeking redress for injustice, their affair is examined, they are returned to the protected status (dhimma), they are given justice against their oppressor, and none of them is to be enslaved, for they are free. If some of them break the covenant and others do not, then whoever does not break it remains upon his covenant, and he is not held responsible for the breaking of others. Their continued adherence to the covenant is known by their denouncing those who break it.

Eleventh: The word jizya is on the pattern fi'lah, from jazā, yajzī, when one repays what was done for him. It is as if they gave it as a repayment for the security they were granted. It is like qi'dah (sitting) and jilsah (sitting). From this meaning is the poet's saying:
"He repays you or praises you, and whoever praises you for what you have done is like one who repaid you."

Twelfth: Muslim narrated from Hisham ibn Hakim ibn Hizam that he passed by some people of the Anbat (the non-Arab farmers of Iraq and Syria) in Syria who had been made to stand in the sun, and in another narration, oil had been poured over their heads. He said: "What is their situation?" It was said: "They are being detained for the jizya." Hisham said: "I bear witness that I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Allah will punish those who punish people in this world.'" In another narration: their commander at that time was 'Umayr ibn Sa'd over Palestine. Hisham entered upon him and related this to him, so he ordered that they be released. Our scholars said: as for punishing them when they refuse to pay while being able to pay, it is permitted. But when their inability is clear, punishing them is not lawful, because whoever is unable to pay the jizya has it dropped from him. The wealthy are not to be made to pay on behalf of the poor. Abu Dawud transmitted from Safwan ibn Sulaym, from a number of the sons of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), from their fathers, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wrongs a person under covenant (mu'ahad), or diminishes his rights, or burdens him beyond his capacity, or takes anything from him without his good will, I will be his adversary on the Day of Resurrection."

Thirteenth: Allah the Exalted says: ﴿from a hand﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he gives it with his own hand, not appointing anyone else to give it. Abu al-Bakhtari narrated from Salman: "Despised." Ma'mar narrated from Qatada: "By force." It has also been said: "from a hand" means by a favour from you to them, because when the jizya is taken from them, a favour has been bestowed upon them by that. 'Ikrimah said: he gives it while standing and the one who takes it is seated. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said the same. Ibn al-'Arabi said: this is not from the words "from a hand," but from the words ﴿and they are humbled﴾.

Fourteenth: The imams narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The upper hand is better than the lower hand. The upper hand is the one that gives, and the lower hand is the one that asks." It is also narrated: "The upper hand is the one that gives." So the hand of the giver in charity is the upper hand, while the hand of the giver in the jizya is the lower hand. The hand of the receiver is the upper hand. That is because He is the Exalter and the Abaser: He raises whom He wills and abases whom He wills; there is no god but Him.

Fifteenth: From Habib ibn Abi Thabit, who said: A man came to Ibn 'Abbas and said: "The land of kharaj (land tax) is one whose people are unable to pay it. Shall I cultivate it, plant it, and pay its kharaj?" He said: "No." Another man came and asked him the same, and he said: "No," and recited the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or the Last Day...﴾ up to His words ﴿and they are humbled.﴾ Does one of you deliberately put humiliation on the neck of one of them and then remove it and place it on his own neck? Kulayb ibn Wa'il said: I said to Ibn 'Umar: "I have bought land." He said: "Buying is good." I said: "I give for every jarib (a unit of land area; some said ten thousand cubits, see al-Misbah, where the disagreement is recorded) of land one dirham and a qafiz of food." (The qafiz is a measure equal to eight makakik.) He said: "Do not place humiliation on your neck." Maymun ibn Mihran narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "It would not please me that I should have all the land in exchange for a jizya of five dirhams, by which I acknowledge humiliation upon myself."

There are seven issues here.

The first concerns the recitation of His words, ﴿Uzayr is the son of God﴾. ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī read "ʿUzayrun" with tanwin (nunation, the final -n sound) on ʿUzayr. On this reading, "ibnan" (a son) is the predicate of a nominal sentence whose subject is ʿUzayr, and ʿUzayr is declined (yanṣarif) whether it is foreign or Arabic in origin. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir read "ʿUzayru ibnu" without tanwin, because two consonants without a vowel between them (ijtimāʿ al-sākinayn) would otherwise meet. An example of this is the reading of whoever reads ﴿Say: He is God, One. God, the Eternal Refuge﴾ [Al-Ikhlas: 1–2]. Abu ʿAli said: "This is common in poetry." Al-Tabari cited in support of this the verse:

"You will find me, by the commander, dutiful,
and with the spear, a skilled thruster, returning to the charge,
when Ghutayf al-Sulami flees."

[A *midʿas* (with s or ṣ) is a man skilled at thrusting with the spear.]

The second issue concerns His words, ﴿And the Jews said﴾. This is a expression in general terms (ʿumūm) whose meaning is specific (khuṣūṣ), since not all Jews said this. It is like His words, ﴿those to whom the people said﴾ [Al ʿImran: 173], when not all the people said it. It is also said that the one who spoke what is reported of the Jews was Sallām ibn Mishkam, Nuʿmān ibn Abi Awfa, Shas ibn Qays and Malik ibn al-Sayf, and that they said it to the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Naqqash said: "No Jew remains who says it; they have died out. If one of them said it, the group is bound by the shame of the saying, because of the prominence of the speaker among them. The sayings of notable people are always famous among the people and are used as evidence. From here it is correct to say that the group said the saying of their notable." And God knows best.

It is reported that the cause of this saying was that the Jews killed the prophets after Moses, peace be upon him. God therefore removed the Torah from them and erased it from their hearts. ʿUzayr then went out wandering the earth, and Gabriel came to him and said: "Where are you going?" He said: "I seek knowledge." So [Gabriel] taught him the whole Torah, and ʿUzayr came to the Children of Israel with the Torah and taught them. It is also said that God preserved the Torah in ʿUzayr's memory as an honour from Him to him, and he told the Children of Israel: "God has preserved the Torah in my memory." So they began to study it from him. The Torah had been buried, which their scholars had buried when the trials, exile and sickness that afflicted them, and what Bukht Nasr did in killing them, befell them. Then the buried Torah was found, and it was found to be identical with what ʿUzayr had been teaching. They went astray at that point and said: "This was not possible for ʿUzayr except that he is the son of God." Al-Tabari related this.

The apparent meaning of the Christians' saying is that the Messiah is the son of God. They meant only filial begetting (bunūwat al-nasl), as the Arabs said about the angels. The saying of al-Dahhak, al-Tabari and others implies the same. This is the most abominable disbelief. Abu al-Maʿali said: "The Christians are unanimous that the Messiah is God and that he is the son of God." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It is said that some of them hold that it is a sonship of tenderness and mercy. This meaning too does not permit that sonship be attributed to him, and it is disbelief."

The third issue: Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "In this is evidence from the words of our Lord, blessed and exalted, that whoever reports the disbelief of others, which it is not permitted for anyone to initiate, bears no blame, for he only speaks of it in order to magnify its enormity and refute it. Had our Lord willed, no one would have spoken it. When He allowed the tongues to utter it, He permitted reporting it in order to denounce it in the heart and on the tongue, and to refute it with proof and argument."

The fourth issue concerns His words, ﴿That is their saying with their mouths﴾. It is said that its meaning is emphasis, as He said: ﴿they write the Book with their own hands﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 79], and ﴿nor any bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [Al-Anʿam: 38], and His words: ﴿And when the Trumpet is blown with one blast﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 13]. Similar examples are numerous. It is also said that the meaning is that it was a bare saying, containing neither explanation nor proof, merely a statement by the mouth, a bare claim without any sound meaning beneath it. For they themselves acknowledge that God, glory be to Him, has taken no consort, so how can they claim that He has a son? It is a lie, a merely verbal saying, unlike the sound sayings that are supported by evidence and established by proof. The scholars of meanings (ahl al-maʿānī) said: "God, glory be to Him, never mentioned a saying linked with mentioning mouths and tongues except that it was a false saying, as in His words: ﴿They say with their mouths what is not in their hearts﴾ [Al ʿImran: 167], and ﴿A grave word it is that comes out of their mouths; they say nothing but a lie﴾ [Al-Kahf: 5], and ﴿They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts﴾ [Al-Fath: 11]."

The fifth issue concerns His words, ﴿they imitate the saying of those who disbelieved before﴾. "Yuḍāhiʾūna" means "they resemble" (yushābihūna). From this is the Arabs' saying: "a woman who is ḍahyaʾ," meaning one who does not menstruate or who has no breasts, as if she resembled men. The scholars differ over "the saying of those who disbelieved" in three views. The first: the saying of the idol-worshippers: "al-Lat, al-ʿUzza and Manat, the third, the other." The second: the saying of the disbelievers: "the angels are the daughters of God." The third: the saying of their forebears, whom they imitated in falsehood and followed in disbelief, as He reported of them in His words: ﴿We found our fathers upon a religion﴾ [Al-Zukhruf: 23].

The sixth issue: The grammarians differed over whether "ḍahyaʾ" is lengthened with a madd (long vowel) or not. Ibn Walladd said: "imraʾa ḍahyaʾ," meaning one who does not menstruate, is hamzated and not lengthened. Others lengthen it, namely Sibawayh, making it on the pattern faʿlāʾ with the lengthening, the hamza in it being an added letter, because they say "nisāʾ ḍuhyun," dropping the hamza. Abu al-Hasan said: "al-Najirami said to me: ḍahyaʾatun, with lengthening and the feminine ending ha. He combined two signs of feminine gender. This he related from Abu ʿAmr al-Shaybani in al-Nawadir," and he recited:

"A ḍahyaʾatun or a barren cow..."

[In the manuscripts it reads *jinād* with nūn, which is an error. *Al-jamād* is a she-camel without milk.]

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "Whoever says that 'yuḍāhiʾūna' is derived from their saying 'imraʾatun ḍahyāʾ' is mistaken, as Abu ʿAli said, because the hamza in *ḍāhaʾa* is original, while in *ḍahyāʾ* it is added, like *ḥamrāʾ*."

The seventh issue concerns His words, ﴿God fight them! How are they deluded?﴾ That is, "May God curse them," meaning the Jews and the Christians, because the one cursed is like the one killed. Ibn Jurayj said: "'Qātalahumu Allah' has the meaning of wonder (taʿajjub)." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Every instance of qatl (killing) in the Qur'an is a curse (laʿn)." From this is the saying of Aban ibn Taghlib:

"God fight her! She blames me, though she knows
that I am the one who ruins myself and sets myself right."

Al-Naqqash related that the original sense of "qātala Allāh" was supplication, but it became so common in their usage that they said it in wonder at both good and evil, without intending supplication. Al-Asmaʿi recited:

"O God fight Layla! How she pleases me,
and I tell the people I do not care for her."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 31:

His saying, exalted is He: (They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah, and the Messiah, son of Mary). Al-Ahbar is the plural of habr, and the habr is one who beautifies speech, arranges it, and perfects it through fine exposition of it. From this comes the expression thawb muhabbar, meaning a garment that has gathered adornment. It has been said concerning the singular of al-ahbar: habr with a kasra on the ha', whereas the exegetes read it with a fatha. The philologists (ahl al-lughah) read it with a kasra. Yunus said: "I have never heard it except with a kasra on the ha'." The evidence for this is that they say midad habr (ink of the scholar), meaning the ink of a learned man; then usage became widespread until they applied habr to ink itself. Al-Farra' said: "The kasra and the fatha are two dialectal forms." Ibn al-Sikkit said: "al-hibr with a kasra means ink, and al-habr with a fatha means the scholar." Al-Ruhban is the plural of rahib, derived from al-rahbah (fear), and it refers to one whom the fear of Allah, exalted is He, has moved to make his intention sincere to Him alone, not to people, to make his time, his work, and his companionship belong to Him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿lords besides Allah﴾. The people of the meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: they made their rabbis and monks like lords, in that they obeyed them in everything. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "Blow," until when He made it fire﴾ [al-Kahf: 96], meaning, like fire. Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said:

"Has anything corrupted religion except kings,
and evil rabbis and their monks?"

Al-A'mash and Sufyan narrated from Habib ibn Abi Thabit, from Abu al-Bakhtari, who said: Hudhayfah was asked about the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: "They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah." Did they worship them? He said: "No, but they made lawful for them what was forbidden, so they deemed it lawful, and they made forbidden for them what was lawful, so they forbade it."

al-Tirmidhi narrated from Adi ibn Hatim, who said: I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while there was a golden cross around my neck. He said: "What is this, O Adi? Cast off this idol from you." And I heard him reciting in Surat Bara'ah: "They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah, and the Messiah, son of Mary." Then he said: "Indeed, they did not worship them, but when they made something lawful for them, they deemed it lawful, and when they made something forbidden for them, they forbade it." He said: "This is a strange hadith, not known except through the narration of Abd al-Salam ibn Harb. And Ghutayf ibn A'yan is not well known in hadith."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the Messiah, son of Mary﴾. The discussion of its derivation has already passed in Al 'Imran. Al-Masih is the sweat that flows from the forehead. Some later scholars expressed this well, saying:

"Rejoice, for you will soon become accustomed to sorrows
when you witness the Gathering and the Balance.
And the masih has flowed from your forehead,
as if it were streams flowing."

And the meaning of its being attributed to Mary, his mother, has already passed in al-Nisa'.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 32:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah﴾, that is, His proof and His evidences of His oneness. He made the proofs like light because of the clarity they contain. It was also said: the meaning is the light of Islam, that is, they wish to extinguish the religion of Allah by denying it.

(بِأَفْواهِهِمْ) [bi-afwāhihim] is the plural of fawh (فَوْه), in its original form, because the original form of fam (فَم, "mouth") is fawh, like ḥawḍ (حَوْض, "pool") and aḥwāḍ (أَحْوَاض, "pools").

(وَيَأْبَى اللَّهُ إِلَّا أَنْ يُتِمَّ نُورَهُ) [wa-ya'bā Allāh illā an yutimma nūrahu] It is said: how did "illā" (إِلَّا, "except") come to be used when there is no negative particle in the sentence, and it is not permitted to say "ḍarabtu illā Zaydan" (I struck except Zayd)? Al-Farra' held that "illā" entered because there is in the sentence a trace of negation (jaḥd). Al-Zajjaj said: negation and affirmation do not have "traces"; the particles of negation are mā, lā, in and laysa, and these have no traces that are pronounced. Had the matter been as he (al-Farra') intended, it would be permitted to say "karihtu illā Zaydan" (I disliked except Zayd). Rather, the answer is that the Arabs omit (the negation) with abā (أَبَى, "refuse"). The implied meaning is: "and Allah refuses everything except that He perfect His light." Ali ibn Sulayman said: this is permitted with abā only because it signifies prevention or refusal, so it resembles negation. Al-Nahhas said: this is good, as the poet said:

وَهَلْ لِي أُمٌّ غَيْرُهَا إِنْ تَرَكْتُهَا ... أَبَى اللَّهُ إِلَّا أن أكون لها ابنما

[Translator's note: the verse is given as transmitted in the source.]

"Allah's words: ﴿He it is who sent His Messenger﴾ means Muhammad ﷺ.

(with guidance) means with the Criterion (al-Furqan).

(and the religion of truth, that He may make it prevail over all religion) means with proof and evidence. He made it prevail over all the sacred laws (shara'i') of religion, so that nothing of them remained hidden from him, according to Ibn 'Abbas and others. It has also been said: "that He may make it prevail" means that He may make the religion of Islam prevail over every religion. Abu Hurayra and al-Dahhak said: this will be at the descent of 'Isa ('alayhi al-salam). al-Suddi said: that will be at the emergence of the Mahdi (the guided one); no one will remain except that he enters Islam or pays the jizya (poll tax). It has been said that the Mahdi is 'Isa alone, but this is not correct, because the sound reports have been transmitted in a mass-transmitted (mutawatir) manner that the Mahdi is from the 'itrah (family) of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so it is not permissible to interpret it as 'Isa. The hadith which has been narrated that "there is no Mahdi except 'Isa" is not sound. al-Bayhaqi said in Kitab al-Ba'th wa al-Nushur: because its narrator Muhammad ibn Khalid al-Jundi is unknown (majhul), he narrates from Aban ibn Abi 'Ayyash, who is abandoned (matruk), from al-Hasan, from the Prophet ﷺ, and it is munqati' (disconnected in its chain). The hadiths before it, which explicitly state the emergence of the Mahdi, and in which it is clarified that the Mahdi is from the 'itrah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, are sounder in their chain. I (al-Qurtubi) say: we have mentioned this, expanded its explanation, in our book (Kitab al-Tadhkira), and we have mentioned the reports about the Mahdi comprehensively, and all praise is due to Allah. It has also been said: He meant "that He may make it prevail over all religion" in the Arabian Peninsula (Jazirat al-'Arab), and it has been done."

**Issue 1 of the commentary on verse 34 (part 1 of 2)**

There are eleven issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** Allah's words, "they devour the wealth of people in falsehood" (*li-ya'kulūna amwāla al-nās bi-l-bāṭil*). The lām (the emphatic lām) has entered upon *yaf'alu* (the present tense form), and it does not enter upon *fa'ala* (the past tense form), because *yaf'alu* resembles nouns. *Al-aḥbār* means the scholars of the Jews. *Al-ruhbān* means the Christians who strive hard in worship.

Regarding "in falsehood," it has been said that they used to take from the wealth of their followers taxes and obligatory payments under the name of churches, places of worship, and other things, leading them to believe that spending on these was part of the religious law and a means of drawing near to Allah the Exalted. Meanwhile, they were hoarding that wealth for themselves, as in the account mentioned by Salman al-Farisi about the monk who dug up his hoard, which Ibn Ishaq related in *al-Sīra*. It has also been said that they took from their crops and wealth taxes under the name of protecting the religion and upholding the law. It has also been said that they took bribes in judicial rulings, as many rulers and judges do today. Allah's words "in falsehood" encompass all of this.

"And they bar from the way of Allah" means they prevent the people of their religion from entering the religion of Islam and following Muhammad (ﷺ).

**The second issue:** Allah's words, "And those who hoard gold and silver" (﴿وَالَّذِينَ يَكْنِزُونَ الذَّهَبَ وَالْفِضَّةَ﴾). The root meaning of *al-kanz* in the language is gathering and accumulating, and this is not restricted to gold and silver. Do you not see the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Shall I inform you of the best thing a man can hoard? A righteous wife"? That is, he gathers her to himself and keeps her. A poet said:

*"And she did not provision herself from all the hoard / except threadbare strands and a worn-out garment."*

Another said:

*"May my fortune not be good if I feed their hungry / with the crumbs of al-Hattī while I have wheat hoarded."*

*Qirf al-Ḥattī* is the porridge of *al-muqill* (the fruit of the doum palm, which ripens and is eaten). He means that he came to a people and their hospitality to him was a porridge of *al-muqill*, which is *al-ḥattī*. When they hosted him with it, he said: "May my fortune not be good..." to the end of the verse.

Gold and silver were singled out for mention because they are things that are not easily noticed, unlike other wealth. Al-Ṭabarī said: *al-kanz* is everything gathered, one part upon another, whether in the belly of the earth or on its surface. Gold is called *dhahab* because it goes away (*yadhhabu*), and silver is called *fiḍḍa* because it breaks apart and scatters (*tanfaḍḍu*). From this is Allah's words: ﴿They dispersed to it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11], and ﴿they would have dispersed from around you﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 159]. This meaning has already passed in Āl ʿImrān.

**The third issue:** The Companions differed over the intended meaning of this verse. Mu'awiyah held that it refers to the People of the Book, and al-Asamm also held this, because Allah's words "And those who hoard" come after His words "Indeed, many of the scholars and the monks devour the wealth of people in falsehood." Abu Dharr and others said that it refers to the People of the Book and other Muslims. This is the correct view, because if He had intended the People of the Book alone, He would have said "and they hoard" without "those who." Since He said "And those who," He has begun a new meaning, indicating that He has joined one sentence to another. So "those who hoard" is a new statement and is in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence. Al-Suddi said: it means the people of the qiblah (Muslims). These are three opinions.

According to the view of the Companions, there is evidence that disbelievers are addressed with the branches of the Sharia. Al-Bukhari related from Zayd ibn Wahb, who said: I passed by al-Rabadhah (a place near Madinah), and there I found Abu Dharr. I said to him: What brought you to this place of yours? He said: I was in Syria and I disagreed with Mu'awiyah over "those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of Allah." Mu'awiyah said: It was revealed concerning the People of the Book. I said: It was revealed concerning us and them. This dispute was between me and him. He wrote to Uthman complaining about me, and Uthman wrote to me: Come to Madinah. I came, and the people crowded around me as if they had never seen me before. I mentioned that to Uthman, and he said: If you wish, you may withdraw and be nearby. That is what led me to this place. Even if they appointed an Abyssinian over me, I would listen and obey.

**The fourth issue:** Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: this verse includes the zakah on cash (*zakāt al-ʿayn*), which is obligatory under four conditions: freedom, Islam, the passing of a full lunar year (*ḥawl*), and a minimum threshold (*niṣāb*) free of debt. The *niṣāb* is two hundred dirhams or twenty dinars, or the threshold of one of them is completed by the other, and one pays a quarter of a tenth from this and a quarter of a tenth from that.

As for why freedom is a condition, it is because the slave lacks full ownership. As for why Islam is a condition, it is because zakah is a purification, and a disbeliever does not receive purification. Also, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 43], so zakah is addressed to whoever is addressed with prayer.

As for why the passing of a year is a condition, it is because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no zakah on property until a year passes over it." As for why the threshold is a condition, it is because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no zakah on less than two hundred dirhams, and there is no zakah on less than twenty dinars."

The completeness of the threshold is not taken into account at the beginning of the year, but is taken into account at the end of the year, because they agree that profit has the ruling of the principal. This is shown by the fact that whoever has two hundred dirhams and trades with them and by the end of the year they have become a thousand, he pays zakah on the thousand and does not begin a new year for the profit. Since this is so, the ruling on profit does not differ whether it arose from a threshold or less than it.

Likewise, they agreed that if someone has forty sheep, and they give birth at the start of the year, and then the mothers die except one of them, and the young ones complete the threshold, zakah is paid on them.

**The fifth issue:** The scholars differed over whether property on which zakah has been paid is called a hoard. One group said yes. It was related by Abu al-Duha from Ja'dah ibn Hubayrah, from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: four thousand (dirhams) and less is spending money, and what exceeds it is a hoard, even if its zakah is paid. But this is not authentic. Another group said: whatever zakah has been paid from it, or on its behalf from something else, is not a hoard. Ibn Umar said: whatever its zakah is paid is not a hoard, even if it is under seven earths, and whatever its zakah is not paid is a hoard, even if it is above the earth. Similar to this is related from Jabir, and this is the correct view.

Al-Bukhari related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever Allah gives wealth but does not pay its zakah, on the Day of Resurrection it will be made into a bald poisonous serpent with two black spots, which will encircle him on the Day of Resurrection, then it will seize him by his two jaws, that is, his cheeks, and then say: I am your wealth, I am your hoard." Then he recited: ﴿And let not those who withhold...﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 180], to the end of the verse.

Also in the same collection, from Abu Dharr, who said: I came to him, that is, the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, or by He other than whom there is no god, or as he swore: there is no man who has camels, cattle, or sheep and does not pay their due, except that they will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, greater and fatter than they were, trampling him with their hooves and goring him with their horns. Whenever the last of them passes, the first of them will be returned to him, until judgment is made among the people."

The implication of these two hadiths supports what we have mentioned. Ibn Umar explained this same meaning in *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī*: a Bedouin said to him: Inform me about Allah's words: "And those who hoard gold and silver." Ibn Umar said: Whoever hoards it and does not pay its zakah, woe to him. This was before zakah was revealed. When it was revealed, Allah made it a purification for wealth.

It has also been said: the hoard is what exceeds one's need. This was related from Abu Dharr, and it is among what is reported of his view, and it is among his strict positions, which he held alone, may Allah be pleased with him.

I say: What was related from Abu Dharr on this may be understood as follows: the verse was revealed at a time of great need and weakness among the Emigrants, and the hand of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was too short to meet their needs, and there was not enough in the public treasury to suffice them, and famines were striking them. So they were forbidden to withhold any wealth except to the extent of need. It is not permitted to store gold and silver in such a time.

When Allah granted victory to the Muslims and expanded their provision, the Prophet (ﷺ) made obligatory five dirhams on two hundred dirhams, and half a dinar on twenty dinars, and he did not make obligatory the whole amount, and he took into consideration the period of growth. This was his clarification (ﷺ).

It has also been said: the hoard is what the obligatory rights arising from it have not been paid, such as freeing a captive, feeding the hungry, and other things. It has also been said: linguistically, the hoard is what is gathered of the two precious metals and other wealth analogous to them by way of analogy. It has also been said: what is gathered of the two metals is what is not jewelry, because jewelry is permitted to be made and has no obligation attached to it. The correct view is what we began by mentioning, namely that all of this is called a hoard both linguistically and in the Sharia. And Allah knows best.

**The sixth issue:** The scholars differed over zakah on jewelry. Malik and his companions, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, and Abu Ubayd held that there is no zakah on it. This is also the view of al-Shafi'i in Iraq, but after that, in Egypt, he paused on it and said: I seek Allah's guidance regarding it. Al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah and his companions, and al-Awza'i said: in all of that there is zakah.

The first group argued: the intention of growth obligates zakah on merchandise, and merchandise is not a place where zakah is obligated, so likewise, cutting off growth in gold and silver by making them into jewelry for personal use (*qinya*) drops the zakah. [Al-qinya: what a person keeps for himself, not for trade.]

Abu Hanifah argued from the general wording of the texts regarding obligating zakah on the two precious metals, and he did not distinguish between jewelry and other forms. Al-Layth ibn Sa'd made a distinction: he obligated zakah on what was made into jewelry in order to evade zakah, and he dropped it on what was worn and lent out. In the school of law there is a detailed treatment of jewelry, which is explained in the books of jurisprudence.

**The seventh issue:** Abu Dawud related from Ibn Abbas, who said: When this verse was revealed, "And those who hoard gold and silver," it was difficult for the Muslims. Umar said: I will relieve you of this. He went and said: O Prophet of Allah, this verse has been difficult for your Companions. He said: "Indeed Allah did not impose zakah except to purify what remains of your wealth, and He imposed inheritance..." and he mentioned a word [what is between the lines is present in the manuscripts of the original, but not in Sunan Abi Dawud; what is in al-Durr al-Manthur of al-Suyuti is: "...and He imposed inheritance from wealth that remains after you"]: "so that it may be for those after you." He said: Umar then exclaimed "Allahu akbar." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Shall I inform you of the best thing a man can hoard? A righteous wife: when he looks at her, she pleases him; when he commands her, she obeys him; and when he is absent from her, she guards him." And he related...

Al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from Thawban that the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah, glorified is He, has censured gold and silver. So if we knew which property is best, we would acquire it." Umar said: "I will ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for you." He asked him, and he said: "A tongue that remembers (Allah), a heart that gives thanks, and a wife who helps the man in his religion." He said: "This is a good (hasan) hadith."

The eighth issue: the words of the Exalted, "and do not spend it in the way of Allah" (wa la yunfiquna-ha fi sabil Allah). He did not say "yunfiquna-huma" (spend them both). On this there are six answers.

The first: Ibn al-Anbari said: He intended the more prevalent and general, which is silver. A similar usage is His saying: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer, and indeed it is difficult﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45], where the pronoun returns to prayer because it is more general. Similar is "But when they see a trade or a diversion, they rush to it" [al-Jumu'ah: 11], where the pronoun ("it," ilayha) returns to trade because it is the more important, and diversion is left out. Many of the exegetes said this. Some of them rejected it and said: "It does not resemble it, because 'aw' (or) has separated trade from diversion, so it is good for the pronoun to return to one of them."

The second: the reverse, namely that "yunfiquna-ha" refers to gold, and the second item is coordinated with it. The Arabs make gold feminine; they say: "hiya al-dhahab al-hamra'" (it is the red gold). It may also be masculine, but the feminine is more common.

The third: that the pronoun refers to the treasures (al-kunuz).

The fourth: that it refers to the hoarded wealth (al-amwal al-maknuzah).

The fifth: that it refers to zakat, the implied meaning being: "and they do not spend the zakat of the hoarded wealth."

The sixth: the sufficiency of a single pronoun in place of the pronoun for the other when the meaning is understood, and this is common in Arabic speech. Sibawayh recited:
"We are content with what we have, and you are content with what you have, though opinions differ."
He did not say "radiyun" (they are content). Another poet said:
"He accused me of a matter from which I and my father were both innocent, and he accused me because of the well (al-tawiyy)."
He did not say "bari'ayn" (both innocent).

[The poet is Ibn Ahmar, whose name is Amr. He described a man with whom he had a quarrel over a well, the Tawiyy. He mentioned that the man had accused him of something he disliked, and accused his father of the same, while both were innocent of it, because of the quarrel between them.
(From Sharh al-Shawahid.)]

Similar is the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit, may Allah be pleased with him: "Indeed the vigor of youth and hair that is black, if it is not disobeyed, is madness." He did not say "yu'asaya" (both disobeyed).

The ninth issue: If it is said: whoever neither hoards nor spends in the way of Allah, but spends on sins, is his ruling regarding the threat the same as that of one who hoards and does not spend in the way of Allah? It is said to him: That is more severe, for whoever squanders his wealth on sins disobeys in two ways: by spending and by consuming, such as buying wine and drinking it. Indeed, there are further ways if the sin extends to others, such as one who helps in the oppression of a Muslim by killing him or taking his property, and so on. The hoarder disobeys in two ways, namely withholding zakat and keeping the wealth locked away, and nothing more. But the keeping of wealth may not be counted (as a sin in itself). And Allah knows best.

The tenth issue: His saying, Exalted is He, "so give them the good news of a painful punishment" (fa-bashshirhum bi-'adhabin alim). Its meaning has already been explained. The Prophet ﷺ explained this punishment by his saying: "Give the hoarders the good news of a brand on their backs; it comes out through their sides, and a brand on their foreheads from behind their necks; it comes out from their foreheads." The hadith... Muslim narrated it. Abu Dharr related in one narration: "Give the hoarders the good news of heated stones heated in the fire of Hell, which are placed on the nipple of one of them until they come out from the top of his shoulder blades, and are placed on the top of his shoulder blades until they come out from the nipple of his chest, and he shakes." The hadith... Our scholars said: the emergence of the heated stone from the nipple of his chest to the top of his shoulder blade is to torment his heart and inner being, when it was filled with joy at the abundance of wealth and happiness in this world, so he is punished in the Hereafter with grief and torment.

The eleventh issue: Our scholars said: The apparent meaning of the verse attaches the threat to whoever hoards and does not spend in the way of Allah, and neglects what is obligatory and other things. However, the attribute of hoarding should not be regarded as a condition, for whoever does not hoard but withholds spending in the way of Allah must be in the same position. Yet what is hidden beneath the earth is what is customarily withheld from spending on obligations, and therefore the threat is specifically attached to it. And Allah knows best.

**First issue: the grammar of "yawma"**

It is a circumstantial adverb (ẓarf), and the implied construction is: "they will be punished on the day it is heated." It cannot be taken as referring to "so give them the good news on the day it is heated," because good tidings are not given at that time.

One says *aḥmaytu al-ḥadīdata fī al-nār* (I heated the iron in the fire), meaning *awqadtu ʿalayhā* (I kindled over it). One also says *aḥmaytuhu*, but not *aḥmaytu ʿalayhi*. Here He says ʿalayhā because He made *ʿalā* belong to the sense of *iḥmāʾ* (heating), and *iḥmāʾ* means *īqād* (kindling): it is kindled over it, and so they are branded (*fa-tuksā*).

*Al-kayy* (branding) is the pressing of hot iron or fire against a limb until the skin burns. *Al-jibāh* is the plural of *al-jabhah*, which is the flat area between the eyebrow and the hairline (*al-nāṣiyah*). One says *jabahtu fulānan bi-kadhā*, meaning I confronted him with it and struck his forehead. *Al-junūb* is the plural of *al-janb* (side).

Branding on the face is more famous and more shameful, while branding on the side and the back is more painful and more agonising. For this reason He specified these parts from among all the other limbs.

The scholars of Sufism (*ʿulamāʾ al-ṣūfiyyah*) said: when they sought wealth and standing, God disfigured their faces; when they turned their sides away (*ṭawaw kashḥan*, meaning they turned away) from the poor when they sat with them, their sides were branded; and when they leaned their backs upon their wealth, trusting in it and relying on it, their backs were branded.

The scholars of the outward (*ʿulamāʾ al-ẓāhir*) said: He specified these limbs because the wealthy man, when he sees the poor man, knits and gathers what is between his eyes (*zawā mā bayna ʿaynayhi*, meaning he contracts it), and tightens his face. As the poet said (the speaker is al-Aʿshā, as in his *Dīwān*):

*Yazīdu yaghuḍḍu al-ṭarfa ʿannī (in another version: dūnī) ka-annamā*
*Zawā bayna ʿaynayhi ʿalayya al-maḥājimu*

*Fa-lā yanbasiṭu min bayna ʿaynayka mā inzawā*
*Wa-lā talqanī illā wa-anfuka rāghimu*

Yazid lowers his gaze from me as though the cuppings (al-maḥājim) had drawn together between his eyes against me.

So what is drawn together between your eyes will not spread out, and he will not meet me except with his nose in the dust.

When he asks him, he turns his side away; and when he increases the request and presses him, he turns his back to him. Thus God linked the punishment to the state of the disobedience.

**The second issue**

The reports differ about the manner of this branding. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from the ḥadīth of Abū Dharr, is what we mentioned about the mention of the *raḍf* (heated stones). In the same source, from the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah, he said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "There is no owner of gold or silver who does not pay its due, except that on the Day of Resurrection plates of fire will be fashioned for him, and they will be heated in the fire of Hell, and his side, his forehead and his back will be branded with them. Whenever they cool, they will be returned to him, on a day whose length is fifty thousand years, until judgement is passed among the servants, and he sees his path, either to Paradise or to the Fire." The ḥadīth continues.

In al-Bukhārī: that his treasure will be presented to him as a bald venomous snake (*shujāʿan aqraʿa*).

It has been mentioned earlier, in a source other than Ṣaḥīḥ, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, that he said: "Whoever has wealth and does not pay its zakat, it will be made a collar for him on the Day of Resurrection, a bald venomous snake that pecks at his head."

I say: This may occur in several situations: in one, the wealth is depicted as a serpent; in another, as plates; and in another, as heated stones. The attributes change, while the substance is one: the snake is a body, and the wealth is a body. This depiction is real, unlike his saying: "Death will be brought as a horned ram, white-black" (*yuʾtā bi-l-mawti ka-annahu kabshun amlaḥu*), for that is another manner, and God, glorified and exalted, may do whatever He wills.

He specified the *shujāʿ* for mention because it is the second enemy of creation. The *shujāʿ* among snakes is the male snake that leaps at the horseman and the pedestrian, rises on its tail, sometimes reaching the rider, and is found in the open deserts. It was also said: it is the *thuʿbān* (large serpent). Al-Liḥyānī said: a snake is called *shujāʿ*, its plural is *thalāthat ashjiʿah*, then *shujʿān*.

The *aqraʿ* among snakes is the one whose head has lost its hair and turned white from its venom. In the Muwaṭṭaʾ: "It has two *zabībatān*," that is, two swollen dots on its cheeks like foam. This occurs on a human's cheeks when he becomes angry and talks excessively. Umm Ghaylān bint Jarīr said: "Often I recited poetry to my father until my cheeks foamed (*tazabbaba shidqāya*)."

It is struck as a parable for the venomous *shujāʿ* whose poison is abundant, so the wealth is depicted as this animal, meeting its owner angry. Ibn Durayd said: "Two black dots above its eyes." In one narration: "A *shujāʿ* was depicted for him, pursuing him and forcing him, so he gives it his hand, and it chews it as a stallion chews."

Ibn Masʿūd said: "By God, God does not punish anyone with a treasure such that a dirham touches a dirham or a dinar touches a dinar, but He widens his skin so that every dirham and dinar is placed on its own separate spot." This applies only to the disbeliever, as stated in the ḥadīth, not to the believer. And God knows best.

**The third issue**

Al-Ṭabarī reported through an isnād to Abū Umāmah al-Bāhilī, who said: A man from the people of the *Ṣuffah* died, and a dinar was found in his cloak. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "A brand (*kayyah*)." Then another died, and two dinars were found with him. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Two brands (*kayyatān*)."

This is either because the two of them lived on charity while having gold (*tibr*) with them, or because this was in the early period of Islam, after which the Sharīʿah established the regulation of wealth and the payment of its due. Had keeping wealth been forbidden, its obligation would have been that all of it be given away, and there is no one in the Ummah who is bound by this. Consider the condition of the Companions and their wealth, may God be pleased with them.

As for what is reported from Abū Dharr, it is his own opinion (*madhhab*), may God be pleased with him. Mūsā ibn ʿUbaydah narrated from ʿImrān ibn Abī Anas, from Mālik ibn Aws ibn al-Ḥadathān, from Abū Dharr, from the Messenger of God ﷺ, who said: "Whoever gathers a dinar, or a dirham, or *tibr*, or silver, and does not set it aside for a debt, nor spends it in the way of God, it is a treasure with which he will be branded on the Day of Resurrection."

I say: This is the view that befits Abū Dharr, may God be pleased with him, to hold: that what exceeds one's need is not a treasure if it is prepared for the way of God.

Abū Umāmah said: "Whoever leaves behind white (silver) or yellow (gold), he will be branded with it, whether forgiven or not forgiven. Indeed, the ornament of the sword is among that."

Thawbān narrated that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "No man dies while having red or white (gold or silver) except that God makes for him, for every *qīrāṭ*, a plate with which he is branded from his *farq* (the parting of his hair) to his foot, and after that he is either forgiven or punished."

I say: This is to be understood as applying to wealth whose zakat has not been paid, based on what we mentioned about the verse before this. So the meaning is: "and he has red or white (wealth) for which he did not pay its zakat." Likewise what is narrated from Abū Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him: "Whoever leaves ten thousand, it will be made into plates with which its owner will be punished on the Day of Resurrection," that is, if he does not pay its zakat, so that the ḥadīths do not contradict one another. And God knows best.

**The fourth issue**

God, exalted, says: ﴿This is what you hoarded for yourselves﴾. That is: it will be said to them, "This is what you hoarded," and the verb is omitted.

(﴿So taste what you used to hoard﴾), that is, the punishment of what you used to hoard.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 36:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the register of Allah from the day He created the heavens and the earth; of them, four are sacred. That is the correct religion. So do not wrong yourselves therein.﴾ In it there are eight issues. [[Note that the manuscripts give seven issues, which is an error.]]

The first: His saying, ﴿Indeed, the number of months﴾. "Months" is the plural of "shahr" (month). If a man says to his brother, "I will not speak to you for months," and he swears to this, then some scholars said he does not speak to him for a year. It was also said: he never speaks to him. Ibn al-Arabi said: I hold that, if he had no intention, this requires three months, because it is the least plural that the form fu'ul, in the plural of fa'l, implies. The meaning of "with Allah" is: in the judgment of Allah and in what He recorded in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

"Twelve months" (ithna 'ashara shahran): "ithna 'ashara shahran" is parsed (i'rab) on its own, without its counterparts, because in it there is the letter of i'rab and its indicator. The majority read "'ashara" with a fatha on the ayn and the shin. Abu Ja'far read "'ashra" with a sukun on the shin.

"In the register of Allah" means the Preserved Tablet. He repeated it after saying "with Allah," because many things are described as being "with Allah," but it is not said that they are written in the register of Allah, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, with Allah is the knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34]. [[See vol. 14, p. 82.]]

The second: His saying, ﴿from the day He created the heavens and the earth﴾. He said "from the day He created the heavens and the earth" to clarify that His decree and His measure existed before that, and that He, glory be to Him, established these months and named them with their names in the order He arranged them on the day He created the heavens and the earth, and sent that down to His prophets in their revealed books. This is the meaning of His saying: "Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months." Its ruling remains as it was, and the alteration of the idolaters in their names, and their advancing of the postponed in name, did not remove it from its arrangement. The purpose of this is to follow the command of Allah regarding them and to reject what the people of pre-Islamic ignorance (jahiliyyah) did of postponing and advancing the names of the months, and attaching rulings to the names they arranged. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said in his sermon at the Farewell Pilgrimage: "O people, indeed time has returned to its form on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth," as will be explained. And what the people of pre-Islamic ignorance did, making the sacred month Safar and making Safar sacred, does not change what Allah described. The factor operating on "day" is the verbal noun which is "in the register of Allah," and it does not mean a single one of the books, because concrete entities do not act upon adverbs of time. The implied meaning is: in what Allah wrote on the day He created the heavens and the earth. "With" (inda) is connected to the verbal noun which is "the number," and it is the operating factor in it. "In" in His saying "in the register of Allah" is connected to an omitted element, which is a qualifier of "twelve." The implied meaning is: twelve months counted or written in the register of Allah. It is not permissible for it to be connected to "number," because of the separation it would cause between the complement and the relative with the predicate of "inna." 

The third: This verse indicates that the obligation of attaching rulings, of acts of worship and others, is only by the months and years known to the Arabs, not the months reckoned by the non-Arabs, the Romans, and the Copts, even if they do not exceed twelve months, because they differ in their number: some of them exceed thirty days and some fall short, whereas the months of the Arabs do not exceed thirty, although some of them fall short. What falls short is not specifically one month; rather, their difference in shortness and fullness follows the variation in the moon's course through the zodiac signs.

The fourth: His saying, ﴿of them, four are sacred﴾. The sacred months mentioned in this verse are Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, al-Muharram, and Rajab, which lies between Jumada al-Akhirah and Sha'ban. This is Rajab of Mudar, and it was called Rajab of Mudar because the Rabi'ah ibn Nizar used to make Ramadan sacred and call it Rajab, while Mudar made Rajab itself sacred. Therefore the Prophet ﷺ said concerning it: "The one that lies between Jumada and Sha'ban," and by this clarification he removed the disorder that occurred in its name. The Arabs also called it "Munsil al-Asinnah" [[Munsil al-asinnah: the removal of the points from their places. When Rajab came, they would remove the points of spears and the blades of arrows, nullifying fighting in it and cutting off the causes of strife because of its sanctity.]]. Al-Bukhari narrated from Abu Raja' al-Utaridi, whose name is Imran ibn Milhan, and it was said Imran ibn Taym, who said: "We used to worship stones. When we found a stone better than it, we would throw away that one and take the other. If we did not find a stone, we gathered a heap of dirt, then brought a sheep and milked over it, then circumambulated it. When the month of Rajab came, we said, 'Munsil al-Asinnah,' and we did not leave a spear with iron in it or an arrow with iron in it without removing it and throwing it away."

The fifth: His saying, ﴿That is the correct religion﴾, i.e., the correct reckoning and the complete count. Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn Abbas: "That is the religion" means that is the decree. Muqatil said: the truth. Ibn Atiyyah said: The most correct in my view is that "religion" here is in its best-known sense, i.e., that is the law and the obedience. "The correct" means the upright, the straight, from qama, yaqumu, in the pattern of sayyid from sada, yasudu. Its origin is qayyum.

The sixth: His saying, ﴿So do not wrong yourselves therein﴾. According to the view of Ibn Abbas, it refers to all the months. According to the view of some, it refers specifically to the sacred months, because it is closer to them and they have a distinction in magnifying wrongdoing, due to His saying: ﴿So there shall be no obscenity, no wickedness, and no quarrelling during the pilgrimage﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197] [[See vol. 2, p. 404 onward.]], not that wrongdoing is permissible in other than these days, as we will explain. Then it was said: concerning "wronging," there are two views. One: do not wrong yourselves therein by fighting, then this was abrogated by the permission of fighting in all the months. This was said by Qatadah, Ata al-Khurasani, al-Zuhri, and Sufyan al-Thawri. Ibn Jurayj said: Ata ibn Abi Rabah swore by Allah that it is not lawful for people to fight in the sanctuary or in the sacred months unless they are fought in them, and it was not abrogated. The correct view is the first, because the Prophet ﷺ fought the Hawazin at Hunayn and the Thaqif at al-Ta'if, and besieged them in Shawwal and part of Dhu al-Qa'dah. This meaning has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. [[See vol. 3, p. 43.]] The second: do not wrong yourselves therein by committing sins, because when Allah magnifies something from one aspect, it has one sanctity, and when He magnifies it from two aspects or more, its sanctity becomes multiple, so the punishment is doubled for an evil deed just as the reward is doubled for a righteous deed. For whoever obeys Allah in the sacred month in the sacred city, his reward is not like the reward of one who obeys Him in a non-sacred month in the sacred city. And whoever obeys Him in a non-sacred month in the sacred city, his reward is not like the reward of one who obeys Him in a non-sacred month in a non-sacred city. Allah, exalted is He, has indicated this by His saying: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear immorality, the punishment will be doubled for her, twice over﴾ [al-Ahzab: 30]. [[See vol. 14, p. 173 onward.]]

The seventh: Scholars have differed, on the basis of this meaning, regarding one who kills by mistake in a sacred month, whether the blood money (diyah) is made more severe for him or not. Al-Awza'i said: killing in a sacred month, the blood money is made more severe in it, as we have been told, and in the sanctuary it is made a diyah and a third. And it is increased in quasi-intentional killing in the number of camels by age. Al-Shafi'i said: the blood money is made more severe for a life and for injuries in the sacred month, in the sacred city, and for kin. It was narrated from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Salim ibn Abd Allah, Ibn Shihab, and Aban ibn Uthman: whoever is killed in the sacred month or in the sanctuary, a third of his blood money is added to it. This is also narrated from Uthman ibn Affan. Malik, Abu Hanifah and their companions, and Ibn Abi Layla said: killing in the non-sacred area and in the sanctuary is equal, and in the sacred month and other than it is equal, and this is the view of a group of the Successors. This is the correct view, because the Prophet ﷺ established the blood money and did not mention in it the sanctuary or the sacred month. They agreed that the expiation (kaffarah) for one who kills by mistake is the same in the sacred month and other than it. So by analogy the blood money should be the same. And Allah knows best.

The eighth: Allah, exalted is He, singled out the four sacred months by mention and forbade wronging in them, honoring them, although it is forbidden at all times, as He said: ﴿So there shall be no obscenity, no wickedness, and no quarrelling during the pilgrimage﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197]. On this view most of the exegetes say: do not wrong yourselves in the four months. Hammad ibn Salamah narrated from Ali ibn Zayd from Yusuf ibn Mihran from Ibn Abbas that he said: "So do not wrong yourselves therein" refers to the twelve. Qays ibn Muslim narrated from al-Hasan from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah that he said: "therein" refers to all of them. If it is said on the first view: why did He say "therein" and not "therein" (feminine singular)? That is because the Arabs say for what is between three and ten: hunna and haula'; when they exceed ten, they say: hiya and hadhihi, intending to make known the naming of the few from the many. It was narrated from al-Kisa'i that he said: I am amazed at this practice of the Arabs. Similarly they say, for fewer than ten nights: khalawna, and for more: khalat. It should not be said: how did He make some times more sacred than others? We say: the Creator, exalted is He, may do what He wills, and single out whatever He wills with excellence; His acts have no cause, and no restriction is upon Him. Rather, He does what He wills by His wisdom, and sometimes the wisdom becomes apparent and sometimes it is hidden.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And fight against the polytheists all together﴾. In it there is one issue. His saying, ﴿fight﴾, is a command to fight. "Kaffah" means all together, and it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial, i.e., surrounding them and gathered. Al-Zajjaj said: similar to this among verbal nouns are "afahu Allah 'afiyah" and "'aqabahu 'aqibah." It is not made dual or plural, and likewise "'ammah" and "khassah." Some scholars said: the obligation of this verse was originally upon each individual, then it was abrogated and made a collective obligation (fard kifayah). Ibn Atiyyah said: This that he said is not known at all from the law of the Prophet ﷺ that he obligated the whole community to go forth. Rather, the meaning of this verse is urging the fight against them, forming alliances against them, and uniting the word. Then he restricted it with His saying: "as they fight you all together," so in proportion to their fighting and their gathering against us, our gathering against them becomes obligatory. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 37:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿Indeed, the postponement (al-nasi') is an increase in disbelief﴾. Most of the imams read it this way. Al-Nahhas said: "To our knowledge, no one transmitted from Nafi' the reading 'innamā al-nasī'' without a hamza except Warsh alone." It is derived from nasa'ahu and an'asahu, meaning to postpone it. Al-Kisa'i related both forms. Al-Jawhari said: "Al-nasi' is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, from your saying: nasa'tu al-shay' fa-huwa mansu' when you postpone it. Then mansu' is changed to nasi', as maqtul is changed to qatil. A man is nasi' and people are nasa'a, like fasiq and fasaqa." Al-Tabari said: "Al-nasi' with the hamza means increase; it is said: nasa'a yansa'u when he increased." He said: "Without the hamza it can only mean forgetting, as the Exalted said: ﴿They forgot Allah, so He forgot them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67][[See p. 199 of this part.]], and he rejected Nafi''s reading and argued that it takes a prepositional complement, one says: nasa'a Allah fi ajalika just as one says zada Allah fi ajalika. From this is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: (Whoever wishes that his provision be expanded for him and that his remaining life (ath̲ar) be extended for him, let him maintain his kinship ties)[[al-Athar: the term (ajal), so called because it follows the lifespan; its origin is from the trace of one's walking on the earth, for when a person dies no movement remains for him, so no trace of his steps remains on the earth. (From Sharh al-Qastallani.)]]." Al-Azhari said: "Ansa'tu al-shay' in'sa'an and nasi'an: a noun placed in the position of the true verbal noun." They used to forbid fighting in al-Muharram; when they needed that, they made Safar sacred in its place and fought in al-Muharram. The reason for this is that the Arabs were people of wars and raids, and it was hard for them to remain three consecutive months without raiding in them. They said: "If three months in a row pass for us without our gaining anything, we will surely perish." So whenever they returned from Mina, a man from Banu Kinanah, then from Banu Fuqaym, called al-Qalammas, would stand up and say: "I am the one whose decision is never rejected." They would say: "Postpone for us a month," meaning: delay the sanctity of al-Muharram for us and place it in Safar, so that al-Muharram becomes permissible for them. They continued this month after month until the prohibition had circled through the whole year. Then Islam came, and al-Muharram had returned to its place that Allah had set for it. This is the meaning of his saying, peace be upon him: (Indeed, time has returned to its form on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth).

Mujahid said: "The polytheists used to perform Hajj every month for two years. They performed Hajj in Dhu al-Hijjah for two years, then in al-Muharram for two years, then in Safar for two years, and likewise for all the months, until the Hajj of Abu Bakr, which he performed before the Farewell Pilgrimage, coincided with Dhu al-Qa'dah of the ninth year. Then the Prophet ﷺ performed Hajj in the following year, the Farewell Pilgrimage, and it coincided with Dhu al-Hijjah. That is the meaning of his saying in his sermon: (Indeed, time has returned...)," the hadith. He meant by this that the months of Hajj had returned to their places, and Hajj returned to Dhu al-Hijjah, and the postponement was nullified.

A third view: Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah said: "The polytheists used to reckon the year as twelve months and fifteen days, so Hajj would fall in Ramadan and in Dhu al-Qa'dah, and in every month of the year by the rotation of the month through the addition of the fifteen days. Abu Bakr performed Hajj in the ninth year in Dhu al-Qa'dah by this rotation, and the Prophet ﷺ did not perform Hajj. When the following year came, Hajj coincided with Dhu al-Hijjah in its tenth days, and this coincided with the crescents. This view is more consistent with the Prophet's saying ﷺ: (Indeed, time has returned), meaning the time of Hajj returned to its original period which Allah appointed on the day He created the heavens and the earth, by the original legislation which His knowledge had preceded and by which His judgment was executed." Then he said: "The year is twelve months." By this he negates the increase they had added to the year, namely the fifteen days, through their arbitrary decision; so the original time was fixed and the jahili arbitrariness was nullified.

Al-Imam al-Mazari related from al-Khwarazmi that he said: "The first thing Allah created was the sun, which He set running in the sign of Aries (al-Hamal), and the time to which the Prophet ﷺ pointed coincided with the sun's entry into the sign of Aries." This requires a fixed revelation, for it cannot be reached except by transmission from the prophets, and there is no sound transmission from them on this; whoever claims it, let him provide its chain. Moreover, reason permits the opposite of what he said: that Allah created the sun before the zodiacal signs, and it is possible that He created all of that at once. Then the scholars of astronomical calculation tested this and found the sun in the sign of Pisces at the time of his saying, peace be upon him: (Indeed, time has returned), and between it and Aries there were twenty degrees. Some of them said ten degrees. And Allah knows best.

The people of interpretation differed about who first practiced the postponement. Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: they were the Banu Malik ibn Kinanah, and they were three. Juwaybir [[In the manuscripts of the original: (Jarir), which is a distortion.]] related from al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas that the first to do this was Amr ibn Luhayy ibn Qam'ah ibn Khindif. Al-Kalbi said: the first to do this was a man from Banu Kinanah called Nu'aym ibn Tha'labah, then after him a man called Junadah ibn 'Awf, who was the one the Messenger of Allah ﷺ met. Al-Zuhri said: a tribe from Banu Kinanah, then from Banu Fuqaym, a man called al-Qalammas, whose name was Hudhayfah ibn Ubayd. In another narration: Malik ibn Kinanah. Whoever was in charge of the postponement would attain leadership, because the Arabs held him in honour. Their poet said about this:

"And among us is the postponer of the month, al-Qalammas."

Al-Kumayt said:

"Are we not the postponers over Ma'add, making the months of lawfulness sacred?"

The Exalted's saying: ﴿an increase in disbelief﴾ is an explanation of what the Arabs did in gathering various kinds of disbelief. For they denied the existence of the Creator, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And what is the Most Merciful?﴾ [al-Furqan: 60][[See vol. 13, p. 64.]] according to the most correct view. And they denied resurrection, saying: ﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 78][[See vol. 15, p. 58.]]. And they denied the sending of messengers, saying: ﴿A human being from among us, a single one, whom we should follow?﴾ [al-Qamar: 24][[See vol. 17, p. 137 onward.]]. And they claimed that permitting and forbidding belonged to them, so they invented it from themselves, following their desires, and made lawful what Allah had forbidden. ﴿And none can change His words, even if the polytheists dislike it.﴾

The Exalted's saying: ﴿Through it those who disbelieve are led astray; they make it lawful one year and forbid it another year, to match the number of what Allah has forbidden, and so make lawful what Allah has forbidden. Their evil deeds have been made attractive to them. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾ There are three readings concerning this. The people of the two sanctuaries (Mecca and Medina) and Abu 'Amr read "yudallu" (passive, with damma on the yā' and fatha on the ḍād in the sense of being led astray). The Kufans read "yudallu" in the passive form. Al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read "yudillu" (active, from aḍalla). Each of the three readings conveys a meaning, except that the third reading has its object omitted. The implied sense is: "And those who disbelieve lead astray through it whoever accepts from them." The phrase "alladhina" is in the nominative position. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers back to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, the sense being: "Allah leads astray through it those who disbelieve," like His saying: ﴿He leads astray whom He wills﴾ [al-Ra'd: 27][[See vol. 14, p. 324 onward.]], and like His saying at the end of the verse: "And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people." The second reading, "yudallu bihi alladhina kafaru," means those to whom it is attributed. Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading because of His saying: "Their evil deeds have been made attractive to them." The first reading was preferred by Abu Hatim, because they were led astray by it, that is, by the postponement, since they used to reckon it and so went astray by it. The pronoun in "yuhillunahu" refers back to the postponement. It is related from Abu Raja' "yadallu" with fatha on the yā' and the ḍād; this is a dialect form, as one says: ḍaliltu adallu and ḍalaltu aḍillu. "Liyuwati'u" is in the subjunctive after the particle of purpose (lam kay), meaning "so that they may agree with" (liyuwafiqu). "Tawata'a al-qawm 'ala kadha" means the people gathered upon it. That is, they would not make one month lawful without making another month forbidden, so that the sacred months would remain four. This is the correct view, not what is mentioned that they made the months five. Qatadah said: they deliberately took Safar and added it to the sacred months, pairing it with al-Muharram in prohibition. Qatrub and al-Tabari also related this from him. And in light of this, the postponement means increase. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 38:

There are two issues here. The first concerns His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿What is [the matter] with you?﴾ "Ma" (مَا) is an interrogative particle whose meaning is affirmation and reproach. The sense is: what prevents you from such-and-such? Just as you say: "What is the matter with you regarding so-and-so, turning away?" There is no disagreement that this verse was revealed as a rebuke for those who stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the expedition of Tabuk, which took place in the ninth year after the Hijrah, a year after the Conquest. Its account will come at the end of the surah, God willing. And "al-nafr" (النَّفْر, setting out) is moving swiftly from one place to another for a matter that has arisen. It is said of a human being: nafara ila al-amr yanfiru nufuran (he went forth toward the matter). A people are called nufur, and from it is His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿They turned their backs in flight, [in] aversion﴾ [al-Isra: 46].[[See vol. 10, p. 721.]] It is said of an animal: nafarat tanfuru (with the "fa" pronounced with a damma and a kasra) nifaran and nufuran. It is said: in the animal there is nifar, which is a noun like al-hiran. And al-Hajj departed from Mina, nafran.

The second issue concerns His, may He be exalted, saying: (اثَّاقَلْتُمْ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ) [you clung heavily to the earth].
