The exegetes said: its meaning is "you clung to the pleasures of the earth," or "to residing on the earth." It is a rebuke for abandoning jihad and a reproach for holding back from hastening to set out, and it is like one who inclines to the earth. Its original form is "tathaqaltum" (تَثَاقَلْتُمْ); the "ta" was assimilated into the "tha" because of their proximity, and it needed an alif of connection so as to be able to pronounce the unvowelled letter. Similar to it is His saying ﴿ad-daraku﴾ [al-A'raf: 38] (ادَّارَكُوا), and ﴿fa-idda-ra'tum﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72] (فَادَّارَأْتُمْ), and ﴿itta-yarna﴾ [al-Naml: 47] (اطَّيَّرْنا), and ﴿izzayyanat﴾ [Yunus: 24] (ازَّيَّنَتْ).[[See vol. 7, p. 204.]][[See vol. 1, p. 455.]][[See vol. 13, p. 214.]][[See vol. 8, p. 326.]] Al-Kisa'i recited:

"She turns away from the reclining one when he smells her, a cool-tasting sweetness, when the kisses follow one another"

[[Sāfa al-shay yasūfuhu and yusāfuhu sawfan, and sāwafa and istāfa, all meaning he smelled it. Al-khasr: whatever is cool.]]

Al-A'mash recited "tathaqaltum" according to the original form; this was related by al-Mahdawi. Tabuk, to which he called the people [[Ibn Ishaq said: ... The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rarely set out on an expedition without concealing it and indicating that he intended a direction other than the one he was facing, except for the expedition of Tabuk, for he made it clear to the people because of the great distance and the severity of the time... etc.]] was in the heat of summer, the ripeness of fruit and the coolness of shade, as came in the sound hadith which will follow. So idleness overcame the people, and they held back and grew heavy. Allah rebuked them with this saying and blamed them for preferring the worldly life over the Hereafter. The meaning of ﴿Are you content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ is: in place of. The sense is: are you content with the pleasures of this world in place of the pleasures of the Hereafter? So "min" (مِنَ) here carries the meaning of substitution, as in His saying ﴿And if We willed, We would have made among you angels upon the earth, succeeding [you]﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 60], meaning: in place of you. The poet said:

"Would that we had a sip of Zamzam's water, cooled, left overnight in a tahayan"

It is also narrated as "from the water of Hamnan" [Hamnan: Mecca]. He meant: would that we had, in place of the water of Zamzam, a cooled sip. The tahayan is a piece of wood set up in a corner of the house for the air, on which water is hung until it cools. Allah rebuked them for preferring ease in this world over ease in the Hereafter, since the ease of the Hereafter is not attained except through the toil of this world. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'A'ishah, when she had performed tawaf while riding: "Your reward is according to your effort." Related by al-Bukhari.

There is one issue here. The words of Allah, the Exalted, "Unless you go forth (illa tanfiru)" form a conditional clause (shart), which is why the nun is dropped from the verb. The response (jawab) is "He will punish you" (yu'adhdhibkum) and "and will replace you with another people" (wa yastabdil qawman ghayrakum). This is a severe threat and a emphatic warning against abandoning the nafir (the call to go forth for jihad).

Ibn al-'Arabi said: Among the established principles of usul al-fiqh is that when a command (amr) is issued, its occurrence implies nothing more than the requirement of the act itself. The punishment for abandoning it is not derived from the command itself, nor is it implied by the requirement. Rather, punishment comes through a statement about it, such as saying: "If you do not do such-and-such, I will punish you with such-and-such," as occurs in this verse. Therefore, by its implication, going forth (nafir) for jihad and setting out against the disbelievers to fight them is obligatory, so that the word of Allah may be the highest.

Abu Dawud related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "'Unless you go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment' and 'It was not for the people of Medina...' up to His words, '...they used to do' [al-Tawbah: 120], were abrogated by the verse that follows it: 'And it is not for the believers to go forth all together' [al-Tawbah: 122]." This is also the view of al-Dahhak, al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah.

"He will punish you": Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the withholding of rain from them. Ibn al-'Arabi said: If this is authentically reported from him, then he knows from where he said it; otherwise, the painful punishment is in this world through the conquest of the enemy, and in the Hereafter through the Fire.

I (al-Qurtubi) say: The statement of Ibn 'Abbas was narrated by the Imam Abu Dawud in his Sunan from Ibn Nufay', who said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas about this verse, "Unless you go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment." He said: "He withheld the rain from them, and that was their punishment." The Imam Abu Muhammad Ibn 'Atiyah also mentioned it as a marfu' report from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called upon a tribe from among the tribes to go forth, but they sat back, so Allah withheld the rain from them and punished them with it. And "painful" (alim) means "causing pain" (mu'lim), i.e., causing suffering. This has been mentioned previously [see vol. 1, p. 198].

(And He will replace you with another people): He threatens that He will bring in place of you for His Messenger a people who will not sit back when he calls them to go forth. It was said: they are the sons of Persia. It was also said: the people of Yemen.

(And they will not harm Him at all): This is a conjunction. The pronoun ("Him") is said to refer to Allah, the Exalted, and it is said to refer to the Prophet (ﷺ). Holding back from jihad while showing aversion is forbidden for everyone. As for holding back without aversion: whoever the Prophet (ﷺ) designates, holding back is forbidden for him; and if he is not designated, the obligation is one of sufficiency (fard kifayah). This was mentioned by al-Qushayri. It has also been said that the intended meaning of this verse is the obligation of going forth when there is need and when the disbelievers become prominent and their strength increases. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that this is by way of a summons (istid'a'). According to this view, it is not appropriate to restrict it to the time when the polytheists are dominant, because the obligation of that does not depend on a summons, since it is already specified. Once this is established, it is unlikely that a summons and a call to go forth would make obligatory something that was not obligatory before, except that when the imam designates a group and calls them to jihad, it is not permissible for them to hold back once they are designated; and by his designation it becomes an obligation upon those he designated, not because of the place of jihad but out of obedience to the imam. And Allah knows best.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 40 (part 1 of 2):

There are eleven issues concerning this verse. The first is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿If you do not support him﴾. It means: you do not help him by going forth with him on the expedition to Tabuk. Allah rebuked them after His Prophet (ﷺ) returned from Tabuk. Al-Naqqash said: this is the first verse revealed of the surah [Bara'ah]. The meaning is: if you abandon supporting him, then Allah will take charge of him, since Allah had already supported him in times of few numbers and made him victorious over his enemy through dominance and might. It was also said: Allah had indeed supported him through his companion in the cave, by giving him companionship and carrying him on his neck, and by his loyalty and by his protecting him with his own self and consoling him with his wealth. Al-Layth ibn Sa'd said: no one accompanied the prophets (peace be upon them) like Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him). Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: Abu Bakr was excluded by this verse from the rebuke contained in the words: "If you do not support him."

The second is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿when those who disbelieved expelled him﴾. He went out by himself, fleeing, but it was by their compulsion that he did so, until he did it. So the act is attributed to them and the ruling is based upon them. For this reason, one who is coerced to kill is killed, and one who destroys property under coercion is liable for it, since the coercer compelled the killer and the destroyer to kill and to destroy.

The third is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿the second of two﴾, meaning one of two. This is like "the third of three" and "the fourth of four." When the wording varies, as when you say "the fourth of three" and "the fifth of four," the meaning is that he made the three into four by himself, and the four into five. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: they expelled him alone from all the people except Abu Bakr. The governing element of this state is "Allah supported him," meaning: He supported him alone, and he was supported as one of two. Ali ibn Sulayman said: the implied construction is "so he went out as the second of two," like the words of Allah: ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17]. The majority of people recited "thani" with a fathah on the ya'. Abu Hatim said: nothing other than this is known. A group recited "thani" with the ya' sukun. Ibn Jinni said: Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' transmitted it, and its basis is that he made the ya' quiescent, likening it to the alif. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is like the recitation of al-Hasan, "ma baqiya mina al-riba," and like the verse of Jarir:

He is the caliph, so be pleased with what pleases you,
one of firm resolve, in whose judgment there is no deviation.

[See vol. 18, p. 305.] [See vol. 3, p. 369.]

The fourth is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿when they were both in the cave﴾. The cave (ghar) is a hole in a mountain, namely the Cave of Thawr. When the Quraysh saw that the Muslims had reached Madinah, they said: this is an unbearable, pressing evil. So they agreed upon killing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They laid siege to him and watched over the door of his house all night so as to kill him when he came out. The Prophet (ﷺ) ordered Ali ibn Abi Talib to sleep on his bed, and he prayed to Allah to blind their sight to his trail. Allah obscured their vision, and he went out while sleep had overcome them. He put dust on their heads and set off. When they awoke, Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) came out to them and informed them that there was no one in the house. They knew then that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had escaped and was safe. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had arranged with Abu Bakr al-Siddiq for the Hijrah, and they gave their two mounts to Abd Allah ibn Ariqit, also said to be Ibn Uraiqit, who was a disbeliever, but they trusted him, for he was a guide through the roads, so they hired him to guide them to Madinah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out through a small door at the back of Abu Bakr's house, which was in the tribe of Banu Jumah, and they set off towards the cave in the mountain of Thawr. Abu Bakr ordered his son Abd Allah to listen to what the people were saying, and ordered his freedman Amir ibn Fuhayrah to graze his sheep and bring them [yurihuha: meaning yaruduha, bring back] to them at night, so that they could take what they needed from them. Then they set off and entered the cave. Asma bint Abi Bakr al-Siddiq used to bring them food, and Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr would bring them news, then Amir ibn Fuhayrah would follow them with the sheep, erasing their tracks. When the Quraysh lost him, they began searching for him with a tracker well known for following tracks, until he stopped at the cave and said: here the trail ends. They looked and saw that a spider had spun a web over the mouth of the cave at that very moment, and for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade killing it. When they saw the spider's web, they were certain that no one was inside, so they returned and set a reward for the Prophet (ﷺ) of one hundred camels for whoever returned him to them.

The report is well known, and the story of Suraqa ibn Malik ibn Ju'shum is mentioned in it. It has also been related from the hadith of Abu al-Darda' and Thawban (may Allah be pleased with them both) [[from h.]]: that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded a dove, and it laid its eggs upon the spider's web and kept brooding over its eggs; when the disbelievers saw it, it turned them away from the cave.

Fifth: al-Bukhari related from Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Abu Bakr hired a man from the Banu al-Dil, a guide, an expert (khirrit) [[al-khirrit: the skilled guide who is adept at the routes of the deserts.]], and he was upon the religion of the disbelievers of Quraysh. They entrusted to him their two riding-camels and set a time with him at the cave of Thawr after three nights. He brought them their two camels on the morning of the third day, and they departed, and 'Amir ibn Fuhayra and the Dili guide set out with them. He took them by the route of the coast [[al-Sahil: a specific place, not the seashore.]].

Al-Muhallab said: In this there is an element of jurisprudence (fiqh): the entrusting of the people of polytheism [[in j: kufr (disbelief).]] with secrets and property when reliability and integrity are known from them, just as the Prophet ﷺ entrusted this polytheist with his secret in the departure from Makkah and with the two camels.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: In this is the hiring of Muslims of disbelievers for guiding the way.

Al-Bukhari said in his chapter heading: [Chapter: Hiring the polytheists in case of necessity, or when people of Islam are not found] — Ibn Battal said: al-Bukhari said in his heading "or when people of Islam are not found" [because the Prophet ﷺ only employed the people of Khaybar in working their land, since there were no Muslims who could take their place in working the land, until Islam grew strong and they were no longer needed, whereupon Umar expelled them]. The majority of jurists permit hiring them in case of necessity and otherwise. And in it: the hiring of two men of one man for one task that is common to both of them. And in it: evidence for the permissibility of fleeing with one's religion out of fear of the enemy, and hiding in caves and other places, and that a person should not hand himself over to the enemy, relying upon Allah and submitting to Him. "And if your Lord had willed, He would have protected him while he was with them, but it is the Sunnah of Allah concerning the prophets and others, and you will not find any change in the Sunnah of Allah." This is the clearest proof against those who forbid that and say: whoever fears anything along with Allah, that is a deficiency in his trust (tawakkul), and he has not believed in divine decree (qadar). All of this is in the meaning of the verse, and to Allah belong praise and guidance.

Sixth: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When he said to his companion, "Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us."﴾ This verse includes the virtues of al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him). Ashhab and Abu Zayd related from Ibn al-Qasim, from Malik: "the second of two, when they were in the cave, when he said to his companion, 'Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us'" refers to al-Siddiq. Thus Allah Exalted affirmed his statement to him with His speech, and described the companionship in His Book. Some scholars said: Whoever denies that Umar and Uthman, or any one of the Companions, was a companion of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is a liar and an innovator. And whoever denies that Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) was a companion of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is a disbeliever, because he has rejected the explicit text of the Qur'an. The meaning of "indeed Allah is with us" is: with support, care, protection and safeguarding.

al-Tirmidhi and al-Harith ibn Abi Usama both related, saying: Ammar ibn... [they said] Affan related to us, saying: Hammam related to us, saying: Thabit informed us, from Anas, that Abu Bakr told him: I said to the Prophet ﷺ while we were in the cave: "If one of them were to look at his feet, he would see us beneath his feet." He said: "O Abu Bakr, what do you think of two whose third is Allah?"

al-Muhasibi said: That is, with them through support and defense, not in the sense of the generality by which He encompasses all creation, when He said: ﴿There is no secret conversation between three but that He is their fourth﴾ [[See vol. 18 p. 289.]] [al-Mujadila: 7]. Its meaning in general is that He hears and sees both the disbelievers and the believers.

Seventh: Ibn al-'Arabi said: The Imamiyya, may Allah disfigure them, said: Abu Bakr's grief in the cave is evidence of his ignorance, his deficiency, the weakness of his heart and his foolishness [[al-kharq (with damma): foolishness and weakness of judgment.]]. Our scholars answered this by saying that attributing grief to him is not a deficiency, just as Ibrahim was not diminished when it was said of him: ﴿He felt apprehension of them and sensed fear. They said, "Do not fear."﴾ [[See vol. 9 p. 62.]] [Hud: 70]. Nor was Musa diminished by his saying: "So Musa felt fear within himself. We said, 'Do not fear.'" [[See vol. 11 p. 221 ff.]] [Ta-Ha: 67, 68]. And concerning Lut: ﴿And do not grieve; indeed we will save you and your family﴾ [[See vol. 13 p. 341 ff.]] [al-'Ankabut: 33]. These great ones, may the blessings of Allah be upon them, were explicitly found to have taqiyya (dissimulation) with them, and that was not a reproach against them nor a description of them as deficient; likewise with Abu Bakr. Moreover, it is a possibility in the case of al-Siddiq, for he said: "If one of them were to look beneath his feet, he would see us."

Second answer: Al-Siddiq's grief was only out of fear for the Prophet ﷺ that harm might reach him, and the Prophet ﷺ at that time was not protected from harm, for the verse ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾ [[See vol. 6 p. 242.]] [al-Ma'ida: 67] had only been revealed to him at Madina [[from b, j, z, k and y.]].

Eighth: Ibn al-'Arabi said: Abu al-Fada'il al-'Adl [[from b, k and y. The names in this have been confused. What is in the printed Ibn al-'Arabi's Ahkam al-Qur'an is "Abu al-Fada'il ibn al-Mu'addal", and in its manuscript "Abu al-Fada'il al-Mu'addal".]] told us, saying: Jamal al-Islam Abu al-Qasim told us, saying: Musa ﷺ said: ﴿By no means! Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me.﴾ [[See vol. 13 p. 100 ff.]] [al-Shu'ara': 62] And of Muhammad ﷺ He said: "Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us." Undoubtedly, when Allah was with Musa alone, his companions apostatized after him; he returned from his Lord and found them worshipping the calf. But when He said of Muhammad ﷺ "Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us," Abu Bakr remained guided, monotheistic, knowledgeable, resolute, standing firm in the matter, and no disorder touched him.

Ninth: al-Tirmidhi related from the hadith of Nubayt ibn Shurayt, from Salim ibn 'Ubayd — who had companionship (suhba) — who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ fainted... the hadith. In it: The Muhajirun gathered, consulting, and they said: "Come, let us go to our brothers among the Ansar and bring them into this matter with us." The Ansar said: "From us a leader, and from you a leader." Then Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Who has the like of these three: 'the second of two, when they were in the cave, when he said to his companion, Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us'? Who are 'they two'?" He said: Then he extended his hand and pledged allegiance to him, and the people pledged allegiance to him with a good and beautiful pledge.

I say: For this reason some scholars said: In His saying, Exalted is He, "the second of two, when they were in the cave," there is an indication that the caliph after the Prophet ﷺ was Abu Bakr al-Siddiq [(may Allah be pleased with him) [[from j and h.]]], because the caliph is never anything except second. I heard our shaykh, the Imam Abu al-'Abbas Ahmad ibn 'Umar say: Al-Siddiq deserved to be called "second of two" only because of his standing with the matter after the Prophet ﷺ, just as the Prophet ﷺ stood with it first. That is because when the Prophet ﷺ died, all the Arabs apostatized, and Islam remained only in Madina, Makkah and Juwatha [[a place in Bahrain.]], so Abu Bakr arose calling the people to Islam and fighting them over entry into the religion, as the Prophet ﷺ had done; thus he deserved from this aspect that "second of two" be said of him.

I say: Sound hadiths have come in the Sunnah whose apparent meaning indicates that he was the caliph after him, and consensus has been established on this, and no dissenter remains among them. Whoever casts doubt on his caliphate is definitively judged to be in error and corrupt. As to whether he becomes a disbeliever or not, that is disputed, and the more apparent view is that he is a disbeliever. A fuller explanation of this meaning will come in surah [al-Fath [[See vol. 16 p. 297.]]], if Allah wills. What is established with certainty from the Book, the Sunnah, and the sayings of the scholars of the Ummah, and what hearts and minds must believe, is the superiority of al-Siddiq over all the Companions. There is no regard for the statements of the Shi'a or of the people of innovation, for they are either disbelievers whose neck is to be struck, or innovators who are deemed corrupt whose word is not accepted. Then after al-Siddiq is 'Umar al-Faruq, then after him 'Uthman. al-Bukhari related from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "In the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ we used to make a comparison among the people, and we would prefer Abu Bakr, then 'Umar, then 'Uthman."

The leading scholars of the early generations [[in j: ahl al-sunna. In z: al-tafsir.]] differed concerning 'Uthman and 'Ali; the majority of them give precedence to 'Uthman. It is related from Malik that he withheld judgment on this, and it is also related from him that he returned to what the majority held. This is the more correct view, if Allah wills.

Tenth: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon him﴾ There are two views on this: one is that it refers to the Prophet ﷺ, and the second is that it refers to Abu Bakr. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Our scholars said, and this is the stronger view, because he feared for the Prophet ﷺ from the people, so Allah sent down His tranquility upon him through the Prophet's ﷺ reassurance, so his heart was calmed, his fright went away, and safety was achieved. Allah, glorified is He, caused the thamam (a plant well known in the desert) to grow, inspired a dove to make its nest there, and sent the spider, which wove a web over it. How weak these soldiers are in outward sensation, and how strong they are in inner meaning! For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said to 'Umar when he quarrelled with al-Siddiq: "Will you leave me my companion? When all the people said, 'You have lied,' Abu Bakr said, 'You have spoken the truth.'" Related by Abu al-Darda'.

Eleventh: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He supported him with soldiers you did not see﴾ meaning of the angels. The pronoun in "supported him" refers to the Prophet ﷺ, and the two pronouns differ; this is common in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs.

(And He made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest) meaning the word of polytheism.

(And the word of Allah is the highest) It has been said: "There is no god but Allah." And it has been said: the promise of victory. al-A'mash and Ya'qub read "and the word of Allah" in the accusative, taking it as governed by "made," while the rest read it in the nominative, as a new sentence. al-Farra' claimed that the accusative reading is remote; he said: "Because you say, 'So-and-so freed the slave of his father,' and you do not say, 'the slave of my father So-and-so.'" Abu Hatim said something similar; he said: It should have been said "and His word is the highest." al-Nahhas said: What al-Farra' mentioned does not resemble the verse, but what Sibawayh recited resembles it:

I do not see death outpacing death, something that embitters death for the rich and the poor alike.

This is good and sound, with no difficulty in it. Indeed, the skilled grammarians say: repeating the noun in such a case has a benefit, which is that it carries the sense of glorification. Allah Exalted said: ﴿When the earth is shaken with its shaking, and the earth brings forth its burdens﴾ [[See vol. 20 p. 147.]] [al-Zalzala: 1, 2]. This has no difficulty. The plural of kalima is kalim. The Tamim say: hiya kilma, with a kasra on the kaf. al-Farra' related three dialects for it: kalima, kilma and kalma, like kabid, kibd and kabd, and warq, wiraq and warq. And kalima also means a poem in its entirety, as al-Jawhari said.

**Issue One:** It concerns the verse on which there are seven issues.

**First issue:** Sufyan narrated from Husayn ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Abu Malik al-Ghifari, who said: "The first part of Surat Bara'a [al-Tawba] to be revealed was ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾." Abu al-Duha also said the same. He said: "Then its beginning and its end were revealed."

**Second issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). There are ten opinions on it.

**The first:** It is related from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿so go forth in companies﴾[[Thus in all the manuscripts. The author, may God have mercy on him, cited the verse of al-Nisa', which is His saying: "So go forth in companies or go forth all together" (4:71). See vol. 5, p. 273. Thubat is the plural of thubah, which means a group of people.]] [al-Nisa’: 71]: "Separate detachments."

**The second:** It is also related from Ibn Abbas and Qatada: "Eager and not eager."

**The third:** "The light one is the wealthy, and the heavy one is the poor." This was said by Mujahid.

**The fourth:** "The light one is the young man, and the heavy one is the elderly man." This was said by al-Hasan.

**The fifth:** "Those who are occupied and those who are not occupied." This was said by Zayd ibn Ali and al-Hakam ibn Utba.

**The sixth:** "The heavy one is the one who has dependents, and the light one is the one who has no dependents." This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

**The seventh:** "The heavy one is the one who has property he is reluctant to leave, and the light one is the one who has no property." This was said by Ibn Zayd.

**The eighth:** "The light ones are the infantry, and the heavy ones are the cavalry." This was said by al-Awza'i.

**The ninth:** "The light ones are those who rush to battle like the advance guard, which is the front of the army, and the heavy ones are the entire army."

**The tenth:** "The light one is the brave, and the heavy one is the coward." This was related by al-Naqqash.

The correct meaning of the verse is that the people were commanded collectively, that is: go forth, whether movement is easy for you or difficult. It is narrated that Ibn Umm Maktum came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and said to him: "Is it obligatory on me to go forth?" He said: "Yes," until God, Exalted is He, revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind﴾[[See vol. 12, p. 311 onwards.]] [al-Nur: 61]. These opinions are only examples of heaviness and lightness.

**Third issue:** This verse has been disputed. It was said that it is abrogated (mansukh) by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak or upon the sick﴾[[See pp. 225 and 293 of this part.]] [al-Tawba: 91]. It was also said that its abrogating verse is His saying: ﴿Why should not a group from every division of them go forth﴾[[See pp. 225 and 293 of this part.]] [al-Tawba: 122]. The correct view is that it is not abrogated. Ibn Abbas related from Abu Talha regarding His saying, Exalted is He: "Go forth, light and heavy," that he said: "Young and old. God has not heard the excuse of anyone." So he went out to Syria and fought until he died, may God be pleased with him. Hammad related from Thabit, and Ali ibn Zayd from Anas, that Abu Talha recited Surat [Bara'a], and when he came to this verse, "Go forth, light and heavy," he said: "O my sons, equip me, equip me." His sons said: "May God have mercy on you! You fought with the Prophet ﷺ until he died, and with Abu Bakr until he died, and with Umar until he died, so we will fight on your behalf." He said: "No, equip me." So he fought at sea and died at sea. They could not find an island to bury him in until after seven days, so they buried him there, and he had not changed, may God be pleased with him.

Al-Tabari related on the authority of one who saw al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad in Homs, on a money-changer's bench, having grown fat beyond the bench, while he was preparing for the campaign. It was said to him: "God has excused you." He said: "The Surah of the Expeditions has come down upon us: 'Go forth, light and heavy.'"

Al-Zuhri said: "Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab went out to the campaign although one of his eyes had been lost. It was said to him: 'You are unwell.' He said: 'God has called forth the light and the heavy. If I cannot fight, I will increase the numbers and guard the baggage.'"

It is related that some people saw in the campaigns of Syria a man whose eyebrows had fallen over his eyes from old age. He was told: "O uncle, God has excused you." He said: "O nephew, we have been commanded to go forth light and heavy."

Ibn Umm Maktum, may God be pleased with him, whose name was Amr, said on the day of Uhud: "I am a blind man, so hand over the banner to me. When the bearer of the banner is defeated, the army is defeated, and I do not know who will strike me with his sword, so I will not leave." On that day Mus'ab ibn Umayr took the banner, as explained earlier in [Al 'Imran].[[See vol. 4, p. 234 onwards.]]

For this reason, and for what is similar to it that has been related from the Companions and the Successors, we say that abrogation is not valid.

**Fourth issue:** There may be a state in which the mobilization of everyone becomes obligatory. This is when jihad becomes an individual obligation (ta'ayyun), by the enemy overcoming a region of the regions, or by his descending upon the very heart of the land. When that happens, it is obligatory upon all the people of that land to go forth and set out against him, light and heavy, young and old, each according to his capacity, whether one has a father who has not given permission or one has no father. No one who is able to set out may remain behind, whether a fighter or one who provides numbers.

If the people of that town are unable to confront their enemy, then it is obligatory upon those who are near them and adjacent to them to set out according to what is binding upon the people of that town, until they know that there is strength among them to stand against the enemy and repel him. Likewise, everyone who knows of their weakness against their enemy, and knows that he can reach them and is able to aid them, is also obligated to set out to them. The Muslims are all a hand against whoever is other than them. Once the people of the area where the enemy has descended and taken up position have risen to repel the enemy, the obligation falls from the others.

If the enemy approaches the abode of Islam but has not entered it, it is also obligatory for them to set out against him, until the religion of God prevails, the homeland is protected, the frontier is guarded, and the enemy is humiliated. There is no disagreement on this.

**Second category of the obligations of jihad:** It is also a collective obligation (fard) upon the imam to dispatch a company to the enemy once every year. He himself goes with them, or he sends one whom he trusts to invite them to Islam and encourage them,[[In B, J and W: "to subdue them" (yurghimahum). In Z and K: "to deter them" (yardaʿahum).]] to restrain their harm, and to make the religion of God prevail over them, until they enter Islam or give the jizya (poll tax) willingly and in submission.

**Also among jihad is what is supererogatory (nafilah):** that the imam sends out one company after another, and dispatches expeditions (sarāyā) at times of heedlessness and when the opportunity arises, and posts watchers for them with ribat (garrison duty) in places of danger, and displays strength.

**Fifth issue:** If it is asked: what should a single person do when all the others fall short? It is said to him: he should aim at one prisoner and ransom him, for when he ransoms one, he has discharged in respect of that one more than would be binding upon him in a group. Indeed, if the wealthy shared among themselves the ransom of the captives, each of them would pay less than one dirham. He should fight himself if he is able, and otherwise equip a fighter. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever equips a fighter has fought, and whoever looks after his family well in his absence has fought." Al-Sahih (Bukhari and Muslim) recorded it. This is because his presence does not suffice in his place, and his wealth does not suffice either.

**Sixth issue:** It is related that a certain king made a treaty with unbelievers that they would not imprison any captive. A Muslim man entered their territory and passed by a closed house. A woman called out to him: "I am a captive, so convey my news to your companion." When he met him and was entertained by him, and they were engaged in conversation, the news reached this tormented woman. Before he had finished his account, the commander rose to his feet and went out to fight immediately, and he marched to the frontier until he freed the captive woman and took control of the place, may God be pleased with him. Ibn al-Arabi mentioned it and said: "The enemy descended upon us—may God break him—in the year 527, and he overran our lands, took our best people captive, and penetrated the middle of our country with a host that frightened the people by its number, though it was not as large as they estimated. I said to the governor and the governed: 'This is the enemy of God who has fallen into the snare and the net, so let there be a blessing among you, and let there be a movement from you toward supporting the religion, which has become binding upon you. Let all the people go out to him, so that not one of them remains in all the regions, and he will be surrounded, for he is certainly doomed if God facilitates him for you.'" But sins prevailed, hearts trembled with disobedience, and every person among the people became a fox retreating to its burrow,[[al-wijar (with kasra or fatha) is the lair of a hyena and the like.]] and if he sees the plot near his burrow... "Surely we belong to God and to Him we shall return. God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs."

**Seventh issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And strive﴾ is a command to jihad, which is derived from effort (jahd). ﴿with your wealth and your lives﴾. Abu Dawud related from Anas that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Strive against the polytheists with your wealth, your lives, and your tongues." This is a description of the most complete form of jihad and the most beloved of it in the sight of God, Exalted is He. He urged the complete qualities, and He mentioned wealth first, since it is the first expense at the time of equipping. Thus He arranged the command as it actually is.

When the Prophet (ﷺ) returned from the expedition of Tabuk, Allah exposed the hypocrisy of a people. Al-'Arad (the goods of this world that are offered) is what is presented of the benefits of this world. The meaning is: a nearby spoil. He informed about them that if they were called to a spoil they would have followed him.

"'Aradan" is the predicate of kana (was). "QarIban" is its adjective. "Wa-safaran qasidan" is coordinated with it. The subject of kana has been omitted because the context indicates it. The estimated sense is: if what was called to were a nearby gain and an easy journey, meaning one whose routes are known and easy, they would have followed you. This allusion is directed at the hypocrites, as we mentioned, because they are included among those who were addressed with the call to march out. This is found in Arabic speech, where they mention a whole and then use a pronoun referring back to a part of it, as was said regarding His saying: ﴿And there is not one of you but will pass over it﴾ [Maryam: 71], that it refers to the Resurrection. Then He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Then We will save those who feared Allah and leave the wrongdoers within it on their knees﴾ [Maryam: 72], meaning Hell, may He be exalted and glorified. A parallel to this verse in the Sunnah, in meaning, is his saying, peace be upon him: ("If one of them knew that he would find a fat bone or two meaty hooves (mirmatayn, with a kasra on the mim, and it may also be fathah; the dual of mirmah, which is the hoof of a sheep, or the meat between its hooves), he would have attended the 'Isha' prayer.") He means: if one of them knew that he would find something present and immediate to take, he would have come to the mosque for its sake.

"But the distance seemed long to them" (wa-lakin ba'udat 'alayhimu al-shuqqah). Abu 'Ubaydah and others related that al-shuqqah is the journey to a distant land; it is said: a shuqqah sha'qqah (a hard, distant journey). All of this refers to the expedition of Tabuk. Al-Kisa'i related that it is said both shuqqah and shiqqah. Al-Jawhari said: al-shuqqah with a damma is a piece of cloth, and al-shuqqah is also a distant journey, and they sometimes say it with a kasra. Al-shiqqah is a splinter split off from a board or a piece of wood. It is said of an angry person: he flared up, and a splinter flew off from him, with a kasra.

"And they will swear by Allah: 'If we had been able, we would have gone out with you.'" That is, if we had had ease in mount and wealth.

"(We would have gone out with you.)" Its parallel is: ﴿And due to Allah from the people is pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to make his way to it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97]. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained it, saying: "Provision and a riding animal." This has already been discussed.

"They destroy themselves" — that is, by lying and hypocrisy.

"And Allah knows that they are liars" — in their excuse.

﴿He has pardoned you, O Muhammad. Why did you grant them permission?﴾

It was said: this is an opening of speech, as you say: "May Allah set you right, strengthen you and have mercy on you! Such-and-such happened." On this interpretation it is good to pause at His words "He has pardoned you." This is related by Makki, al-Mahdawi and al-Nahhas. He informed him of the pardon before the sin so that his heart would not fly away in fear [[al-Faraq (with fatha on the fa) means fear and anxiety.]]. It was also said: the meaning is "Allah has pardoned you for what was done in granting them permission," so on this reading it is not good to pause at "He has pardoned you." This is related by al-Mahdawi, and al-Nahhas preferred it.

Then it was said: regarding the permission there are two views. [The first: "Why did you grant them permission" to go out with you, and their going out without preparation and sincere intention is corruption. The second: "Why did you grant them permission" to remain behind when they pleaded excuses. Al-Qushayri mentioned both and said: this is a gentle rebuke, since He said "He has pardoned you." The Prophet (ﷺ) granted permission without a revelation descending concerning it. Qatadah and Amr ibn Maymun said: there were two things the Prophet (ﷺ) did which he had not been commanded to do: his permission to a group of the hypocrites to stay behind from him, and his taking ransom from the captives; so Allah rebuked him, as you hear.] Some scholars said: what proceeded from him was only leaving the better course, so Allah placed the pardon before the address, which is in the form of a rebuke.

﴿Until those who are truthful become clear to you, and you know the liars.﴾ That is: so that it becomes clear to you who among them was truthful and who was a hypocrite. Ibn Abbas said: on that day the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not yet know the hypocrites; he only came to know them after the revelation of Surah al-Tawbah. Mujahid said: these were people who said, "We will ask permission to sit out; if he permits us we will sit, and if he does not permit us we will still sit." Qatadah said: this verse was abrogated by His words in Surah al-Nur: ﴿So when they ask your permission for some matter of theirs, grant permission to whom you will among them﴾ [al-Nur: 62] [[See vol. 12, p. 320 onward.]]. This was mentioned by al-Nahhas in his Ma'ani al-Quran.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Those who believe in Allah and the Last Day do not ask your permission﴾, meaning, not to remain behind and not to go out. Rather, when you command them to do something, they hasten to it. So asking permission at that time was a sign of hypocrisy without excuse. For this reason He said: ﴿Only those ask your permission who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day, and whose hearts are in doubt, so they waver in their doubt.﴾

Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "﴿Those who believe in Allah do not ask your permission﴾ was abrogated by what is in (Surat al-Nur): ﴿The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger... to His saying... Forgiving, Merciful.﴾" [See vol. 12, p. 320 onward.]

"﴿That they strive﴾" is in a position of accusative by an implied "fi" (in), according to al-Zajjaj. It was also said that the estimate is "out of dislike that they strive," like His saying: ﴿Allah makes clear to you that you may not go astray﴾ [An-Nisa: 176]. [See vol. 6, p. 28.]

"And their hearts were in doubt" means they doubted the religion.

"So they waver in their doubt" means they go back and forth in their doubt.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Those who believe in Allah and the Last Day do not ask your permission﴾, meaning, not to remain behind and not to go out. Rather, when you command them to do something, they hasten to it. So asking permission at that time was a sign of hypocrisy without excuse. For this reason He said: ﴿Only those ask your permission who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day, and whose hearts are in doubt, so they waver in their doubt.﴾

"﴿That they strive﴾" is in a position of accusative by an implied "fi" (in), according to al-Zajjaj. It was also said that the estimate is "out of dislike that they strive," like His saying: ﴿Allah makes clear to you that you may not go astray﴾ [An-Nisa: 176]. [See vol. 6, p. 28.]

"And their hearts were in doubt" means they doubted the religion.

"So they waver in their doubt" means they go back and forth in their doubt.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 46:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had they intended to go forth, they would have made some preparation for it﴾, meaning: had they intended jihad, they would have readied themselves with the readiness of travel. Their neglect of preparation is therefore evidence of their intention to stay behind.

(But Allah disliked their being sent forth), meaning: their going out with you.

(So He held them back), meaning: He kept them from you and forsook them, because they said: "If we are not given permission to sit idle, we will cause corruption and incite the believers against one another." This is supported by what follows: ﴿Had they gone forth among you, they would have added nothing to you but corruption﴾.

(And it was said: "Sit with those who sit"). It was said that this is the words of some of them to others. It was also said that it is the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), and this would be the permission mentioned earlier. It was said: he (ﷺ) said it in anger, so they took the outward wording of it and said: "He has indeed given us permission." It was also said that it is an expression of abandonment, meaning Allah placed sitting idle into their hearts. The meaning of (with those who sit) is: with those who have valid excuses, the blind, the chronically ill, the women and the children.

This is consolation for the believers regarding the hypocrites' staying behind from them. Al-khabal (corruption) means mischief, slander, sowing discord, and spreading rumours. This is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', an exception where what follows is not of the same kind as what precedes it), meaning: "They did not increase you in strength, but they sought corruption." It has also been said that the meaning is: "They increase you only in corruption in what you deliberate upon of opinion," so the exception is not disjunctive.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they would have hastened between you﴾. The meaning is that they would have hurried among you with corruption. Al-ija' is swiftness of travel. The reciter (al-rajiz) said: [[He is Durayd ibn al-Simma, as in Lisan al-Arab.]]

"Would that I were in it a young camel, I would gallop in it and hasten."

It is said: the camel "wada'a" (hastened) when it ran, yet it is "wada'a, yada'u, wad'an and wuqu'an" when it hastened its pace. "Awda'tuhu" means I made him run. It has also been said: al-ijah is a gait like al-khabab (a fast amble). Al-khalal is the gap between two things, and its plural is al-khilal, meaning the gaps that are between the rows, so the meaning is: they would have hastened between you with slander and the spoiling of relations.

﴿they seek to cause you turmoil﴾ is the second object. The meaning is that they seek for you turmoil, that is, corruption and incitement. It is said: "abghaytuhu kadha" means I helped him to seek it, and "baghaytuhu kadha" means I sought it for him. It has been said that fitnah here means shirk (polytheism).

﴿and among you are listeners to them﴾, that is, spies for them who convey news to them from among you. Qatadah said: among you are those who accept their words and obey them. Al-Nahhas said: the first view is better, because it is the more prevalent of its two meanings, that sama' (listening) means hearing speech, and similar to it is ﴿listeners to falsehood﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41]. [[See vol. 6, p. 182.]] As for the second view, it is hardly ever said except as "sami'" (listener), like "qa'il" (speaker).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 48:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, they had sought discord before [this]﴾, meaning: they had sought corruption and turmoil before their affair became manifest and revelation descended concerning what they concealed and what they would do. Ibn Juraij said: He meant twelve men from among the hypocrites who stood at the Thaniyyat al-Wada' (the mountain pass, a path through a mountain, like a notch; it was also said to be the high road in it) on the night of al-Aqabah, intending to assassinate the Prophet (ﷺ). [Al-Wada' is a valley in Makkah, and Thaniyyat al-Wada' is attributed to it.]

﴿And they upset affairs for you﴾, meaning: they turned them over and deliberated on how to nullify what you brought, ﴿until the truth came and the command of Allah prevailed﴾, meaning His religion, ﴿while they were averse.﴾

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 9, verses 49–50:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And among them is he who says, "Grant me permission and do not put me to trial."﴾ It comes from *adhina yu'dhanu* (to grant permission). When you form the imperative, you add a hamza (glottal stop) with a kasra, and after it comes another hamza, which is the first radical of the verb. Two hamzas do not come together, so the second hamza is changed into a *ya'* (y) because of the kasra before it, and you say *i'dhan* (ائذن). When you connect the word to what follows, the reason for avoiding two hamzas disappears, so you pronounce the hamza again and say: "﴿And among them is he who says, 'Grant me permission'﴾" (ائذن لي). Warsh related from Nafi' the reading "﴿And among them is he who says, 'Grant me permission'﴾" (اوذن لي), easing the hamza [[That is, he changed it into a *waw* because of the damma on the lam before it, so that the lam is pronounced as if it were joined to the *waw* of the plural.]]. Al-Nahhas said: It is said *i'dhan li-fulan*, then *i'dhan lahu*. The spelling of the first and the second is the same, with an alif and a ya' before the dhal in the script. If you say *i'dhan li-fulan* and *a'dhan li-ghayrihi*, the second is written without a ya', and so is the fa'. The difference between *thumma* and *wa* is that one may pause on *thumma* and it is separated, whereas one does not pause on *wa* or *fa*, and they are not separated.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Jadd ibn Qays, of Banu Salima, when he wanted to set out for Tabuk: "O Jadd, would you not like to fight the sons of al-Asfar (the Byzantines), and take some of them as concubines and servants?" Jadd said: "My people know that I am enamoured of women, and I fear that if I see the sons of al-Asfar I will not be patient about them, so do not put me to trial, and grant me permission to stay behind, and I will help you with my wealth." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned away from him and said: "I have granted you permission." Then this verse was revealed, meaning: "Do not put me to trial by the beauty of their faces." He had no excuse except hypocrisy.

Al-Mahdawi said: Al-Asfar was a man from Abyssinia who had daughters, and at their time none were more beautiful than them, and he was in the land of the Romans. It was also said: they were named so because the Abyssinians overcame the Romans, and they bore them daughters who took from the whiteness of the Romans and the blackness of the Abyssinians, so they were yellowish and *luʿs* (having dark gums and lips) [[*Al-la'as*: the blackness of the gums and lip. It was also said: *al-la'as* and *al-la'sah*: a darkness that appears on the lip of a white woman. It was also said: it is a blackness within redness.]].

Ibn Atiyya said: There is weakness in the account of Ibn Ibn Ishaq. Al-Tabari related with a chain of narration that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Go out to fight, and you will seize the daughters of al-Asfar." Then Jadd said to him: "Grant us permission and do not put us to trial with women." This is a different line of interpretation, and it is more like hypocrisy and opposition [to Allah and His Messenger].

When this was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Banu Salima, and Jadd ibn Qays was among them: "Who is your chief, O Banu Salima?" They said: "Jadd ibn Qays, but he is stingy and a coward." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "And what disease is more harmful [[That is, what defect is uglier than it. Ibn al-Athir said: (The correct form is *adwa'* with a hamza, and its root is at the beginning of the chapter, but it is narrated thus, unless it is taken from the root *dawa*, *yadwa*, *dawan*, so that *fahuwa dawin* means one who perishes from an internal illness).]] than stinginess? Rather, your chief is the fair youth Bishr ibn al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur." Hassan ibn Thabit al-Ansari said about him:

"Bishr ibn al-Bara' was made a chief because of his generosity,
and Bishr ibn al-Bara' deserved to be made chief.
When the delegations came to him, he gave away his wealth,
and said: 'Take it, for I will return tomorrow.'"

﴿Surely they have fallen into trial﴾ (ألا في الفتنة سقطوا), meaning: they fell into sin and disobedience. This is hypocrisy and staying behind from the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿And indeed Hell encompasses the disbelievers﴾ (وإن جهنم لمحيطة بالكافرين), meaning: their path leads to the Fire, so it surrounds them.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿If good befalls you, it distresses them﴾. This is a conditional sentence with its response. Likewise ﴿and if a misfortune befalls you, they say, "We had already taken our precaution before," and they turn away﴾ is joined to it. *Al-hasanah* (good) is the spoil and victory, and *al-musibah* (misfortune) is defeat. The meaning of their saying "We had already taken our precaution before" (أخذنا أمرنا من قبل) is: we guarded ourselves, we took the path of caution, and so we did not go out to fight.

(And they turn away) means: from faith.

(And they are rejoicing) means: pleased with that and self-satisfied.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 9, verse 51:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Nothing will befall us except what Allah has decreed for us﴾. It was said: "In the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*)." It was also said: "It refers to what He informed us of in His Book, that we will either achieve victory, and victory will be a good outcome (*husna*) for us, or we will be killed, and martyrdom will be an even greater good outcome for us." The meaning is that everything is by decree and predestination (*qada' wa qadar*). This was already discussed in [al-A'raf], that knowledge, predestination and the Book are equivalent. [[See vol. 7, p. 203.]]

﴿He is our Protector (*mawlana*)﴾, i.e., our helper. And *tawakkul* (trust in Allah) is entrusting the matter to Him.

The reading of the majority is *yusibana* in the accusative (*nasb*) after *lan*. Abu Ubayda related that some Arabs use the jussive (*jazm*) with it. Talha ibn Musarrif read *hal yusibuna*. It is related from A'yan, the judge of al-Ray, that he read (*qul lan yusibana*) with a doubled *nun*. This is an error (*lahn*): the *nun* of emphasis (*nun al-tawkid*) is not attached to what is a statement (*khabar*). Had this been in the reading of Talha, it would have been permissible. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Will His scheme remove that which enrages?﴾ [al-Hajj: 15]. [[See vol. 12, p. 21.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 52:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Do you await for us anything but one of the two best things?﴾ The Kufans assimilate the lam into the ta' (idgham, assimilation of one letter into the next). As for the lam of definiteness (lam al-ma'rifa), assimilation is the only permissible form, as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿the repentant ones﴾ [al-Tawba: 112], because the lam of definiteness is very frequent in their speech. Assimilation is not permissible in His saying: ﴿Say: Come﴾ [al-An'am: 151], because "qul" (قُلْ) is weak (mu'tall), so they did not combine two causes for it. Al-tarabbus means waiting (al-intizar). One says: "tarabbasa bi-al-ta'am," meaning he waited with the food until the time of high prices. Al-husna is the feminine of al-ahsan (الأحسن). The singular of al-husnayayn is husna, and the plural is al-husna. It is not permissible to pronounce it except with the definite article (al-husna, الحسنى). One does not say "ra'aytu imra'atan husna" (I saw a woman, husna). The two best things (al-husnayayn) are the booty (al-ghanima) and martyrdom (al-shahada), as related from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others. The wording is a question, but the meaning is rebuke.

﴿And we await for you that Allah will afflict you with a punishment from Him﴾, i.e., a punishment that destroys you, as it struck the earlier nations before you.

﴿Or by our hands﴾, i.e., we are given permission to fight you.

﴿So await﴾: a threat and a warning. That is, await the promises of Satan; indeed we are awaiting the promises of Allah.

In it there are four issues.

**The first:** Ibn ʿAbbas said: It was revealed concerning al-Jadd ibn Qays, when he said, "Grant me leave to stay behind and do not put me to trial. Indeed, I will spend this wealth of mine on you" (Q. 9:49). The word "spend" (anfiqū) is an imperative, but its meaning is a condition and its response (al-sharṭ wa-l-jazāʾ). The Arabs use this construction with "or" (aw), as the poet said¹:

*Treat us harshly or treat us kindly, we will not be blamed*
*by you, nor will we be shunned, however you may turn.*

The meaning is: whether you treat us badly or well, we are as you know us. The meaning of the verse is: whether you spend willingly or under compulsion, it will not be accepted from you. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, explained why it is not accepted from them, saying: ﴿And nothing prevented their contributions from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger﴾ (Q. 9:54). This is therefore the strongest proof.

**The second:** This shows that the deeds of a disbeliever, if they are good deeds such as maintaining family ties, setting a broken bone, or relieving the distressed, are not rewarded in the Hereafter and do not benefit him there, though he is fed (rewarded) for them in this world. The evidence is what Muslim transmitted from ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, Ibn Judʿān used to maintain family ties and feed the poor in the Jahiliyyah. Will that benefit him?' He said: 'It will not benefit him, for he never once said, "My Lord, forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgment."'"

It is also reported from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah does not wrong a believer. A good deed of his is given to him in this world and he is recompensed for it in the Hereafter. As for the disbeliever, he is fed for the good deeds he did for Allah in this world, until when he reaches the Hereafter he has no good deed for which he is recompensed." This is an explicit text.

Then it was asked: Does the certainty of this true promise mean that a disbeliever must be fed and given his good deeds in this world, or is that restricted by the will of Allah mentioned in His saying: ﴿We hasten for him therein whatever We will, for whomever We intend﴾ (Q. 17:18)? This is the sounder of the two opinions, and Allah knows best. Calling what proceeds from a disbeliever a "good deed" is only according to the disbeliever's own assumption; otherwise, nothing of his can be a act of drawing near to Allah, because the condition that validates it, which is faith, is absent. Or it was called a good deed because it resembles the outward form of a believer's good deed. These are also two opinions.

**The third:** If it is said: Muslim transmitted from Hakīm ibn Ḥizām that he said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "O Messenger of Allah, tell me about the matters I used to practise (taḥannuth²) in the Jahiliyyah, such as charity, freeing slaves, or maintaining family ties. Is there a reward for them?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You have become Muslim with whatever good you had already done (aslamta ʿalā mā aslafta min khayr)." We say: his statement, "You have become Muslim with whatever good you had already done," apparently contradicts the principles, because a disbeliever cannot validly draw near to Allah, the Exalted, so he would not be rewarded for his obedience. For it is a condition of one who draws near that he knows the One to whom he draws near, and when the condition is absent, the validity of the conditioned act is negated.

So the meaning of the hadith is: you acquired good dispositions in the Jahiliyyah, which earned you a good habit in Islam. For Ḥakīm, may Allah be pleased with him, lived a hundred and twenty years, sixty in Islam and sixty in the Jahiliyyah. In the Jahiliyyah he freed a hundred slaves and gave a hundred camels as a mount, and he did the same in Islam. This is clear.

It has also been said: It is not unlikely, in the generosity of Allah, that He rewards him for doing that in Islam, just as He removes from him the sins he committed in his state of disbelief. Only the one who did not embrace Islam, did not repent, and died as a disbeliever is not rewarded. This is the apparent meaning of the hadith, and it is the sound view, if Allah wills. The absence of the condition of faith, which prevents reward for good he did before he embraced Islam, does not amount to a rational condition that cannot change once he has become Muslim and died a Muslim. Allah is too generous to waste his deed when his Islam is sound. Al-Ḥarbī interpreted the hadith in this sense, saying: "(You have become Muslim with whatever good you had already done)" means that the good you had previously done, which you performed, belongs to you. It is like saying, "I became Muslim for a thousand dirhams," meaning on condition that he keeps them for himself. And Allah knows best.

**The fourth:** If it is said: Muslim transmitted from al-ʿAbbās, who said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, [indeed] Abū Ṭālib used to protect you and support you. Did that benefit him?' He said: 'Yes. I found him in the depths of the Fire, so I brought him out to a shallow place (ḍaḥḍāḥ³).'" It is said in reply: It is not unlikely that some of the punishment of a disbeliever may be lightened by the good he did, but together with the addition of intercession, as came concerning Abū Ṭālib. As for others, the Revelation has informed us in His saying: ﴿So the intercession of the intercessors will not benefit them﴾ (Q. 74:48). And He said, reporting about the disbelievers: ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor any close friend﴾ (Q. 26:100–101). Muslim also transmitted from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was told about his uncle Abū Ṭālib, and he said: "Perhaps my intercession will benefit him on the Day of Resurrection, so that he will be placed in a shallow place of the Fire reaching to his ankles, whose brain will boil from it." From the hadith of al-ʿAbbās, [may Allah be pleased with him]: "And had it not been for me, he would have been in the lowest level of the Fire."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you were a people of defiant disobedience (qawman fāsiqīn)﴾ (Q. 9:54 cited in the verse text). That is, disbelievers.

---

¹ The poet is Kuthayyir ʿAzza, as in *al-Amālī* of Abū ʿAlī al-Qālī.
² Taḥannuth: worship.
³ Ḍaḥḍāḥ: originally, the thin layer of water on the surface of the ground that reaches up to the ankles; here used metaphorically for the Fire.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 54:

There are three issues in this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And nothing prevented them from having their contributions accepted from them except that they﴾. The first "an" (that) is in the accusative position, and the second is in the nominative position. The meaning is: "And nothing prevented them from having their contributions accepted from them except their disbelief." The Kufans read "an yuqbala minhum" with the ya' (yuqbala, in the masculine form), because "al-nafaqat" (the contributions) and "al-infaq" (the spending) are the same in meaning.

The second: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they do not come to the prayer except while they are lazy﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: If he was in a congregation, he prayed; and if he was alone, he did not pray. This is the one who neither hopes for reward for the prayer nor fears punishment for abandoning it. Hypocrisy therefore inevitably produces laziness in worship. The discussion of all of this has already been presented in [al-Nisa' (the chapter of Women)] [see vol. 5, p. 422]. We have also mentioned there the hadith of al-'Ala' [the correct reading is probably: the hadith of the Bedouin] in full. And all praise is due to Allah.

The third: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they do not spend except while they are unwilling﴾, because they regard it as a loss and withholding it as a gain. When the matter is like this, it is not accepted and no reward is given for it, as has been explained previously.

Therefore let not their wealth or their children impress you. Indeed, Allah intends only to punish them thereby in the life of this world, and that their souls should depart while they are disbelievers. (55) And they swear by Allah that they are surely of you, but they are not of you; rather they are a people who are afraid. (56) That is: do not regard as good what We have given them, nor incline toward it, for it is a gradual leading-on (istidraj). "Indeed, Allah intends only to punish them thereby" — al-Hasan said: the meaning is by paying the zakat and spending in the way of Allah. This is the choice of al-Tabari. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: there is a transposition (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, and the meaning is: "Therefore let not their wealth or their children impress you, in the life of this world. Indeed Allah intends only to punish them thereby in the Hereafter." This is the view of most of the people of Arabic grammar, as mentioned by al-Nahhas. It was also said: He punishes them with the toil of gathering (wealth). According to this interpretation and the view of al-Hasan there is no transposition in it, and it is good. It was also said: the meaning is: "Therefore let not their wealth or their children impress you. Indeed Allah intends only to punish them thereby in this world, because they are hypocrites; they spend unwillingly, so they are punished by what they spend."

(And their souls depart while they are disbelievers) is a clear statement that Allah intends that they should die as disbelievers; that decree has already preceded.

(And they swear by Allah that they are surely of you) It makes clear that among the traits of the hypocrites is swearing that they are believers. Its parallel is the verse: ﴿When the hypocrites come to you, they say: We testify that you are surely the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1] and so on. Al-Faraq means fear; that is, they fear that they will reveal what they are upon and be killed.

Therefore let not their wealth or their children impress you. Indeed, Allah intends only to punish them thereby in the life of this world, and that their souls should depart while they are disbelievers. (55) And they swear by Allah that they are surely of you, but they are not of you; rather they are a people who are afraid. (56) That is: do not regard as good what We have given them, nor incline toward it, for it is a gradual leading-on (istidraj). "Indeed, Allah intends only to punish them thereby" — al-Hasan said: the meaning is by paying the zakat and spending in the way of Allah. This is the choice of al-Tabari. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: there is a transposition (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, and the meaning is: "Therefore let not their wealth or their children impress you, in the life of this world. Indeed Allah intends only to punish them thereby in the Hereafter." This is the view of most of the people of Arabic grammar, as mentioned by al-Nahhas. It was also said: He punishes them with the toil of gathering (wealth). According to this interpretation and the view of al-Hasan there is no transposition in it, and it is good. It was also said: the meaning is: "Therefore let not their wealth or their children impress you. Indeed Allah intends only to punish them thereby in this world, because they are hypocrites; they spend unwillingly, so they are punished by what they spend."

(And their souls depart while they are disbelievers) is a clear statement that Allah intends that they should die as disbelievers; that decree has already preceded.

(And they swear by Allah that they are surely of you) It makes clear that among the traits of the hypocrites is swearing that they are believers. Its parallel is the verse: ﴿When the hypocrites come to you, they say: We testify that you are surely the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1] and so on. Al-Faraq means fear; that is, they fear that they will reveal what they are upon and be killed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 57:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Had they found a refuge﴾. Thus is the pause upon it. In the script it is written with two alifs: the first is a hamza, and the second is a substitute for the tanwin; likewise [I saw] in a part [of the Qur'an]. Al-maljaʼ (refuge) is the fortress, according to Qatadah and others. Ibn ʻAbbas said: it is the shelter (al-hirz), and the two are the same. It is said: "I sought refuge with him (lajaʼtu ilayhi lajaʼan)" [[This is the expression of al-Jawhari in his Sihah. What is in al-Lisan and al-Qamus is that it is said lajaʼa lajaʼan, like manaʻa manʻan; and lajiʼa lajaʼan, like fariha farahan]] and malja'an, and "iltajaʼtu ilayhi" has the same meaning. The place is also called lajaʼan and malja'an. Al-talji'ah means coercion. "Alja'tuhu ila al-shay'" means I compelled him to it. "Alja'tu amri ila Allah" means I entrusted my affair to Allah. ʻAmr ibn Lajaʼ al-Tamimi the poet, according to al-Jawhari [[So it is in the Sihah of al-Jawhari (al-Tamimi). The correct form is (al-Taymi), because he is from Taym ibn ʻAbd Manat ibn Udd Tabikha. ʻAmr ibn Lajaʼ died in al-Ahwaz, and he used to lampoon Jarir. (From Al-Shi'r wa al-Shu'ara').]].

(Or caves) is the plural of maghara, from ghara yaghiru. Al-Akhfash said: it may also be from aghara yughiru, as the poet said:

Praise be to Allah, our evening and our morning [[This is the first half of a lamiyyah verse by Ibn Abi al-Salt. Its second half is: "with good we have been greeted, my Lord, and our evening."]]

Ibn ʻAbbas said: al-maghharat are the caves and the underground passages, which are the places where one hides; and from it come "the water sank (ghara al-ma')" and "the eye sank (ghaarat al-ʻayn)."

(Or a hiding place) is muftaʻal from entering (al-dukhul), i.e., a passage by entering which we would be concealed; and it is repeated because of the difference of wording. Al-Nahhas said: the original form is mudtakhal; the taʼ was changed to dal, because dal is voiced and taʼ is voiceless, and both come from the same place of articulation. It was also said: the original is mutadakhkhal on the pattern mutafaʻʻal, as in the reading of Ubayy: "aw mutadakhkhalan," meaning entry after entry, i.e., a people who would enter with them. Al-Mahdawi: mutadakhkhilan from tadakhkhala, on the pattern of tafaʻʻala, when one exerts oneself to enter. And from Ubayy also: mundakhalan from indakhala, which is anomalous, because its triliteral form is not transitive according to Sibawayh and his companions. Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ibn Muhaysin read: "aw madkhalan" with a fatha on the mim and sukun on the dal. Al-Zajjaj said: it is also read "aw mudkhalan" with a damma on the mim and sukun on the dal. The first is from dakhala yadkhulu; the second from adkhala yudkhilu. Likewise the verbal noun, the place and the time, as Sibawayh recited:

Maghara Ibn Hammam upon the tribe of Khath'am [[This is the second half of a verse by Humayd ibn Thawr. Its first half is: "And she was only in a wrapper and an ʻalaqah."

It describes a woman who was young in age and wore the ʻalaqah, which is a garment of girls: a short tunic without sleeves, worn by a young girl while playing, also called al-atib and al-buqayrah; she wore it at the time of Ibn Hammam's raid on this tribe. Khath'am is a tribe of Yemen.]]

It is narrated from Qatadah, Isa and al-A'mash: "aw mudakhkhalan," with shadda on the dal and the kha'. The majority read with shadda on the dal alone, meaning a place into which they would make themselves enter. These are six readings.

(They would have turned to it) i.e., they would have returned to it.

(While they would rush headlong) i.e., they would hurry, with nothing turning their faces back, from jamaha al-faras, when the bridle does not turn it back. The poet said:

Swift in its gallop, and its charging... like the crackling of the blazing palm fronds [[The verse is by Imru' al-Qays. Al-ihdar means running.]]

The meaning: if they found any of these things mentioned, they would have turned to it hastening in flight from the Muslims.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 58:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities﴾, meaning: who slander you, according to Qatadah. Al-Hasan said: who blames you. Mujahid said: meaning: who asks you (repeatedly)." [Text as given: "وَيَسْأَلُكَ" – "and asks you"]

Al-Nahhas said: The saying among the people of linguistics (ahl al-lughah) is the saying of Qatadah and al-Hasan. It is said: lamazahu yalmizuhu, when he finds fault with him. And al-lamz in the language is blaming in secret. Al-Jawhari said: al-lamz is blaming, and its origin is signaling with the eye or the like. It has been recited as yalmizuhu and yalmizuhu, and both have been read: "And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities." A man who is a lammaz and lumazah means one who blames much. It is also said: lamazahu yalmizuhu, meaning he pushed him and struck him. Al-hamz is like al-lamz. Al-hamiz and al-hammaz mean one who blames, and al-humazah is like it. It is said: a man is humazah, and a woman is humazah as well. And hamazahu means he pushed him and struck him. Then it was said: al-lamz is to the face, and al-hamz is behind one's back.

Allah described a group of the hypocrites as having found fault with the Prophet ﷺ regarding the distribution of the charities, and claiming that they were poor so that he would give to them.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: While the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was dividing some wealth, Hurqus ibn Zuhayr, the origin of the Kharijites, who is also called Dhu al-Khuwaysirah al-Tamimi, came to him and said: "Be just, O Messenger of Allah." He said: (Woe to you! Who would be just if I am not just?) Then the verse was revealed. A sound hadith, related by Muslim in meaning. At that point, Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Let me, O Messenger of Allah, and I will kill this hypocrite." He said: (Allah forbid that people should say that I kill my companions. Indeed this man and his companions recite the Qur'an, but it does not go past their throats; they pass through it as an arrow passes through the game.)

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger had given them⦆. The answer to "law" (if/if only) is omitted; the meaning is: "it would have been better for them."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 60 (part 1 of 7):

There are thirty issues in this verse. The first: His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿Alms are only for the poor﴾. Allah, glorified is He, singled out some people with wealth and not others, as a blessing from Him to them. He made the thanks for this from them to be setting aside a portion to be paid to those who have no wealth, as a deputy for Him, glorified is He, in what He guaranteed by His statement: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah﴾ [Hud: 6].[[See vol. 9, p. 6.]]

The second: His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿for the poor﴾ is a specification of the recipients (masarif) and the place (mahall) of the alms (sadaqat), so that they do not go outside of them. Then, the choice of who distributes them is left to the one who distributes them. This is the view of Malik, Abu Hanifa and their companions, just as one says: "The saddle is for the animal" and "the door is for the house." Al-Shafi'i said: the lam is the lam of ownership (tamlik), as in your saying: "The wealth is for Zayd, 'Amr and Bakr," so it is necessary to equalize among those mentioned. Al-Shafi'i and his companions said: This is like when one bequeaths to specific categories or to specific people. They argued with the word "innama" (only), that it implies restriction of the endowment of alms to the eight categories, and they reinforced this with the hadith of Ziyad ibn al-Harith al-Suda'i, who said: "I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was sending an army to my people. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, hold back your army, for I guarantee their Islam and their obedience.' I wrote to my people, and their Islam and obedience came." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O brother of Sada, obeyed among his people!" He said: I said: "Rather, Allah bestowed favour upon them and guided them." He said: Then a man came to him asking about the alms, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Indeed Allah was not pleased to leave the alms to the judgment of a prophet or anyone else until He divided them into eight portions. So if you are from the people of those portions, I will give you." Narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni, and the wording is that of al-Daraqutni.

It is reported from Zayn al-Abidin that he said: He, the Exalted, knew the amount of zakat that is to be given and what suffices for these categories, and made it a right for all of them. So whoever withholds that from them is the one who wrongs them and deprives them of their provision.

Our scholars held to the statement of the Exalted: ﴿If you disclose your charities, then they are good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 271].[[See vol. 3, p. 332.]] And "sadaqa" wherever it is mentioned without qualification in the Qur'an, it means obligatory charity (sadaqat al-fard). He (ﷺ) said: "I have been commanded to take the charity from your rich and return it to your poor." This is an explicit text that mentions one of the eight categories, in both the Qur'an and the Sunnah. This is the view of Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ali, Ibn Abbas and Hudhayfa, and a group of the Successors (tabi'un) also held it. They said: It is permissible to give it to the eight categories, and if it is given to any one category, it is permissible.

Al-Minhal ibn Amr narrated from Zirr ibn Hubaysh from Hudhayfa, regarding the statement: "Alms are only for the poor and the needy," he said: "Allah only mentioned these charities so that they would be known, and whichever category you give to, it suffices for you." Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn Abbas: "Alms are only for the poor and the needy," he said: "Whichever of them you place it in, it suffices for you." This is also the view of al-Hasan, Ibrahim and others. Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: Malik even claimed consensus on this. I say: He means the consensus of the Companions, for no one is known to have opposed them among them, according to what Abu Umar said. And Allah knows best. Ibn al-'Arabi said: What we have taken as the decisive ruling between us and them is that the community agreed that if each category is given its share, it is not obligatory to generalize it to all of them; likewise, generalizing among the categories is similar to that. And Allah knows best.

The third: The scholars of language and jurisprudence differed on the distinction between the faqir (poor) and the miskin (needy) in nine opinions. Ya'qub ibn al-Sikkit, al-Qutabi and Yunus ibn Habib held that the faqir is in a better condition than the miskin. They said: The faqir is the one who has some of what suffices him and sustains him, while the miskin is the one who has nothing. They cited the verse of al-Ra'i:

As for the faqir whose milch-camel
was sufficient for his dependents, nothing of his hair-wool was left.[[al-Sabad: wool, or it is said hair. The Arabs say: "He has no sabad and no labad," meaning he has no woolly or matted-wool animal, and they refer by these to camels and sheep.]]

A group of the people of language and hadith held this view, among them Abu Hanifa and al-Qadi Abd al-Wahhab. The wafq (sufficiency) from the agreement of two things, like the joining together. It is said: "His milch-camel is wafq (sufficient for) his dependents," meaning it has milk sufficient for their needs with no surplus in it, according to al-Jawhari. Others said the opposite, and made the miskin in a better condition than the faqir. They cited the statement of the Exalted: ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to poor people who worked on the sea﴾ [al-Kahf: 79].[[See vol. 11, p. 33 onward.]] So He informed that they had a boat from the boats of the sea, and perhaps it was equal to a substantial amount of wealth. They reinforced this with what is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he sought refuge from poverty (faqr).
