And it is reported from him that he said: "O Allah, let me live as a miskin and let me die as a miskin." So if the miskin were in a worse condition than the faqir, the two reports would contradict each other, for it is impossible that he seeks refuge from poverty and then asks for what is worse than it. Allah answered his supplication and took him while he had of what Allah had granted him (fai'), but he did not have the full sufficiency, and for this reason he pledged his coat of mail. They said: As for the verse of al-Ra'i, there is no proof in it, because he only mentioned that the faqir had a milch-camel at one time. They said: The faqir in the language of the Arabs means the one whose spine (fiqar) has been removed from his back because of extreme poverty, so there is no state more severe than this. Allah has informed about them with His statement: ﴿They cannot strike about in the land﴾ [al-Baqarah: 273].[[See vol. 3, p. 339.]] And they cited the verse of the poet:

When he saw the vultures of Labad scattering,
he raised his primary feathers like the helpless faqir.[[The verse is by Labid. Labad: the name of the last of the vultures of Luqman ibn Ad, named so because he was (a lasting one), so he remained and neither departed nor died. The qawadim: four or ten feathers at the front of the wing, singular qadima.]]

meaning he was not able to fly, so he became like one whose spine has been severed and clung to the ground. This was the view of al-Asma'i and others, and al-Tahawi reported it from the Kufans. And it is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i and most of his companions. Al-Shafi'i has another opinion: that the faqir and the miskin are equal, with no difference between them in meaning, though they differ in name, and this is the third view. This was also the view of Ibn al-Qasim and the rest of Malik's companions, and Abu Yusuf also said this.

I say: The apparent wording indicates that the miskin is other than the faqir, and that they are two categories, except that one of the two is in greater need than the other. From this aspect, the view of those who made them one category is close to correct. And Allah knows best.

There is no proof in the view of those who argued with the statement of the Exalted: ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to poor people﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], because it is possible that they were renters of it, just as one says: "This is the house of so-and-so" when he is its occupant even if it belongs to someone else. And the Exalted said in describing the people of the Fire: ﴿And for them are hooks of iron﴾ [al-Hajj: 21], attributing them to them. And He said: ﴿And do not give the foolish your wealth﴾ [al-Nisa: 5]. And he (ﷺ) said: "Whoever sells a slave who has wealth..." and this is very common, where a thing is attributed to someone while it is not his. From this come the sayings: "the door of the house," "the saddle-cloth of the animal," "the saddle of the horse," and the like. It is also permissible that they be called masakin out of mercy and pleading, just as one says of someone afflicted with a calamity or subjected to a trial: "miskin." And in a hadith: "The poor (masakin) of the people of the Fire." And the poet said:

The wretched ones of the lovers, even their graves
have upon them the dust of humiliation among the tombs.

As for what they interpreted from his, peace be upon him, saying: "O Allah, let me live as a miskin," the hadith narrated by Anas, it is not so; rather the meaning here is humility before Allah, which has no arrogance in it, no haughtiness, no pride, no vanity, no self-aggrandizement, and no insolence. Abu al-Atahiya said well when he said:

If you want the noblest of all the people,
look at a king in the garb of a miskin.
That is the one whose desire for what is with Allah is great,
and that one is fit for this world and for religion.

And he is not the one who asks, because the Prophet (ﷺ) disliked asking and forbade it, and he said about a black woman who refused to move from the road: "Leave her, for she is a tyrant (jabbara)."[[That is, arrogant and insolent.]] As for the statement of the Exalted: ﴿for the poor who are restricted in the way of Allah, who cannot strike about in the land﴾ [al-Baqarah: 273], it is not impossible that they have wealth. And Allah knows best. What the companions of Malik and al-Shafi'i held, that they are equal, is good. Close to it is what Malik said in the book of Ibn Sahnun: "The faqir is the needy one who abstains (from asking), and the miskin is the one who asks." This was also reported from Ibn Abbas, said by al-Zuhri, and chosen by Ibn Sha'ban,[[This is how it appears in all the manuscripts: he is Muhammad ibn al-Qasim ibn Sha'ban, to whom the leadership of the Malikis in Egypt ended; he died in the year 355. In one manuscript it reads "Ibn Sufyan," which is an error.]] and this is the fourth view.

A fifth view: Muhammad ibn Maslama said: The faqir is the one who has a dwelling and a servant, and what is below that. And the miskin is the one who has no wealth. I say: This view is the reverse of what is established in Sahih Muslim from Abdullah ibn Amr, when a man asked him: "Are we not among the poor emigrants?" Abdullah said to him: "Do you have a wife to whom you return?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Do you have a dwelling in which you live?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then you are among the wealthy." He said: "But I have a servant." He said: "Then you are among the kings."

A sixth view: It is reported from Ibn Abbas that he said: The fuqara' are from the emigrants, and the masakin are from the Bedouins who did not emigrate. Al-Dahhak also said so.

A seventh view: The miskin is the one who is humble and submissive, even if he does not ask. The faqir is the one who bears with patience and accepts a thing in secret and is not humble. This was said by Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hasan.

An eighth view, said by Mujahid, Ikrimah and al-Zuhri: The masakin are the wanderers, and the fuqara' are the poor among the Muslims.

A ninth view, also said by Ikrimah: the fuqara' are the poor of the Muslims, and the masakin are the poor of the People of the Book. This will come later.

The fourth issue: It is the benefit of the disagreement about the poor and the needy, whether they are one category or more. It appears in the case of one who bequeaths a third of his wealth to so-and-so and to the poor and the needy. Whoever says they are one category says: So-and-so receives half of the third, and the poor and the needy receive the second half of the third. Whoever says they are two categories divides the third among them into thirds.

The fifth issue: The scholars differed on the limit of poverty with which it is permissible to take. After the consensus of most of those known from the people of knowledge that whoever has a house and a servant which he cannot do without, he may take from zakat, and the giver may give to him. Malik used to say: If there is no surplus in the price of the house and the servant beyond what he needs of them, it is permissible for him to take; otherwise it is not permissible. Ibn al-Mundhir reported this. An-Nakha'i and al-Thawri also held the view of Malik. Abu Hanifa said: Whoever has twenty dinars or two hundred dirhams, he should not take from zakat.

Al-Qurtubi's commentary on Surah 9, verse 60 (part 2 of 7):

He took the nisab as the basis, based on the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "I have been commanded to take charity from your wealthy and return it to your poor." This is clear, and al-Mughira narrated it from Malik. Al-Thawri, Ahmad, Ishaq and others said: one who has fifty dirhams, or its value in gold, may not take it, and one may not be given more than fifty dirhams from it unless one is a gharim (one in debt). This is what Ahmad and Ishaq said. The evidence for this view is what al-Daraqutni narrated from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Charity is not lawful for a man who has fifty dirhams." In its isnad is Abd al-Rahman ibn Ishaq, who is weak, and from him Bakr ibn Khunays, who is also weak. Hakim ibn Jubayr narrated it from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid, from his father, from Abdullah, from the Prophet ﷺ, something similar, and he said: "fifty dirhams." Hakim ibn Jubayr is weak; Shu'ba and others abandoned him, as al-Daraqutni said, may Allah have mercy on him. Abu Umar said: this hadith revolves around Hakim ibn Jubayr, and he is matruk (abandoned). It is also narrated from Ali and Abdullah that they said: "Charity is not lawful for one who has fifty dirhams or its value in gold," mentioned by al-Daraqutni. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: one who has forty dirhams may not take it. This was narrated by al-Waqidi from Malik. The evidence for this view is what al-Daraqutni narrated from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: "Whoever asks people while he is wealthy will come on the Day of Resurrection with scratches and gashes on his face." It was asked: "O Messenger of Allah, what is his wealth?" He said: "Forty dirhams." In the hadith of Malik, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Ata ibn Yasar, from a man of Banu Asad, the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever among you asks while he has an uqiyya or its equivalent has asked insistently, and the uqiyya is forty dirhams." The well-known position of Malik is what Ibn al-Qasim narrated from him: he was asked, "May one be given from zakat if he has forty dirhams?" He said, "Yes." Abu Umar said: it is possible that the first (group's view) refers to one strong in earning a living and skilled in managing it, and the second to one weak in earning, or one who has dependants. And Allah knows best. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr said: whoever is strong in earning and trading, with physical strength and good management, to the point that this suffices him from people, then charity to him is haram. They argued with the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Charity is not lawful for the wealthy, nor for one who has strength (mirra) and is sound (sawiyy)." This was narrated by Abdullah ibn Umar, and Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Daraqutni recorded it. [Note: al-Mirra (with a kasra): strength and vigour. Sawiyy: one whose limbs are sound.] Jabir narrated: charity came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the people mounted it, and he said: "It is not fit for the wealthy, nor for the able-bodied, nor for a worker," recorded by al-Daraqutni. Abu Dawud narrated from Ubayd Allah ibn Adi ibn al-Khiyar, who said: two men informed me that they came to the Prophet ﷺ during the Farewell Pilgrimage while he was distributing charity, and they asked him for some of it. He looked at us, raising and lowering his gaze, and saw that we were strong, and said: "If you wish, I will give you, but there is no share in it for the wealthy nor for the strong earner." Also, one who has become wealthy through his earnings is like one who is wealthy through his property, so each of them is independent of asking. This was said by Ibn Khuwayz Mindad, and he related it from the school. This should not be relied upon, for the Prophet ﷺ used to give it to the poor, and restricting it to the disabled is invalid. Abu Isa al-Tirmidhi said in his Jami': if a man is strong and in need, and has nothing, and charity is given to him, it suffices for the giver according to the scholars. The meaning of the hadith, according to some scholars, relates to asking. Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: the apparent meaning requires that this is permissible, because he is poor despite his strength and physical health. Abu Hanifa and his companions said the same. Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hasan said: one who does not have what suffices him and maintains him for a year may be given zakat. His evidence is what Ibn Shihab narrated from Malik ibn Aws ibn al-Hadathan, from Umar ibn al-Khattab, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to store from what Allah gave him as spoils a year's provision, then put what was beyond that into al-kura' (horses) and weapons, together with His Exalted saying: ﴿And He found you poor and made you rich﴾ [al-Duha: 8]. [Note: al-Kura' (with a damma): a collective term for horses. It is said: a term for horses and weapons together.] Some scholars said: each person may take from charity what he needs. Some people said: whoever has the dinner of one night is wealthy, and this is narrated from Ali. They argued with the hadith of Ali from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Whoever asks a question while having the means of wealth has amassed for himself hot stones (radf) of Jahannam." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the means of wealth?" He said: "The dinner of one night." [Note: al-Radf: stones heated in the fire.] Al-Daraqutni recorded it and said: its isnad includes Amr ibn Khalid, who is matruk. Abu Dawud also recorded it from Sahl ibn al-Hanzaliyya from the Prophet ﷺ, and in it: "Whoever asks while he has what suffices him is only multiplying for himself from the Fire." Al-Nufayli said in another place: "from the embers of Jahannam." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, what suffices him?" Al-Nufayli said in another place: "What is the wealth which makes asking inappropriate?" He said: "The amount that feeds him at lunch and dinner." Al-Nufayli said in another place: "That he has the fill of a day and a night, or a night and a day." I say: this is what has come regarding the explanation of the poverty which permits taking. The general term "the poor" does not require restriction to Muslims to the exclusion of the People of the Covenant (dhimmis), but the reports are consistent that charities are taken from the wealthy Muslims and returned to their poor. Ikrima said: "the poor" are the poor among the Muslims, and "the needy" (al-masakin) are the poor among the People of the Book. Abu Bakr al-Absi said: Umar ibn al-Khattab saw a blind dhimmi thrown at the gate of Madina, and Umar said to him: "What is your condition?" He said: "They forced me to pay this jizya, and when my sight failed, they abandoned me, and I have no one who gives me anything." Umar said: "You have not been treated justly, then." He ordered that he be given his sustenance and what sustains him. Then he said: "This is one of those of whom Allah the Exalted said: 'Charity is only for the poor and the needy' — the verse," and they are the disabled of the People of the Book. When Allah the Exalted said: "Charity is only for the poor and the needy..." the verse, and matched the sentence with a sentence—the sentence of charity with the sentence of its expenditure—the Prophet ﷺ made that clear, saying to Mu'adh when he sent him to Yemen: "Inform them that Allah has enjoined upon them a charity taken from their wealthy and returned to their poor." So the people of each land are entitled to the zakat of their own land. Abu Dawud narrated that Ziyad, or some of the governors, sent Imran ibn Husayn to collect charity, and when he returned, [the governor] said to Imran: "Where is the wealth?" He said: "Did you send me for wealth! We took it from where we used to take it during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and we placed it where we used to place it during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." Al-Daraqutni and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Awn ibn Abi Juhayfa, from his father, who said: the Prophet's ﷺ collector came to us, took charity from our wealthy and placed it among our poor, and I was an orphan boy, and he gave me a young she-camel from it. Al-Tirmidhi said: and on this subject there is a report from Ibn Abbas; the hadith of Ibn Abi Juhayfa is a hasan hadith.

The sixth issue: The scholars differed about transferring zakat from its place (of collection) into three positions. (First) it may not be transferred; this was said by Sahnun and Ibn al-Qasim, and it is the correct view because of what we have mentioned. Ibn al-Qasim also said: "If some of it is transferred out of necessity, I consider that correct." It is narrated from Sahnun that he said: "If the ruler learns that in some lands there is severe need, it is permissible for him to transfer some of the charity due to those lands to them, for when need arises it becomes obligatory to give priority to those who are in need over those who are not in need (and the Muslim is the brother of the Muslim: he does not abandon him nor wrong him)." [Note: i.e., does not leave him with one who would harm him, but protects him.] The second position: it may be transferred; this was also said by Malik. The evidence for this view is what is reported: that Mu'adh said to the people of Yemen: "Bring me a khamis or labis, which I will take from you instead of maize and barley for the charity, for it is easier for you and more beneficial for the emigrants in Madina." Al-Daraqutni and others recorded it. Khamis is a term with multiple meanings; here it means a garment five cubits long. It is said it was named this because the first to make it was Khumus, a king of the kings of Yemen, as mentioned by Ibn Faris in al-Mujmal and also al-Jawhari. In this hadith there are two proofs. The first: what we have mentioned about transferring zakat from Yemen to Madina, where the Prophet ﷺ would himself take charge of distributing it. This is supported by His saying: ﴿Charity is only for the poor﴾, and He did not distinguish between the poor of one land and the poor of another. And Allah knows best. The second: taking the value in zakat. The reports from Malik differ on paying the value of zakat; he permitted it once and forbade it another time. The basis for permissibility, which is the view of Abu Hanifa, is this hadith. And it is established in Sahih al-Bukhari from the hadith of Anas, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever has reached (the number of camels) for which the due is a jadha'a, but does not have a jadha'a and has a hiqqa, it will be accepted from him, and he will be given two sheep if he can find them, or twenty dirhams" (the hadith). And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Enrich them from begging on this day," meaning the day of Fitr. He only meant that they should be made free of need by what satisfies their need, so whatever satisfies their need is permissible. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [al-Tawba: 103], and did not specify one thing over another. According to Abu Hanifa, it is not permissible to give the use of a dwelling in place of zakat; for example, if five dirhams were due from him and he housed a poor person in a dwelling for a month, this is not permitted, because housing is not property.

**Translation:**

The reasoning of the one who says: "They do not suffice" (and this is the apparent position of the school) is that the Prophet ﷺ said: "For every five camels, a sheep; and for forty sheep, a sheep." He specified the sheep. So if he does not bring it, he has not brought what was commanded, and if he has not brought what was commanded, the obligation remains upon him.

The third opinion is that the share of the poor and the needy is distributed in the locality, while the remaining shares are transferred at the discretion of the ruler (imam).

The first opinion is more sound. And Allah knows best.

**The seventh issue:** Is the consideration the location of the wealth at the completion of the lunar year, so that the charity is distributed there, or the location of the owner, since he is the one addressed? There are two opinions. The second was chosen by Abu Abdullah Muhammad ibn Khuwayz Mandad in his book *Ahkam*. He said: "Because the person is the one addressed with paying it, so the wealth follows him, and therefore the ruling must be according to where the addressee is, like the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil), who is wealthy in his own land and poor in another land, so the ruling applies to him wherever he is."

**Issue:** The reports from Malik differ concerning one who gave to a Muslim poor person and it became clear afterward that he had given to a slave, a non-Muslim, or a wealthy person. On one occasion he said it suffices him, and on another occasion he said it does not suffice him.

The reasoning for sufficiency, which is the more sound view, is what Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "A man said, 'I will surely give charity tonight.' He went out with his charity and placed it in the hand of a prostitute. In the morning the people were talking: 'Charity was given last night to a prostitute.' He said, 'O Allah, all praise is for You; I will give charity again.' He went out with his charity and placed it in the hand of a wealthy person. In the morning the people were talking: 'Charity was given to a wealthy person.' He said, 'O Allah, all praise is for You, for a prostitute and for a wealthy person; I will give charity again.' He went out with his charity and placed it in the hand of a thief. In the morning the people were talking: 'Charity was given to a thief.' He said, 'O Allah, all praise is for You, for a prostitute, a wealthy person, and a thief.' Then he was told: 'As for your charity, it has been accepted. As for the prostitute, perhaps it will keep her chaste from her fornication; perhaps the wealthy person will reflect and spend from what Allah has given him; and perhaps the thief will be kept chaste from his theft.'"

It is also reported that a man paid the zakat of his wealth and gave it to his father. When he awoke, he learned of this, so he asked the Prophet ﷺ, and he said to him: "The reward of your zakat has been recorded for you, and the reward of maintaining the ties of kinship; so you have two rewards."

From the perspective of meaning, the law permits him to exercise ijtihad (independent judgment) in choosing the recipient. So if he exercises ijtihad and gives to one whom he believes to be among its recipients, he has fulfilled what is obligatory upon him.

The reasoning of the one who says: "It does not suffice" is that he did not place it with its rightful recipient, so it resembles deliberate misplacement. Also, deliberate and accidental wrongdoing are equal regarding the liability for property, so he must be liable for what he destroyed, until he delivers it to the poor.

**The eighth issue:** If one pays zakat at its due time and it is then lost without negligence, he is not liable, because he is an agent (wakil) of the poor. If he pays it after a period has passed and it is then lost, he is liable, because he delayed it beyond its due time, so it became attached to his obligation; therefore he is liable. And Allah knows best.

**The ninth issue:** When the ruler is just in collecting and distributing, it is not permissible for the owner to take charge of distribution himself, whether in cash (nadd) or in other forms of property. [Nadd (cash): it refers to dirhams and dinars, and it is called nadd only when it has been converted into money after having been goods.] It has been said: the zakat on cash is owed to its owners. Ibn al-Majishun said: that applies when the distribution is exclusively to the poor and the needy; but if the funds are needed for other categories, then none may distribute them except the ruler. The branches of this topic are many, and these are its foundations.

**The tenth issue:** The words of the Exalted: ﴿And those employed to collect them﴾ refer to the collectors and tax-gatherers whom the ruler sends to collect zakat, by appointment for this task. Al-Bukhari narrated from Abu Humayd al-Sa'idi, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ appointed a man from the Azd tribe over the sadaqat of Banu Sulaym, called Ibn al-Lutbiyyah. When he came back, he settled accounts with him. [The pronunciation of his name differs: some say al-Lutbiyyah with a damma on the lam and a sukun on the taa; it is also reported with a fatha. Some say it is with a fatha on the lam and the letter taa with a mathnah. His name was Abdullah, and he was from Banu Tawlab, a tribe of the Azd. Some say al-Lutbiyyah was his mother.]

The scholars differ about the amount they may take, in three opinions. Mujahid and al-Shafi'i said it is one-eighth. Ibn Umar and Malik said they are given an amount equal to their work as a wage; this is also the view of Abu Hanifah and his companions. They said: "Because he has devoted himself to the interest of the poor, his sustenance and that of his assistants is to be met from their wealth, like a woman who devotes herself to her husband's right, whose maintenance and that of her attendants, one or two servants, is owed by her husband." It is not measured as one-eighth; rather, sufficiency is the criterion, whether it be one-eighth or more, like the provision of a judge. The sufficiency of assistants is not considered in our time, because that would be pure extravagance.

The third opinion: they are given from the public treasury (bayt al-mal). Ibn al-Arabi said: "This is a sound view from Malik ibn Anas, transmitted through Ibn Abi Uways and Dawud ibn Sa'id ibn Zanbu'ah, but it is weak in its evidence, for Allah, glory be to Him, has already stated their share in it explicitly; so how can they be left out by inference and examination?" The sound view is ijtihad regarding the amount of the wage, because the specification in enumerating the categories was for the place (where the funds are spent), not for the entitled person, as previously explained.

They differed concerning the collector if he was a Hashimi (of the Banu Hashim). Abu Hanifah prohibited it, based on the Prophet's words, peace be upon him: "Charity is not lawful for the family of Muhammad; it is only the filth of people." This is charity in one respect, since it is a part of charity, so it is completely equivalent to charity in every respect, as an honour and a purification for the kinship of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from the residue of people. Malik and al-Shafi'i permitted his work, and he is given the wage of his labour, because the Prophet ﷺ sent Ali ibn Abi Talib as a collector, and he sent him as an official to Yemen for zakat; he also appointed a group from Banu Hashim, and the caliphs after him did the same. Moreover, he is a hired worker for a permissible task, so it is necessary that the Hashimi and others be equal in it, by analogy with all other trades. The Hanafiyyah said: the hadith of Ali does not state that he assigned him a share from the charity; if he assigned him from other than charity, it is permissible. This has also been reported from Malik.

**The eleventh issue:** The words of the Exalted: ﴿And those employed to collect them﴾ indicate that every task that is a communal obligation (fard kifayah), such as the collector, the scribe, the divider of shares, the customs officer, and others, the one who performs it may take a wage for it. Among these is leading prayer (imamah), for although prayer is obligatory upon all creation, the leadership of some of them in it is a communal obligation; therefore it is undoubtedly permissible to take a wage for it. This is the foundation of the matter, and the Prophet ﷺ alluded to it when he said: "What I leave after my own expenses and the maintenance of my workers is charity." Ibn al-Arabi said this. [In Ibn al-Arabi: "my dependents" instead of "my workers".]

**The twelfth issue:** The words of the Exalted: ﴿those whose hearts are to be reconciled﴾ are not mentioned in the revelation except in the division of charities. They were people in the early period of Islam who professed Islam, and they are reconciled (mu'allafah) by giving them a portion of charity because of the weakness of their conviction. Al-Zuhri said: "Those whose hearts are reconciled are those who embraced Islam from among Jews or Christians, even if they were wealthy." Some later scholars said: the nature of these people has been disputed. It is said they are a category of disbelievers who are given so that they may be reconciled to Islam, since they would not embrace Islam by force and the sword, but would embrace it through gifts and kindness. It is also said they are people who professed Islam outwardly but whose hearts were not certain, so they are given so that Islam may take firm root in their hearts. It is also said they are people of high standing among the polytheists who had followers, so they are given so that they may reconcile their followers to Islam. He said: "These opinions are close to one another, and the purpose of all of them is giving to those whose Islam cannot be firmly established except through giving; it is thus a kind of jihad." The polytheists are of three types: one type is reached through the establishment of proof; one type through force; and one type through kindness. The imam who looks after the Muslims uses with each type whatever he sees as a means to their salvation and deliverance from disbelief.

In the Sahih of Muslim, from the hadith of Anas, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said (he meant to the Ansar): "I give to men who are recent in their disbelief, to reconcile them..." the hadith continues. Ibn Ishaq said: "He gave them in order to reconcile them, and to reconcile their people through them. They were nobles. He gave Abu Sufyan ibn Harb one hundred camels, gave his son one hundred camels, gave Hakim ibn Hizam one hundred camels, gave al-Harith ibn Hisham one hundred camels, gave Suhayl ibn Amr one hundred camels, gave Huwaytib ibn Abd al-Uzza one hundred camels, and gave Safwan ibn Umayya one hundred camels. Likewise he gave Malik ibn Awf and al-Ala ibn Jariyah." He said: "These are the people of the hundreds." He gave some men of Quraysh less than one hundred, among them Makhramah ibn Nawfal al-Zuhri, Umayr ibn Wahb al-Jumahi, and Hisham ibn Amr al-Amiri. Ibn Ishaq said: "I do not know what he gave these." He gave Sa'id ibn Yarbu' fifty camels, and he gave Abbas ibn Mirdas al-Sulami a few camels, and he was displeased with them, so he said about that:

*They were plunder; I made up for them*
*by my charging on the mare in the wide open plain,*
*and by waking the people when they should sleep,*
*when people were sleeping, I did not sleep.*
*So my plunder and the plunder of the horse* (ʿUbayd, the name of Abbas's horse)
*became between ʿUyaynah and al-Aqraʿ.*
*Indeed, I was in war one who warded off danger,*
*yet I was given nothing and I was not withheld from.*
*Except small young camels that were given to me,*
*counted by the number of their four legs.*
*Neither Husn nor Habis were*
*superior to Mirdas in the gathering.*
*I was not lower than either of them,*
*and whoever is lowered today will not be raised.*

Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Go and cut off his tongue for me." So they gave him [what he asked for],[[In MS B: "gave" (فأعطى).]] until he was satisfied, and that was the cutting off of his tongue.

Abu Umar said: Al-Nadr ibn al-Harith ibn Alqamah ibn Kaldah, the brother of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith who was killed in cold blood at Badr, has been mentioned among those whose hearts are to be won (al-mu'allafah qulubuhum, those whose hearts are inclined toward Islam through gifts). Others have said that he was among those who emigrated to Abyssinia. If he was one of them, it is impossible that he was among those whose hearts are to be won, since whoever emigrated to the land of Abyssinia was among the first emigrants (al-Muhajirun al-Awwalun), in whose heart faith had taken firm root and who fought for it, and he is not one of those who are won over.

Abu Umar said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ appointed Malik ibn Awf ibn Sa'd [ibn Yarbu'[[In MSS J, Z, K and Y. In Usd al-Ghabah: Ibn Rabi'ah ibn Yarbu'.]]] al-Nasri over those of his people from the tribes of Qays who had embraced Islam, and commanded him to raid Thaqif. He did so and pressed them hard. His Islam and the Islam of those whose hearts were to be won was good, except for Uyaynah ibn Hisn, who remained suspect [[al-maghmuz: the one accused.]] in his regard. The rest of those whose hearts were to be won differed in merit. Among them were the excellent and virtuous, whose virtue is agreed upon, such as al-Harith ibn Hisham, Hakim ibn Hizam, Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl and Suhayl ibn Amr, and among them were others lesser than these. Allah has preferred the Prophets and the rest of His believing servants over one another, and He knows them best.

Malik said: It reached me that Hakim ibn Hizam took out what the Prophet ﷺ had given him as one of those whose hearts were to be won, and gave it away in charity after that.

I say: Hakim ibn Hizam and Huwaytib ibn Abd al-Uzza each lived one hundred and twenty years, sixty of them in Islam and sixty in the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam).

I heard our shaykh, the Imam and memorizer (al-Hafiz) Abu Muhammad Abd al-Azim, say: Two of the Companions lived sixty years in the Jahiliyyah and sixty years in Islam, and they both died in Madinah in the year 54 [AH]. One of them was Hakim ibn Hizam, whose birth was inside the Ka'bah thirteen years before the Year of the Elephant. The second was Hassan ibn Thabit ibn al-Mundhir ibn Haram al-Ansari. Abu Umar and Uthman al-Shahrazuri also mentioned this in their book Ma'rifat Anwa' Ilm al-Hadith, and they mentioned no others besides these two. As for Huwaytib, Abu al-Faraj al-Jawzi mentioned him in his book al-Wafa fi Sharaf al-Mustafa. Abu Umar mentioned him in his book al-Sahabah, that he reached Islam at the age of sixty and died at the age of one hundred and twenty. Abu Umar also mentioned Hamman ibn Awf, brother of Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, that he lived sixty years in Islam and sixty years in the Jahiliyyah.

Mu'awiyah and his father Abu Sufyan ibn Harb have been counted among those whose hearts were to be won. As for Mu'awiyah, it is far-fetched that he was among them, for how could he be among them when the Prophet ﷺ entrusted him with the revelation of Allah and its recitation, and mixed him with himself? His standing in the days of Abu Bakr is more famous and more manifest than this. As for his father, there is no dispute that he was among them. There is disagreement about their number. In general, they are all believers, and there was no disbelievers among them, as has been previously stated. Allah knows best and is most wise.

The Third Issue: The scholars differed about whether this category still continues. Umar, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and others said: This category ended with the honour and dominance of Islam. This is well known in the school of Malik and the people of opinion (Ashab al-Ra'y). Some scholars of the Hanafis said: When Allah honoured Islam and its people, and cut off the root of the disbelievers, may Allah curse them, the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, agreed in the caliphate of Abu Bakr [[Thus in the originals. The correct reading is Umar.]], may Allah be pleased with him, that their share had lapsed.

A group of scholars said: They continue, because the Imam may sometimes need to win people over to Islam. Umar only cut them off when he saw the strengthening of the religion. Yunus said: I asked al-Zuhri about them, and he said: I know of no abrogation (naskh, the lifting of a ruling by a later one) regarding this. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: According to this, the ruling concerning them is still valid. If anyone is in need of being won over, and harm is feared that might reach the Muslims from him, or it is hoped that his Islam will become good afterwards, he is given.

Al-Qadi Abd al-Wahhab said: If they are needed at some times, they are given from the zakat. Ibn al-Arabi (al-Qadi) said: What I hold is that if Islam becomes strong, they cease to be given, and if they are needed, they are given their share just as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to give them. For in the Sahih: "Islam began as something strange and will return to being strange as it began" [[Bada' means began. It is also narrated as bada', meaning appeared. Both narrations are sound. Ghurbah (strangeness) can mean a thing being outside its homeland, and it can mean unparalleled.]].

The Fourteenth Issue: If we conclude that their share is not restored to them, it returns to the rest of the categories, or to what the Imam sees fit. Al-Zuhri said: Half of their share is given to those who maintain the mosques. This is one of the things that shows you that the eight categories are places for distribution, not persons who have an equal entitlement. Had they been entitled persons, their share would have lapsed with their disappearance and would not have returned to others, just as if a bequest were made to specific people, and one of them died, his portion would not return to those who remain among them. And Allah knows best.

The Fifteenth Issue: His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And for the slaves﴾ (wa fi al-riqab), that is, for the freeing of slaves. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar, and it is the school of Malik and others. It is permissible for the Imam to buy slaves from the zakat funds and free them on behalf of the Muslims, and their loyalty (wala', the bond of patronage after manumission) will belong to the community of the Muslims. If the owner of the zakat buys them and frees them, it is permissible. This is the essence of Malik's school. It is also narrated from Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan, and this is the view of Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu Ubayd. Abu Thawr said: The owner of the zakat should not buy a soul from it to free, with the drawing of loyalty to himself. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, the people of opinion, and one narration from Malik. The correct view is the first, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "and for the slaves." So if slaves have a share of the charities, it is permissible for him to buy a slave and free him. There is no disagreement among the scholars that a man may buy a horse and ride it in the way of Allah. So if he may buy a horse outright from zakat, it is permissible for him to buy a slave outright, with no difference between the two. And Allah knows best.

The Sixteenth Issue: His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And for the slaves﴾. The origin is concerning loyalty. Malik said: It is the slave who is freed, and his loyalty belongs to the Muslims, and likewise if the Imam frees him. The Prophet ﷺ forbade selling loyalty and gifting it. He, peace be upon him, said: "Loyalty is a bond like the bond of lineage; it is not sold nor given away." He, peace be upon him, also said: "Loyalty belongs to the one who frees." Women do not inherit anything from loyalty, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "Women inherit nothing from loyalty except what they themselves free, or what those they freed free." The Prophet ﷺ gave the daughter of Hamzah half of the inheritance of a freed slave of hers, and to his own daughter the other half. If the one who frees leaves children, male and female, then loyalty belongs to the males among his offspring, to the exclusion of the females. This is the consensus of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. Loyalty is only inherited through pure agnatic succession (ta'sib mahd), and women have no agnatic status, so they inherit nothing from loyalty. So understand, and you will be correct.

The Seventeenth Issue: It has been disputed whether a mukatab (a slave contracted to buy his freedom) may be helped from it. It was said no; this is narrated from Malik, because when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned "the slave," it indicated that He meant full freedom. As for the mukatab, he is included only in the category of the debtors (al-gharimin), on account of the debt of the contract that is upon him, so he does not enter into "the slaves." And Allah knows best. It has also been narrated from Malik, from the narration of the people of Madinah and from Ziyad on his authority, that a mukatab is helped from it in the final part of his contract, by the amount needed to free him.

On this view is the majority of the scholars in interpreting the saying of Allah, the Exalted: "and for the slaves." This was also the view of Ibn Wahb, al-Shafi'i, al-Layth, al-Nakha'i and others. Ali ibn Musa al-Qummi al-Hanafi related in his book Ahkam that they agreed that the mukatab is intended. They differed about freeing slaves. Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: [[That is, al-Qummi.]] He mentioned a reason [[In al-Kiya's Ahkam al-Quran: "and he mentioned clear reasons for prohibiting that..." etc.]] for prohibiting it, saying: Freeing is the cancellation of ownership, and not a transfer of ownership, while what is given to the mukatab is a transfer of ownership, and it is a requirement of charity that it is only valid when the transfer of ownership takes place in it. He strengthened this by saying that if one gave from zakat on behalf of a debtor for his debt without his command, it would not suffice, since he did not own it; so much more so that this would not suffice in freeing. It was also mentioned that in freeing there is the drawing of loyalty to oneself, and that does not occur in giving to the mukatab. It was also mentioned that if the price of the slave is given to the slave, the slave does not own it; and if it is given to his master, then he has given him the freeing. And if it is given after the purchase and the freeing, it is paying a debt, and that does not suffice in zakat.

I say: A hadith has come that explicitly states the meaning of what we have mentioned about the permissibility of both freeing a slave and helping a mukatab. Al-Daraqutni transmitted it from al-Bara', who said: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "Guide me to a deed that brings me near to Paradise and keeps me far from the Fire." He said: "If you have shortened the sermon, you have indeed broadened the request. Free the slave (nasamah) and release the captive (fakk al-raqabah)." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, are these not one thing?" He said: "No. Freeing a soul (nasamah) is that you alone free it, and releasing the neck is that you help in its price." And he mentioned the hadith.

The Eighteenth Issue: They differed about ransoming captives from it. Asbagh said: It is not permitted. This is the view of Ibn al-Qasim. Ibn Habib said: It is permitted, because the captive is a slave owned by ownership of slavery, so he is brought out of slavery into freedom, and that is more deserving and more fitting than releasing the slaves who are in our hands, because if releasing a Muslim from the slavery of a Muslim is an act of worship and permissible from charity, then it is more fitting and more proper that it be so in releasing a Muslim from the slavery and humiliation of a disbeliever.

The Nineteenth Issue: His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And for the debtors (al-gharimin)﴾. They are those whom debt has overwhelmed and who have no means of repaying it. There is no disagreement on this, except for one who incurred debt in extravagance (safahah), for he is not given from it or from anything else, unless he repents.

Someone who has property but is also under debt that exceeds it is given from it, to pay his debt. If he has no property and is under debt, he is poor and a debtor, so he is given on both counts. Muslim transmitted from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: A man was afflicted in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in fruits he had bought, and his debt increased. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Give charity to him." The people gave charity to him, but it did not reach the amount of his debt. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to his creditors: "Take what you have found, and you have no more than that."

The Twentieth Issue: It is permissible for one who has taken on a burden for a good and righteous cause to be given from charity what pays what he has taken on, when it becomes due upon him, even if he is wealthy, if that would strip him of his wealth, like the debtor. This is the view of al-Shafi'i and his companions, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others. Those who held this view argued from the hadith of Qabisah ibn Mukhariq, who said: "I took on a hamalah" [[The hamalah (with a fatha) is what a person takes upon himself on behalf of another, such as blood money or a fine, like when war breaks out between two parties in which blood is shed, and a man steps between them to bear the blood-money of the slain in order to reconcile them. Tahammul means taking it upon oneself on their behalf.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 60 (part 5 of 7):

(from the Nihaya of Ibn al-Athir).]] I came to the Prophet ﷺ to ask him about it, and he said: "Remain until the sadaqah (charity) comes to us, and we will order that some be given to you." Then he said: "O Qabisah, begging is not permitted except for one of three: a man who has taken on a hamalah (a debt of compensation) so begging becomes lawful for him until he obtains it, and then he refrains; a man whom a jaihah (a calamity) has struck, destroying his wealth, so begging becomes lawful for him until he obtains qiwam (sufficiency) of living, or he said sidad (a sufficiency) of living; and a man who has been struck by faqah (destitution) until three people of sound judgment from his people [[i.e., until they stand before the assembly saying: 'Such-and-such a man has been struck by destitution, etc.']] say: 'Verily, so-and-so has been struck by destitution, so begging becomes lawful for him until he obtains qiwam of living, or he said sidad of living.' Whatever is beyond these is begging, O Qabisah, and it is suht (unlawful gain), which its possessor consumes as suht." So his saying "then he refrains" is evidence that he is wealthy, because the poor man is not required to refrain. And Allah knows best. It is also related from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "Begging is not permitted except for one of three: a person in severe poverty (faqr mudqi'), or a person under a heavy burden of debt (ghurm mufzi'), or a person bearing a painful blood-money (dam mujey')." [[Mudqi': severe, leading its possessor to the daqa'a, which is dust. It is said: it is the poor handling of poverty. Mufzi': severe and dreadful. Dam mujey': it is that one bears a diyah (blood-money), strives to pay it until he delivers it to the heirs of the slain; if he does not pay it, the one who bore it on behalf of another is killed, and his killing causes him pain.]] It is also related from him, peace be upon him: "Charity is not lawful for a wealthy person except for five," and the hadith continues, and it will come.

The twenty-first issue: They differed over whether the debt of a deceased person is paid from it or not. Abu Hanifa said: the debt of a deceased person is not paid from sadaqah. This is the view of Ibn al-Mawwaz. Abu Hanifa said: nor is one given from it who owes an expiation (kaffarah) or the like of the rights of Allah the Exalted; the gharim (debtor) is only one who owes a debt for which he is imprisoned. Our scholars and others said: the debt of a deceased person is paid from it, because he is among the ghariminf (debtors). The Prophet ﷺ said: "I am closer to every believer than himself. Whoever leaves wealth, it belongs to his family; and whoever leaves debt or dependants (diya') [[al-Diya' (with a fatha): the dependants; its origin is the verbal noun of da'a yadi'u diya'an, and the dependants are named by the verbal noun, just as you say: whoever dies and leaves fuqar, i.e., poor people.]], then it is for me and upon me."

The twenty-second issue: The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿وَفِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ [and in the way of Allah]. They are the ghuzat (fighters) and the places of ribat (frontier garrisoning). They are given what they spend on their campaign, whether they are wealthy or poor. This is the view of most scholars, and it is the essence of the school of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him. Ibn Umar said: they are the pilgrims (hajjaj) and the performers of umrah. It is related from Ahmad and Ishaq, may Allah have mercy on them both, that they said: "The way of Allah is the Hajj." In al-Bukhari: "It is mentioned from Abu Las [[with a non-dotted letter, as in al-Taj: Abu Muhammad al-Khuza'i, a Companion]]: the Prophet ﷺ carried us on camels of charity for the Hajj." And it is mentioned from Ibn Abbas: "He frees [from the zakah [[the addition is from Sahih al-Bukhari]]] of his wealth and gives for the Hajj." Abu Muhammad Abd al-Ghani al-Hafiz narrated: Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Khayyash narrated to us: Abu Ghassan Malik ibn Yahya narrated to us: Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us: Mahdi ibn Maymun informed us, from Muhammad ibn Abi Ya'qub, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Nu'm, who is kunyah Abu al-Hakam, who said: "I was sitting with Abd Allah ibn Umar, when a woman came to him and said: 'O Abu Abd al-Rahman, my husband bequeathed his wealth for the way of Allah.' Ibn Umar said: 'It is as he said, for the way of Allah.' I said to him: 'You have only increased her in grief regarding what she asked about.' He said: 'Then what do you order me to do? Should I order her to give it to those armies who go out and cause corruption in the land and cut off the road?' He said: I said: 'Then what do you order?' He said: 'I order her to give it to righteous people, to the pilgrims of the Sacred House of Allah. They are the delegation of the Most Merciful, they are the delegation of the Most Merciful, they are the delegation of the Most Merciful, not like the delegation of Satan,'" saying it three times. I said: "O Abu Abd al-Rahman, what is the delegation of Satan?" He said: "People who enter upon these rulers and carry tales to them, and strive among the Muslims with lies, so they are rewarded with gifts and given grants for it."

Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hakam said: It is given from sadaqah for horses, weapons, and whatever is needed of instruments of war, and for repelling the enemy from the protected territory, because all of that is part of the way of the campaign and its benefit. The Prophet ﷺ gave one hundred camels in the case of Sahl ibn Abi Hathma, to extinguish a flame of strife. I say: Abu Dawud narrated this hadith from Bashir ibn Yasar, that a man from the Ansar called Sahl ibn Abi Hathma informed him that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ paid for him one hundred camels from the camels of charity, meaning the blood-money of the Ansari who was killed at Khaybar.

Isa ibn Dinar said: "Charity is lawful for a fighter in the way of Allah, who has become needy in his campaign and whose assistance and abundance have been absent from him." He said: "It is not lawful for one whose wealth is with him among the fighters; it is only lawful for one whose wealth is absent from him among them." This is the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, and the majority of scholars. Abu Hanifa and his two companions said: "The fighter is not given except when he is poor and cut off from his means." This is an addition to the text, and an addition to the text is, in their view, naskh (abrogation), and abrogation can only occur by the Qur'an or a mutawatir (widely transmitted) report, and that is absent here. Rather, in the sound Sunnah there is what contradicts that, in his saying, peace be upon him: "Charity is not lawful for a wealthy person except for five: a fighter in the way of Allah, or one who works on it (the collection), or a debtor, or a man who bought it with his wealth, or a man who has a poor neighbour, so the poor man gives charity to him and he gives a gift to the wealthy man." Malik narrated it as mursal (with a missing companion link) from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Ata ibn Yasar. And Ma'mar raised it, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Ata ibn Yasar, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet ﷺ. So this hadith explains the meaning of the verse, and that it is permissible for some wealthy people to take it, and it explains his peace-be-upon-him saying: "Charity is not lawful for a wealthy person nor for one with sound strength," because this saying is general (mujmal) and not on its generality, by the evidence of the five wealthy persons mentioned.

Ibn al-Qasim used to say: "It is not lawful for a wealthy person to take from charity what he uses to aid himself in jihad and spends in the way of Allah; it is only lawful for a poor person." He said: "Likewise the debtor, it is not lawful for him to take from charity what preserves his wealth and pays his debt from it while he is wealthy in it." He said: "If the fighter becomes needy in his campaign while he is wealthy, with wealth absent from him, he does not take anything from charity by borrowing; when he reaches his own land, he pays that from his wealth." All of this Ibn Habib mentioned from Ibn al-Qasim, and he claimed that Ibn Nafi and others opposed him in that. Abu Zayd and others narrated from Ibn al-Qasim that he said: "The fighter is given from zakah even if he has with him in his campaign what suffices him from his wealth, and he is wealthy in his own land." And this is the sound view, for the apparent meaning of the hadith: "Charity is not lawful for a wealthy person except for five." Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik that the fighters and places of ribat are given from it, whether poor or wealthy.

The twenty-third issue: The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿وَابْنِ السَّبِيلِ﴾ [and the wayfarer]. The sabil is the road, and the traveller is attributed to it because of his constant presence on it and his passing over it, as the poet said:

If you ask me about passion, then I am passion,
and the son of passion, and its brother, and its father.

The meaning of "the one whose means are cut off" (ibn al-sabil, the wayfarer) is the traveller who is stranded during his journey, away from his city, his home and his wealth. He is given from the zakat (obligatory almsgiving) even if he is wealthy in his own city, and he is not obliged to burden himself with a loan. Mālik said in the Kitāb of Ibn Saḥnūn: "If he finds someone who will lend to him, he is not given." The first view is more correct, for he is not obliged to place himself under anyone's obligation when he has found the favour of God Most High.

If he has what suffices him, there are two reports concerning whether it is permitted to take from zakat for him because he is ibn al-sabil. The well-known view is that he is not given. If he takes it anyway, he is not obliged to return it once he reaches his city, nor to pay it out again.

Twenty-fourth issue: If someone comes and claims one of the qualifying attributes, is his word accepted or not? He is told: "Prove what you say." As for debt, he must prove it. As for the other attributes, the apparent state of affairs bears witness to him, and this suffices for them. The evidence for this is two authentic hadiths, recorded by the compilers of the Ṣaḥīḥ, and the apparent meaning of the Qur'an.

Muslim narrated from Jarīr [from his father] who said: "We were with the Prophet ﷺ early in the day. A people came to him, barefoot and naked, wearing striped cloaks or abās (cloaks), with swords slung on their shoulders, most of them, indeed all of them, from Muḍar. The face of the Messenger of God ﷺ changed (tamaʿara, i.e. altered) because of the poverty he saw in them. He went in, then came out, and commanded Bilāl, who called the adhān and iqāmah, and he prayed. Then he gave a sermon and said: 'O people, fear your Lord who created you,' up to His words 'watchful over you' [al-Nisā' 1]. And the verse in al-Ḥashr: 'Let every soul look to what it has sent forward for tomorrow' [al-Ḥashr 18]. A man gives in charity from his dinar, from his dirham, from his garment, from his measure of wheat… until he said: 'even with half a date.' Then a man from the Anṣār came with a purse whose hand almost could not hold it, indeed it could not. Then the people followed one after another, until I saw two heaps of food and clothing, and I saw the face of the Messenger of God ﷺ glowing as if it were polished gold. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: '(Whoever establishes a good practice in Islam will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it after him, without anything being diminished from their rewards. And whoever establishes an evil practice in Islam will bear its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it after him, without anything being diminished from their burdens.)'"

So the Prophet ﷺ was content with their apparent state, urged them to give charity, did not ask them for proof, and did not inquire whether they had wealth or not.

Similar to this is the hadith of the leper, the bald man and the blind man, which Muslim and others recorded. This is its wording: from Abū Hurayrah that he heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: "Among the Children of Israel there was a leper, a bald man and a blind man. God wished to test them, so He sent an angel to them. He came to the leper and said: 'What do you love most?' He said: 'A good colour, good skin, and that the thing which people loathe in me be removed.' He wiped him and the loathsomeness left him, and he was given a good colour and good skin. He said: 'What wealth do you love most?' He said: 'Camels' – or he said 'cattle' (Isḥāq was uncertain), except that the leper or the bald man said one of them was camels and the other said cattle. He was given a pregnant she-camel [of ten months]. He said: 'May God bless you in it.' Then he came to the bald man and said: 'What do you love most?' He said: 'Good hair, and that the thing which people loathe in me be removed.' He wiped him and it left him, and he was given good hair. He said: 'What wealth do you love most?' He said: 'Cattle,' so he was given a pregnant cow. He said: 'May God bless you in it.' Then he came to the blind man and said: 'What do you love most?' He said: 'That God return my sight to me so that I may see the people.' He wiped him and God returned his sight to him. He said: 'What wealth do you love most?' He said: 'Sheep,' so he was given a sheep that had young. These two [i.e. the owners of the camels and the cattle] had offspring, and this one [the sheep] multiplied. So one of them had a valley full of camels, another a valley full of cattle, and another a valley full of sheep. Then he came to the leper in his form and appearance and said: 'A poor man whose means have been cut off on my journey; there is no provision for me today except through God and then through you. I ask you, by the One who gave you the good colour, the good skin and the wealth, for a camel by which I may complete my journey.' He said: 'The rights (of others) are many.' He said: 'It seems to me that I know you. Were you not a leper whom people loathed, poor, and then God gave you wealth?' He said: 'I inherited this wealth from my forefathers, generation after generation.' He said: 'If you are lying, may God return you to what you were.' Then he came to the bald man in his form and said to him the same as he had said to this one, and he replied as this one had replied, and he said: 'If you are lying, may God return you to what you were.' Then he came to the blind man in his form and appearance and said: 'A poor man and a wayfarer whose means have been cut off on my journey; there is no provision for me today except through God and then through you. I ask you, by the One who returned your sight, for a sheep by which I may complete my journey.' He said: 'I was blind and God returned my sight to me, so take what you wish and leave what you wish. By God, I will not hold anything against you today for what you take for God's sake.' He said: 'Keep your wealth, for you were only tested. God is pleased with you and displeased with your two companions.'"

This is among the clearest evidence that whoever claims more than his poverty, whether dependants or otherwise, is not investigated about it, contrary to those who say he is investigated if it is possible. In the hadith there is: "A poor man and a wayfarer, I ask you for a sheep," and the Prophet did not require him to prove the journey.

As for the mukātab (a slave who has contracted to buy his own freedom), he is required to prove the contract, because slavery is the original state until freedom is established.

Twenty-fifth issue: It is not permitted to give zakat to those whose maintenance is obligatory upon the giver, namely parents, children and the wife. If the imam gives a man's charity to his child, parent or wife, it is permitted. As for the man himself taking it, that is not permitted, because by it he would discharge an obligation from himself.

Abū Ḥanīfah said: One does not give from it to one's son's child or one's daughter's child, nor to one's mukātab, nor to one's mudabbar (a slave freed upon the owner's death), nor to one's umm walad (a slave-mother of his child), nor to a slave of whom he has freed half, because he is commanded to give and to bring it out to God Most High through the hand of the poor person, and the benefits of possessions are shared between him and these people. For this reason the testimony of some of them is not accepted for others. He said: The mukātab remains a slave as long as a dirham is owed upon him, and he may fail, in which case the earnings become his. The one partly freed is, according to Abū Ḥanīfah, in the position of the mukātab. According to his two companions, Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad, he is in the position of a free man who has a debt, so it is permitted to pay it to him.

Twenty-sixth issue: If he gives it to those whose maintenance is not obligatory upon him, there is disagreement about it. Some permitted it and some disliked it. Mālik said: "(The concern is) fear of praise (for it)." Muṭarrif reported that he said: "I saw Mālik giving his zakat to his relatives." Al-Wāqidī reported that Mālik said: "The best place to put your zakat is your relatives whom you do not support."

The Prophet ﷺ said to the wife of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd: "You have two rewards: the reward of kinship and the reward of charity."

They differed concerning a woman giving her zakat to her husband. It is reported from Ibn Ḥabīb that he used to be helped in maintaining his household by what she gave him. Abū Ḥanīfah said: It is not permitted, but his two companions disagreed and said: It is permitted. This is the more correct view, because it is established that Zaynab, the wife of ʿAbd Allāh, came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and said: "I wish to give charity to my husband; will it count for me?" He, peace be upon him, said: "Yes, you have two rewards: the reward of charity and the reward of kinship." The charity is zakat, and because the husband has no obligation of maintenance towards her, she is in the position of a stranger.

Abū Ḥanīfah argued: The benefits of possessions are shared between them, so that the testimony of one of them for the other is not accepted. The hadith is to be understood as voluntary charity.

Al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Thawr and Ashhab held that this is permitted, provided that she does not spend it on what is obligatory for her to provide, and that he spends what he receives from her on his own maintenance and clothing, and maintains her from his own wealth.

Twenty-seventh issue: They also differed concerning the amount to be given. The gharim (debtor) is given the amount of his debt, and the poor (faqīr) and the needy (miskīn) are given what suffices them and their dependants. There is disagreement over whether it is permitted to give a nisab (the minimum threshold of zakat-liable wealth) or less than it, and this disagreement rests on the earlier disagreement about the degree of poverty which permits taking. ʿAlī ibn Ziyād and Ibn Nāfiʿ reported: There is no fixed limit in this; it is left to the judgement of the ruler. When the needy are few and the charity abundant, the poor person is given a year's sustenance. Al-Mughīrah reported: He is given less than the nisab and does not reach it. Some later scholars said: If the town has two zakats, one on cash and one on crops, he takes what will bring him to the other. Ibn al-ʿArabī said: "What I think is that he should be given a nisab, even if the town has two or more zakats, for the aim is to make the poor person rich until he becomes wealthy. When he has taken that, if the other zakat arrives and he has what suffices him, someone else takes it."

I say: This is the view of the people of opinion (ḥanafīs) regarding giving a nisab. Abū Ḥanīfah disliked it while permitting it, and Abū Yūsuf permitted it, saying: "Because part of it is occupied with his present need, so the surplus beyond his present need is less than two hundred dirhams. And if he gives him more than two hundred dirhams in total, the surplus beyond his present need is an amount…"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 60 (part 7 of 7):

...al-mi'atayn (two hundred), then it is not permissible. Among the later Hanafis is one who said: this applies when he has no dependents and no debt. If he has a debt, there is no harm in giving him two hundred dirhams or more, in an amount which, if he paid his debt with it, would leave him with less than two hundred. And if he has dependents, there is no harm in giving him an amount which, if it were distributed among his dependents, would give each one of them less than two hundred, because giving charity to him is, in meaning, giving charity to him and to his dependents. This is a good view.

The twenty-eighth issue: Know that the words of His, the Exalted, ﴿for the poor﴾ are unrestricted, with no condition or qualification attached. Rather, they indicate the permissibility of giving to the whole category of the poor, whether they are from the Banu Hashim or others. However, the Sunnah has come with considerations of conditions. Among them: that they are not from the Banu Hashim, and that they are not among those whose maintenance the giver is obliged to provide. There is no disagreement about this. A third condition: that the recipient is not strong enough to earn a living, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Charity is not lawful for the rich, nor for one who has the strength of a sound, able-bodied person." This has been discussed earlier.

There is no disagreement among the scholars of the Muslims that obligatory charity (zakat) is not lawful for the Prophet (ﷺ), nor for the Banu Hashim, nor for their clients (mawali). It has been related from Abu Yusuf the permission of a Hashimi giving his charity to a Hashimi; this was related by al-Kiya al-Tabari. Some scholars held an anomalous view, saying: the clients of the Banu Hashim are not forbidden any kind of charity. This contradicts what is established from the Prophet (ﷺ), for he said to his client Abu Rafi': "Indeed, the client of a people is one of them."

The twenty-ninth issue: The scholars differed on the permissibility of voluntary charity (sadaqat al-tatawwu') for the Banu Hashim. The view held by the majority of scholars, and it is the sound one, is that voluntary charity is permissible for the Banu Hashim and their clients, because Ali, al-Abbas and Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with them, gave charity and established endowments (awqaf) for a group of the Banu Hashim, and their endowed charities are well known and famous. Ibn al-Majishun, Mutarrif, Asbagh and Ibn Habib said: the Banu Hashim are not to be given from either obligatory charity or voluntary charity. Ibn al-Qasim said: the Banu Hashim are to be given from voluntary charity. Ibn al-Qasim said: the hadith that came from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Charity is not lawful for the family of Muhammad" refers only to zakat, not to voluntary charity. Ibn Khuwaiz Mindad chose this view, and Abu Yusuf and Muhammad also held it. Ibn al-Qasim said: their clients are to be given from both kinds of charity. Malik said in al-Wadihah: Nothing is to be given to the family of Muhammad from voluntary charity. Ibn al-Qasim said: it was said to him, meaning Malik, "What about their clients?" He said: "I do not know what the clients are." So I argued against him with his saying, peace be upon him: "The client of a people is one of them." He said: "He has said: 'The sister's son of a people is one of them.'" Asbagh said: that applies to kindness and respect.

The thirtieth issue: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿a duty from Allah﴾ is in the accusative according to Sibawayh, as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: Allah has prescribed the charities as an obligation. It is permissible to read it in the nominative according to al-Kisa'i, as a predicate, meaning: they are an obligation. Al-Zajjaj said: I do not know that it was read this way. I say: Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Abla recited it so, making it a predicate, just as you say: "Indeed Zayd is going out."

Allah, exalted is He, explained that among the hypocrites there was one who would loosen his tongue to slander the Prophet (ﷺ), saying: "If he rebukes me, I will swear to him that I did not say this," and he would accept it from him, for "he is an ear" (*udhun*) that listens. Al-Jawhari said: One says "a man is *udhun*" when he listens to everyone's speech, and the word is used the same for the singular and the plural. Ali ibn Abi Talha narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning Allah's words ﴿He is an ear﴾, that he said: "one who listens and accepts."

This verse was revealed concerning Attab ibn Qushayr, who said: "Muhammad is only an ear; he accepts whatever is said to him." It is also said that it was about Nabtal ibn al-Harith. Ibn Ishaq said: Nabtal was a large man, with bushy hair on his head and beard, dark-skinned, with red eyes, a blackened-reddish complexion and a deformed appearance. It was about him that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wishes to look at the devil, let him look at Nabtal ibn al-Harith." *Al-Sufa* (with a *damma* on the *sin*) is a blackness tinged with redness; and "a man *asfa'*" is how al-Jawhari defined it.

It is read *udhun* with a *damma* on the *dhal* and also with it *sakin* (sukun).

(﴿Say: "An ear of good for you"﴾) meaning: he is an ear of good, not an ear of evil; that is, he hears good and does not hear evil.

Al-Hasan and Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read *"Qul udhunun khayrun lakum"* (﴿Say: an ear of good for you﴾) with *raf'* (nominative) and *tanwin* (nunation). The rest read it with *idafah* (genitive construction). Hamza read *"wa rahmatin"* (﴿and mercy﴾) in the genitive (*khafd*). The rest read it in the nominative (*raf'*), as a conjunction to *"udhun"*, and the implied meaning is: "Say: he is an ear of good and he is mercy," that is, he is a listener to good, not a listener to evil; that is, he listens to what it is loved that he listen to, and he is mercy. Whoever reads it in the genitive does so as a conjunction to *"khayr"*. Al-Nahhas said: This is far-fetched according to the grammarians of Arabic (*ahl al-'arabiyyah*), because the two nouns have been separated by distance, and this is considered ugly with the genitive. Al-Mahdawi said: Whoever puts *rahmah* in the genitive does so as a conjunction to *"khayr"*, and the meaning is "a listener of good and a listener of mercy," since mercy is part of good. It is not valid to conjoin *rahmah* to *"lil-mu'minin"* (﴿for the believers﴾), because the meaning would be "he believes in Allah and believes the believers," so the *lam* would be extra (*za'idah*) according to the Kufans. A similar usage is Allah's words ﴿for their Lord they fear﴾ [al-A'raf: 154], meaning: they fear their Lord. Abu Ali said: It is like His words ﴿followed closely﴾ [al-Naml: 72]. According to al-Mubarrad, the *lam* is connected to a verbal noun (*masdar*) implied by the verb, the estimate being: "his believing (*iman*) is for the believers," that is, his affirmation is for the believers and not for the disbelievers. Or it is taken according to the sense: the meaning of *yu'minu* is *yusaddiqu* (affirms), so it takes the *lam* as it does in Allah's words ﴿confirming what is before it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 46].

There are three issues here.

The first: it is related that a group of the hypocrites gathered, among them al-Jullas ibn Suwayd and Wadi'ah ibn Thabit, and among them a youth from the Ansar called Amir ibn Qays. They belittled him, and they spoke and said: "If what Muhammad says is true, then we are worse than donkeys." The youth became angry and said: "By God, what he says is true, and you are worse than donkeys." The Prophet (ﷺ) was informed of their words, and they swore that Amir was lying. Amir said: "They are the liars," and he swore to that, and said: "O God, do not separate us until the truthfulness of the truthful and the lying of the liar become clear." So God revealed this verse, and in it: ﴿They swear to God to you, to please you﴾.

The second: God's statement ﴿And God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ is an inchoate sentence (mubtada') and its predicate (khabar). The view of Sibawayh is that the implied construction is: "God has more right that they should please Him, and His Messenger has more right that they should please Him," and then something was omitted, as one of them said:

"We are content with what we have, and you with what you have, though our opinions differ."

Muhammad ibn Yazid said: there is no omission in the speech; the implied meaning is "God has more right that they should please Him, and His Messenger," by way of inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir). Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "His Messenger has more right that they should please Him, and God is the opening of the speech," as you say: "What God wills, and you willed." Al-Nahhas said: Sibawayh's view is the best of these, because it is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he forbade saying "What God wills and you willed," and nothing in it should be assumed to be fronted or delayed, and its meaning is sound. I say: it has also been said that God, glorified is He, made His pleasure to be in His Messenger's pleasure. Do you not see that He said: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God﴾ [An-Nisa' 80]. Al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham, whenever he passed by this verse, would pause and then say: "A letter, and what a letter; it has been entrusted to him, so he commands us only with good."

The third: our scholars said: this verse includes the acceptance of the oath of one who swears, even if the one to whom the oath is made is not obliged to be satisfied. The oath is a right of the claimant. It also includes that the oath be by God, Mighty and Majestic, as previously mentioned. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever swears, let him swear by God or remain silent, and whoever is sworn to, let him accept it." The discussion of oaths and exception within them has already been covered fully in Surat al-Ma'idah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 63:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did they not know﴾, meaning the hypocrites. Ibn Humayd and al-Hasan read "tu'lamu" with the ta' (ت), in the second person address.

(That) is in the accusative position, governed by "ya'lamu" (they know), and the pronoun (ha') refers back to the matter (al-hadith).

(Whoever opposes Allah) is in the nominative position as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'). Al-muhaddada (opposition) means that one party stands on one boundary (hadd) and the other on a different boundary, like al-mushaqqa (hostility). It is said: "Fulan haadda Fulanan," meaning he came to be on a boundary other than his boundary.

(Then indeed for him is the fire of Hell.) It is said: what follows the fa' in a conditional sentence is a subject (mubtada'), so it should have been "fa-inna" with a kasra on the hamza. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh permitted "fa-inna lahu nara jahannam" with a kasra. Sibawayh said: "It is good," and he recited:

"My knowledge of the stagnant waters, and the camels that hasten along the road, worn out (by travel)...

And that when my mounts tire of their resting places, then indeed I am, regarding my fortune in the matter, one who presses on."

[[The two verses are by Ibn Muqbil. The evidence in them is the kasra of the second "inna". Al-asdam: waters that have changed due to scarcity of arrivals, singular sadam. Takhdi: they hasten. Al-talaih: those worn out by long travel. The meaning of "mallat rikabi munakhaha": the continuous travel, making them kneel and departing. Al-jamih: one who presses on in his course, i.e., long travel does not break me, but I proceed forward for the fortune I hope for in my affair. (From Sharh al-Shawahid.)]]

However, the common reading is "fa-anna" with a fatha on the hamza. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh also said: the second "anna" is a substitution (badal) for the first. Al-Mubarrad claimed that this view is rejected, and that the correct view is what al-Jarmi said: the second is repeated for emphasis because the speech has been lengthened. Its parallel is ﴿And they in the Hereafter are the greatest losers﴾ [An-Naml: 5] (see vol. 13, p. 154 onward). Likewise ﴿So the outcome of both was that they would be in the Fire, abiding therein﴾ [Al-Hashr: 17] (see vol. 18, p. 37). Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is "so the obligation of the Fire is for him." Al-Mubarrad rejected this and said: this is an error, because "anna" with a fatha and shadda cannot begin a sentence with the predicate omitted. Ali ibn Sulayman said: the meaning is "so what is necessary is that for him is the fire of Hell," the second "inna" being the predicate of an omitted subject. It was also said: the estimate is "fa-lahu anna lahu nara jahannam," with "fa" governing a preposition omitted between the fa' and anna, so that the clause is in the nominative by settling (al-istiqrar).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 64:

There are three issues concerning this verse. The first is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The hypocrites fear﴾. It is a report, not a command. What indicates that it is a report is that what follows it, "Allah will bring out what you fear," [applies to them], because they disbelieved out of obstinacy. Al-Suddi said: Some of the hypocrites said, "By Allah, I wish I had been brought forward and given a hundred lashes, and that nothing would be revealed about us that exposes us," so the verse was revealed. "Yahdharu" means yataharras (takes precaution). Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is liyahdhar (let him beware), so it is a command, as one says, "Let him do that" (yaf'al dhalika).

The second is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that there be sent down upon them﴾. "An" (that) is in the accusative position, meaning "from [the fact] that there be sent down." According to the view of Sibawayh, it may also be in the genitive position, with min (from) elided. It may also be in the accusative position as the object of yahdhar, because Sibawayh permitted "hadhirtu Zaydan" (I was wary of Zayd), and he cited the verse:

Wary of matters that do no harm, yet secure in what cannot save him from decrees.

Al-Mubarrad did not permit it, because hadhar (caution) is a matter of state (hay'a). The meaning of "upon them," i.e., upon the believers, concerning the affair of the hypocrites, informing them of their disgraces, their evil deeds and their faults. For this reason the surah was called al-Fadiha (the Exposer), al-Muthira (the Stirrer) and al-Mubatthira (the Unveiler), as was mentioned at the beginning of the surah. Al-Hasan said: the Muslims used to call this surah al-Haffara (the Digger), because it dug up what was in the hearts of the hypocrites and brought it to light.

The third is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Mock﴾. This is a command of warning and threat.

(Allah will bring out) i.e., will make manifest "what you fear" to become apparent. Ibn Abbas said: Allah revealed the names of the hypocrites, and they were seventy men, then He abrogated those names from the Qur'an out of compassion and mercy, because their children were Muslims and people would taunt one another. Accordingly, Allah has fulfilled His promise of making that manifest, when He said, "Allah will bring out what you fear." It has also been said: Allah's bringing out [the matter] is that He informed His Prophet, peace be upon him, of their states and their names, not that they were revealed in the Qur'an. Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿And you will surely recognize them by the tone of their speech﴾ [Muhammad: 30], and this is a kind of inspiration.
