Among the hypocrites were those who wavered and did not decisively judge Muhammad, peace be upon him, to be either a liar or truthful. Among them were those who recognized his truthfulness yet were obstinate.

**Chapter 1: This verse was revealed concerning the expedition of Tabuk.** al-Tabari and others related from Qatadah: While the Prophet (ﷺ) was marching in the expedition of Tabuk, a group of the hypocrites were riding ahead of him, and they said, "Look at him! He thinks he will conquer the palaces of Syria and seize the fortresses of the Banu al-Asfar!" God, glorified is He, informed him of what was in their hearts and what they were discussing. So he said, "Hold back the riders for me," and then he came to them and said, "You said such-and-such." They swore, "We were only plunging and playing," meaning, "We were not being serious."

al-Tabari also mentioned from Abdullah ibn Umar, who said: "I saw the speaker of this statement, Wadi'ah ibn Thabit, clinging to the strap of the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) she-camel, walking alongside it while the stones were striking him, and he was saying, 'We were only plunging and playing.' And the Prophet (ﷺ) was saying, '﻿Was it God, His signs, and His Messenger that you were mocking?'"

al-Naqqash mentioned that this clinging man was Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. al-Qushayri also mentioned this from Ibn Umar. Ibn Atiyyah said: "That is an error, because he did not witness Tabuk."

al-Qushayri said: "It has been said that the Prophet (ﷺ) said this only to Wadi'ah ibn Thabit, who was one of the hypocrites and was present at the expedition of Tabuk."

*Al-khawd* (plunging) means entering the water; then it was used for any entry into something that involves defilement and harm.

**Issue two:** Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: "What they said was either in earnest (*jidd*) or in jest (*hazl*). Either way it is disbelief, for jesting with disbelief is disbelief, and there is no disagreement about this among the community. Seriousness is the companion of knowledge and truth, while jest is the companion of falsehood and ignorance. Our scholars said: Consider His words, ﴿Do you take us for a mockery?﴾ He said, ﴿I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant.﴾" [See vol. 1, p. 444] [al-Baqarah: 67]

**Issue three:** The scholars differed about jest in the remaining rulings, such as sale, marriage, and divorce, in three positions:
1. It is binding in no case.
2. It is binding in every case.
3. A distinction is made between sale and other contracts. It is binding in marriage and divorce, but not in sale.

Malik said in the *Kitab Muhammad*: the marriage of one who is jesting is binding. Abu Zayd, from Ibn al-Qasim, in *al-Utbiyyah*, said: it is not binding. Ali ibn Ziyad said: it is annulled both before and after. For al-Shafi'i there are two opinions concerning the sale of one who is jesting. The two opinions can likewise be derived from the statements of our scholars. Ibn al-Mundhir reported a consensus that the serious and the jesting divorce are the same.

Some of our later scholars said: If both parties agree on jest in marriage and sale, it is not binding. If they disagree, earnestness prevails over jest.

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Daraqutni narrated from Abu Hurairah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Three things, whether done in earnest or in jest, are taken seriously: marriage, divorce, and taking back (a divorced wife)." al-Tirmidhi said: "It is a hasan gharib hadith, and this is the practice of the people of knowledge among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and others."

I say: This is how it appears in the hadith, "and taking back," but in the *Muwatta'* of Malik, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, he said: "Three things have no play in them: marriage, divorce, and manumission." It is likewise reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, and Abu al-Darda', all of whom said: "There are three things in which there is no play [and no retraction in them]," and the one who plays with them is serious: marriage, divorce, and manumission. And from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Umar, who said: "Four things are binding on everyone: manumission, divorce, marriage, and vows." And from al-Dahhak, who said: "Three things have no play in them: marriage, divorce, and vows."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 9, verse 66:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not make excuses; you have disbelieved after your belief.﴾ This is said in the manner of reproach, as if He were saying: "Do not do what will not benefit you." Then He judged them to be disbelievers and to be unable to make excuse for their sin. The verb *i'tadhara* is used with the meaning of *a'dhara*, that is, he became one who has an excuse. Labid said:

*"Ila al-hawli thumma ism al-salami 'alaykuma*
*Wa man yabki hawlan kamilan faqad i'tadhara"*

[This is the second half of a verse whose first half is: "Until the year's end, then the greeting of peace upon you both."]

*I'tidhar* (making an excuse) means the erasing of the trace of resentment (*mawjida*). It is said: "The dwellings *i'tadharat*," meaning they were effaced. *I'tidhar* also means the obliteration (of traces). The poet said:

*"Am kunta ta'rifu ayatin faqad ja'alat
Atlalu ilfika bil-Wadkaa ta'taadhiru"*

Ibn al-A'rabi said: its original meaning is cutting. One says *i'tadhartu ilayhi*, meaning "I cut off what was in his heart of resentment." From this comes *'udhrat al-ghulam*, which is what is cut from a boy during circumcision, and from this comes *'udhrat al-jariya*, because it cuts her hymen.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If We pardon a group among you, We will punish another group because they were criminals.﴾ It has been said: they were three men. Two of them mocked and one laughed, so the one who was pardoned was the one who laughed and did not speak. The word *ta'ifa* (group) means a company, and it may be applied to one person in the sense of "a soul" (*nafs*). Ibn al-Anbari said: the plural form may be used for the singular, as when you say, "So-and-so went out on mules." He said: it is also possible that *ta'ifa*, when intended for one person, is *ta'if*, and the *ha'* is for emphasis (intensification).

The scholars differed concerning the name of this man who was pardoned, giving several views. It is said he was Makhshi ibn Humayyir, as stated by Ibn Ishaq. Ibn Hisham said: it is also said Ibn Makhshi. Khalifa ibn Khayyat said in his *Tarikh*: his name was Mukhashin ibn Humayyir. Ibn Abd al-Barr mentioned Mukhashin al-Himyari, and al-Suhayli mentioned Mukhashshin ibn Khumayyir [from manuscripts B and J]. All of them mentioned that he was martyred at al-Yamama, and that he had repented and was named Abd al-Rahman. So he asked Allah to be killed as a martyr and that his grave not be known.

It has been disputed whether he was a hypocrite or a Muslim. It has been said he was a hypocrite who then repented a sincere repentance. It has also been said he was a Muslim, except that he heard the hypocrites and laughed with them and did not denounce them.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women﴾ is a subject (mubtada'). "Some of them" (ba'duhum) is a second subject. It is also permissible for it to be a substitute (badal), with the predicate being "from one another" (min ba'd). The meaning of "some of them are from some" is that they are like one thing in departing from the religion.

Al-Zajjaj said: this is connected to His saying: ﴿They swear by Allah that they are surely of you, and they are not of you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 56], meaning they are not among the believers, but some of them are from some, that is, they resemble one another in enjoining what is evil (al-munkar) and forbidding what is good (al-ma'ruf).

"Qabḍ aydīhim" (their hands being withheld) is an expression for [leaving off] jihad and for what is obligatory upon them of rights. "Nasiya" (forgot) here means "left/abandoned": they abandoned what Allah commanded them, so He abandoned them in doubt. It was also said: they abandoned His command until it became like something forgotten, so He made them in the position of those forgotten from His reward. Qatadah said: ﴿so He forgot them﴾ means from good, but as for evil, He did not forget them.

Al-fisq (wickedness, transgression) is departing from obedience and from the religion. This has been discussed before [[See vol. 1, p. 244.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 68:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has promised the hypocrites﴾. It is said: "Allah promised (wa'd) good (bi-l-khayr) as a promise (wa'dan), and promised evil (bi-l-sharr) as a threat (wa'idan)." "Khalidin" (abiding eternally) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and its governing verb is omitted, meaning: they will burn therein, abiding eternally.

(Hiya hasbuhum) is a subject and predicate: meaning, it is sufficient recompense and a full requital for their deeds. "Al-la'n" (cursing) is distance, meaning distance from the mercy of Allah, and it has been mentioned before [[see vol. 2, p. 25.]].

(Wa-lahum 'adhabun muqim) means: and for them is a lasting, enduring punishment.

**First issue:** The verse concerns three matters.

**The first matter:** God's words ﴿like those before you﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the *kaf* (the particle "like") is in the accusative position, meaning: God promised the disbelievers the Fire of Hell as a promise, just as He promised those before them. It was also said that the meaning is: you have acted like the deeds of those before you, in abandoning enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, so the object was omitted. It was also said: "you are like those before you," in which case the *kaf* is in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject. The word *ashadd* (أَشَدَّ) is not declined because it is an elative adjective (*af'al*). Its original form is *ashadd* (أَشَدَّدُ), meaning: they were stronger than you in power, so it was not possible for them, nor could they prevent God's punishment, the Mighty and Majestic.

**The second matter:** Sa'id narrated from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "You will follow the ways of the nations before you, span by span and cubit by cubit, to the extent that if they had entered the hole of a lizard, you would enter it." Abu Hurayra said: "If you wish, recite the Qur'an: ﴿Like those before you, who were stronger than you in power and greater in wealth and children, and they enjoyed their portion﴾." Abu Hurayra said: "*al-khalaq* (الْخَلَاقُ) means the religion." So the verse means: you have enjoyed your portion, just as those before you enjoyed theirs, until he finished the verse. They said: "O Prophet of God, what did the Jews and Christians do?" He said: "And who are the people but they?"

In the Sahih, on the authority of the same, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "You will certainly follow the ways of those before you, span by span and cubit by cubit, to the extent that if they had entered the hole of a lizard, you would enter it." They said: "O Messenger of God, the Jews and Christians?" He said: "Who else?"

Ibn 'Abbas said: "How similar tonight is to last night! These are the Children of Israel, and we have been likened to them." A similar statement is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud.

**The third matter:** God's words ﴿so they enjoyed their portion﴾, meaning they benefited from their share of the religion, as those before them did. ﴿And you indulged﴾ is a shift from the third person (absence) to the second person (address). ﴿as those who indulged﴾, meaning like their indulgence. So the *kaf* is in the accusative position as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: you indulged in an indulgence like that of those who indulged. The word *alladhi* (الَّذِي) is a defective noun like *man*, used for both the singular and the plural. It has already been discussed in *al-Baqara* (see vol. 1 p. 212).

It is said: *khudtu al-ma'* (خُضْتُ الْمَاءَ) "I waded the water," *akhudhu-hu khawdan wa khiyadan*. *Al-mawdi'* (the place) is a *makhadah* (مَخَاضَةٌ), a ford where people cross on foot or on riding animals. Its plurals are *al-makhad* and also *al-makhawid*, according to Abu Zayd. *Akhadtu dabbati fi al-ma'* means "I made my animal wade into the water." *Akhada al-qawm* means their horses waded. *Khudtu al-ghamarat* means I plunged into the difficulties. It is said: *khadahu bi al-sayf* means he moved his sword in the one struck. *Khawwada fi najī'ihi* (he plunged into his blood), with the doubled letter for emphasis. The blood (*najī'*) means blood, and it is said specifically the blood of the abdomen. *Al-mikhawd* is for drink, like the *mijdah* (a wooden stick with two crossed pieces at its head) for barley gruel; from it one says *khudtu al-sharab*, "I stirred the drink." *Khada al-qawm fi al-hadith* and *takhawadu* mean they discussed it together. So the meaning is: you plunged into the affairs of this world with frivolity and play. It was also said: into the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) by denying him.

﴿Those—their deeds have become void﴾, meaning they became null. This has been discussed before (see vol. 3 p. 46).

﴿their deeds﴾, meaning their good deeds.

﴿And those—they are the losers﴾. This has also been discussed before (see vol. 1 p. 248).

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿Has there not come to them the news of those before them?﴾ That is, the report of those who came before them. The alif here is for affirmation and warning, meaning: have they not heard of Our destruction of the disbelievers before them?

(﴿the people of Noah, ʿAd, and Thamud﴾) is a substitution (badal) for "those."

(﴿and the people of Abraham﴾) means Nimrod son of Kanaan and his people.

(﴿and the companions of Madyan﴾) Madyan is the name of the town in which Shuʿayb was. They were destroyed by the punishment of the Day of the Cloud.

(﴿and the overturned cities﴾) It has been said that this refers to the people of Lot, because their land was overturned with them, meaning it was inverted. This is the view of Qatadah. It has also been said that "the overturned cities" means everyone who was destroyed, just as one says, "the world turned upside down on them."

(﴿their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾) This means all the prophets. It has been said that the messengers came to the companions of the overturned cities, and on this view their messenger was Lot alone, but he was sent to each town as a messenger, and there were three towns, and it has been said four. The Exalted's statement elsewhere, ﴿And the overturned cities﴾ [al-Najm: 53], is in the manner of a collective noun. It has also been said that by "messengers" is meant one messenger, as in His statement, ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 51], and there was no one else in his era. I say: this view is open to question, because of the authentic (ṣaḥīḥ) hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "God addressed the believers with what He commanded the messengers," and so on. It has already been mentioned in "al-Baqarah." The intended meaning is all the messengers, and God knows best.

The Exalted's statement: ﴿It was not God who would wrong them﴾ means it was not God who would destroy them until He sent to them the prophets.

(﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾) meaning they wronged themselves after the proof (ḥujjah, decisive evidence) had been established against them.

**Fourth issue (masa'il)**, or: The first issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Some of them are allies of others﴾, meaning their hearts are united in affection, love and mutual compassion. He said regarding the hypocrites: "Some of them are from others," because their hearts are divided, but they are grouped together in ruling. The second issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They enjoin what is right﴾, meaning [they enjoin] the worship of God Exalted and His Oneness, and everything that follows from that.

(And they forbid what is wrong) [they forbid] the worship of idols and everything that follows from that. Al-Tabari reported from Abu al-'Aliyah that he said: Everything God mentions in the Quran concerning enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong refers to forbidding the worship of idols and devils. The discussion of enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong has already passed in the commentary on Surat al-Ma'idah [see vol. 6, p. 242 and following] and Al 'Imran [see vol. 4, p. 47], and praise be to God. The third issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they establish prayer﴾, which was discussed at the beginning of al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 164]. Ibn 'Abbas said: It refers to the five daily prayers, and according to this the zakat mentioned here is the obligatory zakat. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: In my view, praise for voluntary acts is more eloquent, since whoever establishes voluntary acts is more deserving of establishing obligatory ones. The fourth issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they obey God﴾ in the obligatory matters, (and His Messenger) in what he has prescribed for them. The "sin" in His saying, "God will surely have mercy on them" (sa-yarhamuhumu Allah), introduces the promise with a delay, so that souls may delight in hoping for it, and God's grace is guaranteed to fulfil it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 72:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah has promised the believing men and the believing women gardens﴾, that is, orchards, (﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾), that is, from beneath their trees and their mansions the rivers flow. It has already been mentioned in "al-Baqarah" that they flow in a controlled manner by [Allah's] power, without a trench [[See vol. 1, p. 239.]].

(﴿Abiding therein, and pleasant dwellings﴾) palaces of chrysolite, pearls and rubies, whose fragrance diffuses from a distance of five hundred years.

(﴿In gardens of Eden﴾), that is, in an abode of residence. It is said: "ʿadana bi-l-makan" when one stays in a place, and from it comes "al-maʿdin" (the mine). ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurasani said: "Gardens of Eden" is the capital of Paradise, and its ceiling is the Throne of the Most Merciful, Mighty and Majestic. Ibn Masʿud said: it is the innermost part of Paradise, that is, its middle. al-Hasan said: it is a palace of gold, which none enters except a prophet, a truthful one (ṣiddiq), a martyr, or a just ruler. Similar to this is reported from al-Dahhak. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: ʿAdn is the highest level in Paradise, and in it is the spring of Tasnim, while the gardens surround it and encompass it, and it has been covered since the day Allah created it until the prophets, the truthful ones, the martyrs, the righteous and whomever Allah wills descend to it.

(﴿And the good pleasure of Allah is greater﴾), that is, greater than that. ﴿That is the great triumph.﴾

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 73:

There are two issues here. The first concerns His statement, exalted is He: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers﴾. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and his community after him is included in it. It has been said: the meaning is, strive against the disbelievers together with the believers. Ibn 'Abbas said: he was commanded to strive against the disbelievers with the sword, and against the hypocrites with the tongue and by severe rebuke and harshness. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Strive against the hypocrites with your hand; if you cannot, then with your tongue; if you cannot, then frown in their faces" [[Ikfaharra al-rajul: if the man scowled.]]. Al-Hasan said: strive against the hypocrites by enforcing the prescribed punishments (hudud) upon them and with the tongue, and Qatadah chose this view, and they were the most frequent to incur the prescribed punishments. Ibn al-'Arabi said: as for establishing the proof with the tongue, it was constant; as for the prescribed punishments, since most of those who incurred them were among them, this is an assertion without evidence. A sinner is not a hypocrite; the hypocrite is defined by what is in his heart of hypocrisy, hidden, not by what the limbs manifestly commit. The reports about those who received the prescribed punishments, their context shows, indicate that they were not hypocrites.

The second issue concerns His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and be harsh with them﴾. Ghilaz (harshness) is the opposite of ra'fah (tenderness), and ra'fah is a softness of heart that leads to lenience toward the one who deserves punishment. Harshness is not in the tongue, for the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If the slave-girl of one of you commits fornication, let him flog her with the prescribed punishment and not reproach her [[That is, not rebuke or censure her for the fornication after striking her. It was also said: he meant that in punishing her he should not be satisfied with reproach but should apply the prescribed punishment, for fornication by slave-women was not regarded by the Arabs as reprehensible or objectionable, so he commanded them to apply the prescribed punishment to slave-women just as they were commanded to apply it to free women. (Ibn al-Athir's Nihayah.)]] for it." From the same root is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159] [[See vol. 4, p. 248.]]. And from it is the statement of the women to 'Umar: "You are more severe and harsher than the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." [[Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated this report in the "Chapter on the virtues of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him," both saying: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab asked permission to enter upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while with him were some women of Quraysh asking him for things, their voices raised above his voice. When 'Umar asked permission, they rose and hastened to the veil, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) permitted him, so 'Umar entered while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was laughing. 'Umar said: "May Allah make you laugh, O Messenger of Allah!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I am amazed at these women who were with me; when they heard your voice, they hastened to the veil." 'Umar said: "You are more deserving that they should fear you, O Messenger of Allah." Then 'Umar said: "O enemies of their own selves, do you fear me and not fear the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?" They said: "Yes, you are more severe and harsher than the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Enough, O son of al-Khattab! By He in whose hand my soul is, Satan never met you travelling a path but that he took a path other than yours."]]

The meaning of ghilaz is roughness of the side. It is the opposite of His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and lower your wing to those of the believers who follow you﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 215] [[See vol. 13, p. 134.]], and ﴿and lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾ [al-Isra': 24] [[See vol. 10, p. 236.]]. This verse abrogated every form of pardon, reconciliation, and forgiveness.

There are six issues in this passage.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They swear by Allah that they did not say﴾. It is reported that this verse was revealed concerning al-Jullas ibn Suwayd ibn al-Samit and Wadi'ah ibn Thabit, who attacked the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "By Allah, if Muhammad is truthful about our brothers, who are our masters and our best, then we are worse than donkeys." 'Amir ibn Qays said to him: "Indeed! By Allah, Muhammad is truthful and believed, and you are worse than a donkey." 'Amir reported that to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Jullas came and swore by Allah beside the pulpit of the Prophet (ﷺ) that 'Amir was lying. 'Amir swore that he had indeed said it, and said: "O Allah, send down upon Your truthful Prophet something." So it was revealed. It is also said that the one who heard it was 'Asim ibn 'Adi, and it is said Hudhayfah. It is said: rather, it was heard by the son of his wife, whose name was 'Umayr ibn Sa'd, according to what Ibn Ishaq said; others said his name was Mus'ab. Al-Jullas resolved to kill him lest he inform of the report, and concerning this it was revealed: "And they planned what they could not attain." Mujahid said: when his companion told him, "I will inform the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of your words," al-Jullas intended to kill him, but then did not do it, being unable to do so. He said: that is the indication of His saying, "And they planned what they could not attain." It is also said that it was revealed concerning 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy, who saw a man of Ghifar fighting with a man of Juhayna, and Juhayna were allies of the Ansar, and the Ghifari overpowered the Juhani. Ibn Ubayy said: "O sons of al-Aws and al-Khazraj, help your brother! By Allah, our situation and Muhammad's is only like the saying of the speaker: 'Fatten your dog and it will devour you.' If we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it." The Prophet (ﷺ) was informed of this, and 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy came and swore that he had not said it. This was related by Qatadah. A third view is that it was the saying of all the hypocrites; this was related by al-Hasan. Ibn al-'Arabi said: this is the sound view, because of the generality of the saying and the presence of the meaning in him and in them, and the sum of it is their belief about him, that he is not a prophet.

The second: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they uttered a word of disbelief﴾. al-Naqqash said: their denial of what Allah promised of victory. It is also said that "the word of disbelief" is the saying of al-Jullas: "If what Muhammad brought is true, then we are worse than donkeys," and the saying of 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy: "If we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it." al-Qushayri said: the word of disbelief is cursing the Prophet (ﷺ) and attacking Islam.

(And they disbelieved after their Islam) that is, after the ruling that they were Muslims. This indicates that the hypocrites are disbelievers. In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿That is because they believed and then disbelieved﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 3] there is a decisive proof. The verse also indicates that disbelief occurs through anything that contradicts affirmation and knowledge, although faith is not established except by "There is no god but Allah" alone, apart from other statements and actions, except in the prayer. Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said: they agreed concerning the prayer on something on which they did not agree in the rest of the laws, for they all said: whoever is known for disbelief and then is seen performing the prayer at its time, praying many prayers, and no verbal declaration of his is known, he is judged to be a believer; and they did not judge in the case of fasting and zakat by the like of that.

The third: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they planned what they could not attain﴾, meaning the hypocrites' plan to kill the Prophet (ﷺ) on the night of the 'Aqabah during the expedition of Tabuk; they were twelve men. Hudhayfah said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named them until he counted them all. I said: "Will you not send to them and kill them?" He said: "I dislike that the Arabs should say, when he prevailed over his companions, he began to kill them; rather, Allah suffices them with the Dubaylah." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the Dubaylah?" He said: "A flame from Hell that will be placed upon the sinew of the heart of one of them until his soul departs." And so it was. Muslim recorded it in meaning. It is also said that they planned to place the crown on the head of Ibn Ubayy so that they might gather around him. The saying of Mujahid on this has already been mentioned.

The fourth: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they did not resent except that Allah and His Messenger enriched them from His bounty﴾. That is, they have nothing to resent, as al-Nabighah said:

"And there is no fault in them, except that their swords have notches from the clashing of the battalions."

It is said: naqama yanqimu and naqima yanqamu. A poet said [in the kasra form]:

"They resented nothing from the Banu Umayyah, except that they are forbearing when they are angry."

Zuhayr said:

"He is delayed, placed in a book, and stored for the Day of Reckoning, or hastened and then requited."

It is recited with kasra and with fatha of the qaf. al-Sha'bi said: they used to seek blood-money, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would decide it for them, and they became rich. 'Ikrimah mentioned that it was twelve thousand. It is said that the slain man was a client of al-Jullas. al-Kalbi said: before the coming of the Prophet (ﷺ) they were in hardship of life, not riding horses and not obtaining booty; when the Prophet (ﷺ) came to them they became rich through the spoils. This saying is well known: "Beware the evil of one to whom you have shown kindness." al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: it was said to al-Bajali, "Do you find in the Book of Allah, 'Beware the evil of one to whom you have shown kindness'?" He said: yes, "And they did not resent except that Allah and His Messenger enriched them from His bounty."

The fifth: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So if they repent, it is better for them﴾. It is reported that when this verse was revealed, al-Jullas stood up, sought forgiveness, and repented. This indicates the repentance of the disbeliever who conceals disbelief and displays faith, whom the jurists call the zindiq. The scholars differed on this. al-Shafi'i said: his repentance is accepted. Malik said: the repentance of the zindiq is not recognized, because he used to display faith and conceal disbelief, and his faith is known only by his speech. Likewise he acts now at all times: he says, "I am a believer," while he conceals the opposite of what he displays. When he is caught and says, "I repent," his state does not change from what it was. If he comes to us repentant of his own accord before he is caught, his repentance is accepted, and this is what is meant by the verse. And Allah knows best.

The sixth: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And if they turn away﴾, that is, they turn away from faith and repentance, (Allah will punish them with a painful punishment) in this world by killing, and in the Hereafter by the Fire.

(And they have no protector on earth) that is, no one who prevents them, (nor any helper) that is, no supporter. This has already been mentioned.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verses 75–78 (part 1 of 2):

There are eight issues concerning this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah﴾. Qatadah said: This was a man from the Ansar (the Helpers of Madinah) who said: "If Allah grants me some wealth, I will surely give its due [[In MS ʿayn: "منه" and in MS hāʾ: "لله حقه."]] and I will surely give charity." But when Allah gave him that, he did what is stated about you. So beware of lying, for it leads to wickedness.

And ʿAlī ibn Yazīd [[Thus in MSS b, j, ʿayn, k; in MS alif: "Zayd." Both narrated from al-Qasim.]] narrated from al-Qasim, from Abu Umamah al-Bahili, that Thaʿlabah ibn Hatib al-Ansari (he named him) said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Pray to Allah that He grants me wealth." He said, (ﷺ): "Woe to you, O Thaʿlabah! A little that you can thank for is better than a lot that you cannot bear." Then he came back a second time, and the Prophet ﷺ said: (ﷺ) "Are you not content to be like the Prophet of Allah? If I wished, mountains would travel with me, made of gold, and they would travel." He said: "By the One who sent you with the truth, if you pray to Allah and He grants me wealth, I will surely give every person with a right his due." So the Prophet ﷺ prayed for him. He acquired sheep, and they multiplied as worms multiply, so Madinah became too narrow for him. He withdrew from it and settled in one of its valleys, until he began to pray Dhuhr and ʿAsr in congregation and abandoned everything other than them. Then they multiplied and increased until he abandoned the prayers except Friday, and they kept increasing until he abandoned Friday too. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (ﷺ) "Woe to Thaʿlabah!" three times. Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103]. So the Prophet ﷺ sent two men to collect the charity, and he said to them: (ﷺ) "Pass by Thaʿlabah and by so-and-so, a man of Banu Sulaym, and take their charities." So they went to Thaʿlabah and read him the letter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He said: "This is nothing but a sister of the jizyah (poll tax)! Go on until you are finished, then come back." The hadith is long, and it is well known.

It has also been said: the cause of Thaʿlabah's wealth was that he inherited from a paternal cousin of his. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: It has been said that Thaʿlabah ibn Hatib is the one about whom the verse "And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah" was revealed, when he withheld zakat. But Allah knows best. What has come concerning those who witnessed Badr is contradicted by His saying in the verse: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts﴾, and so on.

I say: It is also mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the occasion of revelation of the verse that Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah had his wealth delayed from him in Syria, so he swore in one of the gatherings [[In MSS j and ʿayn: "two gatherings."]] of the Ansar: "If that is secured for me, I will surely give charity from it and surely maintain ties of kinship with it." But when it was secured, he was stingy with it, so the verse was revealed.

I say: Thaʿlabah was a Badri and an Ansari, and among those whom Allah and His Messenger testified to as believers, as will be explained at the beginning of al-Mumtahanah [[The author will mention at the beginning of surat al-Mumtahanah that it is Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, not Thaʿlabah ibn Hatib.]]. So what is narrated about him is not sound. Abu ʿUmar said: Perhaps the view of those who said that Thaʿlabah was the withholder of zakat about whom the verse was revealed is not sound. But Allah knows best.

Al-Dahhak said: The verse was revealed concerning some men among the hypocrites: Nabtal ibn al-Harith, Jadd ibn Qays, and Muʿattib ibn Qushayr.

I say: This is more fitting to the revelation of the verse concerning them. However, His saying "So He caused hypocrisy to follow" indicates that the one who made the covenant with Allah was not a hypocrite before that, unless the meaning is: He increased them in hypocrisy, which they persisted in until death. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until the Day they meet Him﴾, as will come.

The second: Our scholars said: When Allah, exalted is He, said "And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah," it is possible that he made the covenant with Allah by his tongue without believing it in his heart. And it is possible that he made the covenant with both, then a bad ending overtook him, for actions are by their endings and days are by their outcomes. "Man" (من) is in the nominative case as the subject, and the predicate is in the prepositional phrase.

The word "oath" (yamin) occurs in the hadith, and there is no oath in the apparent wording of the Qur'an except by mere binding and commitment. As for it being in the form of an oath in meaning, the lam indicates it. He used two lams: the first is the lam of the oath, and the second is the lam of the response, and both are for emphasis. Some said: They are both lams of the oath, and the first is more apparent. But Allah knows best.

The third: A vow of divorce (talaq) and every ruling that a person undertakes alone, without needing anyone else in it, binds him to what he intends to commit to, even if he does not utter it, as our scholars said. Al-Shafiʿi and Abu Hanifah said: No ruling binds anyone unless he utters it. This is the other view of our scholars. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: The evidence for the soundness of what we have taken is what Ashhab narrated from Malik, when he was asked about a man who intends divorce in his heart but does not utter it with his tongue, and he said: It binds him, just as he is a believer in his heart or a disbeliever in his heart. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: This is a wonderful principle, and its formulation is: A contract in which a person does not need anyone else for his commitment to it is concluded by intention. Its origin is faith and disbelief.

I say: The argument of the second view is what Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (ﷺ) "Indeed Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper about, so long as they do not act upon it or speak it." Al-Tirmidhi narrated it and said: It is a good, sound hadith. And the practice according to the people of knowledge is that if a man speaks to himself about divorce, it is nothing until he speaks it. Abu ʿUmar said: Whoever believes in his heart in divorce but his tongue does not pronounce it, it is nothing. This is the more famous view from Malik. It has also been narrated from him that divorce binds him if he intends it in his heart, just as he disbelieves in his heart even if his tongue does not utter it. The first view is more correct in reasoning and in the path of the transmitted reports, based on the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: (ﷺ) "Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper about, so long as no tongue utters it or hand does it."

The fourth: If it is a vow (nadhr), then fulfilling a vow is obligatory without disagreement, and abandoning it is disobedience. If it is an oath (yamin), then fulfilling an oath is not obligatory by consensus. However, the meaning here is: if the man was poor, zakat was not obligatory upon him, so he asked Allah for wealth on which zakat would become obligatory for him, and he would pay what became obligatory upon him of his duty. When Allah gave him what He willed of that, he abandoned what he had committed himself to, which would not have been binding upon him in the basic religion had he not committed himself to it. But the striving to seek wealth for paying the rights was what ensnared him, since his request from Allah, exalted is He, was without a sincere intention, or with an intention but the beginning that was written for him had already preceded in it, in which was wretchedness. We seek refuge in Allah from that.

I say: From this meaning is His saying, peace be upon him: (ﷺ) "When one of you wishes, let him consider what he wishes for, for he does not know what has been written for him in the unseen of Allah, mighty and majestic, from his wish." That is, from its consequence. For many a wish a person is tempted by, or becomes arrogant, and so it becomes a cause of ruin in this world and the next, because the affairs of this world are obscure, their outcomes are uncertain, and their harms are dangerous. As for wishing for matters of religion and the Hereafter, wishing for them has a praiseworthy outcome, is encouraged, and is recommended.

The fifth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity﴾ is evidence that whoever says, "If I own such and such, then it is charity," it binds him. This is the view of Abu Hanifah. Al-Shafiʿi said: It does not bind him. The disagreement regarding divorce is similar, and likewise regarding manumission (ʿitq). Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: It binds him regarding manumission but does not bind him regarding divorce, because manumission is an act of devotion, and such devotion is established in one's obligation through a vow, unlike divorce, which is a disposition over a subject, and it is not established in one's obligation.

Al-Shafiʿi used as evidence what Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (ﷺ) "There is no vow for the son of Adam regarding what he does not own, nor manumission for him regarding what he does not own, nor divorce for him regarding what he does not own." This is the wording of al-Tirmidhi. He said: On this subject there are also reports from ʿAli, Muʿadh, Jabir, Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAʾishah. The hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr is a good hadith, and it is the best that has been narrated on this subject. And it is the view of most people of knowledge among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ and others.

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: The companions of al-Shafiʿi have cited many hadiths on this subject, none of which is authentic, so one should not rely upon them, and nothing remains except the apparent meaning of the verse.

The sixth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But when He gave them of His bounty﴾, meaning He gave them.

(They were stingy with it): meaning with giving charity and spending wealth in good, and with fulfilling what they had guaranteed and committed to. Stinginess has already been discussed in Surat Al ʿImran [[See vol. 4, p. 290.]].

(And they turned away): meaning from obedience to Allah.

(While they were refusing): meaning from Islam, that is, showing aversion to it.

The seventh: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow﴾ has two objects: that is, Allah, exalted is He, caused hypocrisy in their hearts to follow. It has been said: that is, He caused stinginess to follow them as hypocrisy, and for this He said "they were stingy with it."

(Until the Day they meet Him): it is in the position of a genitive, that is, they meet their stinginess, meaning the recompense of their stinginess, as one says, "Tomorrow you will meet your deeds." It has also been said: (Until the Day they meet Him) means they meet Allah. In this there is evidence that he died a hypocrite. And it is unlikely that the one about whom it was revealed was Thaʿlabah or Hatib, because the Prophet ﷺ said to ʿUmar: (ﷺ) "And what makes you know? Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do what you wish, for I have forgiven you." And Thaʿlabah and Hatib were among those who were present at Badr and witnessed it.

(Those] because they broke their promise to God and because they lied. Their lying was their breaking of the covenant and their failure to fulfil what they had bound themselves to.

Eighth issue: His saying, ﴿hypocrisy (nifaq)﴾. Nifaq (hypocrisy) is disbelief when it lies in the heart. When it lies in actions, it is a sin. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever has four traits will be a pure hypocrite, and whoever has one of them has one trait of hypocrisy until he gives it up: when he is entrusted, he betrays; when he speaks, he lies; when he makes a covenant, he breaks it; and when he disputes, he is treacherous." Al-Bukhari transmitted it. The derivation of this word has already been discussed in [al-Baqarah] [[See vol. 1 pp. 178, 98 1.]], so there is no point in repeating it.

People differ on the interpretation of this hadith. One group said: this applies only to someone who tells a story knowing it is false, makes a covenant he does not intend to keep, and waits for a trust in order to betray it. They relied on a hadith with a weak chain, that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, met Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, as they were coming out from the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and they were downcast [[In MS ʿAyn: "weeping" / "they weep" / "they are weeping."]]. ʿAlī said: "What is the matter with you two, that I see you downcast?" They said: "A hadith we heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the traits of the hypocrites: 'When he speaks he lies, when he makes a covenant he breaks it, when he is entrusted he betrays, and when he promises he fails to keep it.'" ʿAlī said: "Did you not ask him?" They said: "We were in awe of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." He said: "But I will ask him." He went in to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar went out and they were downcast," and then he mentioned what they had said. He said: "I have spoken to them, but I did not put it in the sense they understood. Rather, the hypocrite, when he speaks while speaking to himself that he is lying, when he promises while speaking to himself that he will fail, and when he is entrusted while speaking to himself that he will betray." 

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: Clear evidence has established that one who deliberately commits these traits does not become a disbeliever; he becomes a disbeliever only through a belief that goes back to ignorance of Allah and His attributes, or to denying Him. [Exalted is Allah above the belief of the ignorant and above the deviation of the deviators] [[From MS ʿAyn.]].

Another group said: this is specific to the hypocrites of the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. They relied on what Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān transmitted from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "We came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with some of his companions and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you said: "Three, whoever has them is a hypocrite even if he fasts, prays, and claims to be a believer: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he fails, and when he is entrusted he betrays; and whoever has one of them has a share of hypocrisy."' We thought that we were not free of them, or of some of them, and that many people were not free of them." He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ laughed and said: "What is the matter with you and them? I only singled out the hypocrites with them, as Allah singled them out in His Book. As for my saying, 'When he speaks he lies,' that is His saying, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿When the hypocrites come to you...﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn: 1], to the end of the verse. Are you like that?" We said: "No." He said: "Do not worry, you are free of that. As for my saying, 'When he promises he fails,' that concerns what Allah revealed to me: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with God: "If He gives us of His bounty..."﴾ [at-Tawbah: 75], the three verses. Are you like that?" We said: "No. By Allah, if we made a covenant with God regarding something, we would fulfil it." He said: "Do not worry, you are free of that. As for my saying, 'When he is entrusted he betrays,' that concerns what Allah revealed to me: ﴿Indeed, We offered the Trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains...﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 72], to the end of the verse. Every person is entrusted with his religion. The believer washes from major impurity in private and in public, while the hypocrite does so only in public. Are you like that?" We said: "No." He said: "Do not worry, you are free of that."

Many of the Successors and the imams held this view.

Another group said: this applies to one in whom these traits predominate. It appears from the position of al-Bukhārī and other scholars that whoever is characterised by these blameworthy traits is a hypocrite until the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: What I hold is that if sins predominate over a person, he does not become a disbeliever through them, so long as they do not affect his belief.

Our scholars said: The brothers of Yūsuf, upon him be peace, made a covenant with their father and broke it, they told him something and lied to him, and he entrusted them with Yūsuf and they betrayed him, yet they were not hypocrites.

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ said: The brothers of Yūsuf did these traits, and they were not hypocrites; rather they were prophets [[The correct view is that they were not prophets, because their action contradicts infallibility.]].

Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said: Hypocrisy is of two kinds: hypocrisy of lying and hypocrisy of action. As for hypocrisy of lying, it existed in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. As for hypocrisy of action, it does not end until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Bukhārī transmitted from Ḥudhayfah that hypocrisy existed in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but today it is only disbelief after belief.

His saying, ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows their secret and their private conversation?﴾ This is a rebuke, and since He is knowing, He will requite them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verses 75–78 (part 1 of 2):

There are eight issues concerning this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah﴾. Qatadah said: This was a man from the Ansar (the Helpers of Madinah) who said: "If Allah grants me some wealth, I will surely give its due [[In MS ʿayn: "منه" and in MS hāʾ: "لله حقه."]] and I will surely give charity." But when Allah gave him that, he did what is stated about you. So beware of lying, for it leads to wickedness.

And ʿAlī ibn Yazīd [[Thus in MSS b, j, ʿayn, k; in MS alif: "Zayd." Both narrated from al-Qasim.]] narrated from al-Qasim, from Abu Umamah al-Bahili, that Thaʿlabah ibn Hatib al-Ansari (he named him) said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Pray to Allah that He grants me wealth." He said, (ﷺ): "Woe to you, O Thaʿlabah! A little that you can thank for is better than a lot that you cannot bear." Then he came back a second time, and the Prophet ﷺ said: (ﷺ) "Are you not content to be like the Prophet of Allah? If I wished, mountains would travel with me, made of gold, and they would travel." He said: "By the One who sent you with the truth, if you pray to Allah and He grants me wealth, I will surely give every person with a right his due." So the Prophet ﷺ prayed for him. He acquired sheep, and they multiplied as worms multiply, so Madinah became too narrow for him. He withdrew from it and settled in one of its valleys, until he began to pray Dhuhr and ʿAsr in congregation and abandoned everything other than them. Then they multiplied and increased until he abandoned the prayers except Friday, and they kept increasing until he abandoned Friday too. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (ﷺ) "Woe to Thaʿlabah!" three times. Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103]. So the Prophet ﷺ sent two men to collect the charity, and he said to them: (ﷺ) "Pass by Thaʿlabah and by so-and-so, a man of Banu Sulaym, and take their charities." So they went to Thaʿlabah and read him the letter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He said: "This is nothing but a sister of the jizyah (poll tax)! Go on until you are finished, then come back." The hadith is long, and it is well known.

It has also been said: the cause of Thaʿlabah's wealth was that he inherited from a paternal cousin of his. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: It has been said that Thaʿlabah ibn Hatib is the one about whom the verse "And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah" was revealed, when he withheld zakat. But Allah knows best. What has come concerning those who witnessed Badr is contradicted by His saying in the verse: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts﴾, and so on.

I say: It is also mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the occasion of revelation of the verse that Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah had his wealth delayed from him in Syria, so he swore in one of the gatherings [[In MSS j and ʿayn: "two gatherings."]] of the Ansar: "If that is secured for me, I will surely give charity from it and surely maintain ties of kinship with it." But when it was secured, he was stingy with it, so the verse was revealed.

I say: Thaʿlabah was a Badri and an Ansari, and among those whom Allah and His Messenger testified to as believers, as will be explained at the beginning of al-Mumtahanah [[The author will mention at the beginning of surat al-Mumtahanah that it is Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, not Thaʿlabah ibn Hatib.]]. So what is narrated about him is not sound. Abu ʿUmar said: Perhaps the view of those who said that Thaʿlabah was the withholder of zakat about whom the verse was revealed is not sound. But Allah knows best.

Al-Dahhak said: The verse was revealed concerning some men among the hypocrites: Nabtal ibn al-Harith, Jadd ibn Qays, and Muʿattib ibn Qushayr.

I say: This is more fitting to the revelation of the verse concerning them. However, His saying "So He caused hypocrisy to follow" indicates that the one who made the covenant with Allah was not a hypocrite before that, unless the meaning is: He increased them in hypocrisy, which they persisted in until death. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until the Day they meet Him﴾, as will come.

The second: Our scholars said: When Allah, exalted is He, said "And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah," it is possible that he made the covenant with Allah by his tongue without believing it in his heart. And it is possible that he made the covenant with both, then a bad ending overtook him, for actions are by their endings and days are by their outcomes. "Man" (من) is in the nominative case as the subject, and the predicate is in the prepositional phrase.

The word "oath" (yamin) occurs in the hadith, and there is no oath in the apparent wording of the Qur'an except by mere binding and commitment. As for it being in the form of an oath in meaning, the lam indicates it. He used two lams: the first is the lam of the oath, and the second is the lam of the response, and both are for emphasis. Some said: They are both lams of the oath, and the first is more apparent. But Allah knows best.

The third: A vow of divorce (talaq) and every ruling that a person undertakes alone, without needing anyone else in it, binds him to what he intends to commit to, even if he does not utter it, as our scholars said. Al-Shafiʿi and Abu Hanifah said: No ruling binds anyone unless he utters it. This is the other view of our scholars. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: The evidence for the soundness of what we have taken is what Ashhab narrated from Malik, when he was asked about a man who intends divorce in his heart but does not utter it with his tongue, and he said: It binds him, just as he is a believer in his heart or a disbeliever in his heart. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: This is a wonderful principle, and its formulation is: A contract in which a person does not need anyone else for his commitment to it is concluded by intention. Its origin is faith and disbelief.

I say: The argument of the second view is what Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (ﷺ) "Indeed Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper about, so long as they do not act upon it or speak it." Al-Tirmidhi narrated it and said: It is a good, sound hadith. And the practice according to the people of knowledge is that if a man speaks to himself about divorce, it is nothing until he speaks it. Abu ʿUmar said: Whoever believes in his heart in divorce but his tongue does not pronounce it, it is nothing. This is the more famous view from Malik. It has also been narrated from him that divorce binds him if he intends it in his heart, just as he disbelieves in his heart even if his tongue does not utter it. The first view is more correct in reasoning and in the path of the transmitted reports, based on the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: (ﷺ) "Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper about, so long as no tongue utters it or hand does it."

The fourth: If it is a vow (nadhr), then fulfilling a vow is obligatory without disagreement, and abandoning it is disobedience. If it is an oath (yamin), then fulfilling an oath is not obligatory by consensus. However, the meaning here is: if the man was poor, zakat was not obligatory upon him, so he asked Allah for wealth on which zakat would become obligatory for him, and he would pay what became obligatory upon him of his duty. When Allah gave him what He willed of that, he abandoned what he had committed himself to, which would not have been binding upon him in the basic religion had he not committed himself to it. But the striving to seek wealth for paying the rights was what ensnared him, since his request from Allah, exalted is He, was without a sincere intention, or with an intention but the beginning that was written for him had already preceded in it, in which was wretchedness. We seek refuge in Allah from that.

I say: From this meaning is His saying, peace be upon him: (ﷺ) "When one of you wishes, let him consider what he wishes for, for he does not know what has been written for him in the unseen of Allah, mighty and majestic, from his wish." That is, from its consequence. For many a wish a person is tempted by, or becomes arrogant, and so it becomes a cause of ruin in this world and the next, because the affairs of this world are obscure, their outcomes are uncertain, and their harms are dangerous. As for wishing for matters of religion and the Hereafter, wishing for them has a praiseworthy outcome, is encouraged, and is recommended.

The fifth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity﴾ is evidence that whoever says, "If I own such and such, then it is charity," it binds him. This is the view of Abu Hanifah. Al-Shafiʿi said: It does not bind him. The disagreement regarding divorce is similar, and likewise regarding manumission (ʿitq). Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: It binds him regarding manumission but does not bind him regarding divorce, because manumission is an act of devotion, and such devotion is established in one's obligation through a vow, unlike divorce, which is a disposition over a subject, and it is not established in one's obligation.

Al-Shafiʿi used as evidence what Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (ﷺ) "There is no vow for the son of Adam regarding what he does not own, nor manumission for him regarding what he does not own, nor divorce for him regarding what he does not own." This is the wording of al-Tirmidhi. He said: On this subject there are also reports from ʿAli, Muʿadh, Jabir, Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAʾishah. The hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr is a good hadith, and it is the best that has been narrated on this subject. And it is the view of most people of knowledge among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ and others.

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: The companions of al-Shafiʿi have cited many hadiths on this subject, none of which is authentic, so one should not rely upon them, and nothing remains except the apparent meaning of the verse.

The sixth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But when He gave them of His bounty﴾, meaning He gave them.

(They were stingy with it): meaning with giving charity and spending wealth in good, and with fulfilling what they had guaranteed and committed to. Stinginess has already been discussed in Surat Al ʿImran [[See vol. 4, p. 290.]].

(And they turned away): meaning from obedience to Allah.

(While they were refusing): meaning from Islam, that is, showing aversion to it.

The seventh: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow﴾ has two objects: that is, Allah, exalted is He, caused hypocrisy in their hearts to follow. It has been said: that is, He caused stinginess to follow them as hypocrisy, and for this He said "they were stingy with it."

(Until the Day they meet Him): it is in the position of a genitive, that is, they meet their stinginess, meaning the recompense of their stinginess, as one says, "Tomorrow you will meet your deeds." It has also been said: (Until the Day they meet Him) means they meet Allah. In this there is evidence that he died a hypocrite. And it is unlikely that the one about whom it was revealed was Thaʿlabah or Hatib, because the Prophet ﷺ said to ʿUmar: (ﷺ) "And what makes you know? Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do what you wish, for I have forgiven you." And Thaʿlabah and Hatib were among those who were present at Badr and witnessed it.

(Those] because they broke their promise to God and because they lied. Their lying was their breaking of the covenant and their failure to fulfil what they had bound themselves to.

Eighth issue: His saying, ﴿hypocrisy (nifaq)﴾. Nifaq (hypocrisy) is disbelief when it lies in the heart. When it lies in actions, it is a sin. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever has four traits will be a pure hypocrite, and whoever has one of them has one trait of hypocrisy until he gives it up: when he is entrusted, he betrays; when he speaks, he lies; when he makes a covenant, he breaks it; and when he disputes, he is treacherous." Al-Bukhari transmitted it. The derivation of this word has already been discussed in [al-Baqarah] [[See vol. 1 pp. 178, 98 1.]], so there is no point in repeating it.

People differ on the interpretation of this hadith. One group said: this applies only to someone who tells a story knowing it is false, makes a covenant he does not intend to keep, and waits for a trust in order to betray it. They relied on a hadith with a weak chain, that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, met Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, as they were coming out from the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and they were downcast [[In MS ʿAyn: "weeping" / "they weep" / "they are weeping."]]. ʿAlī said: "What is the matter with you two, that I see you downcast?" They said: "A hadith we heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the traits of the hypocrites: 'When he speaks he lies, when he makes a covenant he breaks it, when he is entrusted he betrays, and when he promises he fails to keep it.'" ʿAlī said: "Did you not ask him?" They said: "We were in awe of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." He said: "But I will ask him." He went in to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar went out and they were downcast," and then he mentioned what they had said. He said: "I have spoken to them, but I did not put it in the sense they understood. Rather, the hypocrite, when he speaks while speaking to himself that he is lying, when he promises while speaking to himself that he will fail, and when he is entrusted while speaking to himself that he will betray." 

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: Clear evidence has established that one who deliberately commits these traits does not become a disbeliever; he becomes a disbeliever only through a belief that goes back to ignorance of Allah and His attributes, or to denying Him. [Exalted is Allah above the belief of the ignorant and above the deviation of the deviators] [[From MS ʿAyn.]].

Another group said: this is specific to the hypocrites of the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. They relied on what Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān transmitted from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "We came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with some of his companions and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you said: "Three, whoever has them is a hypocrite even if he fasts, prays, and claims to be a believer: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he fails, and when he is entrusted he betrays; and whoever has one of them has a share of hypocrisy."' We thought that we were not free of them, or of some of them, and that many people were not free of them." He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ laughed and said: "What is the matter with you and them? I only singled out the hypocrites with them, as Allah singled them out in His Book. As for my saying, 'When he speaks he lies,' that is His saying, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿When the hypocrites come to you...﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn: 1], to the end of the verse. Are you like that?" We said: "No." He said: "Do not worry, you are free of that. As for my saying, 'When he promises he fails,' that concerns what Allah revealed to me: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with God: "If He gives us of His bounty..."﴾ [at-Tawbah: 75], the three verses. Are you like that?" We said: "No. By Allah, if we made a covenant with God regarding something, we would fulfil it." He said: "Do not worry, you are free of that. As for my saying, 'When he is entrusted he betrays,' that concerns what Allah revealed to me: ﴿Indeed, We offered the Trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains...﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 72], to the end of the verse. Every person is entrusted with his religion. The believer washes from major impurity in private and in public, while the hypocrite does so only in public. Are you like that?" We said: "No." He said: "Do not worry, you are free of that."

Many of the Successors and the imams held this view.

Another group said: this applies to one in whom these traits predominate. It appears from the position of al-Bukhārī and other scholars that whoever is characterised by these blameworthy traits is a hypocrite until the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: What I hold is that if sins predominate over a person, he does not become a disbeliever through them, so long as they do not affect his belief.

Our scholars said: The brothers of Yūsuf, upon him be peace, made a covenant with their father and broke it, they told him something and lied to him, and he entrusted them with Yūsuf and they betrayed him, yet they were not hypocrites.

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ said: The brothers of Yūsuf did these traits, and they were not hypocrites; rather they were prophets [[The correct view is that they were not prophets, because their action contradicts infallibility.]].

Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said: Hypocrisy is of two kinds: hypocrisy of lying and hypocrisy of action. As for hypocrisy of lying, it existed in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. As for hypocrisy of action, it does not end until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Bukhārī transmitted from Ḥudhayfah that hypocrisy existed in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but today it is only disbelief after belief.

His saying, ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows their secret and their private conversation?﴾ This is a rebuke, and since He is knowing, He will requite them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verses 75–78 (part 1 of 2):

There are eight issues concerning this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah﴾. Qatadah said: This was a man from the Ansar (the Helpers of Madinah) who said: "If Allah grants me some wealth, I will surely give its due [[In MS ʿayn: "منه" and in MS hāʾ: "لله حقه."]] and I will surely give charity." But when Allah gave him that, he did what is stated about you. So beware of lying, for it leads to wickedness.

And ʿAlī ibn Yazīd [[Thus in MSS b, j, ʿayn, k; in MS alif: "Zayd." Both narrated from al-Qasim.]] narrated from al-Qasim, from Abu Umamah al-Bahili, that Thaʿlabah ibn Hatib al-Ansari (he named him) said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Pray to Allah that He grants me wealth." He said, (ﷺ): "Woe to you, O Thaʿlabah! A little that you can thank for is better than a lot that you cannot bear." Then he came back a second time, and the Prophet ﷺ said: (ﷺ) "Are you not content to be like the Prophet of Allah? If I wished, mountains would travel with me, made of gold, and they would travel." He said: "By the One who sent you with the truth, if you pray to Allah and He grants me wealth, I will surely give every person with a right his due." So the Prophet ﷺ prayed for him. He acquired sheep, and they multiplied as worms multiply, so Madinah became too narrow for him. He withdrew from it and settled in one of its valleys, until he began to pray Dhuhr and ʿAsr in congregation and abandoned everything other than them. Then they multiplied and increased until he abandoned the prayers except Friday, and they kept increasing until he abandoned Friday too. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (ﷺ) "Woe to Thaʿlabah!" three times. Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103]. So the Prophet ﷺ sent two men to collect the charity, and he said to them: (ﷺ) "Pass by Thaʿlabah and by so-and-so, a man of Banu Sulaym, and take their charities." So they went to Thaʿlabah and read him the letter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He said: "This is nothing but a sister of the jizyah (poll tax)! Go on until you are finished, then come back." The hadith is long, and it is well known.

It has also been said: the cause of Thaʿlabah's wealth was that he inherited from a paternal cousin of his. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: It has been said that Thaʿlabah ibn Hatib is the one about whom the verse "And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah" was revealed, when he withheld zakat. But Allah knows best. What has come concerning those who witnessed Badr is contradicted by His saying in the verse: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts﴾, and so on.

I say: It is also mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the occasion of revelation of the verse that Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah had his wealth delayed from him in Syria, so he swore in one of the gatherings [[In MSS j and ʿayn: "two gatherings."]] of the Ansar: "If that is secured for me, I will surely give charity from it and surely maintain ties of kinship with it." But when it was secured, he was stingy with it, so the verse was revealed.

I say: Thaʿlabah was a Badri and an Ansari, and among those whom Allah and His Messenger testified to as believers, as will be explained at the beginning of al-Mumtahanah [[The author will mention at the beginning of surat al-Mumtahanah that it is Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, not Thaʿlabah ibn Hatib.]]. So what is narrated about him is not sound. Abu ʿUmar said: Perhaps the view of those who said that Thaʿlabah was the withholder of zakat about whom the verse was revealed is not sound. But Allah knows best.

Al-Dahhak said: The verse was revealed concerning some men among the hypocrites: Nabtal ibn al-Harith, Jadd ibn Qays, and Muʿattib ibn Qushayr.

I say: This is more fitting to the revelation of the verse concerning them. However, His saying "So He caused hypocrisy to follow" indicates that the one who made the covenant with Allah was not a hypocrite before that, unless the meaning is: He increased them in hypocrisy, which they persisted in until death. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until the Day they meet Him﴾, as will come.

The second: Our scholars said: When Allah, exalted is He, said "And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah," it is possible that he made the covenant with Allah by his tongue without believing it in his heart. And it is possible that he made the covenant with both, then a bad ending overtook him, for actions are by their endings and days are by their outcomes. "Man" (من) is in the nominative case as the subject, and the predicate is in the prepositional phrase.

The word "oath" (yamin) occurs in the hadith, and there is no oath in the apparent wording of the Qur'an except by mere binding and commitment. As for it being in the form of an oath in meaning, the lam indicates it. He used two lams: the first is the lam of the oath, and the second is the lam of the response, and both are for emphasis. Some said: They are both lams of the oath, and the first is more apparent. But Allah knows best.

The third: A vow of divorce (talaq) and every ruling that a person undertakes alone, without needing anyone else in it, binds him to what he intends to commit to, even if he does not utter it, as our scholars said. Al-Shafiʿi and Abu Hanifah said: No ruling binds anyone unless he utters it. This is the other view of our scholars. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: The evidence for the soundness of what we have taken is what Ashhab narrated from Malik, when he was asked about a man who intends divorce in his heart but does not utter it with his tongue, and he said: It binds him, just as he is a believer in his heart or a disbeliever in his heart. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: This is a wonderful principle, and its formulation is: A contract in which a person does not need anyone else for his commitment to it is concluded by intention. Its origin is faith and disbelief.

I say: The argument of the second view is what Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (ﷺ) "Indeed Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper about, so long as they do not act upon it or speak it." Al-Tirmidhi narrated it and said: It is a good, sound hadith. And the practice according to the people of knowledge is that if a man speaks to himself about divorce, it is nothing until he speaks it. Abu ʿUmar said: Whoever believes in his heart in divorce but his tongue does not pronounce it, it is nothing. This is the more famous view from Malik. It has also been narrated from him that divorce binds him if he intends it in his heart, just as he disbelieves in his heart even if his tongue does not utter it. The first view is more correct in reasoning and in the path of the transmitted reports, based on the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: (ﷺ) "Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper about, so long as no tongue utters it or hand does it."

The fourth: If it is a vow (nadhr), then fulfilling a vow is obligatory without disagreement, and abandoning it is disobedience. If it is an oath (yamin), then fulfilling an oath is not obligatory by consensus. However, the meaning here is: if the man was poor, zakat was not obligatory upon him, so he asked Allah for wealth on which zakat would become obligatory for him, and he would pay what became obligatory upon him of his duty. When Allah gave him what He willed of that, he abandoned what he had committed himself to, which would not have been binding upon him in the basic religion had he not committed himself to it. But the striving to seek wealth for paying the rights was what ensnared him, since his request from Allah, exalted is He, was without a sincere intention, or with an intention but the beginning that was written for him had already preceded in it, in which was wretchedness. We seek refuge in Allah from that.

I say: From this meaning is His saying, peace be upon him: (ﷺ) "When one of you wishes, let him consider what he wishes for, for he does not know what has been written for him in the unseen of Allah, mighty and majestic, from his wish." That is, from its consequence. For many a wish a person is tempted by, or becomes arrogant, and so it becomes a cause of ruin in this world and the next, because the affairs of this world are obscure, their outcomes are uncertain, and their harms are dangerous. As for wishing for matters of religion and the Hereafter, wishing for them has a praiseworthy outcome, is encouraged, and is recommended.

The fifth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity﴾ is evidence that whoever says, "If I own such and such, then it is charity," it binds him. This is the view of Abu Hanifah. Al-Shafiʿi said: It does not bind him. The disagreement regarding divorce is similar, and likewise regarding manumission (ʿitq). Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: It binds him regarding manumission but does not bind him regarding divorce, because manumission is an act of devotion, and such devotion is established in one's obligation through a vow, unlike divorce, which is a disposition over a subject, and it is not established in one's obligation.

Al-Shafiʿi used as evidence what Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (ﷺ) "There is no vow for the son of Adam regarding what he does not own, nor manumission for him regarding what he does not own, nor divorce for him regarding what he does not own." This is the wording of al-Tirmidhi. He said: On this subject there are also reports from ʿAli, Muʿadh, Jabir, Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAʾishah. The hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr is a good hadith, and it is the best that has been narrated on this subject. And it is the view of most people of knowledge among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ and others.

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: The companions of al-Shafiʿi have cited many hadiths on this subject, none of which is authentic, so one should not rely upon them, and nothing remains except the apparent meaning of the verse.

The sixth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But when He gave them of His bounty﴾, meaning He gave them.

(They were stingy with it): meaning with giving charity and spending wealth in good, and with fulfilling what they had guaranteed and committed to. Stinginess has already been discussed in Surat Al ʿImran [[See vol. 4, p. 290.]].

(And they turned away): meaning from obedience to Allah.

(While they were refusing): meaning from Islam, that is, showing aversion to it.

The seventh: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow﴾ has two objects: that is, Allah, exalted is He, caused hypocrisy in their hearts to follow. It has been said: that is, He caused stinginess to follow them as hypocrisy, and for this He said "they were stingy with it."

(Until the Day they meet Him): it is in the position of a genitive, that is, they meet their stinginess, meaning the recompense of their stinginess, as one says, "Tomorrow you will meet your deeds." It has also been said: (Until the Day they meet Him) means they meet Allah. In this there is evidence that he died a hypocrite. And it is unlikely that the one about whom it was revealed was Thaʿlabah or Hatib, because the Prophet ﷺ said to ʿUmar: (ﷺ) "And what makes you know? Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do what you wish, for I have forgiven you." And Thaʿlabah and Hatib were among those who were present at Badr and witnessed it.

(Those] because they broke their promise to God and because they lied. Their lying was their breaking of the covenant and their failure to fulfil what they had bound themselves to.

Eighth issue: His saying, ﴿hypocrisy (nifaq)﴾. Nifaq (hypocrisy) is disbelief when it lies in the heart. When it lies in actions, it is a sin. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever has four traits will be a pure hypocrite, and whoever has one of them has one trait of hypocrisy until he gives it up: when he is entrusted, he betrays; when he speaks, he lies; when he makes a covenant, he breaks it; and when he disputes, he is treacherous." Al-Bukhari transmitted it. The derivation of this word has already been discussed in [al-Baqarah] [[See vol. 1 pp. 178, 98 1.]], so there is no point in repeating it.

People differ on the interpretation of this hadith. One group said: this applies only to someone who tells a story knowing it is false, makes a covenant he does not intend to keep, and waits for a trust in order to betray it. They relied on a hadith with a weak chain, that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, met Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, as they were coming out from the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and they were downcast [[In MS ʿAyn: "weeping" / "they weep" / "they are weeping."]]. ʿAlī said: "What is the matter with you two, that I see you downcast?" They said: "A hadith we heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the traits of the hypocrites: 'When he speaks he lies, when he makes a covenant he breaks it, when he is entrusted he betrays, and when he promises he fails to keep it.'" ʿAlī said: "Did you not ask him?" They said: "We were in awe of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." He said: "But I will ask him." He went in to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar went out and they were downcast," and then he mentioned what they had said. He said: "I have spoken to them, but I did not put it in the sense they understood. Rather, the hypocrite, when he speaks while speaking to himself that he is lying, when he promises while speaking to himself that he will fail, and when he is entrusted while speaking to himself that he will betray." 

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: Clear evidence has established that one who deliberately commits these traits does not become a disbeliever; he becomes a disbeliever only through a belief that goes back to ignorance of Allah and His attributes, or to denying Him. [Exalted is Allah above the belief of the ignorant and above the deviation of the deviators] [[From MS ʿAyn.]].

Another group said: this is specific to the hypocrites of the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
