They relied on what Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān transmitted from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "We came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with some of his companions and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you said: "Three, whoever has them is a hypocrite even if he fasts, prays, and claims to be a believer: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he fails, and when he is entrusted he betrays; and whoever has one of them has a share of hypocrisy."' We thought that we were not free of them, or of some of them, and that many people were not free of them." He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ laughed and said: "What is the matter with you and them? I only singled out the hypocrites with them, as Allah singled them out in His Book. As for my saying, 'When he speaks he lies,' that is His saying, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿When the hypocrites come to you...﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn: 1], to the end of the verse. Are you like that?" We said: "No." He said: "Do not worry, you are free of that. As for my saying, 'When he promises he fails,' that concerns what Allah revealed to me: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with God: "If He gives us of His bounty..."﴾ [at-Tawbah: 75], the three verses. Are you like that?" We said: "No. By Allah, if we made a covenant with God regarding something, we would fulfil it." He said: "Do not worry, you are free of that. As for my saying, 'When he is entrusted he betrays,' that concerns what Allah revealed to me: ﴿Indeed, We offered the Trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains...﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 72], to the end of the verse. Every person is entrusted with his religion. The believer washes from major impurity in private and in public, while the hypocrite does so only in public. Are you like that?" We said: "No." He said: "Do not worry, you are free of that."

Many of the Successors and the imams held this view.

Another group said: this applies to one in whom these traits predominate. It appears from the position of al-Bukhārī and other scholars that whoever is characterised by these blameworthy traits is a hypocrite until the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: What I hold is that if sins predominate over a person, he does not become a disbeliever through them, so long as they do not affect his belief.

Our scholars said: The brothers of Yūsuf, upon him be peace, made a covenant with their father and broke it, they told him something and lied to him, and he entrusted them with Yūsuf and they betrayed him, yet they were not hypocrites.

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ said: The brothers of Yūsuf did these traits, and they were not hypocrites; rather they were prophets [[The correct view is that they were not prophets, because their action contradicts infallibility.]].

Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said: Hypocrisy is of two kinds: hypocrisy of lying and hypocrisy of action. As for hypocrisy of lying, it existed in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. As for hypocrisy of action, it does not end until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Bukhārī transmitted from Ḥudhayfah that hypocrisy existed in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but today it is only disbelief after belief.

His saying, ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows their secret and their private conversation?﴾ This is a rebuke, and since He is knowing, He will requite them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verses 75–78 (part 1 of 2):

There are eight issues concerning this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah﴾. Qatadah said: This was a man from the Ansar (the Helpers of Madinah) who said: "If Allah grants me some wealth, I will surely give its due [[In MS ʿayn: "منه" and in MS hāʾ: "لله حقه."]] and I will surely give charity." But when Allah gave him that, he did what is stated about you. So beware of lying, for it leads to wickedness.

And ʿAlī ibn Yazīd [[Thus in MSS b, j, ʿayn, k; in MS alif: "Zayd." Both narrated from al-Qasim.]] narrated from al-Qasim, from Abu Umamah al-Bahili, that Thaʿlabah ibn Hatib al-Ansari (he named him) said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Pray to Allah that He grants me wealth." He said, (ﷺ): "Woe to you, O Thaʿlabah! A little that you can thank for is better than a lot that you cannot bear." Then he came back a second time, and the Prophet ﷺ said: (ﷺ) "Are you not content to be like the Prophet of Allah? If I wished, mountains would travel with me, made of gold, and they would travel." He said: "By the One who sent you with the truth, if you pray to Allah and He grants me wealth, I will surely give every person with a right his due." So the Prophet ﷺ prayed for him. He acquired sheep, and they multiplied as worms multiply, so Madinah became too narrow for him. He withdrew from it and settled in one of its valleys, until he began to pray Dhuhr and ʿAsr in congregation and abandoned everything other than them. Then they multiplied and increased until he abandoned the prayers except Friday, and they kept increasing until he abandoned Friday too. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (ﷺ) "Woe to Thaʿlabah!" three times. Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103]. So the Prophet ﷺ sent two men to collect the charity, and he said to them: (ﷺ) "Pass by Thaʿlabah and by so-and-so, a man of Banu Sulaym, and take their charities." So they went to Thaʿlabah and read him the letter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He said: "This is nothing but a sister of the jizyah (poll tax)! Go on until you are finished, then come back." The hadith is long, and it is well known.

It has also been said: the cause of Thaʿlabah's wealth was that he inherited from a paternal cousin of his. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: It has been said that Thaʿlabah ibn Hatib is the one about whom the verse "And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah" was revealed, when he withheld zakat. But Allah knows best. What has come concerning those who witnessed Badr is contradicted by His saying in the verse: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts﴾, and so on.

I say: It is also mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the occasion of revelation of the verse that Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah had his wealth delayed from him in Syria, so he swore in one of the gatherings [[In MSS j and ʿayn: "two gatherings."]] of the Ansar: "If that is secured for me, I will surely give charity from it and surely maintain ties of kinship with it." But when it was secured, he was stingy with it, so the verse was revealed.

I say: Thaʿlabah was a Badri and an Ansari, and among those whom Allah and His Messenger testified to as believers, as will be explained at the beginning of al-Mumtahanah [[The author will mention at the beginning of surat al-Mumtahanah that it is Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, not Thaʿlabah ibn Hatib.]]. So what is narrated about him is not sound. Abu ʿUmar said: Perhaps the view of those who said that Thaʿlabah was the withholder of zakat about whom the verse was revealed is not sound. But Allah knows best.

Al-Dahhak said: The verse was revealed concerning some men among the hypocrites: Nabtal ibn al-Harith, Jadd ibn Qays, and Muʿattib ibn Qushayr.

I say: This is more fitting to the revelation of the verse concerning them. However, His saying "So He caused hypocrisy to follow" indicates that the one who made the covenant with Allah was not a hypocrite before that, unless the meaning is: He increased them in hypocrisy, which they persisted in until death. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until the Day they meet Him﴾, as will come.

The second: Our scholars said: When Allah, exalted is He, said "And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah," it is possible that he made the covenant with Allah by his tongue without believing it in his heart. And it is possible that he made the covenant with both, then a bad ending overtook him, for actions are by their endings and days are by their outcomes. "Man" (من) is in the nominative case as the subject, and the predicate is in the prepositional phrase.

The word "oath" (yamin) occurs in the hadith, and there is no oath in the apparent wording of the Qur'an except by mere binding and commitment. As for it being in the form of an oath in meaning, the lam indicates it. He used two lams: the first is the lam of the oath, and the second is the lam of the response, and both are for emphasis. Some said: They are both lams of the oath, and the first is more apparent. But Allah knows best.

The third: A vow of divorce (talaq) and every ruling that a person undertakes alone, without needing anyone else in it, binds him to what he intends to commit to, even if he does not utter it, as our scholars said. Al-Shafiʿi and Abu Hanifah said: No ruling binds anyone unless he utters it. This is the other view of our scholars. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: The evidence for the soundness of what we have taken is what Ashhab narrated from Malik, when he was asked about a man who intends divorce in his heart but does not utter it with his tongue, and he said: It binds him, just as he is a believer in his heart or a disbeliever in his heart. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: This is a wonderful principle, and its formulation is: A contract in which a person does not need anyone else for his commitment to it is concluded by intention. Its origin is faith and disbelief.

I say: The argument of the second view is what Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (ﷺ) "Indeed Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper about, so long as they do not act upon it or speak it." Al-Tirmidhi narrated it and said: It is a good, sound hadith. And the practice according to the people of knowledge is that if a man speaks to himself about divorce, it is nothing until he speaks it. Abu ʿUmar said: Whoever believes in his heart in divorce but his tongue does not pronounce it, it is nothing. This is the more famous view from Malik. It has also been narrated from him that divorce binds him if he intends it in his heart, just as he disbelieves in his heart even if his tongue does not utter it. The first view is more correct in reasoning and in the path of the transmitted reports, based on the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: (ﷺ) "Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper about, so long as no tongue utters it or hand does it."

The fourth: If it is a vow (nadhr), then fulfilling a vow is obligatory without disagreement, and abandoning it is disobedience. If it is an oath (yamin), then fulfilling an oath is not obligatory by consensus. However, the meaning here is: if the man was poor, zakat was not obligatory upon him, so he asked Allah for wealth on which zakat would become obligatory for him, and he would pay what became obligatory upon him of his duty. When Allah gave him what He willed of that, he abandoned what he had committed himself to, which would not have been binding upon him in the basic religion had he not committed himself to it. But the striving to seek wealth for paying the rights was what ensnared him, since his request from Allah, exalted is He, was without a sincere intention, or with an intention but the beginning that was written for him had already preceded in it, in which was wretchedness. We seek refuge in Allah from that.

I say: From this meaning is His saying, peace be upon him: (ﷺ) "When one of you wishes, let him consider what he wishes for, for he does not know what has been written for him in the unseen of Allah, mighty and majestic, from his wish." That is, from its consequence. For many a wish a person is tempted by, or becomes arrogant, and so it becomes a cause of ruin in this world and the next, because the affairs of this world are obscure, their outcomes are uncertain, and their harms are dangerous. As for wishing for matters of religion and the Hereafter, wishing for them has a praiseworthy outcome, is encouraged, and is recommended.

The fifth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity﴾ is evidence that whoever says, "If I own such and such, then it is charity," it binds him. This is the view of Abu Hanifah. Al-Shafiʿi said: It does not bind him. The disagreement regarding divorce is similar, and likewise regarding manumission (ʿitq). Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: It binds him regarding manumission but does not bind him regarding divorce, because manumission is an act of devotion, and such devotion is established in one's obligation through a vow, unlike divorce, which is a disposition over a subject, and it is not established in one's obligation.

Al-Shafiʿi used as evidence what Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (ﷺ) "There is no vow for the son of Adam regarding what he does not own, nor manumission for him regarding what he does not own, nor divorce for him regarding what he does not own." This is the wording of al-Tirmidhi. He said: On this subject there are also reports from ʿAli, Muʿadh, Jabir, Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAʾishah. The hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr is a good hadith, and it is the best that has been narrated on this subject. And it is the view of most people of knowledge among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ and others.

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: The companions of al-Shafiʿi have cited many hadiths on this subject, none of which is authentic, so one should not rely upon them, and nothing remains except the apparent meaning of the verse.

The sixth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But when He gave them of His bounty﴾, meaning He gave them.

(They were stingy with it): meaning with giving charity and spending wealth in good, and with fulfilling what they had guaranteed and committed to. Stinginess has already been discussed in Surat Al ʿImran [[See vol. 4, p. 290.]].

(And they turned away): meaning from obedience to Allah.

(While they were refusing): meaning from Islam, that is, showing aversion to it.

The seventh: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow﴾ has two objects: that is, Allah, exalted is He, caused hypocrisy in their hearts to follow. It has been said: that is, He caused stinginess to follow them as hypocrisy, and for this He said "they were stingy with it."

(Until the Day they meet Him): it is in the position of a genitive, that is, they meet their stinginess, meaning the recompense of their stinginess, as one says, "Tomorrow you will meet your deeds." It has also been said: (Until the Day they meet Him) means they meet Allah. In this there is evidence that he died a hypocrite. And it is unlikely that the one about whom it was revealed was Thaʿlabah or Hatib, because the Prophet ﷺ said to ʿUmar: (ﷺ) "And what makes you know? Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do what you wish, for I have forgiven you." And Thaʿlabah and Hatib were among those who were present at Badr and witnessed it.

(Those] because they broke their promise to God and because they lied. Their lying was their breaking of the covenant and their failure to fulfil what they had bound themselves to.

Eighth issue: His saying, ﴿hypocrisy (nifaq)﴾. Nifaq (hypocrisy) is disbelief when it lies in the heart. When it lies in actions, it is a sin. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever has four traits will be a pure hypocrite, and whoever has one of them has one trait of hypocrisy until he gives it up: when he is entrusted, he betrays; when he speaks, he lies; when he makes a covenant, he breaks it; and when he disputes, he is treacherous." Al-Bukhari transmitted it. The derivation of this word has already been discussed in [al-Baqarah] [[See vol. 1 pp. 178, 98 1.]], so there is no point in repeating it.

People differ on the interpretation of this hadith. One group said: this applies only to someone who tells a story knowing it is false, makes a covenant he does not intend to keep, and waits for a trust in order to betray it. They relied on a hadith with a weak chain, that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, met Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, as they were coming out from the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and they were downcast [[In MS ʿAyn: "weeping" / "they weep" / "they are weeping."]]. ʿAlī said: "What is the matter with you two, that I see you downcast?" They said: "A hadith we heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the traits of the hypocrites: 'When he speaks he lies, when he makes a covenant he breaks it, when he is entrusted he betrays, and when he promises he fails to keep it.'" ʿAlī said: "Did you not ask him?" They said: "We were in awe of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." He said: "But I will ask him." He went in to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar went out and they were downcast," and then he mentioned what they had said. He said: "I have spoken to them, but I did not put it in the sense they understood. Rather, the hypocrite, when he speaks while speaking to himself that he is lying, when he promises while speaking to himself that he will fail, and when he is entrusted while speaking to himself that he will betray." 

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: Clear evidence has established that one who deliberately commits these traits does not become a disbeliever; he becomes a disbeliever only through a belief that goes back to ignorance of Allah and His attributes, or to denying Him. [Exalted is Allah above the belief of the ignorant and above the deviation of the deviators] [[From MS ʿAyn.]].

Another group said: this is specific to the hypocrites of the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. They relied on what Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān transmitted from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "We came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with some of his companions and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you said: "Three, whoever has them is a hypocrite even if he fasts, prays, and claims to be a believer: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he fails, and when he is entrusted he betrays; and whoever has one of them has a share of hypocrisy."' We thought that we were not free of them, or of some of them, and that many people were not free of them." He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ laughed and said: "What is the matter with you and them? I only singled out the hypocrites with them, as Allah singled them out in His Book. As for my saying, 'When he speaks he lies,' that is His saying, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿When the hypocrites come to you...﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn: 1], to the end of the verse. Are you like that?" We said: "No." He said: "Do not worry, you are free of that. As for my saying, 'When he promises he fails,' that concerns what Allah revealed to me: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with God: "If He gives us of His bounty..."﴾ [at-Tawbah: 75], the three verses. Are you like that?" We said: "No. By Allah, if we made a covenant with God regarding something, we would fulfil it." He said: "Do not worry, you are free of that. As for my saying, 'When he is entrusted he betrays,' that concerns what Allah revealed to me: ﴿Indeed, We offered the Trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains...﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 72], to the end of the verse. Every person is entrusted with his religion. The believer washes from major impurity in private and in public, while the hypocrite does so only in public. Are you like that?" We said: "No." He said: "Do not worry, you are free of that."

Many of the Successors and the imams held this view.

Another group said: this applies to one in whom these traits predominate. It appears from the position of al-Bukhārī and other scholars that whoever is characterised by these blameworthy traits is a hypocrite until the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: What I hold is that if sins predominate over a person, he does not become a disbeliever through them, so long as they do not affect his belief.

Our scholars said: The brothers of Yūsuf, upon him be peace, made a covenant with their father and broke it, they told him something and lied to him, and he entrusted them with Yūsuf and they betrayed him, yet they were not hypocrites.

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ said: The brothers of Yūsuf did these traits, and they were not hypocrites; rather they were prophets [[The correct view is that they were not prophets, because their action contradicts infallibility.]].

Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said: Hypocrisy is of two kinds: hypocrisy of lying and hypocrisy of action. As for hypocrisy of lying, it existed in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. As for hypocrisy of action, it does not end until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Bukhārī transmitted from Ḥudhayfah that hypocrisy existed in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but today it is only disbelief after belief.

His saying, ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows their secret and their private conversation?﴾ This is a rebuke, and since He is knowing, He will requite them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 79:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who find fault with those of the believers who give charity voluntarily, and with those who find nothing to give except their effort⦆... Actually, the verse begins: ﴿Those who find fault with the volunteers among the believers regarding charities﴾. This too is among the attributes of the hypocrites. Qatadah said: "yalmizun" means they criticize (ya'ibun). He said: This is because 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf (may Allah be pleased with him) gave charity of half his wealth, and his wealth was eight thousand, so he gave four thousand of it in charity. Some people said: How great is his show-off (riya'). So Allah revealed: ﴿Those who find fault with the volunteers among the believers regarding charities﴾.

A man from the Ansar came with half a ṣubra [[al-ṣubra (with a damma): what is gathered of food without measuring or weighing, some of it piled on top of other.]] of his dates, and they said: Allah is not in need of this. So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿And those who find nothing to give except their effort﴾, the verse.

Muslim transmitted from Abu Mas'ud, who said: We were commanded to give charity. He said: We used to carry loads on our backs (in another narration: "on our backs") – he said: So Abu 'Aqil gave half a ṣā'. He said: Another person came with something more than that, and the hypocrites said: Indeed Allah is not in need of the charity of this one, and this other one did only out of show-off. So it was revealed: ﴿Those who find fault with the volunteers among the believers regarding charities, and those who find nothing to give except their effort﴾. He means Abu 'Aqil, whose name was al-Habhab. Al-juhd (or al-jahd) means: a little thing by which the one of little means subsists; al-juhd and al-jahd have the same meaning. It has been mentioned before [[See vol. 7, p. 62.]]. And "yalmizun" means they blame (ya'ibun); it has been mentioned before. And "al-muṭṭawwi'in" is originally al-mutatawwi'in, with the ta' assimilated into the ta'; they are those who do a thing voluntarily without it being obligatory upon them. And "alladhina" is in the genitive position as a conjunction with "al-mu'minin". It is not permissible for it to be a conjunction with the noun before its completion. "Fa-yaskharun" is a conjunction with "yalmizun". ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ is the predicate of the subject, and it is a supplication against them. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a report, meaning He mocked them when they came to the Fire. The meaning of Allah's mocking is His recompensing them for their mockery. It has been mentioned in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 3, p. 29.]].
His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them﴾. Its explanation will come at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And never pray over any of them who has died, ever﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 81:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who were left behind rejoiced in their sitting (maq'ad) behind⦆ means: in their sitting. He sat (qa'ada) a sitting and a maq'ad, meaning he sat down. Another made him sit (aq'adahu), according to al-Jawhari. The mukhallaf is the one who is left behind, meaning God left them behind and discouraged them, or the Messenger of God and the believers left them behind when they knew of their reluctance to fight in jihad (jihad, struggle in the way of God). There are two opinions. This took place during the Battle of Tabuk.

(Khilafa Rasul Allah) is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi, the object expressing the reason for the action), and if you wish it may be a verbal noun (masdar). Al-khilaf means opposition. Whoever recited "khalfa Rasul Allah" (behind the Messenger of God) meant lagging behind from jihad.

(And they said: Do not go forth in the heat) means that some of them said this to others.

(Say: The fire of Hell) means: say to them, O Muhammad, the fire of Hell.

(Is more intense in heat, if only they understood) is a subject and predicate (ibtida' wa khabar, a nominal sentence). "Harran" is in the accusative as an explicative (al-bayan, specification of what is meant). That is, whoever abandons the command of God exposes himself to that fire.

**First issue:** the words ﴿فَلْيَضْحَكُوا قَلِيلًا﴾ are an imperative, ﴿So let them laugh a little﴾. Its meaning is one of threat, and it is not a command to laugh. The original form is with a kasra on the lam, *fa-li*, and the kasra was dropped because it is heavy. Al-Hasan said: ﴿So let them laugh a little﴾ in this world, ﴿and let them weep much﴾ in Jahannam. It is also said that it is an imperative in the sense of a statement, meaning that they will laugh a little and weep much. ﴿جَزاءً﴾ (jaza'an) is an object of purpose (*maf'ul min ajlihi*), meaning ﴿as a recompense﴾.

**Second issue:** Among people there are those who do not laugh, out of concern for themselves and for the corruption of their state in their own belief, from the intensity of fear, even if they are righteous servants. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By Allah, if you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much, and you would go out to the *ṣuʿudāt* [[The *ṣuʿudāt* are the roads, the plural of *ṣaʿd*, and *ṣaʿd* is the plural of *ṣaʿīd*, like *ṭarīq* and *ṭuruq* and *ṭuruqāt*. It is also said that it is the plural of *ṣaʿda*, like *ẓulma*, and it is the open space in front of the house door and the passage of people before it.]] crying out to Allah the Exalted. I wish I were a tree that is cut down" [[al-Tirmidhi said: It is also narrated through another route that Abu Dharr said: "I wish I were a tree that is cut down."]]. This was related by al-Tirmidhi.

Al-Hasan al-Basri, may Allah be pleased with him, was among those whom sorrow had overcome, so he did not laugh. Ibn Sirin used to laugh and argued with al-Hasan, saying: "Allah causes laughter and causes weeping." The Companions used to laugh, but excessive laughter and persistence in it until it overcomes a person is blameworthy and forbidden; it is the behaviour of fools and idlers. In a report: "Its excess kills the heart." As for weeping out of fear of Allah, His punishment and the severity of His retribution, it is praiseworthy. He, peace be upon him, said: "Weep, and if you cannot weep, then feign weeping, for the people of the Fire weep until their tears flow down their faces like streams, until the tears run out, and then blood flows, and the eyes become sore; were ships to be sailed upon them, they would sail." This was related by Ibn al-Mubarak from the hadith of Anas, and by Ibn Majah as well.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 83:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So if Allah returns you to a faction of them﴾, that is, of the hypocrites. He said "to a faction" because not all of those who remained in Madinah were hypocrites; among them were those with valid excuses and those who had no excuse but whom He then pardoned and accepted their repentance, like the three who were left behind (al-thalatha alladhina khullifu). This will come later.

﴿Then they ask your permission to go out, so say: Never shall you go out with me, nor fight with me any enemy﴾; that is, punish them by never letting them accompany you. This is like what He said in Surah al-Fath: ﴿Say: You shall never follow us﴾ [al-Fath: 15].[[See vol. 16, p. 270 onwards.]] "Al-khalifin" is the plural of khalif, as if they remained behind (khalafu) those who went out. Ibn Abbas said: "Al-khalifin" refers to those among the hypocrites who stayed behind. Al-Hasan said: "with the women and the weak among the men," so the masculine was given precedence. It was also said: the meaning is, "Sit with the corrupt ones," from the saying, "So-and-so is a khalifa of his household" when he is corrupt among them, from the khulufu of the mouth of one who fasts (the change in the breath of a fasting person), and from your saying: "The milk has spoiled" (khalafa al-laban), meaning it became spoiled from long staying in the waterskin. Accordingly, the meaning is: "Sit with the corrupt." This indicates that taking along one who discourages others in the raids is not permissible.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 84 (part 1 of 2):**

There are eleven issues concerning it.

The first issue: It is related that this verse was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul and the Prophet's ﷺ prayer over him. This is established in the two Sahihs (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) and elsewhere. The reports are consistent that the Prophet ﷺ prayed over him and that the verse was revealed after that. It is also related from Anas ibn Malik that when the Prophet ﷺ moved forward to pray over him, Jibril came to him, pulled his garment, and recited to him, "And never pray over any of them who has died, ever" (the verse), so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ turned away without having prayed over him. But the established reports contradict this. In al-Bukhari, from Ibn Abbas, he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed over him and then departed, and he had not remained long before the two verses from [Bara'ah] were revealed: "And never pray over any of them who has died, ever." The same is reported from Ibn Umar, and Muslim recorded it. Ibn Umar said: When Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul died, his son Abdullah came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and asked him to give him his shirt in which to shroud his father. He gave it to him. Then he asked him to pray over him, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood up to pray over him. Umar stood up, took hold of the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ garment, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, will you pray over him when Allah has forbidden you to pray over him?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah the Exalted has only given me a choice, when He said: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them. Even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times﴾ [al-Tawbah: 80]. And I will add beyond seventy." Umar said: "He is a hypocrite." Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed over him, and Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed: "And never pray over any of them who has died, and do not stand at his grave," so he abandoned praying over them. Some scholars said: The Prophet ﷺ only prayed over Abdullah ibn Ubayy on the basis of the apparent outward profession of his Islam. Then he did not do this once he was forbidden from it.

The second issue: If someone says, how could Umar say, "Will you pray over him when Allah has forbidden you to pray over him," when no prohibition had yet been issued concerning praying over them? It is said in reply: It is possible that this occurred to him as an inspiration (ilham) and a kind of inner speaking (tahdith) for which the Prophet ﷺ bore witness to him. The Qur'an used to descend in accordance with his opinion, as he said: "I agreed with my Lord in three matters," and it came in four. This has already been discussed in al-Baqarah (see vol. 2, p. 113), so this is one of those cases. It is also possible that he understood this from the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 80], and so on, not that a prohibition had preceded it, as the report of al-Bukhari and Muslim indicates. And Allah knows best. I say: It is also possible that he understood it from the words of Allah the Exalted: "It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists" [al-Tawbah: 113], because that was revealed in Mecca. This will be discussed later.

The third issue: The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them﴾ and so on. He made clear that even if he asked forgiveness for them, it would not benefit them, even if he asked it excessively. Al-Qushayri said: What is reported, that he said, "I will surely add more than seventy," is not established. I say: This contradicts what is established in the hadith of Ibn Umar ("And I will add beyond seventy") and in the hadith of Ibn Abbas ("If I knew that if I added beyond seventy they would be forgiven, I would add beyond it"). He said: Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed over him. Al-Bukhari recorded it.

The fourth issue: The scholars differed concerning the interpretation of his words, "Ask forgiveness for them." Is it a despair (iyas) or a choice (takhyir)? One group said: What is meant by it is despair, as evidenced by the words of Allah the Exalted: "So Allah will never forgive them." The mention of seventy is a customary figure of speech, or it is their habit in expression for the many and for excess. So when one of them says, "I will not speak to him for seventy years," it is equivalent for them to saying, "I will never speak to him." Similar to this in the sense of excess are the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿In a chain whose length is seventy cubits﴾ [see vol. 18, p. 268 onwards], and His words ﷺ: "Whoever fasts one day in the way of Allah, Allah will distance his face from the Fire by seventy autumns." Another group said: It is a choice, and among them were al-Hasan, Qatadah and Urwa: "If you wish, ask forgiveness for them, and if you wish, do not ask forgiveness." For this reason, when he intended to pray over Ibn Ubayy, Umar said: "Will you pray over the enemy of Allah who said on such and such a day such and such?" He said: "I was given a choice, so I chose." They said: Then this was abrogated when there was revealed: ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [see vol. 18, p. 128].

(That is because they disbelieved) meaning Allah will not forgive them because of their disbelief.

The fifth issue: The words of Allah the Exalted: "It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists" and so on. This verse was revealed in Mecca at the death of Abu Talib, as will be explained. From it is understood the prohibition of asking forgiveness for one who died in disbelief. This precedes this verse, from which the choice was understood by his words, "Allah has only given me a choice," and this is problematic. It is said: His seeking forgiveness for his uncle was intended as a forgiveness that is hoped to be answered, so that forgiveness might be attained for him. In this seeking of forgiveness, he ﷺ asked his Lord for permission to seek forgiveness for his mother, but He did not grant him permission. As for asking forgiveness for the hypocrites, which he was given a choice about, it is a verbal seeking of forgiveness that does not benefit, and its purpose is only to console the hearts of some of the living relatives of the one for whom forgiveness is sought. And Allah knows best.

The sixth issue: It was disputed concerning the Prophet's ﷺ giving his shirt to Abdullah. It is said: He gave it only because Abdullah had given his shirt to al-Abbas, the paternal uncle of the Prophet ﷺ, on the day of Badr. That is because when al-Abbas was taken captive on the day of Badr, as has been mentioned earlier, and his garment was stripped off, the Prophet ﷺ saw him in that state and pitied him. He sought a shirt for him, but no shirt was found that would fit him except the shirt of Abdullah, because they were similar in height. The Prophet ﷺ intended by giving the shirt to lift the obligation of him in this world, so that he would not meet him in the Hereafter while he had a favor upon him that he would reward him for. It is also said: He gave him the shirt only as an honor to his son, a help to him in his request, and a consoling of his heart. The first is more correct. Al-Bukhari recorded from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: On the day of Badr, prisoners were brought, and al-Abbas was brought, and he had no garment on him. The Prophet ﷺ [looked for (fa-nazar) in the manuscripts of the original] a shirt for him, and they found the shirt of Abdullah ibn Ubayy which fit him, so the Prophet ﷺ clothed him with it. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ took off the shirt which he had put on him. In the hadith, the Prophet ﷺ said: [Indeed my shirt will not avail him anything from Allah, but I hope that by this act of mine a thousand men of my people will become Muslims]. In some reports it is (of my people), meaning from the hypocrites of the Arabs, but the correct version is that he said: "men of his people." It occurs in the Maghazi of Ibn Ishaq and in some books of tafsir: "So a thousand men of the Khazraj became Muslim and repented because of this act of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ."

The seventh issue: When Allah the Exalted said: "And never pray over any of them who has died, ever," our scholars said: This is an explicit text regarding refraining from praying over the disbelievers, and there is no evidence in it for praying over the believers. It was disputed whether the obligation of praying over the believers is derived from its implication (mafhum), on two views. One view: It is derived, because He gave as the reason for prohibiting prayer over the disbelievers their disbelief, by the words of Allah the Exalted: "Because they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger." So when disbelief is removed, prayer becomes obligatory. This is like the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿No! Indeed, they, that Day, will be veiled from their Lord﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 15], meaning the disbelievers, so this indicates that others than the disbelievers will see Him, and they are the believers. That is similar to it. And Allah knows best. Or the prayer is derived from evidence outside the verse, namely the hadiths transmitted on the subject and the consensus. The source of the disagreement is the view on argument from implication (dalil al-khitab, the reasoning from what a text implies by contrast) and abandoning it. Muslim transmitted from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Your brother has died, so stand up and pray over him." He said: So we stood and formed two rows, meaning for al-Najashi. And from Abu Hurayra that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ announced the death of al-Najashi to the people on the day he died, went out with them to the prayer ground (musalla), and said the takbir four times. The Muslims have agreed that it is not permissible to abandon the prayer over the funerals of Muslims, whether they were among the people of major sins or righteous, inheriting this from their Prophet ﷺ in word and deed. And praise be to Allah. The scholars agreed upon this, except regarding the martyr, as has been mentioned earlier, and except for the people of innovation (ahl al-bid'ah) and rebels (al-bughat).

The eighth issue: The majority of scholars hold that the takbir is four. Ibn Sirin said: The takbir was three, then they added one. Another group said: One says the takbir five times, and this is reported from Ibn Mas'ud and Zayd ibn Arqam. From Ali: six takbirs. From Ibn Abbas, Anas ibn Malik and Jabir ibn Zayd: three takbirs. The reliable position is four. Al-Daraqutni transmitted from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The angels prayed over Adam and said the takbir four times over him, and they said: This is your sunnah, O children of Adam."

The ninth issue: In the well-known position of the school of Malik, there is no recitation in this prayer. Likewise Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri hold this, based on his ﷺ saying: "When you pray over the dead, make your supplication sincere for him." Abu Dawud transmitted it from the hadith of Abu Hurayra. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Muhammad ibn Maslamah, Ashhab from among our scholars, and Dawud went to the view that one recites al-Fatihah, based on his peace be upon him saying: "There is no prayer without the Opening of the Book (al-Fatihah)," taking it in its general sense. And on what al-Bukhari transmitted from Ibn Abbas: he prayed over a funeral, recited al-Fatihah, and said: "So that you may know that it is a sunnah." Al-Nasai transmitted from the hadith of Abu Umama, who said: The sunnah in the funeral prayer is that one recites Umm al-Qur'an (al-Fatihah) quietly in the first takbir, then says takbir three times, and the salam is at the end. Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazi also mentioned from Abu Umama, who said: The sunnah in the funeral prayer is that you say takbir, then recite Umm al-Qur'an, then send blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ, then make your supplication sincere for the deceased, and you recite only in the first takbir, then you say the salam. Our shaykh Abu al-Abbas said: These two hadiths are sound, and they are considered by the usulis (scholars of legal theory) as connected to the musnad (chain-attested reports). The practice according to the hadith of Abu Umama is preferable, since in it there is a combination between his peace be upon him saying "There is no prayer" and making the supplication for the deceased sincere. The recitation of al-Fatihah in it is only as an opening to the supplication. And Allah knows best.

The tenth issue: The sunnah for the imam is to stand at the head of a man and at the waist (ajizah) of a woman, based on what Abu Dawud transmitted from Anas, who prayed over a funeral, and al-Ala ibn Ziyad said to him: "O Abu Hamza, was this how the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to pray over funerals, like your prayer, saying the takbir four times, and standing at the head of a man and the waist of a woman?" He said: "Yes." And Muslim transmitted from Samura ibn Jundab, who said: I prayed behind the Prophet ﷺ, and he prayed over Umm Ka'b, who died while in postnatal bleeding, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood for the prayer over her in the middle of her body (wasatiha).

The Eleventh issue: His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And do not stand over his grave﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to stand over the grave when he had buried the deceased, and he would supplicate for him to be made firm (in his answer), as we have explained [in al-Tadhkira]. And praise be to Allah.
He repeated it for emphasis. The discussion of it has already come earlier.

The believers hastened to respond, while the hypocrites made excuses. So the command is addressed to the believers to persist in faith, and to the hypocrites to begin faith. The word "an" (that) is in a position of accusative, meaning: "that believe." Al-tawl means wealth, and it has been mentioned before. He singled them out for mention because one who has no tawl does not need permission, since he is excused. "(And they said, 'Leave us, that we may be with those who sit back.')" That is, those unable to go out.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran, "The Collection of Rulings of the Qur'an") on Surah 9, verses 87–89:**

Allah the Exalted says: "(They are content to be with the women who stay behind)." *Al-khawalif* is the plural of *khalifah*, meaning with the women, the children, and the men who have excuses. The word may also be used for a man, as *khalifah* and *khalif*, when he is not noble, as has already been mentioned. It is said: "So-and-so is *khalifat ahlihi*," meaning that he is left behind his family.

Al-Nahhas said: Its origin is from *khalafa al-laban yakhlufu*, meaning that the milk turned sour from being left for a long time. *Khalafa fam al-sa'im* means that the breath of the fasting person changed in smell. From this comes the saying "so-and-so is a *khalaf sew*," meaning a bad successor. However, *fawa'il* is the plural of *fa'ilah*. The plural *fawa'il* is not formed from the adjective *fa'il* except in poetry, with two exceptions: *faris* (rider/knight) and *halik* (perishing one).

As for Allah's words describing the fighters for the cause: "And those, for them are the good things" (*al-khayrat*), it has been said, on the authority of al-Hasan, that this means "the beautiful women." The evidence for this is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿In them are good [women], beautiful [women]﴾ [al-Rahman: 70]. It is said: "She is *khayrat al-nisa'*" (the best of women). The original form is *khayyirah*, which was lightened, like *hayyinah* and *haynah*. It has also been said that it is the plural of *khayr* (good). So the meaning is that for them are the benefits of both abodes. The meaning of *al-falah* (success) has already been explained [See vol. 1, pp. 182, 392]. *Al-jannat* means the gardens and orchards, and this has also been mentioned before [See vol. 1, pp. 182, 392].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 90:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there came those who make excuses among the Bedouins﴾. Al-A'raj and al-Dahhak read "al-Mu'dharun" (those who make excuses) with a light (unshadda) pronunciation. Abu Kurayb related it from Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and the transmitters of the readings related it from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Jawhari said: Ibn 'Abbas used to read "wa-ja'a al-mu'dhirun" with a light pronunciation, from a'dhara (to give a valid excuse), and he would say: "By Allah, it was revealed in exactly this way." Al-Nahhas said: However, its transmission goes back to al-Kalbi. It is from a'dhara, and from it comes the saying "qad a'dhara man andhara," meaning: the one who has warned you has fully discharged the excuse, that is, the one who came before you and warned you has made his case completely clear.

As for "al-Mu'adhdhirun" with the shadda, there are two views. The first is that it refers to the one who is truthful, so in meaning it is the same as al-mu'tadhir (the one making an excuse), because he has a genuine excuse. Thus "al-Mu'adhdhirun" according to this reading originally is al-mu'tadhirun, but the ta' was changed into dhal, assimilated into it, and its vowel was placed on the 'ayn, as was read in ﴿yukhsamun﴾ [Ya-Sin: 49] with a fatha on the kha'. [[See vol. 15, p. 36 onward.]] It is also permissible to read "al-Mu'idhdhirun" with a kasra on the 'ayn, due to the meeting of two sukun. It is also permissible to read it with a damma on it, following the mim. This was mentioned by al-Jawhari and al-Nahhas, though al-Nahhas transmitted it from al-Akhfash, al-Farra', Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd. It is also possible that the original is al-mu'tadhirun, then the ta' was assimilated into the dhal, and they would be those who have a genuine excuse. Labid said:

Until the year is complete, then greetings upon you both... and whoever weeps a full year has made an excuse (i'tadhara).

The second view is that the one who makes excuses (al-mu'adhdhir) may not be truthful, and this is the one who makes an excuse while having no excuse. Al-Jawhari said: So he is al-mu'adhdhir in the pattern of mufa"il, because he is the one who feigns sickness and falls short, making an excuse without a valid reason. Another said: It is said 'udhira fulan fi amr kadha ta'dhiran, meaning he fell short in it and did not exert himself. The meaning is that they made excuses with falsehood. Al-Jawhari said: Ibn 'Abbas used to say: "May Allah curse the al-mu'adhdhirin." It seems that in his view al-mu'adhdhir with the shadda is the one who displays an excuse, offering pretexts without any real excuse. Al-Nahhas said: Abu al-'Abbas Muhammad ibn Yazid said: It is not permissible that the original be al-mu'tadhirin, for the idgham would not be permissible and confusion would result. Isma'il ibn Ishaq reported that idgham is avoided according to the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, once the context of the speech indicates that they are blameworthy and have no excuse. He said: because they came seeking permission to stay behind; had they been among the weak, the sick, and those who cannot find anything to spend, they would not have needed to ask permission. Al-Nahhas said: The root of al-mu'dharah, al-i'dhar and al-ta'dhir is one and the same, and it comes from what is difficult and hard to achieve (yata'adhdhar). The Arab saying "man 'adhiri min fulan" means: he has committed a grave act deserving that I punish him for it, and people do not know about it; "so who will excuse me if I punish him?"

On the reading with the light pronunciation, Ibn 'Abbas said: They are those who stayed behind with a genuine excuse, so the Prophet ﷺ granted them permission. It was also said: they are the company of 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl, who said: "O Messenger of Allah, if we went out with you, the Bedouins of Tayy would raid our wives, our children and our livestock," so the Prophet ﷺ excused them.

On the reading with the shadda, in the second view, they are a people from Ghifar who made excuses, and the Prophet ﷺ did not excuse them, because he knew that they were not truthful, and Allah knows best. Another group stayed behind without any excuse, even displaying one, out of audacity towards the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and they are those whom Allah, exalted is He, described when He said: ﴿And those who lied to Allah and His Messenger stayed behind﴾. The intended meaning of their lie is their saying: "We are believers." And "li-yu'dhana" is in the accusative after the lam of purpose (lam kay).

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 9, verses 91–92:**

There are six issues (masa'il) in this passage.

**The first issue:** God's statement: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak...﴾ (the verse). This is a basic principle concerning the removal of legal obligation (taklif) from the incapable. Whoever is unable to do something has that obligation lifted from him. Sometimes it is replaced by an act, and sometimes by a compensatory payment (gharm). There is no difference between incapacity arising from physical weakness and incapacity arising from lack of wealth. A parallel to this verse is God's statement: ﴿God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 286], and His statement: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick﴾ [An-Nur: 61]. [See vol. 3, p. 424 onward.] [See vol. 12, p. 311 onward.]

Abu Dawud related from Anas that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, there are people you left behind in Madinah [in other manuscripts: after you] who did not march any march, nor spend any expenditure, nor cross any valley, except that they were with you in it." They said: "O Messenger of God, how can they be with us while they are in Madinah?" He said: "The excuse held them back."

This verse, together with the similar verses mentioned, shows that there is no blame upon those who have valid excuses. These are people whose excuses are known, such as the chronically ill, the elderly, the blind, and the lame, and also people who did not find anything to spend. So He says: "There is no blame upon these."

﴿When they are sincere to God and His Messenger﴾: when they know the truth, love His friends, and hate His enemies. The scholars said: God, may He be glorified, excused the people with valid excuses, and the hearts were not patient [to go out]. Ibn Umm Maktum went out to Uhud and asked to be given the banner, so Mus'ab ibn Umayr took it. A man from the unbelievers came and struck his hand that held the banner and cut it off. He then held it with the other hand, and [the enemy] struck the other hand, so he held it to his chest, and he recited: ﴿Muhammad is only a messenger; the messengers have passed away before him﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 144]. These were the resolves of these people.

God says: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind﴾ [An-Nur: 61], and this applies to the first case. ﴿Nor upon the lame﴾ [An-Nur: 61]: 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh, one of the chiefs (nuqaba') of the Ansar, was lame, yet he was at the front of the army. The Messenger, peace be upon him, said to him: "Indeed God has excused you." He said: "By God, I will walk with this limp of mine into Paradise." [Note: "hafara" means that one leaves an impression on the path by walking on it.] This is in accordance with what has preceded in this surah concerning them, may God be pleased with them.

'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: "A man would be brought, supported between two men, until he was stood up in the row."

**The second issue:** God's statement: ﴿When they are sincere﴾. Nusḥ (sincerity) is the purification of action from deceit, and from it comes "sincere repentance" (tawbah nasuh). Nafṭawayh said: "Nasaḥa the thing" means it became pure. "Nasaha lahu al-qawl" means he made the speech pure for him.

In Sahih Muslim, from Tamim al-Dari, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The religion is sincere advice (nasihah)," three times. We said: "To whom?" He said: "To God, to His Book, to His Messenger, to the leaders of the Muslims, and to their common folk."

The scholars said: Sincere advice to God is the purification of belief in His oneness, attributing to Him the attributes of divinity, declaring Him free from deficiencies, desiring what He loves, and distancing oneself from what provokes His anger. Sincere advice to His Messenger is affirming his prophethood, committing to obey his commands and prohibitions, loyalty to whoever he is loyal to, enmity toward whoever is his enemy, honoring him, loving him and loving the people of his household, glorifying him and glorifying his Sunnah, reviving it after his death by researching it, understanding it, defending it, spreading it, calling to it, and adopting his noble character (ﷺ). Likewise, sincere advice to the Book of God is reciting it, understanding it, defending it, teaching it, honoring it, and adopting its character. Sincere advice to the leaders of the Muslims is not rebelling against them, guiding them to the truth, alerting them to matters of the Muslims that they have neglected, adhering to obedience to them, and fulfilling their due rights. Sincere advice to the common people is not being hostile to them, guiding them, loving the righteous among them, praying for all of them, and wishing good for all of them.

In the authentic hadith: "The likeness of the believers in their mutual affection, mercy, and compassion is like the body: when one of its limbs complains, the rest of the body responds to it with wakefulness and fever."

**The third issue:** God's statement: ﴿There is no path (against) the good-doers﴾. The word "min sabil" (from a path) is in the position of the subject of "ma" (there is not), meaning: no path to punishment. This verse is a basic principle for lifting punishment from every good-doer. For this reason, our scholars said regarding one who takes retaliation (qisas) from the one who cut off his hand, and that leads, through spreading infection, to the destruction of his own life: he owes no blood money (diyah), because he acted well in taking retaliation against the one who wronged him. Abu Hanifah said: he is liable for blood money. Similarly, if a stallion attacks a man and he kills it in defending himself, there is no liability upon him, and this is also the view of al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah said: he is liable to pay its owner the value of the animal. Ibn al-'Arabi said: the same applies to all matters of the Shari'ah.

**The fourth issue:** God's statement: ﴿Nor upon those who came to you that you might provide them with mounts﴾. It is related that this verse was revealed concerning 'Irbad ibn Sariyah. It was also said: it was revealed concerning 'A'idh ibn 'Amr. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the sons of Muqarrin, and this is the view of the majority of the exegetes. They were seven brothers, all of whom accompanied the Prophet (ﷺ), and there were no seven brothers among the Companions other than them. They were: al-Nu'man, Ma'qil, 'Aqil, Suwayd, Sinan, and a seventh who was not named. [The author mentions only five. What is in al-Qamus (under the root q-r-n) is: 'Abdullah, 'Abd al-Rahman, 'Aqil, Ma'qil, al-Nu'man, Suwayd, and Sinan, the sons of Muqarrin, are Companions.] The sons of Muqarrin al-Muzani were seven brothers who emigrated and accompanied the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and no one else shared with them in this honor, according to what Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and a group [of scholars] mentioned. It has been said that all of them witnessed the Battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq).

It was also said: it was revealed concerning seven men from various tribes, and they are the Weepers (al-Bakka'un). They came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) during the Battle of Tabuk, asking him to provide them with mounts, but he did not find anything to mount them on. So they turned away with their eyes overflowing with tears out of grief that they could not find anything to spend, and so they were called the Weepers. They were: Salim ibn 'Umayr from Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf; 'Ulbah ibn Zayd, brother of Banu Harithah; Abu Layla 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ka'b from Banu Mazin ibn al-Najjar; 'Amr ibn al-Hammam from Banu Salamah; 'Abdullah ibn al-Mughaffal al-Muzani, although it was also said: rather, he is 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr al-Muzani; Hermi ibn 'Abdullah, brother of Banu Waqif; and 'Irbad ibn Sariyah al-Fazari. This is how Abu 'Umar named them in his book al-Durar. There is disagreement about them. Al-Qushayri said: Ma'qil ibn Yasar, Sakhr ibn Khansa', 'Abdullah ibn Ka'b al-Ansari, Salim ibn 'Umayr, Tha'labah ibn Ghanamah, 'Abdullah ibn Mughaffal, and another. They said: "O Prophet of God, you have called us to go out with you, so provide us with mounts, and we will fight with you." He said: "I do not find anything to mount you on," so they turned away weeping.

Ibn 'Abbas said: they asked him to provide them with animals to ride, and a man needed two camels: one to ride and one to carry his water and provisions because the road was long.

Al-Hasan said: it was revealed concerning Abu Musa and his companions. They came to the Prophet (ﷺ) asking him to provide them with mounts, and it coincided with his anger, so he said: "By God, I will not mount you, and I do not find anything to mount you on." So they turned away weeping. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) called them back and gave them camels (dhawd). [Note: "dhawd" among camels refers to between three and ten; the word is feminine, has no singular of its own form, and the plural is adhwad.] Abu Musa said: "Did you not swear, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Indeed, if God wills, I do not swear an oath and then see something other than it as better, except that I do what is better and make expiation for my oath."

I say: this is an authentic hadith, related by al-Bukhari and Muslim in its wording and meaning. In Muslim: "He called us and commanded that we be given five camels with white humps..." (the hadith), and at its end: "Go, for God has given you [the mount]."

Al-Hasan also said, and Bakr ibn 'Abdullah: it was revealed concerning 'Abdullah ibn Mughaffal al-Muzani, who came to the Prophet (ﷺ) asking him for a mount.

Al-Jurjani said: the meaning is: "Nor upon those who came to you that you might provide them with mounts, and you said, 'I do not find...'" So it is a subject (mubtada') conjoined to what precedes it without a conjunction (waw), and the answer (jawab) is "they turned away."

**(And their eyes overflow with tears):** this clause is in the position of an accusative of circumstance (hal). "Hazanan" (out of grief) is a verbal noun (masdar). "Alla yajidu" ("that they do not find") is in the accusative with "an." Al-Nahhas said: al-Farra' said it is permissible to say "an la yajiduna," making "la" mean "laysa" (not). According to the Basrans, it means that they do not find.

**The fifth issue:** The majority of scholars hold that whoever does not find what he can spend on his military campaign is not obligated to [go]. Our scholars said: if his habit is to beg, then it becomes obligatory upon him, like the Hajj, and it proceeds according to the custom, because if his situation does not change, the obligation is directed toward him just as it is toward the one who has means. And God knows best.

**The sixth issue:** In God's statement: ﴿And their eyes overflow with tears﴾ there is an indication of the use of circumstantial evidence (qara'in al-ahwal). Among these are some that give necessary knowledge ('ilm darury), and some that admit of doubt. The first is like someone who passes by a house in which wailing has risen, cheeks have been scratched, hair has been shaved, voices have been raised in shrill cries (salq), garments have been torn, and people call out to the owner of the house with cries of destruction (thubur). He knows that someone has died. The second is like the tears of orphans at the doors of rulers. God, may He be exalted, said, reporting about the brothers of Yusuf, peace be upon him: ﴿And they came to their father in the evening, weeping﴾ [Yusuf: 16]. And they were liars. God said, reporting about them: ﴿And they brought his shirt with false blood﴾ [Yusuf: 18].

Nevertheless, these are indications that are generally relied upon, and testimony is built upon them, based on the apparent and generally prevailing circumstances. The poet said:

*When tears mingle upon cheeks,*
*it becomes clear who weeps from who feigns weeping.*

This meaning will come again in [the commentary on] Surah Yusuf in full, God willing.

For this reason, our scholars said regarding one who takes retaliation (qisas) from the one who cut off his hand, and that leads, through spreading infection, to the destruction of his own life: he owes no blood money (diyah), because he acted well in taking retaliation against the one who wronged him. Abu Hanifah said: he is liable for blood money. Similarly, if a stallion attacks a man and he kills it in defending himself, there is no liability upon him, and this is also the view of al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah said: he is liable to pay its owner the value of the animal. Ibn al-'Arabi said: the same applies to all matters of the Shari'ah.

**The fourth issue:** God's statement: ﴿Nor upon those who came to you that you might provide them with mounts﴾. It is related that this verse was revealed concerning 'Irbad ibn Sariyah. It was also said: it was revealed concerning 'A'idh ibn 'Amr. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the sons of Muqarrin, and this is the view of the majority of the exegetes. They were seven brothers, all of whom accompanied the Prophet (ﷺ), and there were no seven brothers among the Companions other than them. They were: al-Nu'man, Ma'qil, 'Aqil, Suwayd, Sinan, and a seventh who was not named. [The author mentions only five. What is in al-Qamus (under the root q-r-n) is: 'Abdullah, 'Abd al-Rahman, 'Aqil, Ma'qil, al-Nu'man, Suwayd, and Sinan, the sons of Muqarrin, are Companions.] The sons of Muqarrin al-Muzani were seven brothers who emigrated and accompanied the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and no one else shared with them in this honor, according to what Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and a group [of scholars] mentioned. It has been said that all of them witnessed the Battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq).

It was also said: it was revealed concerning seven men from various tribes, and they are the Weepers (al-Bakka'un). They came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) during the Battle of Tabuk, asking him to provide them with mounts, but he did not find anything to mount them on. So they turned away with their eyes overflowing with tears out of grief that they could not find anything to spend, and so they were called the Weepers. They were: Salim ibn 'Umayr from Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf; 'Ulbah ibn Zayd, brother of Banu Harithah; Abu Layla 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ka'b from Banu Mazin ibn al-Najjar; 'Amr ibn al-Hammam from Banu Salamah; 'Abdullah ibn al-Mughaffal al-Muzani, although it was also said: rather, he is 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr al-Muzani; Hermi ibn 'Abdullah, brother of Banu Waqif; and 'Irbad ibn Sariyah al-Fazari. This is how Abu 'Umar named them in his book al-Durar. There is disagreement about them. Al-Qushayri said: Ma'qil ibn Yasar, Sakhr ibn Khansa', 'Abdullah ibn Ka'b al-Ansari, Salim ibn 'Umayr, Tha'labah ibn Ghanamah, 'Abdullah ibn Mughaffal, and another. They said: "O Prophet of God, you have called us to go out with you, so provide us with mounts, and we will fight with you." He said: "I do not find anything to mount you on," so they turned away weeping.

Ibn 'Abbas said: they asked him to provide them with animals to ride, and a man needed two camels: one to ride and one to carry his water and provisions because the road was long.

Al-Hasan said: it was revealed concerning Abu Musa and his companions. They came to the Prophet (ﷺ) asking him to provide them with mounts, and it coincided with his anger, so he said: "By God, I will not mount you, and I do not find anything to mount you on." So they turned away weeping. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) called them back and gave them camels (dhawd). [Note: "dhawd" among camels refers to between three and ten; the word is feminine, has no singular of its own form, and the plural is adhwad.] Abu Musa said: "Did you not swear, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Indeed, if God wills, I do not swear an oath and then see something other than it as better, except that I do what is better and make expiation for my oath."

I say: this is an authentic hadith, related by al-Bukhari and Muslim in its wording and meaning. In Muslim: "He called us and commanded that we be given five camels with white humps..." (the hadith), and at its end: "Go, for God has given you [the mount]."

Al-Hasan also said, and Bakr ibn 'Abdullah: it was revealed concerning 'Abdullah ibn Mughaffal al-Muzani, who came to the Prophet (ﷺ) asking him for a mount.

Al-Jurjani said: the meaning is: "Nor upon those who came to you that you might provide them with mounts, and you said, 'I do not find...'" So it is a subject (mubtada') conjoined to what precedes it without a conjunction (waw), and the answer (jawab) is "they turned away."

**(And their eyes overflow with tears):** this clause is in the position of an accusative of circumstance (hal). "Hazanan" (out of grief) is a verbal noun (masdar). "Alla yajidu" ("that they do not find") is in the accusative with "an." Al-Nahhas said: al-Farra' said it is permissible to say "an la yajiduna," making "la" mean "laysa" (not). According to the Basrans, it means that they do not find.

**The fifth issue:** The majority of scholars hold that whoever does not find what he can spend on his military campaign is not obligated to [go]. Our scholars said: if his habit is to beg, then it becomes obligatory upon him, like the Hajj, and it proceeds according to the custom, because if his situation does not change, the obligation is directed toward him just as it is toward the one who has means. And God knows best.

**The sixth issue:** In God's statement: ﴿And their eyes overflow with tears﴾ there is an indication of the use of circumstantial evidence (qara'in al-ahwal). Among these are some that give necessary knowledge ('ilm darury), and some that admit of doubt. The first is like someone who passes by a house in which wailing has risen, cheeks have been scratched, hair has been shaved, voices have been raised in shrill cries (salq), garments have been torn, and people call out to the owner of the house with cries of destruction (thubur). He knows that someone has died. The second is like the tears of orphans at the doors of rulers. God, may He be exalted, said, reporting about the brothers of Yusuf, peace be upon him: ﴿And they came to their father in the evening, weeping﴾ [Yusuf: 16]. And they were liars. God said, reporting about them: ﴿And they brought his shirt with false blood﴾ [Yusuf: 18].

Nevertheless, these are indications that are generally relied upon, and testimony is built upon them, based on the apparent and generally prevailing circumstances. The poet said:

*When tears mingle upon cheeks,*
*it becomes clear who weeps from who feigns weeping.*

This meaning will come again in [the commentary on] Surah Yusuf in full, God willing.

Almighty Allah's words: ﴿Only upon﴾, i.e., the punishment and the sin.

(Upon those who ask your permission while they are wealthy) and what is meant is the hypocrites. He repeated their mention for emphasis in warning against the evil of their deeds.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 94:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿They will make excuses to you﴾ — meaning the hypocrites (al-munafiqun).

(﴿We will not believe you﴾) i.e., we will not believe you (sadaqa-kum, "we will not confirm you as truthful").

(﴿Allah has already informed us of your news﴾) i.e., He has informed us of your inner secrets (sara'ir-kum).

(﴿And Allah will see your deed﴾) in what you resume (fa-ma tasta'nifun).

(﴿Then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do﴾) i.e., He will recompense you for your deeds. All of this has already passed in full detail.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 95:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will swear to you by Allah when you return to them﴾, that is, from Tabuk. The thing sworn to is omitted, meaning: they will swear that they were not able to go out.

(﴿That you may leave them alone﴾), that is, that you may overlook their blame. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, do not speak to them. There is a report that when he (ﷺ) arrived from Tabuk, he said: "Do not sit with them and do not speak to them."

(﴿Indeed, they are filth﴾), that is, their deeds are filth. The implied meaning is: indeed, they are people of filth, that is, their deeds are abominable.

(﴿And their refuge is Hell﴾), that is, their abode and their place. Al-Jawhari said: al-ma'wa (refuge) is every place to which a thing resorts by night or by day. Fulan resorted (awa) to his dwelling, yaʾwi awiyyan, on the pattern fa'ul, and iwa'an. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I will take refuge in a mountain that will protect me from the water﴾ [Hud: 43]. I caused him to resort (awaytuhu iwa'an), and awaytuhu, when I lodged him with you, fa'ala and af'ala have the same meaning, according to Abu Zayd. And ma'wi al-ibil, with a kasra on the waw, is a dialect form for ma'wa al-ibil specifically, and it is anomalous (shadh).
Abdullah ibn Ubayy swore that he would not lag behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after that, and he sought that the Prophet be pleased with him.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary on the verse: "The Bedouins are the most intense in disbelief and hypocrisy" (Qur'an 9:97)**

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿The Bedouin Arabs are more intense in disbelief and hypocrisy﴾. On this there are two issues.

**The first issue:** When Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioned the condition of the hypocrites in Medina, He then mentioned those Bedouins (*a'rab*) who lived outside it and far from it, and said that their disbelief is more intense. Qatada said: "Because they are further from knowing the ways (*sunan*)." It was also said: "Because they are harder of heart, coarser in speech, more brutish in nature, and further from hearing the revelation (*tanzil*)." For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said concerning them: ﴿and more likely (*wa-ajdaru*)﴾, that is, more fitting (*akhlaq*).

﴿Allā ya'lamū﴾: the word *an* is in a position of accusative through the deletion of the preposition *bi* (with). You say: "You are deserving (*jadir*) to do" and "to do," so when you delete the *bi*, only *an* is suitable. If you use the *bi*, then *an* and other forms are suitable. You say: "You are deserving that you stand" and "deserving of standing." If you said "You are deserving the standing," it would be an error. *An* is suitable with it because *an* indicates the future, so it is as if it were a substitute for the deleted element.

﴿ḥudūda mā anzala Allāh﴾: that is, the obligations (*fara'id*) of the Law. It was also said: the proofs of Allah regarding lordship and the sending of the messengers, because of their little reflection.

**The second issue:** Since this indicates their deficiency and their lowering below the complete rank that others have, certain rulings follow from it, three in number.

The first: they have no right to the *fay'* (property taken from the enemy without battle) and the *ghanima* (spoils of war), as the Prophet (ﷺ) said in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Buraydah, in which: "Then invite them to move from their dwellings to the abode of the emigrants (*muhajirun*), and inform them that if they do so, they will have what the emigrants have and they will bear what the emigrants bear. If they refuse to move from it, then inform them that they will be like the Bedouins of the Muslims: the rule of Allah that applies to the believers will apply to them, and they will have no share in the spoils or the *fay'* unless they fight with the Muslims."

The second: the testimony (*shahada*) of the people of the desert (*badiya*) is excluded against the people of the settled communities (*hadara*), because of the certainty of suspicion in that. Abu Hanifa permitted it, saying: "Because not every suspicion is taken into account, and all Muslims are, in his view, upright (*'adl*)." Al-Shafi'i permitted it when the person is upright and acceptable, and this is the correct view, for the reason we explained in (*al-Baqara*) [[See vol. 3, p. 396.]]. Allah, the Exalted, has described the Bedouins here with three attributes: first, with disbelief and hypocrisy; second, that ﴿he takes what he spends as a loss and waits for misfortunes to befall you﴾ (9:98); third, with belief in Allah and the Last Day, and ﴿he takes what he spends as means of nearness to Allah and as prayers of the Messenger﴾ (9:99). Whoever has this description, it is unlikely that his testimony would not be accepted, so he is joined to the second and first categories, and that is invalid. The discussion of this has passed in (*al-Nisa'*) [[See vol. 5, p. 410 and following.]].

The third: their leading the people of the settled communities in prayer is prohibited, because of their ignorance of the Sunnah and their abandoning of the Friday prayer (*jumu'a*). Abu Mijlaz disliked a Bedouin leading the prayer. Malik said: "He should not lead, even if he is the best reciter among them." Sufyan al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i, Ishaq, and the companions of opinion (*ashab al-ra'y*) said: "Praying behind a Bedouin is permissible." Ibn al-Mundhir chose this view, provided he maintains the limits of the prayer.

﴿Ashaddu﴾: its origin is *ashaddu* (with a doubled letter), and this has been discussed before.

(*kufran*): put in the accusative as a specification (*bayan*).

(*wa-nifaqan*): conjoined to it.

(*wa-ajdaru*): conjoined to *ashaddu*, and its meaning is *akhlaq* (more fitting). It is said: "So-and-so is *jadir* with such a thing," meaning fitting for it, and "You are *jadir* to do such a thing." The plural is *judara'* and *jadiruna*. Its origin is from *judur al-ha'it* (the foundations of the wall), which is raising it by building. So the saying "He is *ajdaru* with such a thing" means he is closer to it and more entitled to it.

(*allā ya'lamū*): that is, "by not knowing." *Al-'Arab* is a folk of people, and the adjective referring to them is *'arabi*, clearly Arab, and they are the people of the cities. *Al-A'rab* is specifically the inhabitants of the desert. In eloquent poetry the form *a'arib* has come. The adjective referring to *al-a'rab* is *a'rabi*, because it has no singular, and *al-a'rab* is not a plural of *al-'arab* as *al-anbat* was the plural of *nabat*; rather *al-'arab* is a collective noun (*ism jins*). *Al-'Arab al-'aribah* are the pure ones among them, derived from the same root and emphasized by it, as in your saying: "a night that is truly night" (*layl la'il*). They sometimes say: *al-'Arab al-'arba'*. *Ta'arraba* means he made himself resemble the Arabs. "*Ta'arraba* after his emigration" means he became a Bedouin. *Al-'Arab al-musta'ribah* are those who are not pure, and likewise *al-muta'arribah*. *Al-'Arabiyya* is this language. Ya'rub ibn Qahtan was the first to speak Arabic, and he is the father of all of Yemen. *Al-'Arab* and *al-'Urb* are one, like *al-'Ajam* and *al-'Ujm*. *Al-'Uraib* is the diminutive of *al-'Arab*. The poet said:

*"Wa-makn al-dibab ta'am al-'Uraib... wa-la tashtahihi nufus al-'Ajam"*
(The eggs of the locust are the food of the little Arabs, and the souls of the non-Arabs do not desire them.) [[The verse is by 'Abd al-Mu'min ibn 'Abd al-Quddus. *Makn*: the eggs of the lizard, the locust, and the like.]]

He used the diminutive for them as an honour, as in the saying: "I am its *judhayl* (little trunk) that is rubbed, and its *udhayq* (little palm) that is propped up" [[*Judhayl* is the diminutive of *jidhl*, the base of a tree. *Al-muhakkak* is that against which mangy camels rub themselves, a stick planted in the camels' resting places for this purpose. *Udhayq* is the diminutive of *idhq*, a palm tree. *Al-murajjab* is that which has been given a *rujba*, a support built around it with stones. This is from the saying of al-Habbab ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Jamuh al-Ansari on the day of Saqifa at the pledge of allegiance to Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, meaning that affairs have tested him and he has opinion and knowledge by which people are healed, as mangy camels are healed by rubbing against the stick.]]. All of this is from al-Jawhari. Al-Qushayri related that the plural of *al-'arabi* is *al-'arab*, and the plural of *al-a'rabi* is *a'rab* and *a'arib*. When the *a'rabi* is addressed as "O Arab," he is pleased, and when the *'arabi* is addressed as "O Bedouin," he becomes angry. The Emigrants (*muhajirun*) and the Helpers (*ansar*) are Arabs, not Bedouins. The Arabs were named *'arab* because the descendants of Isma'il grew up in *'Araba*, which is in Tihama, so they were attributed to it. Quraysh settled in *'Araba*, which is Makka, and the rest of the Arabs spread throughout its peninsula.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 98:

God Most High says: ﴿And among the desert Arabs is one who takes what he spends as a loss﴾. "Min" (from) is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'). "Ma yunfiqu maghraman" (what he spends as a loss) has two objects, and the implied meaning is "yunfiquhu" (he spends it), so the pronoun (the ha') was dropped because the phrase is long. "Maghraman" means loss (ghurman) and ruin (khusranan). Its root meaning is the necessity (luzum) of a thing, and from it comes: ﴿Indeed, its punishment is ever adhering (gharaman)﴾ [al-Furqan: 65] [[see vol. 13, p.]], that is, constant. The meaning is that they regard what they spend in jihad and charity as a loss, and they do not hope for any reward for it.

(And they await misfortunes to befall you.) Tarabbus (awaiting) means waiting, and it has been discussed before [[see vol. 3, p. 108.]]. Dawa'ir is the plural of dA'ira, which is the state that turns from blessing to affliction. That is, they combine ignorance of giving with a bad disposition and a corrupt heart.

(Upon them is a circle of evil.) Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a dammah on the sin (as-sau') here and in the fath (fatha) form, while the rest read it with a fatha on the sin. They agreed on the fatha on the sin in His words: ﴿Your father was not a man of evil (imra' sau')﴾ [Maryam: 28] [[see vol. 11, p. 99.]].
