The difference between them is that as-su' with a dammah means what is disliked. Al-Akhfash said: that is, upon them is a circle of defeat and evil. Al-Farra' said: that is, upon them is a circle of punishment and affliction. Both said: it is not permissible to say imra' su' with a dammah, just as one does not say "huwa imru' 'adhab" or "wa la sharr" (he is a man of punishment or of evil). It is related from Muhammad ibn Yazid that he said: as-saw' with a fatha means badness (radd'a). Sibawayh said: "I passed by a man of sidq (righteousness)," meaning a man of goodness, and it is not from the truthfulness of the tongue; had it been from the truthfulness of the tongue, I would not have said "I passed by a garment of sidq." And "I passed by a man of saw'" is not from its being a derivative of su'a, rather its meaning is "I passed by a man of corruption." Al-Farra' said: as-saw' with a fatha is the verbal noun of sü'tuhu sau'an, masa'atan, and suwa'iyyatan. Others said: the verb from it is sa'a yasu'u. As-su' with a dammah is a noun, not a verbal noun, and it is like your saying: upon them is a circle of calamity and what is disliked.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 99:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among the Bedouins are those who believe in Allah﴾, meaning: who affirm (ṣaddaqa). The intended ones are the Banu Muqarrin of Muzayna, as mentioned by al-Mahdawi. "Qurubat" is the plural of qurbah (qurbah: that by which one draws near to Allah, the Exalted), and its plurals are qurab, qurubat, qarabat and qurbat, as related by al-Nahhas. And al-qurubat (with a ḍamma) are that by which one draws near to Allah, the Exalted; you say from it: "qarrabtu li-Llahi qurbanan" (I offered to Allah an offering). And al-qirbah (with a kasra on the qaf) is that in which water is drawn, and its plural for small numbers is qurubat, qarabat and qurbat, and for large numbers qurub. Likewise the plural of every word of the form fi'lah, such as sidrah and fiqrah, you may open the ʿayn, or kasra it, or sukoon it, as related by al-Jawhari. Nafi', in the narration of Warsh, read "qurubah" with a ḍamma on the rāʾ, and this is the original form. The rest read it with sukoon for lightness, like kutub and rusul, and there is no disagreement regarding qurubat. Ibn Saʿdan related that Yazid ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ read: "Ala innaha qurbatun lahum." The meaning of "wa-salawat al-Rasul" is his seeking forgiveness for them and his supplication. Salah (prayer, blessing) falls under several meanings: the salah from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is mercy, goodness and blessing; Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿It is He who sends blessings upon you, and His angels﴾ [al-Ahzab: 43]. The salah from the angels is supplication, and likewise it is from the Prophet (ﷺ), as He said: ﴿And pray for them; indeed, your prayer is a comfort for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103], meaning: your supplication is a source of steadfastness and tranquillity for them.

(Ala innaha qurbatun lahum) meaning: it brings them near to the mercy of Allah, that is, their expenditures.

**Question 1:** When Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioned the categories of the Bedouin Arabs, He mentioned the Muhajirun (Emigrants) and the Ansar (Helpers), and made clear that among them are the foremost to emigrate (al-sabiqun) and those who followed them, and He praised them. The scholars differ on the number of their ranks and categories. We will mention a portion of that, explaining its purpose, if Allah the Exalted wills. Umar ibn al-Khattab related that he recited "wal-Ansari" (and the Ansar) in the nominative, as a conjunction to "al-sabiqun." Al-Akhfash said: "The genitive (al-khafd) in 'al-Ansar' is the preferable reading, because the foremost (al-sabiqun) are from both groups." "Ansar" is an Islamic name. Anas ibn Malik was asked: "Tell us, the people say of you 'al-Ansar': is this a name Allah gave you, or were you called by it in the Jahiliyyah (Age of Ignorance)?" He said: "Rather, it is a name Allah gave us in the Qur'an." Abu Umar mentioned this in al-Istidhkar.

**Question 2:** The Qur'an explicitly states the superiority of the first foremost ones (al-sabiqun al-awwalun) among the Muhajirun and the Ansar, namely those who prayed toward both qiblahs (the Qiblah of Jerusalem and the Ka'bah), according to the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and a group. According to the view of the followers of al-Shafi'i, they are those who witnessed the Pledge of Ridwan (Bay'at al-Ridwan), which is the Pledge of al-Hudaybiyyah; this was also said by al-Sha'bi. From Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Ata' ibn Yasar: they are the people of Badr. There is agreement that whoever emigrated before the change of the qiblah is among the first Muhajirun, with no disagreement among them.

**Question 3:** As for their most excellent ones: Abu Mansur al-Baghdadi al-Tamimi said: "Our companions (scholars) are unanimous that the most excellent of them are the four Caliphs, then the remaining six (of the ten promised Paradise), up to the completion of the ten, then the people of Badr, then the people of Uhud, then the people of the Pledge of Ridwan at al-Hudaybiyyah."

**Question 4:** As for the first of them to embrace Islam: Mujalid related from al-Sha'bi, who said: "I asked Ibn Abbas: 'Who was the first of the people to embrace Islam?' He said: 'Abu Bakr. Have you not heard the words of Hassan:

When you recall a grief from a trusted brother,
then remember your brother Abu Bakr for what he did,
the best of creation, the most pious and most just of them after the Prophet,
and the most faithful in what he bore.
The second, the companion of the cave, whose station is praised,
and the first of the people to affirm the Messengers.'"

Abu al-Faraj al-Jawzi related from Yusuf ibn Ya'qub ibn al-Majishun that he said: "I met my father and our shaykhs, Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, Rabi'ah ibn Abi Abd al-Rahman, Salih ibn Kaysan, Sa'd ibn Ibrahim, and Uthman ibn Muhammad al-Akhnasi, and they had no doubt that the first of the people to embrace Islam was Abu Bakr." This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Hassan, Asma' bint Abi Bakr, and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i. It was also said: "The first to embrace Islam was Ali," which was related from Zayd ibn Arqam, Abu Dhar, al-Miqdad, and others. Al-Hakim Abu Abd Allah said: "I know of no disagreement among the historians that Ali was the first of them to embrace Islam." It was also said: "The first to embrace Islam was Zayd ibn Harithah." Ma'mar related something similar from al-Zuhri. This is also the view of Sulayman ibn Yasar, Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, and Imran ibn Abi Anas. It was also said: "The first to embrace Islam was Khadijah, the Mother of the Believers." This was related through several channels from al-Zuhri, and is the view of Qatadah, Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Yasar, and a group; it was also related from Ibn Abbas. Al-Tha'labi, the exegete, claimed that the scholars agree that the first to embrace Islam was Khadijah, and that their disagreement concerns only those who embraced Islam after her. Ishaq ibn Ibrahim ibn Rahawayh al-Hanzali would reconcile these reports, saying: "The first of the men to embrace Islam was Abu Bakr, of the women Khadijah, of the boys Ali, of the freed slaves Zayd ibn Harithah, and of the slaves Bilal." And Allah knows best.

Muhammad ibn Sa'd related: "Musab ibn Thabit informed me, saying: Abu al-Aswad Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Nawfal told me, saying: The Islam of al-Zubayr came after Abu Bakr, and he was fourth or fifth." Al-Laith ibn Sa'd said: "Abu al-Aswad told me: al-Zubayr embraced Islam when he was eight years old." It was related that Ali embraced Islam at the age of seven, and it was also said at ten.

**Question 5:** The known position of the people of hadith is that every Muslim who saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is one of his Companions (Sahabah). Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: "Whoever accompanied the Prophet ﷺ or saw him from among the Muslims is one of his Companions." It is related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab that he would not count as a Companion anyone except one who stayed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for a year or two, and fought alongside him in one or two campaigns. If this statement is authentically from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, it would require that Jarir ibn Abd Allah al-Bajali, or someone who shared with him, not be counted among the Companions, since he lacks the apparent conditions that Sa'id stipulated for them, though there is no known disagreement about counting him among the Companions.

**Question 6:** There is no disagreement that the first of the foremost Muhajirun was Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. Ibn al-Arabi said: "Precedence (al-sabq) occurs in three ways: by attribute, which is faith; by time; and by place. The most excellent of these aspects is precedence in attributes. The evidence for this is the Prophet's ﷺ saying in the Sahih: 'We are the last (in time) and the first (in merit), except that they were given the Book before us, and we were given it after them. This is their day about which they differed, and Allah guided us to it. So the Jews are tomorrow, and the Christians the day after tomorrow.' The Prophet ﷺ informed us that although the nations before us preceded us in time, we preceded them in faith, in obedience to the command of Allah the Exalted, in submission to Him, in surrender to His command, in contentment with His obligations, and in bearing His duties. We do not object to Him, nor do we choose against Him, nor do we replace His law with opinion, as the People of the Book did. This is by the grace of Allah in what He decreed, and by His facilitation of what He is pleased with. 'And we would not have been guided had Allah not guided us.'"

**Question 7:** Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: "This verse includes the superiority of the foremost in every virtue of the Sharia, whether in knowledge, religion, courage, or other matters, such as the giving of wealth and the rank of honor." There is a disagreement between Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, on this matter. The scholars differed on whether the foremost should be preferred in giving (stipends) over others. It is related that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, did not prefer among the people in giving, some over others, according to precedence. Umar would say to him: "Will you make the one with precedence equal to the one with no precedence?" Abu Bakr said: "They worked for Allah, and their reward is upon Him." Umar used to prefer (in giving) during his caliphate, then he said at his death: "If I live until tomorrow, I will bring the lowest of the people up to the highest of them," and he died that night. The matter (of the stipends) has remained under this disagreement until this day of ours.

**Commentary on Allah's words:** ﴿And those who followed them in excellence﴾. On this there are two issues.

**First:** Umar recited "wal-Ansaru" in the nominative, and "alladhina" without the conjunction "wa," as a qualifier of the Ansar. Zayd ibn Thabit objected to him, so Umar asked Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who confirmed Zayd's reading. Umar returned to it and said: "We did not think except that we had been raised to a rank that no one with us can attain." Ubayy said: "I find confirmation of this in the Book of Allah, in the beginning of Surat al-Jumu'ah: ﴿And others among them who have not yet joined them﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 3]. And in Surat al-Hashr: ﴿And those who came after them say: 'Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith'﴾ [al-Hashr: 10]. And in Surat al-Anfal, with His saying: ﴿And those who believed afterward and emigrated and fought alongside you, they are of you﴾ [al-Anfal: 75]." Thus the reading with the conjunction "wa" was established. By His saying "in excellence," Allah the Exalted specified what they follow of their actions and words, not of the slips and errors that proceeded from them, since they were not infallible, may Allah be pleased with them.

**Second:** The scholars differed about the Successors (al-tabi'un) and their ranks. The Hafiz al-Khatib said: "The Successor is one who accompanied a Companion, and one of them may be called tabi' or tabi'i." The words of al-Hakim Abu Abd Allah and others imply that it is sufficient that one hears from a Companion or meets him, even if the customary companionship is not found. It has also been said that the designation of Successors applies to those who embraced Islam after al-Hudaybiyyah, such as Khalid ibn al-Walid, Amr ibn al-As, and those similar to them among the people of the Conquest (of Makkah), because it is established that Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf complained to the Prophet ﷺ about Khalid ibn al-Walid, and the Prophet ﷺ said to Khalid: "Leave my Companions alone! By Him in whose hand my soul is, if one of you spent gold equal to Mount Uhud every day, it would not reach the mudd of one of them, nor half of it." It is strange that al-Hakim Abu Abd Allah counted al-Nu'man and Suwayd, the two sons of Muqarrin al-Muzani, among the Successors, when he mentioned the brothers among the Successors, though both are well-known Companions mentioned among the Companions, and both witnessed the Battle of the Trench, as already mentioned. And Allah knows best.

The greatest of the Successors are the seven jurists of Madinah: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, Kharijah ibn Zayd, Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Rahman, Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Utbah ibn Mas'ud, and Sulayman ibn Yasar. One of the eminent scholars has put them into a single verse:

So take them: Ubayd Allah, Urwah, al-Qasim,
Sa'id, Abu Bakr, Sulayman, and Kharijah.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: "The best of the Tabi'un (the Successors, those who met the Companions) is Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab." It was said to him: "Then 'Alqama and al-Aswad?" He said: "Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, and 'Alqama and al-Aswad."

And from him also, that he said: "The best of the Tabi'un are Qays, Abu 'Uthman, 'Alqama and Masruq. These were excellent men and among the elite of the Tabi'un."

He also said: "'Ata' was the mufti of Makkah and al-Hasan was the mufti of Basra, and these two are the ones from whom people narrated the most." And he left it at that (without specifying further).

It is narrated from Abu Bakr ibn Abi Dawud that he said: "The leading women among the Tabi'un are Hafsa bint Sirin and 'Amra bint 'Abd al-Rahman, and the third of them, though she is not like them, is Umm al-Darda' [[Umm al-Darda' al-Sughra al-Dimashqiyya.]]."

It is narrated from al-Hakim Abu 'Abd Allah that he said: "There is a class counted among the Tabi'un, but the hearing of any of them from the Companions is not authentically established. Among them are Ibrahim ibn Suwayd al-Nakha'i, and he is not Ibrahim ibn Yazid al-Nakha'i the jurist; and Bukayr ibn Abi al-Samit [[In al-Taqrib: (al-Samit with an unpointed initial letter, and it is also said with a damma).]], and Bukayr ibn 'Abd Allah al-Ashajj." He mentioned others besides them, and said: "This class is counted by people among the followers of the Tabi'un (Atba' al-Tabi'in)."

Some of them did meet Companions: Abu al-Zinad 'Abd Allah ibn Dhakwan, who met 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar and Anas; Hisham ibn 'Urwa, who was brought in to 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, and Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah; Musa ibn 'Uqba, who reached Anas ibn Malik; and Umm Khalid bint Khalid ibn Sa'id.

Among the Tabi'un there is a class called the Mukhadramun (those who lived across two eras), who are those who lived through the Jahiliyya and the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), embraced Islam, but had no companionship (with him). Its singular is mukhadram, with a fatha on the ra', as if he had been "cut off" (khudrima), that is, cut off from his peers who attained companionship and other things. Muslim mentioned them and their number reached twenty persons, among them Abu 'Amr al-Shaybani, Suwayd ibn Ghafala al-Kindi, 'Amr ibn Maymun al-Awdi, Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi, 'Abd Khayr ibn Yazid al-Khayrani (with a fatha on the kha', a branch of Hamdan), and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mull. And Abu al-Hilal al-Ataki Rabi'a [[In al-Mizan: Rabi'a ibn Abi al-Hilal.]] ibn Zurara. Among those whom Muslim did not mention are Abu Muslim al-Khawlani 'Abd Allah ibn Thawb, and al-Ahnaf ibn Qays.

This is a brief account of the knowledge of the Companions and the Tabi'un whose excellence the Noble Qur'an has declared, may Allah be pleased with them all. And for us is the sufficiency of His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾[[See vol. 4, p. 170.]] [Al 'Imran: 110], as previously discussed, and His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And thus We have made you a justly balanced nation﴾[[See vol. 2, p. 152.]] [al-Baqara: 143], and so on. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I wish that we had seen our brothers..." [[The narration of Ahmad: "I wish that I had met my brothers.." It is also narrated as: "I have seen.."]] — the hadith. So he made us his brothers. If we fear Allah and follow his footsteps, Allah will gather us in his company, and will not divert us from his path and his creed, by the right of Muhammad and his family.

**The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites﴾.** This is a subject and predicate (*mubtada'* and *khabar*, the topic and comment of the sentence). The meaning is: "a people among them are hypocrites." He means Muzaynah, Juhaynah, Aslam, Ghifar and Ashja'.

﴿And among the people of Madinah are those who persisted in hypocrisy﴾. That is, "a people who persisted in hypocrisy." It has been said that *maradu* (persisted) is a qualifier of the hypocrites, so there is an inversion in the sentence. The meaning would then be: "Among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites who persisted in hypocrisy, and among the people of Madinah are the like of them." The meaning of *maradu* is that they remained in it and did not repent, according to Ibn Zayd. Others said: they clung stubbornly to it and refused anything other than it. The meanings are close. The root of the word comes from smoothness, touching, and being stripped bare, as if they had stripped themselves bare for hypocrisy. From the same root comes *ramlatun mar'da'*, a sand dune with no vegetation on it; *ghusnun amrad*, a branch with no leaves; *faras amrad*, a horse with no hair on its *thunnah* (the tufts of hair hanging at the back of the fetlock); and *ghulam amrad*, a clearly beardless young man, though one does not say *jariyah mar'da'* (for a girl). *Tamrid* of a building means smoothing it, and from this is His saying: ﴿a palace made smooth (*mumarrad*)﴾ [An-Naml: 44] [See vol. 13, p. ]. *Tamrid* of a branch means stripping it of its leaves. It is said: *marada* (he became rebellious/stripped) *yamruadu murudan wa muradah*.

**The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿You do not know them; We know them﴾.** This is like His saying: ﴿You do not know them; Allah knows them﴾ [Al-Anfal: 60], as already explained [See pp. 35 and 164 of this part]. It has also been said that the meaning is: "O Muhammad, you do not know the final outcome of their affairs, and only We have exclusive knowledge of it." This prevents anyone from being judged as destined for Paradise or the Fire.

**The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿We will punish them twice; then they will be returned to a great punishment﴾.** Ibn 'Abbas said: with sicknesses in this world and the punishment of the Hereafter. The sickness of a believer is an expiation, while the sickness of a disbeliever is a punishment. It has been said that the first punishment is the disgrace of the Prophet ﷺ having knowledge of them, as will be explained regarding the hypocrites. The second punishment is the punishment of the grave. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the punishment of this world and the punishment of the grave. Ibn Zayd said: the first is through calamities affecting their wealth and their children, and the second is the punishment of the grave. Mujahid said: hunger and killing. Al-Farra' said: killing and the punishment of the grave. It has also been said: captivity and killing. It has been said: the first is taking zakat from their wealth and carrying out the prescribed punishments upon them, and the second is the punishment of the grave. It has also been said: one of the two punishments is what Allah, the Exalted, said: "So let not their wealth impress you..." up to His saying: ﴿Allah only intends to punish them through them in the life of this world﴾ [At-Tawbah: 55] [See pp. 35 and 164 of this part]. The purpose of the verse is either the continuity of the punishment, or the doubling of the punishment upon them.

And others have acknowledged their sins: they mixed a righteous deed with another that was evil. Perhaps Allah will turn to them in forgiveness. Indeed, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful. (102)

That is: among the people of Madinah and those around you are a people who acknowledged their sins, and others who are left in suspense awaiting the command of Allah, who will judge them as He wills. The first category may have been hypocrites who persisted in hypocrisy, and it is also possible that they were believers.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning ten men who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk, and seven of them tied themselves to the pillars of the mosque. Qatadah said something similar and added: "And concerning them was revealed: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103]," as mentioned by al-Mahdawi. Zayd ibn Aslam said they were eight. It was also said they were six, and it was said they were five.

Mujahid said: the verse was revealed specifically concerning Abu Lubabah al-Ansari regarding his situation with Banu Qurayzah, for they spoke to him about descending to the judgment of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, and he gestured to them toward his throat, meaning that the Prophet ﷺ would slaughter them if they came down. When he was exposed, he repented and regretted, and he tied himself to one of the pillars of the mosque, and swore that he would neither eat nor drink until Allah pardoned him or he died. He remained so until Allah pardoned him, the verse was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered that he be untied. This was mentioned by al-Tabari from Mujahid, and Ibn Ishaq mentioned it in the Sirah in more detail than this.

Ashhab related from Malik: "And others" was revealed concerning Abu Lubabah and his companions, and when he committed the sin he said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall I stay near you and strip myself of my wealth?" He said: "A third of it will suffice you," and Allah the Exalted has said: "Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow" [al-Tawbah: 103]. Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn Wahb narrated this from Malik.

The majority hold that the verse was revealed concerning those who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk, and they had tied themselves as Abu Lubabah did, and they pledged to Allah that they would not release themselves until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ himself released them and was pleased with them. The Prophet ﷺ said: "I swear by Allah I will not release them nor excuse them until I am commanded to release them; they turned away from me and stayed behind from the campaign with the Muslims." Then Allah revealed this verse, and when it was revealed the Prophet ﷺ sent for them, released them and excused them. When they were released, they said: "O Messenger of Allah, these are our wealth which kept us away from you; give charity from it on our behalf, purify us and ask forgiveness for us." He said: "I have not been commanded to take anything from your wealth." Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103], the verse.

Ibn 'Abbas said: they were ten men, among them Abu Lubabah, and he took a third of their wealth, and it was an expiation for the sins they had committed.

Their evil deed was staying behind, by the consensus of the proponents of this view. They differed regarding the righteous deed. Al-Tabari and others said: it is the acknowledgment, repentance and regret. It was also said: their righteous deed was that they joined the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and tied themselves to the pillars of the mosque, saying: "We will not approach a family or a child until Allah reveals our excuse." Another group said: rather, the righteous deed was their earlier participation in the campaigns of the Prophet ﷺ.

And this verse, although it was revealed concerning the Bedouins, is general until the Day of Resurrection for whoever has both righteous and evil deeds, so such a person is hoped for. Al-Tabari related from Hajjaj ibn Abi Zaynab who said: I heard Abu 'Uthman say: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more hopeful to me for this Ummah than His saying the Exalted: 'And others have acknowledged their sins; they mixed a righteous deed with another that was evil.'"

In al-Bukhari, from Samurah ibn Jundub, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to us: "Last night two visitors came to me, took me up, and we reached a city built of gold brick and silver brick. We were met by men, half of whose form was as beautiful as the most beautiful you have seen, and half as ugly as the ugliest you have seen. The two said to them: 'Go and plunge into that river,' so they plunged into it, then returned to us, the evil having gone from them, and they were in the most beautiful form. The two said to me: 'This is the Garden of Eden, and that is your abode.' They said: 'As for the people who were half beautiful and half ugly, they mixed a righteous deed with another that was evil; Allah has overlooked them.'"

Al-Bayhaqi also mentioned, from the hadith of al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, the hadith of the Night Journey, in which he said: "Then I was taken up to the heaven..." and then mentioned the hadith until he mentioned his ascent to the seventh heaven, and they said: "Welcome to a brother and a successor, what an excellent brother and excellent successor, and what an excellent arrival!" Then he came upon a gray-haired man sitting on a chair at the gate of Paradise, and near him were a people with white faces and a people with dark faces and something in their colors. They came to a river and bathed in it, and came out with some of the colors removed; then they came to another river and bathed in it, and came out with more of the colors removed; then they entered a third river and came out with their colors like the colors of their companions, and they sat with their companions. He said: "O Jibril, who are these with white faces, and these who have something in their colors?" He said: "As for these with white faces, they are a people who did not mix their faith with injustice." He said: "And as for those who have something in their colors, they mixed a righteous deed with another that was evil, then they repented, and Allah accepted their repentance. As for the first river, it is the mercy of Allah; as for the second river, it is the blessing of Allah; and as for the third river, their Lord gave them a pure drink." And he mentioned the hadith.

Regarding the "wa" in His saying "and another that was evil," it was said: it has the meaning of "bi" (with), and it was said: it has the meaning of "ma'a" (with), as in your saying: "the water and the wood are level." The Kufans rejected this and said: because the wood cannot be placed before the water, whereas "another" in the verse may be placed before the first, so it is like "I mixed the water with the milk."

In this verse there are eight issues.

The first issue concerns the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾. Scholars differ about this charity that was commanded. It is said that it is the obligatory charity (ṣadaqat al-farḍ), as reported by Juwaybir from Ibn ʿAbbas, and this is also the view of ʿIkrimah, as mentioned by al-Qushayri. It is also said that it is specific to those about whom the verse was revealed, since the Prophet (ﷺ) took from them a third of their wealth, and this is not from the obligatory zakat (obligatory almsgiving) in any way. For this reason Malik said: "If a man gives away all his wealth in charity, it suffices for him to pay out a third." He relied on the hadith of Abu Lubabah.

On the first view, the verse is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), which by its apparent meaning requires that he alone be the one to take it, so no one else may take the charity. It follows from this that the charity lapses when he is gone and ceases with his death. On this basis, those who withheld zakat took their stand against Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), and they said: "He used to give us in return for it purification, growth, and prayers upon us, and we have now lost these from anyone else." Their poet composed on this subject and said:

"We obeyed the Messenger of Allah as long as he was among us,
so how strange is the rule of Abu Bakr!
What they asked of you and you refused them
is to them like dates, or sweeter than dates.
We shall withhold from them as long as a remnant of us remains,
noble in adversity and in ease."

This is a group among those who opposed Abu Bakr, the best of them in conduct. Concerning them Abu Bakr said: "By Allah, I will fight whoever separates the prayer from the zakat."

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: As for their claim that this is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), so that no one else is included in it, this is the speech of one ignorant of the Qur'an, heedless of the sources of the Shariʿa (sharīʿah), and trifling with religion. The address in the Qur'an does not come in one single form, but its occurrences vary in several ways. Among them is an address directed to the whole community, such as His words: ﴿O you who have believed, when you rise to prayer﴾ [al-Maʾidah: 6] and His words: ﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183], and similar verses. Among them is an address specific to him, in which no one else shares, either in wording or in meaning, such as His words: ﴿And from the night, pray with it as an additional prayer for you﴾ [al-Isra': 79] and His words: ﴿As a privilege for you alone﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50]. Among them is an address specific to him in wording, but the whole community shares it in meaning and in action, such as His words: ﴿Establish prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ [al-Isra': 78], and the verse continues, and His words: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 98], and His words: ﴿And when you are among them and lead them in prayer﴾ [al-Nisa': 102]. So everyone upon whom the sun has declined is addressed with the prayer, and likewise everyone who recites the Qur'an is addressed with the seeking of refuge, and likewise everyone who fears establishes prayer in that manner. Of this kind is His words, the Exalted: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow, and pray for them﴾. On this meaning come His words, the Exalted: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 1] and ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq: 1].

The second issue concerns His words: ﴿from their wealth﴾. Some Arabs, namely the tribe of Daws, held that "māl" (wealth) means garments, goods, and merchandise, and that they do not call gold or silver "māl." This meaning is also found in the established Sunnah, in the narration of Malik from Thawr ibn Zayd al-Dili, from Abu al-Ghayth Salim, mawla of Ibn Mutiʿ, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the year of Khaybar, and we did not gain any gold or silver, only goods, garments, and merchandise," and he related the hadith.

Others held that "māl" (wealth) is specifically coined wealth of gold and silver. It is also said that it refers specifically to camels, and from this comes their saying: "māl" is camels. It is also said that it refers to all livestock. Ibn al-Anbari reported from Ahmad ibn Yahya Thaʿlab, the grammarian, who said: "Whatever falls short of reaching the amount at which zakat becomes due in gold or silver is not wealth." And he recited:

"By Allah, no livestock of mine has ever reached
the threshold of zakat, nor camels, nor wealth."

Abu 'Umar said: In the usage of the Arabs, whatever is possessed and owned is called *mal* (wealth), based on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The son of Adam says, 'My wealth, my wealth,' but he has from his wealth only what he eats and so consumes it, or wears and so wears it out, or gives in charity and so sends it ahead." And Abu Qatada said: "He gave me the coat of mail, and I sold it and bought with its price an orchard (*makhraf*)[[The *makhraf* (with a fatha on the mim) is a small portion of palm trees, six or seven, that a man buys for picking dates (*al-kharfah*). It was also said that it is a group of palm trees, however many they are.]] in the territory of Banu Salima. It was indeed the first wealth I acquired (*ta'assaltuhu*)[[*Ta'assala mālan* means he acquired it, took it as his own, and developed it.]] in Islam."

Whoever swears by giving in charity all of his wealth, that applies to every kind of his property, whether or not it is subject to zakat, unless he intends a specific thing, in which case it is according to what he intended. It has also been said that it applies only to the kinds of property that are subject to zakat. Knowledge is comprehensive, and the language testifies that whatever is owned is called *mal*. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: the words of the Exalted, ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾, are unrestricted, not limited by any condition regarding what is taken or from whom it is taken, nor do they specify the amount taken or the property it is taken from. Their explanation is found in the Sunnah and the consensus, as we will mention. Accordingly, zakat is taken from all kinds of wealth. The Prophet ﷺ made zakat obligatory on livestock, grain and gold and silver coinage, and there is no disagreement about this. They differed concerning other things, such as horses and all kinds of goods (*'urūd*). The mention of horses[[See vol. 10, p. 73, and p. 135 onward.]] and honey[[See vol. 10, p. 73, and p. 135 onward.]] will come, Allah willing, in [the chapter on bees (*al-naḥl*)]. The imams related from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "There is no charity on less than five *awsuq* of dates, nor on less than five *awāqī* of silver (*al-warq*), nor on less than five *dhawd* of camels."[[Dhawd: between three and nine camels, a small herd.]] The discussion on the zakat of grains and what the earth produces has already been completed in [Surat al-An'am][[See vol. 7, p. 98 and what follows.]], and on minerals in [Surat al-Baqarah][[See vol. 3, p. 321 and what follows.]], and on ornaments in this surah.

The scholars agreed that the *uqiyya* is forty dirhams. So when a free Muslim possesses two hundred dirhams of minted silver, which are the five *awāqī* mentioned in the hadith, for a full lunar year, zakat becomes obligatory on him, and it is one-fortieth of it, which is five dirhams. The condition of a full year is based on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "There is no zakat on property until a year passes over it." Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it. As for what exceeds two hundred dirhams of silver, it is calculated proportionally, so from each portion of it is one-fortieth, whether little or much. This is the view of Malik, al-Layth, al-Shafi'i, most of the followers of Abu Hanifa, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abu Thawr, Ishaq and Abu 'Ubayd. This has been related from Ali and Ibn 'Umar. But a group said: there is nothing due on what exceeds two hundred dirhams until the excess reaches forty dirhams, and when it reaches that, there is one dirham in it, which is one-fortieth of it. This is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan, 'Ata', Tawus, al-Sha'bi, al-Zuhri, Makhul, 'Amr ibn Dinar and Abu Hanifa.

The fourth issue: As for the zakat on gold, the majority of scholars hold that when gold reaches twenty dinars, whose value is two hundred dirhams or more, zakat on it is obligatory, based on the hadith of Ali, which al-Tirmidhi transmitted from Damra and al-Harith, from Ali. Al-Tirmidhi said: "I asked Muhammad ibn Isma'il about this hadith, and he said: 'Both of them are sound in my view, from Abu Ishaq, and it is possible that it comes from both of them together.'" Al-Baji said in *al-Muntaqa*: "The chain of this hadith is not strong there, but the agreement of the scholars on acting upon it is evidence of the soundness of its ruling, and Allah knows best." It has been related from al-Hasan and al-Thawri, and some of the followers of Dawud ibn Ali inclined to it, that gold has no zakat until it reaches forty dinars. This is refuted by the hadith of Ali, the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, and the hadith of 'A'isha, that the Prophet ﷺ used to take from every twenty dinars half a dinar, and from forty dinars one dinar. On this is the body of the people of knowledge, except for those mentioned.

The fifth issue: The community agreed that what is less than five *dhawd* of camels has no zakat. When they reach five, then in them is a sheep. The sheep (*shāh*) applies to one of the small livestock, and small livestock includes both sheep (*ḍa'n*) and goats (*ma'z*). Also the scholars agreed that in five camels there is only one sheep, and it is their prescribed due. The charity of livestock is explained in the document which Abu Bakr al-Siddiq wrote for Anas when he sent him to Bahrain. Al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Daraqutni, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and others transmitted it, and all of it is agreed upon. The disagreement concerning it lies in two places. The first is the zakat on camels, which is when they reach one hundred and twenty-one. Malik said: the collector has the choice; if he wishes he may take three *banāt labūn*, and if he wishes he may take two *ḥiqqa*.[[*Ibn labūn*: the offspring of a she-camel that has completed its second year and entered its third. *Al-ḥiqq* (with a kasra): the one that has completed three years and entered its fourth.]] Ibn al-Qasim said: and Ibn Shihab said: In it are three *banāt labūn* until it reaches one hundred and thirty; then there is one *ḥiqqa* and two *banāt labūn*. Ibn al-Qasim said: and I hold the view of Ibn Shihab. Ibn Habib mentioned that 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi Salama, 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi Hazim and Ibn Dinar held the view of Malik. As for the second place, it concerns the zakat on sheep, which is when they exceed three hundred plus one sheep. Al-Hasan ibn Salih ibn Hayy said: in them are four sheep. And when they are four hundred plus one sheep, in them are five sheep, and so on, whenever they increase, for every hundred there is one sheep. This is also related from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i. The majority said: for two hundred plus one sheep there are three sheep; then there is nothing due until four hundred, when there are four sheep; then whenever they increase by a hundred, there is one sheep. This is by consensus and agreement. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: "This is an issue in which Ibn al-Mundhir made an error, reported the mistake of the scholars concerning it, confused matters, and committed many errors."

The sixth issue: Neither al-Bukhari nor Muslim mentioned in their *Sahih* collections the details of the zakat on cattle. It was transmitted by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, al-Daraqutni and Malik in his *Muwatta'*, and it is mursal, maqtu' and mawquf.[[*Mursal*: a hadith in which the Successor omits the Companion. *Maqtu'*: a report ending at a Successor or later. *Mawquf*: a report ending at a Companion.]] Abu 'Umar said: Some people transmitted it from Tawus from Mu'adh, but those who transmitted it as mursal are more reliable than those who linked it. Among those who linked it is Baqiyya, from al-Mas'udi, from al-Hakam, from Tawus. The narrators have differed concerning what Baqiyya transmits alone from reliable transmitters. Al-Hasan ibn 'Umara transmitted it from al-Hakam in the same way as Baqiyya transmitted it from al-Mas'udi from al-Hakam, and al-Hasan is agreed to be weak. This report has also been transmitted with a connected, sound and established chain, not through Tawus. 'Abd al-Razzaq mentioned it, saying: Ma'mar and al-Thawri informed us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Wa'il, from Masruq, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent me to Yemen and ordered me to take from every thirty cows a *tabī'* or a *tabī'a*[[*Al-tabī'*: the calf in its first year. *Al-musinn*: one that has completed two years and entered its third.]], and from forty a *musinna*, and from every adult (*ḥālim*) a dinar[[An addition from the two *Sahih*s of al-Daraqutni and al-Tirmidhi.]] or its equivalent in *ma'āfir*[[*Ma'āfir*: striped garments from Yemen, named after Ma'afir, a tribe in Yemen.]]." Al-Daraqutni and Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi transmitted it and declared it sound. Abu 'Umar said: There is no disagreement among the scholars that the zakat on cattle, as from the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions, is what Mu'adh ibn Jabal said: for thirty cows a *tabī'*, and for forty a *musinna*, except for an opinion narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Abu Qilaba, al-Zuhri and Qatada, who obligate for every five cows a sheep up to thirty.

This is a summary of the details of zakat with its roots and branches, found in the books of jurisprudence. The discussion of partnership (*khulṭa*)[[See vol. 15, p. 165.]] will come, Allah willing, in [Surat Sad][[See vol. 15, p. 165.]].

The seventh issue: The words of the Exalted, ﴿ṣadaqatan﴾ (a charity), are derived from *ṣidq* (truthfulness), since it is evidence of the soundness of his faith, the truthfulness of his inner state along with his outward state, and that he is not among the hypocrites who find fault with the believers who give voluntarily in charity. The words ﴿tuṭahhiruhum wa tuzakkīhim bihā﴾ ("you purify them and cause them to grow through it") are two circumstantial clauses (*ḥālān*) for the addressee; the sense is: take it while purifying them and causing them to grow by it. It is also permissible to make them two attributes of the charity, meaning a charity that purifies them and causes them to grow, and then the subject of *tuzakkīhim* would be the addressee, and the pronoun in *bihā* would refer back to the indefinite noun it describes. Al-Nahhas and Makki related that ﴿tuṭahhiruhum﴾ is an attribute of the charity, and ﴿tuzakkīhim bihā﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿khudh﴾, which refers to the Prophet ﷺ. It is also possible that it is a circumstantial clause from the charity, but that is weak, because it is a circumstantial clause from an indefinite noun. Al-Zajjaj said: "The better view is that the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: 'Indeed you purify them and cause them to grow through it,' as a new independent statement (*qaṭ' wa-istiʼnāf*). It is also permissible to read it in the jussive as a response to the imperative, and the meaning would be: if you take from their wealth a charity, you will purify them and cause them to grow." From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*Qifā nabki min dhikrā ḥabībin wa manzili*
("Halt, let us weep at the remembrance of a beloved and a dwelling.")

Al-Hasan read ﴿tuṭhirahum﴾ with a sukun on the ṭā', and it is transmitted with a hamza from *ṭahara* and *aṭhartuhu*, like *ẓahara* and *aẓhartuhu*.

The eighth issue: The words of the Exalted, ﴿wa ṣalli 'alayhim﴾ ("and pray for them"), are the basis for the action of every imam who receives the charity, that he should supplicate for the giver for blessing. Muslim transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa, who said: "When people came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with their charity, he would say: 'O Allah, send Your blessings upon them.' Ibn Abi Awfa came to him with his charity, and he said: 'O Allah, send Your blessings upon the family of Abi Awfa.'" Some people adopted this view, while others held that it was abrogated (*mansūkh*) by the words of the Exalted: ﴿And never pray over any of them who dies, ever﴾ [al-Tawba: 84]. They said: "It is not permissible to pray over anyone except the Prophet ﷺ alone, since he was singled out for that." They used as evidence the words of the Exalted: ﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among yourselves like the calling of some of you to others﴾ [al-Nur: 63], the verse, and that 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas used to say: "No one is to be prayed for except the Prophet ﷺ." The first view is more correct, since the address is not restricted to him, as has already been mentioned, and will come in the verse after this. So it is obligatory to follow the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and to emulate him, because he would carry out the command: ﴿And pray for them; indeed your prayer is a comfort for them﴾, meaning: when you supplicate for them when they bring their charities, that calms their hearts and they rejoice in it. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah related: "The Prophet ﷺ came to me, and I said to my wife: 'Do not ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for anything.' She said: 'The Messenger of Allah ﷺ leaves our house and we do not ask him anything!' Then she said: 'O Messenger of Allah, pray for my husband.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'May Allah send His blessings upon you and upon your husband.'" The word *ṣalāh* here means mercy and compassion. Al-Nahhas said: "All the lexicographers, as far as we know, agreed that *ṣalāh* in the speech of the Arabs means supplication, and from it is the funeral prayer (*ṣalāt al-janā'iz*)." Ḥafs, Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿inna ṣalātaka﴾ in the singular, while the rest read it in the plural. The same disagreement applies to ﴿aṣalātuka ta'muruka﴾ [Hud: 87][[See vol. 9, p. 84 and what follows.]]. And *sakan* was read with a sukun on the kaf. Qatada said: its meaning is tranquillity (*waqār*) for them. *Al-sakan* is that by which souls are calmed and hearts are reassured.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 104:

There are two issues in this.

The first: It has been said that those among the staying-behind who had not repented said: "These people were with us yesterday; they are not spoken to and not sat with. So what is their state now? And what is this special status with which they have been singled out over us?" Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Did they not know﴾. The pronoun in "ya'lamu" (they know) refers to those among the staying-behind who had not repented. This is the view of Ibn Zayd. It is also possible that it refers to those who repented and bound themselves [to the pillars of the mosque].

His exalted words ﴿He﴾ are an emphasis on God, glorified and exalted be He, being alone in these matters. The explanation is that if He had said, "Indeed God accepts repentance," it would have been possible that the acceptance of His Messenger is an acceptance from Him; so the verse makes clear that this is something that neither a prophet nor an angel can reach.

The second: His exalted words ﴿and takes the charities﴾. This is a clear text that God, exalted be He, is the One who takes them and the One who rewards for them, and that the right in them belongs to Him, mighty and majestic. The Prophet (ﷺ) is an intermediary; if he dies, his agent (ʿāmil) is the intermediary after him; but God, mighty and majestic, is Living and does not die. This shows that His words, glorified and exalted be He, ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ are not restricted to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed God accepts charity and takes it with His right hand, then nurtures it for one of you as one of you nurtures his foal, until a morsel becomes like Uhud." And the confirmation of this in the Book of God is: ﴿He it is who accepts repentance from His servants and takes the charities﴾ and ﴿God deprives usury of blessing and makes charities grow﴾. He said: This is a hadith ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. In Sahih Muslim: "No one gives a date from good earnings, except that God takes it with His right hand" — in another narration — "and it grows in the palm of the Merciful until it becomes greater than a mountain," the hadith. It is also narrated: "Indeed the charity falls into the palm of the Merciful before it falls into the palm of the beggar, and He nurtures it as one of you nurtures his colt or his young camel, and God multiplies for whom He wills." Our scholars, may God have mercy on them, said in interpreting these hadiths: this is a metaphor (kinaya) for acceptance and reward for it, just as He expressed by His noble, sanctified Self [a metaphor] for the sick, out of tenderness toward him, in His words: "O son of Adam, I was sick and you did not visit Me," the hadith. This meaning has already been mentioned in [al-Baqarah]. The right hand and the palm are singled out for mention because every recipient of something takes it with his palm and his right hand, or it is placed into them; so it came in terms they know. God, mighty and majestic, is exempt from any organ (jāriḥa). The word "yamīn" (right hand) has come in Arabic speech with meanings other than the physical organ, as the poet said:

"When a banner is raised for glory, / ʿArabah receives it with the right hand."

That is, he is qualified for glory and nobility; he did not mean the physical right hand, because glory is a meaning, so the right hand that receives its banner is a meaning. Likewise the "right hand" with respect to God, exalted be He. It has also been said that the meaning of "it grows in the palm of the Merciful" is an expression for the pan of the scale in which deeds are weighed; this would then be an instance of omitting the modifier, as if he said: "so the pan of the Merciful's scale grows." It is related from Malik, al-Thawri and Ibn al-Mubarak that they said regarding the interpretation of these hadiths and similar ones: "Pass them on without asking how." Al-Tirmidhi and others related this. And this is the position of the people of knowledge from the People of the Sunnah and the Community.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary on Surah 9, verse 105:**

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And say, "Work"﴾ is an address to everyone.

(﴿So Allah will see your deed, and [so will] His Messenger and the believers﴾) meaning: by His making them aware of your deeds. And in a report: "If a man were to work inside a rock that has no door and no window, his deed would come out to the people, whatever it may be."

It was revealed concerning the three who were forgiven: Ka'b ibn Malik, Hilal ibn Umayya of the Banu Waqif, and Murara ibn al-Rabi'; it was also said: Ibn Ribi'i al-'Umari, as mentioned by al-Mahdawi. They had remained behind from Tabuk, and they were ... (as will come from their mention below). The implied meaning is: "and among them are others whose matter is deferred" (murjawn), from arjaʾtuhu, meaning I postponed him. From this comes the term Murji'a (the Murji'ah), because they postponed deeds.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "murjawn" without a hamza. It was said that it is from arjaytuhu, meaning I postponed him. Al-Mubarrad said: arjaytuhu is not said in the sense of "I postponed him"; rather it comes from al-raja' (hope).

﴿Either He will punish them or He will accept their repentance.﴾ "Imma" in Arabic is used for one of two matters. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knows the outcome of things, but the address to the servants is according to what they understand; that is, let their matter be, in your view, one of hope, because the servants have no more than this.

*Note on the passage's wording:* the Arabic text contains the phrase "مياسر", which appears to be a corrupted word and whose meaning could not be reliably determined from the text provided; the translation above renders it as "..." accordingly.

**Tenth-century footnote-free translation follows.**

There are ten issues (masa'il) in this verse.

**The first issue:** God's words, ﴿Those who took a mosque﴾, are coordinated (ma'tuf), meaning: "And among them are those who took a mosque," a clause coordinated with a preceding clause. It may also be read in the nominative (raf') as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), with the predicate (khabar) omitted, as if it were "they are punished" or something similar. As for whoever reads ﴿alladhina﴾ without the conjunction "wa," which is the reading of the people of Medina (al-Madaniyyun), it is in the nominative as a subject, and its predicate is "do not stand." The intended meaning is: "Those who took a mosque, do not stand in it ever," that is, do not stand in their mosque. This was said by al-Kisa'i. Al-Nahhas said: the predicate of the subject is ﴿their building which they built will not cease to be a doubt in their hearts﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:110]. It was also said that the predicate is "they are punished," as already mentioned.

The verse was revealed, as it is narrated, concerning Abu 'Amir al-Rahib (the monk), because he went out to Caesar (Qaysar), became Christian, and Caesar promised them that he would come to them. So they built the Mosque of Harm (Masjid al-Dirar), watching for his arrival in it. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and others. Its story has already been mentioned in al-A'raf [[see vol. 7, p. 320]].

The people of tafsir (Ahl al-Tafsir) said: The Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf built the Mosque of Quba' and sent to the Prophet ﷺ asking him to come to them. He came and prayed in it. Their brothers, the Banu Ghanm ibn 'Awf, envied them and said: "We will build a mosque and send to the Prophet ﷺ, that he may come to us and pray for us as he prayed in our brothers' mosque, and Abu 'Amir will pray in it when he comes from Syria." So they came to the Prophet ﷺ while he was preparing for Tabuk and said: "O Messenger of God, we have built a mosque for the one who has need, the sick, and the rainy night, and we wish that you would pray for us in it and invoke blessing." The Prophet ﷺ said: "I am on a journey and occupied with affairs; if we return, we will come to you and pray for you in it." When the Prophet ﷺ returned from Tabuk, they came to him, having finished it and having prayed in it on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday. He asked for his shirt to put it on and go to them, but the Qur'an was revealed to him about the matter of the Mosque of Harm. The Prophet ﷺ summoned Malik ibn al-Dukhshum, Ma'n ibn 'Adi, 'Amir ibn al-Sakan, and Wahshi, the slayer of Hamzah, and said: "Go to this mosque whose people are wrongdoers, demolish it and burn it." So they set out quickly. Malik ibn al-Dukhshum took a flame of fire from his house, and they rose up, burned the mosque, and demolished it.

Those who had built it were twelve men: Hizam ibn Khalid of the Banu 'Ubayd ibn Zayd, one of the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf, and from his house the Mosque of Harm was brought out; Mu'attib ibn Qushayr; Abu Habibah ibn al-Az'ar; 'Abbad ibn Hunayf, brother of Sahl ibn Hunayf, of the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf; Jariyah ibn 'Amir and his two sons Mujammi' and Zayd, the sons of Jariyah; Nabtal ibn al-Harith; Bahzaj; Bijad ibn 'Uthman; Wadi'ah ibn Thabit; and Tha'labah ibn Hatib is mentioned among them. Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: "There is consideration in this, because he witnessed Badr."

'Ikrimah said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab asked a man among them: "With what did you help in this mosque?" He said: "I helped in it with a pillar." He said: "Rejoice in it! A pillar of fire of Hell in your neck."

**The second issue:** God's words, ﴿harm﴾ (dirar), is a verbal noun (masdar) functioning as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). ﴿Disbelief and dividing among the believers and waiting in ambush﴾ are all coordinated (ma'tuf). The people of ta'wil (interpretation) said: harm to the mosque, yet there is no harm to the mosque; it is only to its people.

Al-Daraqutni narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "There shall be neither harming nor reciprocal harming. Whoever harms, God will harm him; and whoever is hostile, God will be hostile to him."

Some scholars said: Darar is that from which you gain benefit while your neighbor suffers harm from it. Dirar is that from which you gain no benefit while your neighbor suffers harm from it. It has also been said: both have the same meaning, and both were spoken together for emphasis.

**The third issue:** Our scholars (ulama'una) said: It is not permissible to build a mosque beside a mosque, and it is obligatory to demolish it and prohibit its construction, lest the people of the first mosque turn away from it and it remain empty. Except if the neighborhood is large and one mosque is not sufficient for its people, then it may be built at that time. Likewise they said: It is not appropriate that two or three congregational mosques (jami'ayn) be built in one city, and the second must be prohibited; and whoever prays Friday prayer (Jumu'ah) in it, his prayer is not valid. The Prophet ﷺ burned the Mosque of Harm and demolished it.

Al-Tabari narrated from Shaqiq that he came to pray in the mosque of the Banu Ghadirah [[so in ب, ج and ك; in هـ: Banu 'Amirah; what is in al-Tabari: Banu 'Amir]] and found that the prayer had already passed him. It was said to him: "The mosque of the Banu so-and-so has not yet been prayed in." He said: "I do not like to pray in it, because it was built on harm."

Our scholars said: Every mosque built on harm or on show and reputation (riya' wa-sum'ah) has the ruling of the Mosque of Harm; prayer in it is not permissible. Al-Naqqash said: It follows from this that one should not pray in a church (kanisah) or the like, because they were built on evil.

I say: This does not follow, because the church was not built with the intention of harming others, even if its original construction was on evil. The Christians take the church, and the Jews take the synagogue (bay'ah), as a place of worship according to their claim, like our mosque. So the two differ. The scholars have agreed that whoever prays in a church or synagogue, in a clean place, his prayer is valid and permissible. Al-Bukhari mentioned that Ibn 'Abbas used to pray in a synagogue when there were no images (tamathil) in it. Abu Dawud narrated from 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'As that the Prophet ﷺ ordered him to make the mosque of al-Ta'if where their idols (tawaghit) had been.

**The fourth issue:** The scholars said: Whoever is an imam for an oppressor (zalim), one does not pray behind him unless his excuse becomes evident or he repents. The Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf, who built the Mosque of Quba', asked 'Umar ibn al-Khattab during his caliphate to permit Mujammi' ibn Jariyah to lead them in prayer in their mosque. He said: "No, and not a delight to the eye! Is he not the imam of the Mosque of Harm?" Mujammi' said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, do not hasten against me. By God, I prayed in it while I did not know what they had concealed. If I had known, I would not have prayed with them in it. I was a young man who recited the Qur'an, and they were elders who had lived in their pre-Islamic ignorance [[in ب and ج: ghashsu; in هـ: 'ashu; in ع: nashu]], and they did not recite anything of the Qur'an. So I prayed, and I do not reckon what I did to be a sin, and I do not know what is in their souls." So 'Umar excused him, believed him, and ordered him to pray in the Mosque of Quba' [[may God be pleased with them both]].

**The fifth issue:** Our scholars, may God's mercy be upon them, said: When a mosque that is made for worship, and the Law (al-shar') encouraged its construction, saying: "Whoever builds a mosque for God, even if it is like the nest of a sandgrouse (mafhas qata), God will build for him a house in Paradise," is demolished and removed when it contains harm to others, then what do you think of other than it! Rather, it is more fitting that it be removed and demolished, so that harm does not enter upon the older one. This is like one who builds an oven, a mill, or digs a well, or other things by which he brings harm upon others. The governing principle of this chapter is: whoever brings harm upon his brother is prevented. If he brings harm upon his brother by an action which he was permitted to do with his property, and that harms his neighbor or someone other than his neighbor, the action is examined. If leaving it is a greater harm than the harm inflicted on the actor, the greater of the two harms is cut off, and the one of greater sanctity in the principles (fi al-usul) is preferred.

An example of that: a man opens a window in his house overlooking his brother's house, where there are his family and women. It is the custom of women in their houses to take off some of their clothes and move about for their needs. It is known that looking upon nakedness ('awrat) is forbidden, and a prohibition regarding it has been reported [[in ع: "about it"]]. So, for the sanctity of looking upon nakedness, the scholars decided that one should close, upon the one who opened the door and the window, what he opened, though he had benefit and comfort in it, because closing it upon him causes harm; they intended to cut off the greater of the two harms, since it was necessary to cut off one of them. This is the ruling in this chapter, contrary to al-Shafi'i and whoever says what he says.

The companions of al-Shafi'i said: If a man digs a well on his property, and another digs a well on his property to steal the water of the first well, it is permitted, because each of them dug on his own property, so neither is prevented from that. Similar to this among them: if he digs beside his neighbor's well a latrine (kanif) that spoils it for him, he cannot be prevented, because he acted within his own property. The Qur'an and the Sunnah refute this view. And success is from God.

Among this chapter is another kind of harm that the scholars prevented: such as the smoke of the oven and the bathhouse, the dust of the threshing floor (andar), and the worms that breed from dung spread in open courtyards. Whatever is like this, the part whose harm is evident and whose continuation is feared is cut off. As for what is a brief, light matter, like shaking out clothes and mats at the doors, this is something people cannot do without, and it does not warrant anything; so preventing harm by prohibiting such a thing is greater and more important than enduring it for a brief, light time. The neighbor's duty toward his neighbor, according to the etiquette of the Sunnah, is to be patient with his harm as far as he is able, just as it is incumbent upon him not to harm him and to do good to him.

**The sixth issue:** Among what enters this chapter is a question narrated by Isma'il ibn Abi Uways from Malik, that he was asked about a woman who was afflicted (by a touch from the jinn), meaning a touch from the jinn, so that whenever her husband had intercourse with her, or she became impure (ajnabat), or he approached her, it would distress her greatly. Malik said: "I do not think he should approach her, and I think it is for the ruler to come between him and her."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 107 (part 2 of 2):

The seventh matter: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and disbelief﴾. Since their belief was that the mosque of Quba' and the mosque of the Prophet ﷺ had no sanctity, they disbelieved by this belief. This is said by Ibn al-'Arabi. It is also said: "and disbelief" means disbelief in the Prophet ﷺ and in what he brought. This is said by al-Qushayri and others.

The eighth matter: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and to cause division among the believers﴾, meaning they use it to divide their community, so that groups would stay behind from the Prophet ﷺ. This shows you that the greatest purpose and the most evident aim of establishing the congregation is the bringing together of hearts and of the word upon obedience, and the binding of covenant and sanctity through the act of religious duty, until familiarity comes through association and hearts are cleansed of the filth of rancor.

The ninth matter: Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, perceived from this verse and said: two congregations are not to be prayed in one mosque with two imams. This is contrary to all other scholars. It has been narrated from al-Shafi'i the prohibition, where it leads to scattering the word, nullifying this wisdom, and being a pretext for saying: whoever wants to separate from the congregation has an excuse, so he establishes his own congregation and puts forward his own leadership, so disagreement occurs and order collapses. This was hidden from them. Ibn al-'Arabi said: this was his practice with them, and he was firmer of footing than they were in wisdom and more knowledgeable of the limits of the Shari'ah.

The tenth matter: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and as an ambush for those who warred against Allah and His Messenger﴾. It refers to Abu 'Amir the monk, and he was named so because he used to worship and seek knowledge; he died a disbeliever in Qinnasrin [[Qinnasrin (with a kasra on its first letter, a fatha on its second, and doubled, and it may be pronounced with a kasra): a district in Syria.]] through the supplication of the Prophet ﷺ. He had said to the Prophet ﷺ: "I do not find a people who will fight you except that I will fight you alongside them." So he continued fighting him until the day of Hunayn. When Hawazin were defeated, he went out to Syria seeking support, and he sent to the hypocrites and said: "Prepare whatever strength and weapons you can, and build a mosque, for I am going to Caesar to bring back an army of Romans to expel Muhammad from Madinah." So they built the mosque of harm. This Abu 'Amir is the father of Hanzalah, the washed one of the angels [[He was called "the washed one of the angels" because he was martyred on the day of Uhud, and the angels washed him. That was because he had been intimate with his wife at the time of his departure for Uhud, and then the call to march out in the levy came upon him, which made him forget the ritual bath and hastened him away from it. When he was killed as a martyr, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ informed them that the angels had washed him. (From al-Isti'ab.)]]. And al-Irsad means waiting. You say: "I prepared such-and-such" if you readied it, awaiting it for that purpose. Abu Zayd said: it is said "rasadtuhu" and "arsadtuhu" concerning good, and "arsadtu lahu" concerning evil. Ibn al-A'rabi said: it is only said "arsadtu," and its meaning is "irtaqabtu" (I watched/waited). And His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿from before﴾ means from before the building of the mosque of harm.

﴿And they will surely swear, "We intended nothing but goodness"﴾, meaning we did not intend by its construction anything but the good deed, which is ease for the Muslims, as they mentioned for the one with a sickness and need. This shows that actions differ according to their aim and intentions, and for this reason He said: "And they will surely swear, 'We intended nothing but goodness.'" ﴿And Allah testifies that indeed they are liars﴾, meaning He knows the corruption of their inner thoughts and their lying in what they swear to.

**Issue 1: The Tafsir of "Never stand therein"**

There are eleven issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** Allah's words, ﴿Never stand therein﴾. This refers to the Mosque of Harm (masjid al-dirar), meaning: do not stand in it for prayer. Prayer is sometimes expressed by the word "standing." It is said: "So-and-so stands the night," meaning he prays through the night. From this is the authentic hadith: "Whoever stands in prayer during Ramadan out of faith and seeking reward, his previous sins will be forgiven." Al-Bukhari narrated it from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said... and then he mentioned it. It is also narrated that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would not pass by the road where the mosque was, and he ordered that its site be made into a dunghill, where carrion, filth and refuse would be thrown.

**The second issue:** Allah's words, ﴿ever﴾. "Abadan" (ever) is an adverb of time. Adverbs of time are of two kinds: a defined one, such as "day," and an indefinite one, such as "time" (hin) and "period" (waqt). "Abad" (eternity) belongs to this second kind, as does "dahr" (age). Here arises a question of legal theory (usuli): although "abadan" is an indefinite adverb with no generality in itself, when it is joined to the negative particle "la" it conveys generality. If he had said "do not stand," that would have sufficed for an unconditional prohibition. When he says "abadan," it is as if he said: "at no time and in no period." As for an indefinite noun in an affirmative statement reporting an actual event, it does not carry generality. The people of the language understood this, and the jurists of Islam ruled accordingly. They said: if a man says to his wife, "You are divorced forever," she is divorced with one divorce.

**The third issue:** Allah's words, ﴿a mosque founded upon piety﴾. That is, its walls were built and its foundations raised. "Ass" (foundation) is the origin of a building, and so is "asas." "Assas" is a shortened form of it. The plural of "ass" is "isas," like "uss" and "isas." The plural of "asas" is "usus," like "qadhal" and "qudhul." The plural of "usus" is "asas," like "sabab" and "asbab." One says "assastu al-binā'" (I founded the building), meaning "ta'sis." The expression "kāna dhālika 'alā uss al-dahr," "assi al-dahr," and "issi al-dahr" are three dialect forms, meaning "from the beginning of time" and "the face of time." The "lam" in "lamasjidun" is the lam of oath, and it has also been said to be the lam of inception, as when you say, "Indeed Zayd is the best of people in conduct." It implies emphasis. "Ossisa 'alā al-taqwā" (founded upon piety) is an attribute of "masjid." "Aḥaqq" (more worthy) is the predicate of the subject "lamasjidun." The meaning of piety here is the qualities by which punishment is averted; it is an intensive form from "waqaytu" (I protected), and this was discussed earlier.

**The fourth issue:** The scholars differed about the mosque that was founded upon piety. One group said it is the Mosque of Quba. This is narrated from Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and al-Hasan. They relied on Allah's words, ﴿from the first day﴾, and the Mosque of Quba was founded in Medina on the first day, since it was built before the Mosque of the Prophet (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn Umar, Ibn al-Musayyab, and Malik according to what Ibn Wahb, Ashhab and Ibn al-Qasim narrated from him. al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that he said: Two men disputed (tamārā, meaning argued) about the mosque founded upon piety from the first day. One man said it is the Mosque of Quba, and the other said it is the Mosque of the Prophet (ﷺ). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It is this mosque of mine." [He said: this is a sound hadith.] The first opinion is more fitting to the story, because of the words, ﴿therein﴾, and the pronoun of place requires men who purify themselves. Thus it is the Mosque of Quba. The evidence for this is the hadith of Abu Hurayra, who said: This verse was revealed about the people of Quba, ﴿therein are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾. He said: They used to cleanse themselves with water, so this verse was revealed about them. al-Sha'bi said: They are the people of the Mosque of Quba, and Allah revealed this about them. Qatada said: When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the people of Quba: "Indeed Allah, glorified is He, has praised you well concerning purification. What do you do?" They said: "We wash the trace of excrement and urine with water." It was narrated by Abu Dawud. al-Daraqutni narrated from Talha ibn Nafi', who said: Abu Ayyub, Jabir ibn Abdullah and Anas ibn Malik, the Ansar, told me from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning this verse, ﴿therein are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾, that he said: "O assembly of the Ansar, indeed Allah has praised you well concerning purification. What is this purification of yours?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah, we perform ablution for prayer and bathe from major impurity." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Is there anything beyond that?" They said: "No, except that when one of us comes out from defecating, he likes to cleanse himself with water." He said: "That is it, so keep to it." This hadith implies that the mosque mentioned in the verse is the Mosque of Quba. However, the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri is explicit that the Prophet (ﷺ) stated it is his mosque, so there is no room for argument with it. Abu Kurayb narrated: Abu Usama told us, Salih ibn Hayyan told us, Abdullah ibn Buraydah told us, concerning the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿in houses which Allah has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned﴾ [al-Nur: 36]: He said: They are only four mosques, which none but a prophet built: the Ka'bah, built by Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them; Jericho, the Bayt al-Maqdis, built by Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them; and the Mosque of Medina and the Mosque of Quba, which were founded upon piety, built by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

**The fifth issue:** ﴿from the first day﴾. "Min" (from), according to the grammarians, corresponds to "mundhu" (since). So "mundhu" for time is equivalent to "min" for place. It was said that its meaning here is "mundhu," and the implied phrase is: "since the first day its construction began." It was also said that the meaning is "from the founding of the first days," so it was attached to the verbal noun of the verb "ossisa" (was founded), as the poet said:

*Li-man al-diyāru bi-qunnati al-ḥijri*
*Aqwayna min ḥijaji wa min dahri*

(To whom belong these abodes at the summit of al-Hijr? They have become desolate since the passing of years and the passing of ages.) This is the opening line of an ode by Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma in praise of Harim ibn Sinan. "Qunna" (with a damma) means the top of a mountain, and he means here the high part of the land. "Al-Hijr" (with a kasra on the ha) is the dwelling place of Thamud in the region of al-Sham near Wadi al-Qura. "Aqwayna" means: became empty and desolate. "Hijaj" means years. (See this line and its discussion in the fourth-and-seventy-ninth witness, after the seven hundredth, in al-Baghdadi's Khizanat al-Adab.) This means: since the passage of years and since the passage of ages. What led to this view is that among the principles of the grammarians is that "min" does not govern times; rather, times are governed by "mundhu." You say: "I have not seen him since a month, a year, or a day," and you do not say "min shahrin," "min sanatin," or "min yawmin." So when it appears in a sentence and a time-word follows it, an implied element that can be governed by "min" is supposed, as we mentioned in the line's interpretation. (Ibn Atiyya.) It seems good to me that in this verse one can dispense with an assumption, and that "min" governs the word "awwal" (first), because it carries the sense of a starting point. It is as if he said: "from the beginning of the days."

**The sixth issue:** Allah's words, ﴿more worthy that you stand therein﴾. That is, "that you stand," and it is in the accusative position. "Aḥaqq" is the comparative form of "ḥaqq" (truth/right). The comparative form is used only between two things that share a quality, one of which has more of that shared quality than the other. The Mosque of Harm, though false, has no right to it, yet both share the truth in terms of the belief of its builder, or the belief of those who thought standing in it was permissible because it was a mosque. But one of the two beliefs is false inwardly before Allah, while the other is true inwardly and outwardly. A similar example is Allah's words: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day are better in their abode and finer in their resting place﴾ [al-Furqan: 24]. It is known that goodness in comparison with the Fire is absurd. But this was phrased according to the belief of each group that they are upon good, and that their destination is good, since ﴿every party rejoices in what they have﴾. This is not of the kind of "honey is sweeter than vinegar," for honey, though sweet, makes everything agreeable sweet. Do you not see that some people prefer vinegar to honey, singly against singly and paired against paired?

**The seventh issue:** Allah's words, ﴿therein﴾. Whoever says that the mosque meant is the Mosque of the Prophet (ﷺ), the pronoun in "therein you should stand" refers to it, and "therein are men" refers to it as well. Whoever says it is the Mosque of Quba, the pronoun in "therein" refers to it, according to the earlier disagreement.

**The eighth issue:** In this verse Allah, glorified and exalted is He, praised those who love purity and prefer cleanliness. This is a human virtue and a legal duty. In al-Tirmidhi, from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, she said: "Command your husbands to cleanse themselves with water, for I am shy of them." He said: This is a sound hadith. It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to carry water with him for istinja' (cleansing after excretion). He used stones for lightness and water for purification. Ibn al-'Arabi said: The scholars of Qayrawan used to place stones in sand in their washing places, with which they cleaned themselves, and then cleansed themselves with water.

**The ninth issue:** What is required for the impurity of the excretory passage is lightening (of the requirement), while for the impurity of the rest of the body and clothing, purification is required. This is a concession from Allah to His servants, in both situations of the presence of water and its absence. This is what the majority of scholars said. Ibn Habib was an outlier, saying: one may cleanse with stones (istijmar) only when water is absent. The established reports on cleansing with stones even when water is present refute him.

**The tenth issue:** The scholars differed in this area about removing impurity from bodies and clothes, after agreeing to overlook and pardon the blood of fleas as long as it is not excessive, into three opinions.

*The first:* It is an obligatory duty (fard). It is not valid to pray in a garment that is impure, whether the one praying knows it or forgets. This was narrated from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin, and it is the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Abu Thawr. Ibn Wahb narrated it from Malik. It is also the view of Abu al-Faraj al-Maliki and al-Tabari, except that al-Tabari said: if the impurity is the size of a dirham, one must repeat the prayer. It is also the view of Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf regarding the consideration of the size of a dirham, by analogy with the ring of the anus.

*The second:* Removing impurity from clothes and bodies is obligatory according to the Sunnah, an obligation of Sunnah and not of fard. They said: whoever prays in impure clothing must repeat the prayer within its time; if the time has passed, there is nothing upon him. This is the view of Malik and his companions, except Abu al-Faraj, and it is a narration from Ibn Wahb from him. Malik said concerning small amounts of blood: the prayer is not repeated from it, within the time or after it, but it is repeated from small amounts of urine and excrement. All of this from the school of Malik is the view of al-Layth. Ibn al-Qasim said from him: removing it is required when one remembers, not when one forgets. This opinion is unique to him.

*The third*, and the first is more correct, if Allah wills. This is because the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by two graves and said: "Indeed they are both being punished, and they are not being punished for something great.
