As for one of them, he used to walk about with slander; as for the other, he did not protect himself from his urine." The hadith, narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim, is sufficient for you. It will come in Surah [al-Isra'] (Subhan). They said: A person is only punished for abandoning an obligation, and this is clear.

Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba related from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Most of the punishment of the grave is from urine" [Narrated by Ahmad, Ibn Majah and al-Hakim. In the manuscripts it reads "from urine" (fi al-bawl), which is a scribal error.]. The others argued from the Prophet's (ﷺ) removal of his sandals during prayer, when Jibril (peace be upon him) informed him that there was filth and harm on them... the hadith. Abu Dawud and others transmitted it from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and it will come in Surah Ta-Ha, God willing [See vol. 11, p. 171 onward.]. They said: Since he did not repeat the prayer he had performed, this indicates that removing it is a sunna and that the prayer is valid, and one repeats it as long as the time remains, seeking perfection. And God knows best.

The eleventh issue: Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: As for distinguishing between the little and the much by the size of the Baghli dirham [dirhams struck by the head of a mule for our master Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him.], [meaning the large dirhams which are the size of the circumference of a dinar [addition from Ibn al-Arabi.]], by analogy with the anus opening [al-masruba (with the ra vowelled either way): the passage of waste from the rear, meaning the upper edge of the ring.], it is flawed on two counts. The first: measures determined by analogy are not established, so this estimate is not accepted. The second: what was relaxed for him regarding the anal opening is a concession due to necessity, and necessity and concessions are not to be analogized from, because they fall outside analogy and so are not referred back to it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 110:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Their building which they have built will never cease to be a cause of doubt in their hearts﴾, meaning the mosque of harm (masjid al-dirar).

(Rība) means doubt in their hearts and hypocrisy. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak. Al-Nabigha said:

I swore an oath, and I left no doubt (rība) for your self, and for a man there is no refuge except in God.

Al-Kalbi said: it means regret and remorse, because they regretted their building it. Al-Suddi, Habib and al-Mubarrad said: "rība" means resentment and rage.

(Illa an taqatta'a qulubuhum) Ibn Abbas said: that is, their hearts will split apart so that they die, like His saying: ﴿Then We would have cut off from him the aorta﴾ [al-Haqqah: 46], because life is cut off when the aorta is severed (al-watin: a vein that feeds the liver, according to al-Raghib; and the watin is a vein in the heart, according to al-Qamus). This was also said by Qatada, al-Dahhak and Mujahid. Sufyan said: "illa an yatubu" (unless they repent). Ikrima said: unless their hearts are cut apart in their graves. The companions of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud used to recite it: "rība fi qulubihim wa law taqatta'at qulubuhum" (a doubt in their hearts, even if their hearts were cut apart). Al-Hasan, Ya'qub and Abu Hatim read "ila an taqatta'" as a limit (ghaya), meaning they will continue in doubt about it until they die, and then they will become certain and it will become clear to them. The readers differed regarding the word "taqatta'": the majority read "tuqatta'" with a damma on the taa', a fatha on the qaf and a shadda on the ta', as a passive verb. Ibn Amir, Hamza, Hafs and Ya'qub read it likewise, except that they put a fatha on the taa'. It is reported from Ya'qub and Abu Abd al-Rahman "tuqta'" as a passive verb with a light qaf. It is reported from Shibl and Ibn Kathir "taqta'" with a light qaf and "qulubahum" in the accusative, meaning: you are the one who does this to them. We have already mentioned the reading of the companions of Abdullah.

(Wa Allahu 'Alimun Hakim) has already been explained.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 111:

There are eight issues in this verse. The first: the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties⦆. It has been said: this is a figure of speech (tamthil), like the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16]. [[See vol. 1, p. 21.]] The verse was revealed concerning the second pledge, which is the Great Pledge of al-ʿAqabah, in which the men of the Ansar outnumbered the seventy, and the youngest of them in age was ʿUqbah ibn ʿAmr. This is because they gathered before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at al-ʿAqabah, and ʿAbdullah ibn Rawahah said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Stipulate for your Lord and for yourself whatever you wish." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I stipulate for my Lord that you worship Him and do not associate anything with Him, and I stipulate for myself that you protect me from what you protect your own selves and your wealth from." (They said: "If we do that, what will we have?" He said:) "Paradise." They said: "The sale is profitable; we will neither cancel it nor ask for its cancellation." So the verse was revealed: "Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties, for that they will have Paradise," to the end of the verse. Then, after that, it is general for every one who strives in the way of Allah from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) until the Day of Resurrection.

The second: this verse is evidence for the permissibility of a master dealing with his slave, although everything belongs to the master; but when he makes his worker the owner of what he has delegated to him. What is permissible between a master and his slave is not permissible between him and others, because his property is his, and he has the right to take it back.

The third: the basic principle of buying among created beings is that what leaves their hands is compensated by something more beneficial to them, or by something equal in benefit to what left them. Allah, glorified is He, bought from the servants the destruction of their lives and properties in His obedience and their ruin in seeking His pleasure, and He gave them Paradise as recompense for it when they do that. It is a great recompense, to which the thing exchanged cannot come close nor be compared. So He applied to that the figurative sense of what they customarily know in buying and selling: from the servant is the surrender of self and wealth, and from Allah is the reward and bounty. This was therefore named a purchase (shira').

It is related from al-Hasan who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Above every righteousness is another righteousness, until the servant gives his blood; when he does that, there is no righteousness above that." And a poet said [on the meaning of righteousness [[from ʿ.]]]:

Giving away water is a generosity with honour in it,
but giving away the self is the utmost limit of generosity.

Al-Asmaʿi recited for Jaʿfar al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him:

I sell the precious self, its own owner,
and there is no price for it among all creation.
Through it Gardens are bought, if I sell it
for something other than it—indeed, that is a loss.
If my self departs for a worldly thing I have obtained,
then my self has indeed departed, and the price has departed too.

Al-Hasan said: A Bedouin passed by the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was reciting this verse: "Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives," and he said: "Whose speech is this?" He said: "The speech of Allah." He said: "By Allah, it is a profitable sale; we will not cancel it nor ask for its cancellation." So he went out to fight and was martyred.

The fourth: the scholars said: just as He purchased from the believers who are adults and legally responsible, so He purchases from children, afflicting them and making them ill, because of the benefit in that and the lesson for adults. For they are never more upright in patience, nor less prone to corruption, than when they witness the pain of children; and the reward that the two parents who support them obtain for the distress that befalls them and the upbringing and care that is their responsibility. Then He, Mighty and Majestic, compensates these children with a recompense when they come to Him. A parallel to this among creatures is that you hire a labourer to build and carry earth, and in all of that he experiences pain and harm; yet that is permissible because of the benefit in his work and because of the wage that reaches him.

The fifth: the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They fight in the way of Allah﴾ is an explanation of what they fight for and upon, and this has already been mentioned.

(So they kill and are killed.) Al-Nakhaʿi, al-Aʿmash, Hamzah, al-Kisaʾi and Khalaf read it with the object preceding the subject. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"If you kill us, we will kill you..."

That is: if some of us kill some of you, some of us will kill you. The rest read it with the subject preceding the object.

The sixth: the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿A promise binding upon Him in the Torah, the Gospel and the Quran﴾ is a report from Allah the Exalted that this was in these books, and that jihad and resisting enemies originated from the time of Musa, peace be upon him. "Waʿdan" and "haqqan" are emphatic verbal nouns (masdars).

The seventh: the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And who is more faithful to his covenant than Allah?﴾ means: no one is more faithful to his covenant than Allah. It includes fulfilling the promise and the threat, but it does not include the Creator's fulfilment of all of them: as for His promise, it is for all; as for His threat, it is specific to some of the wrongdoers, some sins, and some circumstances. This meaning has already been discussed fully. [[See vol. 5, p. 333 onward.]]

The eighth: the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So rejoice in your transaction which you have made﴾ means: show joy at that. Glad tidings (bushra) is the manifestation of joy in the face. This has already been mentioned. [[See vol. 1, p. 238.]] Al-Hasan said: By Allah, there is no believer on earth but that he enters into this pledge.

(That is the great triumph) meaning: attaining Paradise and abiding eternally therein.

**First issue: the verse 9:112 descriptions.** There are three questions here.

**The first question:** the words of God, Exalted is He, ﴿The repentant, the worshippers﴾. "The repentant" (al-tā'ibūn) are those who turn back from the blameworthy state of disobedience to God to the praiseworthy state of obedience to God. The one who repents (al-tā'ib) is the one who returns (al-rāji'). Whoever returns to obedience is better than whoever merely returns from disobedience, because he combines the two matters. "The worshippers" (al-'ābidūn) means the obedient, who intend God, glorified is He, by their obedience. "The praisers" (al-ḥāmidūn) means those who are content with His decree, who spend His blessing in obedience to Him, and who praise God in every state. "The wanderers" (al-sā'iḥūn) means those who fast, according to Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and others. From the same usage is God's words: ﴿worshipping, wandering﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5] [see vol. 18, p. 192].

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: "The fasting person is only called a wanderer (sā'iḥ) because he gives up all pleasures: food, drink and marriage." Abu Talib said:

*"By the wanderers who do not taste a drop, for their Lord, and by the women who remember and work."*

Another said:

*"A pious one who prays his night and his day, always much in the remembrance of God, a wanderer."*

It is related from 'Aisha that she said: "The wandering (siyāḥa) of this community is fasting." Al-Tabari transmitted it with a chain of narration. Abu Hurayra related it as a raised report (marfū') from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The wandering of my community is fasting." Al-Zajjaj said: "The view of al-Hasan is that they are those who fast the obligatory fast." It has also been said that they are those who make fasting continuous. 'Ata' said: "The wanderers are the fighters (mujāhidūn)." Abu Umama related that a man asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for permission to go wandering, and he said: "The wandering of my community is struggle in the way of God." Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Haqq authenticated it. It has also been said: "The wanderers are the emigrants (muhājirūn)," said by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd. It has been said: "They are those who travel in search of hadith and knowledge," said by 'Ikrima. It has been said: "They are those who direct their thoughts to the oneness of their Lord, His dominion, and the signs and proofs He created which point to His oneness and His greatness." Al-Naqqash related this. It is also reported that one of the worshippers took a cup to perform ablution for the night prayer, put his finger into the handle of the cup, and sat contemplating until dawn broke. He was asked about this and said: "I put my finger into the handle of the cup, and I remembered the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿When the shackles are on their necks and the chains﴾ [Ghafir: 71] [see vol. 15, p. 331 onward], and I thought how I would receive the shackle, and I remained all my night in that."

I say: the root *s-y-ḥ* supports the soundness of all these views, for siyāḥa originally means going over the face of the earth, as water flows (yasīḥ). The fasting person persists in obedience by abstaining from food and other things, so he is in the position of a wanderer. Those who reflect have their hearts roaming over what they have mentioned. In a hadith: "God has angels who wander and travel through the horizons, conveying to me the prayer of my community." It is also narrated as *ṣayyāḥīn* with a *ṣād*, from *ṣiyāḥ* (shouting).

﴿The bowers, the prostrators﴾ means in the obligatory prayer and other prayers. ﴿Those who enjoin the right﴾ means to the Sunna; it has also been said: to faith. ﴿And those who forbid the wrong﴾ has been said to mean forbidding innovation (bid'a); it has also been said: forbidding disbelief; and it has been said: it is general to every right and wrong. ﴿And those who guard the limits of God﴾ means those who carry out what He commanded and refrain from what He forbade.

**The second question:** The scholars of interpretation disagreed about whether this verse is connected to what precedes it or separate from it. A group said: this verse is independent in itself; under that pledge falls every monotheist who fights in the way of God so that the word of God is supreme, even if he does not possess these attributes in this verse or in most of them. Another group said: these descriptions came as conditions, and the two verses are linked, so only the believers who have these attributes and who give themselves in the way of God enter under the pledge. This was said by al-Dahhak. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This view is restrictive and constricting. The meaning of the verse, according to what the views of the scholars and the Sharia require, is that these are the attributes of the perfect among the believers, which God mentioned so that the people of monotheism would race toward them until they reach the highest rank."

Al-Zajjaj said: "What I hold is that His words ﴿The repentant, the worshippers﴾ are in the nominative by way of the inceptive, and its predicate is elided, meaning: ﴿the repentant, the worshippers﴾ up to the end of the verse, for them is also Paradise, even if they do not fight, when there is no obstinacy or intention among them to abandon fighting, because some Muslims suffice for others in fighting." Al-Qushayri chose this view and said: "This is good, for if it were an attribute of the believers mentioned in His words ﴿God has bought from the believers﴾, the promise would be specific to the fighters."

In the codex of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) it reads ﴿the repentant (al-tā'ibīn), the worshippers (al-'ābidīn)﴾ to the end. For this there are two possibilities: first, it is an attribute of the believers by way of following (ittibā'); second, it is in the accusative by way of praise (madḥ).

**The third question:** The scholars disagreed about the *wāw* in His words ﴿and those who forbid the wrong﴾. It was said: it entered into the attribute of those who forbid, as it entered in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Ḥā Mīm. The revelation of the Book from God, the Mighty, the Knowing. Forgiver of sin and Accepter of repentance﴾ [Ghafir: 1–3] [see vol. 15, p. 289]; so He mentioned some of them with *wāw* and some without it. This is permissible and customary in speech, and no wisdom or cause is sought for the like of it. It was also said: it entered because the one who forbids wrong is accompanied by the one who enjoins right, so one of them is hardly mentioned alone. Similarly in ﴿previously married and virgins﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5] [see vol. 18, p. 193]. And it entered into His words ﴿and those who guard﴾ because of its closeness to what is conjoined. It has also been said that it is superfluous, but this is weak and has no meaning. It has been said: it is the *wāw* of the eighth (wāw al-thamāniya), because seven is a complete and sound number among the Arabs. Likewise they said concerning His words ﴿previously married and virgins﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5], and His words about the gates of Paradise: ﴿and its gates were opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73] [see vol. 15, pp. 382–843], and His words: ﴿They will say: they are seven, and their eighth is their dog﴾ [al-Kahf: 22] [see vol. 10, p. 382]. Ibn Khalawayh mentioned this in his debate with Abu 'Ali al-Farisi concerning the meaning of His words ﴿and its gates were opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], and Abu 'Ali denied it.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "My father, may God be pleased with him, related to me from the grammarian teacher Abu 'Abd Allah al-Kafif al-Malaqi, who was among those who settled in Granada and taught there during the period of Ibn Ḥabūs, that he said: 'It is an eloquent dialect of some Arabs, whose custom when counting is to say: wāḥid, ithnān, thalātha, arba'a, khamsa, sitta, sab'a, wa-thamāniya, tis'a, 'ashara, and so their dialect is.' Whenever the matter of eight comes in their speech, they insert the *wāw*."

I say: this is the dialect of Quraysh. Its explanation and refutation will come, God willing, in Surat al-Kahf [see vol. 10, p. 382], and likewise in al-Zumar, also by God's power [see vol. 15, pp. 382–843].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 9, verse 113:

There are three issues (*masa'il*) in this verse.

**The first issue:** Muslim narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from his father, who said: When Abu Talib was on the point of death, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to him and found with him Abu Jahl and Abdullah ibn Abi Umayya ibn al-Mughira. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O uncle, say: There is no god but Allah, a word by which I will testify for you before Allah." Abu Jahl and Abdullah ibn Abi Umayya said: "O Abu Talib, will you turn away from the religion of Abd al-Muttalib?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kept presenting it to him and repeating that statement, until Abu Talib said, as the last thing he spoke to them: "He is upon the religion of Abd al-Muttalib," and he refused to say, "There is no god but Allah." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Allah, I will certainly ask forgiveness for you, so long as I am not forbidden from doing so." Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were close relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Blazing Fire﴾ [At-Tawba: 113]. And Allah revealed concerning Abu Talib, saying to His Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills, and He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾ [Al-Qasas: 56]. [See vol. 13, p.]

Accordingly, the verse abrogates (*nasikha*, i.e. *naskh*, abrogation) the Prophet's (ﷺ) seeking forgiveness for his uncle, for he had asked forgiveness for him after his death, as narrated in sources other than the Sahih. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: "This is far-fetched, because this surah is among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed, whereas Abu Talib died at the beginning of Islam while the Prophet (ﷺ) was in Makkah."

**The second issue:** This verse includes the severing of ties of allegiance (*muwala*) with disbelievers, whether living or dead. Allah has not permitted the believers to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, so seeking forgiveness for a polytheist is not permissible.

If it is said: It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) said on the day of Uhud, when they broke his incisor and wounded his face: "O Allah, forgive my people, for they do not know." How does this agree with Allah's prohibition to His Messenger and the believers from seeking forgiveness for the polytheists?

It is answered: That statement of the Prophet (ﷺ) was only by way of relating (*hikaya*) what was said by those prophets who came before him. The evidence for this is what Muslim narrated from Abdullah, who said: "It is as if I am looking at the Prophet (ﷺ) relating (the story of) a prophet among the prophets, whom his people struck, and he was wiping the blood from his face and saying: 'My Lord, forgive my people, for they do not know.'" In al-Bukhari it is also related that the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned a prophet before him whose people had wounded him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) began to report about him that he said: "O Allah, forgive my people, for they do not know." I say: This is clear in relating what was said by one who came before him, not that he said it at the outset from himself, as some have supposed. And Allah knows best.

The prophet whom he related was Nuh (Noah), peace be upon him, as will be explained, God willing, in Surah Hud. [See vol. 9, p. 43.]

It has also been said that the meaning of "seeking forgiveness" (*istighfar*) in the verse is prayer (*salat*, i.e. funeral prayer). Some of them said: "I would not refrain from praying over anyone from the People of the Qiblah, even if she were an Abyssinian woman pregnant from fornication, because I have not heard that Allah prohibited prayer except for the polytheists, by His saying: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾, and so on." Ata ibn Abi Rabah said: "The verse is about the prohibition of praying over the polytheists, and 'seeking forgiveness' here means prayer."

A third answer: seeking forgiveness for the living is permissible, because there is hope for their faith, and they may be won over (*ta'alluf*) through kind words and encouraged toward the religion. Many scholars have said: "There is no harm in a man invoking for his two disbelieving parents and asking forgiveness for them so long as they are alive. But as for one who has died, hope has been cut off from him, so he is not to be invoked for." Ibn Abbas said: "They used to ask forgiveness for their dead, so the verse was revealed, and they refrained from seeking forgiveness, but he did not forbid them from seeking forgiveness for the living until they die."

**The third issue:** The people of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said: The phrase "*ma kana*" (it was not) in the Qur'an comes in two ways. One is as negation, like His saying: ﴿It was not for you to cause its trees to grow﴾ [An-Naml: 60], and ﴿No soul could die except by the permission of Allah﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 145]. The other is in the sense of prohibition (*nahy*), like His saying: ﴿It is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 53], and "It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists." [See vol. 14, p.]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 114:

There are three issues concerning this verse.

The first: al-Nasa'i narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "I heard a man asking forgiveness for his two parents while they were polytheists, so I said: 'Do you ask forgiveness for them while they are polytheists?' He said: 'Did not Ibrahim (peace be upon him) ask forgiveness for his father?' So I went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him [[from manuscript ʿayn]], and then this was revealed: ﴿And the request for forgiveness by Ibrahim for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 114]." The meaning is: O believers, you have no proof in the asking of forgiveness by Ibrahim the Friend of Allah (peace be upon him) for his father, for that was only because of a promise. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Ibrahim's father had promised Ibrahim the Friend that he would believe in Allah and renounce the rival gods. When he died upon disbelief, Ibrahim knew that he was an enemy of Allah, so he abandoned supplicating for him. Thus the pronoun in ﴿promise he had made to him﴾ refers to Ibrahim, while the one who made the promise was his father. It was also said: the one who made the promise was Ibrahim, that is, Ibrahim had promised his father that he would ask forgiveness for him, and when he died as a polytheist, he disassociated himself from him. This promise is indicated by His saying: ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord﴾ [Maryam: 47].

The qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi said: The Prophet (ﷺ) relied, in asking forgiveness for Abu Talib, on the Most High's saying: ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord﴾ [Maryam: 47]. Allah informed him that Ibrahim's asking forgiveness for his father was a promise made before the disbelief of his father became clear to him. When the disbelief became clear to him, he disassociated himself from him. So how can you ask forgiveness for your uncle, O Muhammad, when you have witnessed his death as a disbeliever?

The second: the outward state of a person at the time of death is the basis on which he is judged. If he dies upon faith, he is judged as a believer, and if he dies upon disbelief, he is judged as a disbeliever, while your Lord knows best the inner state of his heart. Nevertheless, al-ʿAbbas said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Messenger of Allah, did you benefit your uncle with anything?" He said: "Yes." This was an intercession (shafaʿah, meaning mediation or advocacy) for the lightening of the punishment, not for leaving the Fire, as we have explained in the book "al-Tadhkirah."

The third: the Most High's saying: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was awwah, forbearing﴾. The scholars differed concerning the meaning of awwah (ʿawwāh, one who laments much and turns to Allah in sorrow) into fifteen opinions.

The first: it is the one who supplicates much. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr.

The second: it is the one merciful to the servants of Allah. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah, and it was narrated from Ibn Mas'ud. The first is more authentic in its chain from Ibn Mas'ud, as said by al-Nahhas.

The third: it is the one who is certain (of his faith). This was said by ʿAta' and ʿIkrimah, and Abu Zabyan narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The fourth: it is the believer in the language of Abyssinia (Ethiopia). This was also said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The fifth: it is the one who glorifies (Allah), who remembers Allah in desolate, lonely deserts. This was said by al-Kalbi and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.

The sixth: it is the one who remembers Allah much. This was said by ʿUqbah ibn ʿAmir. A man who remembers Allah much and glorifies Him was mentioned in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "Indeed he is awwah."

The seventh: it is the one who recites the Qur'an much. This is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. I say: these opinions overlap, and the recitation of the Qur'an encompasses them.

The eighth: it is the one who groans (mutaʾawwih). This was said by Abu Dharr. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) used to say: "Oh, from the Fire, before oh avails nothing." Abu Dharr also said: A man used to circumambulate the House (the Kaʿbah) much and say in his supplication: "Awh, awh." Abu Dharr complained about him to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "Leave him, for he is awwah." Then one night I went out and found the Prophet (ﷺ) burying that man at night, with a lamp with him.

The ninth: it is the jurist (faqih). This was said by Mujahid and al-Nakhaʿi.

The tenth: it is the one who is humble and submissive (mutadarriʿ khashiʿ). ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaddad ibn al-Hadi narrated it from the Prophet (ﷺ). Anas said: A woman spoke in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ) with something he disliked, so ʿUmar forbade her, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Leave her, for she is awwahah." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is awwahah?" He said: "The humble one (al-khashiʿah)."

The eleventh: it is the one who, when he remembers his sins, seeks forgiveness for them. This was said by Abu Ayyub.

The twelfth: it is the one who laments much over sins. This was said by al-Farra'.

The thirteenth: it is the one who guides to good (muʿallim li-l-khayr; the word muʿallim means the one who is the source or indicator of it). This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The fourteenth: it is the compassionate. This was said by ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Yahya. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) was called al-Awwah for his compassion and tenderness.

The fifteenth: it is the one who turns back from everything Allah dislikes. This was said by ʿAta'.

Its root is from taʾawwuh, which is that a sound is heard from the chest, like the exhalation of one in distress. Kaʿb said: Ibrahim (peace be upon him), whenever he mentioned the Fire, would groan (taʾawwaha).

Al-Jawhari said: The expression people use when complaining, "awh min kadha" (with the waw silent), is only an expression of pain. The poet said:

So, awh at the remembrance of her whenever I recall her,
and across a distance of land and sky between us.

Sometimes they change the waw into an alif and say: "ah min kadha." Sometimes they double the waw and vowel it with a kasra and make the ha' sukun, saying: "awwih min kadha." Sometimes they drop the ha' with doubling and say: "awwi min kadha" without the mad (elongation). Some say: "awwah" with the mad, doubling, a fatha on the waw, and the ha' sukun, to prolong the sound in complaint. Sometimes they add a ta' to it and say: "awwatah," which may be elongated or not. The man has said awwah (ta'wih), and has groaned (ta'awwuh) when he says awwah, and the noun from it is ahah, with the mad. Al-Muthaqqab al-ʿAbdi said:

When I rise at night to saddle her,
she groans the groan of a grieving man.

Al-Halim is one who has much forbearance (hilm). He is the one who overlooks sins and endures harm patiently. It was also said: he is the one who never punished anyone except for the sake of Allah, and never avenged anyone except for the sake of Allah. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was like that, and when he stood to pray, the pounding of his heart (wajib qalbih, its throbbing and agitation) could be heard from two miles away.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verses 115–116:

I.e., Allah would not cause misguidance to fall into their hearts after guidance until He makes clear to them what they should fear (yattaqun), so that they do not fear Him; at that point they deserve being led astray (al-idlal).

I say: In this there is the clearest proof that sins, when they are committed and their veil is violated, become a cause of misguidance and ruin, and a ladder to abandoning right guidance and direction. We ask Allah for rectitude, success and right guidance by His grace.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala (may Allah have mercy on him) said concerning His words, "until He makes clear to them": i.e., until He establishes proof against them through His command, as He said: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones, but they defiantly transgress therein﴾ [Al-Isra: 16]. [See vol. 10, p. 232.]

Mujahid said: "until He makes clear to them": i.e., the command of Ibrahim that they should not seek forgiveness for the polytheists specifically, and that He makes clear to them obedience and disobedience in general.

It is related that when the prohibition of wine was revealed and stressed, they asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about those who died while drinking it, and Allah, exalted is He, revealed: "And Allah would not misguide a people after He has guided them until He makes clear to them what they should fear." This verse is a refutation of the Mu'tazilah and others who say that Allah creates their guidance and their misguidance, as has preceded. [See vol. 1, pp. 149, 186.]

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things. Indeed, to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; He gives life and causes death; and you have not, besides Allah, any protector or helper﴾ — its meaning has been explained more than once. [See vol. 1, pp. 249, 261; vol. 2, p. 69.]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verses 115–116:

I.e., Allah would not cause misguidance to fall into their hearts after guidance until He makes clear to them what they should fear (yattaqun), so that they do not fear Him; at that point they deserve being led astray (al-idlal).

[See vol. 10, p. 232.]

Mujahid said: "until He makes clear to them": i.e., the command of Ibrahim that they should not seek forgiveness for the polytheists specifically, and that He makes clear to them obedience and disobedience in general.

It is related that when the prohibition of wine was revealed and stressed, they asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about those who died while drinking it, and Allah, exalted is He, revealed: "And Allah would not misguide a people after He has guided them until He makes clear to them what they should fear." His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things. Indeed, to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; He gives life and causes death; and you have not, besides Allah, any protector or helper﴾ — its meaning has been explained more than once. [See vol. 1, pp. 249, 261; vol. 2, p. 69.]

Al-Tirmidhi narrated: Abd ibn Humayd narrated to us, Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, Ma'mar informed us, from al-Zuhri, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ka'b ibn Malik, from his father, who said: "I did not stay behind from the Prophet (ﷺ) in any battle he fought, until the Battle of Tabuk, except for Badr. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not reproach anyone who stayed behind from Badr. He had only set out aiming for the caravan, and then Quraysh went out to protect their caravan, and they met without an appointment, as Allah the Exalted said." "By my life, the most honourable of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) battles among the people is Badr, and I do not wish that I had witnessed it instead of my pledge at the night of al-Aqabah, when we made a covenant upon Islam. Then I did not stay behind from the Prophet (ﷺ) until the Battle of Tabuk, which was the last battle he fought." The Prophet (ﷺ) announced the departure, and he mentioned the hadith in full. He said: "So I went to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he was sitting in the mosque with the Muslims around him, and he was radiant like the light of the moon. When he was pleased about something, he would become radiant. I came and sat before him, and he said: 'Rejoice, O Ka'b ibn Malik, at the best day that has come upon you since your mother bore you.' I said: 'O Prophet of Allah, is this from Allah or from you?' He said: 'Rather, it is from Allah.' Then he recited this verse: ﴿Allah has certainly turned in forgiveness to the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of difficulty﴾ until he reached ﴿Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾." He said: "And concerning us was also revealed: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and be with the truthful﴾ [al-Tawbah: 119]," and he mentioned the hadith. It will come in full from the Sahih of Muslim, in the story of the three, if Allah the Exalted wills.

The scholars differed about this repentance that Allah turned to the Prophet, the Emigrants and the Helpers, and they held several opinions. Ibn Abbas said: the repentance toward the Prophet was because of his granting permission to the hypocrites to remain behind. The evidence is His saying: ﴿May Allah forgive you; why did you grant them permission?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43], and toward the believers, because of the inclination of some of their hearts toward staying away from him. It was said: Allah's turning toward them was rescuing them from the severe hardship. It was also said: it was their deliverance from the harm of the enemy, and this was expressed as repentance even though it departs from its usual sense, because the meaning of repentance is present in it, which is returning to the former state. The scholars of meanings (Ahl al-Ma'ani) said: the Prophet (ﷺ) is mentioned in the repentance only because, since he was the cause of their repentance, he was mentioned with them, as in His saying: ﴿Then a fifth of it is for Allah and for the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 41]. [See p. 154 and p. 1 of this part.]

His saying the Exalted: ﴿who followed him in the hour of difficulty﴾ means: in the time of difficulty. The intended meaning is all the times of that expedition, and it does not mean one specific hour. It was said: the hour of difficulty is the hardest of the hours they passed through in that expedition. Al-Usrah (difficulty) is the hardship of the matter. Jabir said: the difficulties of mount, provisions and water gathered upon them. Al-Hasan said: the difficulty among the Muslims was that they went out with one camel which they rode in turns among themselves. Their provisions were spoiled dates, moldy barley and foul-smelling rendered fat (al-Ihalah: fat). Each group would bring out what they had, except for a few dates, and when one of them was overcome by hunger, he would take a date, chew it until he tasted it, then give it to his companion, who would drink a sip of water after it, and so on, until it reached the last of them, and nothing of the date remained but the pit. They went with the Prophet (ﷺ) in their sincerity and certainty, may Allah be pleased with them.

Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), when asked about the hour of difficulty, said: "We went out in intense summer heat, and we stopped at a place where we were struck with severe thirst, until we thought our necks would be cut off from thirst. A man would slaughter his camel, squeeze out its dung-contents (al-Farth: the dung while it is still in the stomach) and drink it, and put what remained on his liver." Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of Allah, Allah has accustomed you to good in supplication, so supplicate for us." He said: "Do you want that?" He said: "Yes." So he raised his hands and did not lower them until the sky overshadowed them, then it poured, and they filled what they had with them. Then we went to look, and we did not find that it had passed beyond the camp.

Abu Hurayrah and Abu Sa'id narrated, both saying: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) in the Battle of Tabuk, and the people were struck with hunger. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if you permit us, we will slaughter our water-camels (al-Nawadih: the camel used for drawing water, then the term was applied to any camel even if it does not carry water) and eat and use their fat.'" [The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do it."] [Then Umar came and said (addition from Sahih Muslim): "O Messenger of Allah, if they do it, the mounts will become few. Rather, call them to bring the surplus of their provisions, and supplicate to Allah over it for blessing, perhaps Allah will place blessing in that."] He said: "Yes." Then he called for a leather mat (al-Nut': a mat made of leather), which was spread out. Then he called for the surplus of the provisions. A man would come with a handful of millet, another would come with a handful of dates, another would come with a piece of bread, until there gathered on the mat a small amount of that. Abu Hurayrah said: "I estimated it, and it was about the size of a goat's resting place (rabdat al-anz: its body when it lies down)." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) supplicated for blessing. Then he said: "Take in your containers." So they took in their containers, until, by Him besides Whom there is no god, not a single container remained in the camp without being filled. The people ate until they were satisfied, and some surplus remained. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that I am the Messenger of Allah. No servant meets Allah with these two, without doubting them, and is barred from Paradise." Muslim recorded it in his Sahih with its wording and meaning, and all praise is due to Allah.

Ibn Arafah said: the army of Tabuk was called the army of difficulty because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called the people to the expedition in the peak of the summer heat, so it was hard and difficult for them, and it was the season for purchasing the dates. He said: the proverb about the army of difficulty was coined because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had not gone on an expedition with a number like it before. His companions on the day of Badr were three hundred and some, on the day of Uhud seven hundred, on the day of Khaybar one thousand five hundred, on the day of the Conquest ten thousand, on the day of Hunayn twelve thousand, and his army in the Battle of Tabuk was thirty thousand and more. It was his last expedition. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out in Rajab, stayed at Tabuk during Sha'ban and some days of Ramadan, dispatched his detachments, and made peace with some peoples in exchange for the jizyah (poll tax). In this expedition he appointed Ali over Madinah, and the hypocrites said: "He left him out of hatred for him." So Ali went out after the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and he (peace be upon him) said: "Are you not pleased to be to me in the position of Harun to Musa?" He made clear that his remaining behind by his command equals in reward going out with him, because the matter depends on the command of the Lawgiver. It was called the Battle of Tabuk because the Prophet (ﷺ) saw some of his companions making a well of Tabuk (hisy Tabuk) run, meaning they inserted a cup into it and stirred it so the water would come out, and he said: "You have kept making it flow (tabukuna-ha bawkan)," so that expedition was named the Battle of Tabuk. Al-Hisy (with a kasra) is what the earth absorbs of sand; when it reaches hardness and the ground holds it, one digs away the sand to extract it, and this is al-ihtisa', as al-Jawhari said.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿after the hearts of a faction of them had almost swerved﴾. The reading of "قُلُوبُ" (hearts) is in the nominative case (ruffi'a) by "تَزِيغُ" according to Sibawayh. The subject (al-hadith) is implied in "كادَ" by analogy with "كانَ", because the predicate necessarily follows it just as it follows "كانَ". If you wish, you may make it nominative by "كادَ", and the reading would be: "after the hearts of a faction of them had almost swerved." Al-A'mash, Hamzah and Hafs read "يَزِيغُ" with the letter ya'. Abu Hatim claimed that whoever reads "يَزِيغُ" with ya' is not permitted to make "القُلُوبُ" nominative by "كادَ". Al-Nahhas said: what he disallowed is permissible according to others, on the basis of making the whole group masculine. Al-Farra' related: "رَحُبَ الْبِلَادُ وَأَرْحَبَتْ" (the lands were wide and became wide), and "رَحُبَتْ" is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. The meaning of "تَزِيغُ" was differed over: it was said: it means perish through strain, hardship and severity. Ibn Abbas said: it means deviate (ta'dilu, i.e. incline) from the truth in resisting and supporting.

It was also said: after a faction of them had resolved to stay behind and disobey, then they joined him. It was said: they resolved to turn back, so Allah turned toward them and directed them to it.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿Then He turned in forgiveness toward them﴾. It was said: His turning toward them was that He mended their hearts so that they did not swerve. Likewise is the way of the Truth with His friends: when they come near destruction and prepare themselves for death, He sends down clouds of generosity upon them and revives their hearts. It is recited:

*From You I hope, and I know no Lord*
*from whom is hoped some of what I hope from You*

*When the hardships in the land intensify upon creation, and they cry out and wail,*
*and You test the servants with fear and hunger, and they persist in sins and insist.*

*I had no refuge but You, my Lord,*
*so I became certain that through You I am saved.*

Regarding the three, He said: ﴿Then He turned in forgiveness toward them that they might repent﴾. It was said: the meaning of "Then He turned toward them" is that He enabled them to repent, so that they would repent. It was said: the meaning is He turned toward them, i.e. He gave them room and did not hasten their punishment, so that they would repent. It was said: He turned toward them so that they would remain steadfast in repentance. It was said: the meaning is He turned toward them so that they would return to the state of His being pleased with them. In sum, were it not for what had preceded in His knowledge, that He had decreed repentance for them, they would not have repented. The evidence for this is his (peace be upon him) saying: "Act, for each is made easy for what he was created for."

Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 9, verse 118 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And upon the three who were left behind﴾. It was said: [this refers to] the repentance (tawbah), from Mujahid and Abu Malik. Qatadah said: [this refers to] the expedition of Tabuk.

It is related from Muhammad ibn Zayd [[In (ʿ) [a manuscript]: Ibn Jarir.]] that the meaning of "khullifu" (were left behind) is "turukū" (were left), because the meaning of "khallaftu fulanan" is "I left him and separated from him, remaining behind from what I had risen to in it."

ʿIkrimah ibn Khalid recited "khullifu," meaning they remained in the wake of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

It is related from Ja'far ibn Muhammad that he recited "khalafū."

It was also said that "khullifu" means they were deferred and delayed, set apart from the hypocrites, so no judgment was passed concerning them.

This is because the repentance of the hypocrites was not accepted, while some people offered excuses and their excuses were accepted, and the Prophet (ﷺ) deferred these three until the Qur'an was revealed concerning them.

This is the sound view, based on what Muslim, al-Bukhari and others narrated.

The wording is that of Muslim. Ka'b said:

"We were left behind, O you three, from the matter of those who had sworn oaths to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), whose oaths he accepted; he gave them allegiance and asked forgiveness for them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) deferred our matter until Allah decided concerning it. Therefore Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And upon the three who were left behind﴾. What Allah mentioned was not our staying behind from the expedition; rather, it was His leaving us [in suspense] and His deferring our matter, in contrast to those who swore to him, made excuses to him, and he accepted from them."

This narration is long; this is its end. [[See Sahih Muslim, Kitab al-Tawbah.]]

The three who were left behind were:
Ka'b ibn Malik, Murarah ibn Rabi'ah al-'Amiri, and Hilal ibn Umayyah al-Waqifi, and all of them were from the Ansar.

Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated their account. Muslim said, from Ka'b ibn Malik, who said:

"I never stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in any expedition he undertook, except the expedition of Tabuk. However, I did stay behind in the Battle of Badr, and he did not reproach anyone who stayed behind from it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out seeking the caravan of Quraysh, until Allah brought them together with their enemy without prior arrangement. I witnessed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) the Night of al-'Aqabah, when we pledged ourselves to Islam, and I do not wish that I had instead the witnessing of Badr, though Badr is more mentioned among the people than it. As for my account when I stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the expedition of Tabuk:

I had never been stronger or more affluent than when I stayed behind from him in that expedition. By Allah, I had never before gathered two riding beasts, but I gathered two in that expedition. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out on it in intense heat, facing a long journey and a desert waste, and facing a numerous enemy. So he made clear to the Muslims their situation, so that they might prepare for their expedition, and informed them of the direction he intended. The Muslims with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were numerous, and no written register [[Ka'b refers by this to the register (diwan)]] gathered them."

Ka'b said: "Few men wished to absent themselves, thinking that this would remain hidden from them, so long as no revelation from Allah the Exalted had come down about it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out on that expedition when the fruits and shade were ripe, and I was inclined toward them [[i.e., inclined to them]]. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prepared for it, and the Muslims with him. I began going out in the mornings to equip myself with them, but I would return without having accomplished anything, and I would say to myself: 'I am capable of that whenever I wish!'

This continued to drag on with me until the people were fully engaged in the effort, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out to fight with the Muslims accompanying him, while I had not accomplished anything of my equipment. Then I went out and returned without accomplishing anything. This continued to drag on with me until they hurried away and the expedition had passed me by. I intended to set out and catch up with them, but I wish I had done so! However, that was not decreed for me. So when I went out among the people after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had departed, it grieved me that I saw no one like me except a man accused [[i.e., one accused of hypocrisy in his religion]] of hypocrisy, or a man among those whom Allah excused from the weak. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not mention me until he reached Tabuk, and then he said while sitting among the people at Tabuk:

(What has Ka'b ibn Malik done?)

A man from Banu Salamah said: 'O Messenger of Allah, his two cloaks and his admiring glances at his sides have held him back.' [[This is a metaphor for his being self-admiring, full of pride and arrogance.]]

Mu'adh ibn Jabal said to him: 'Evil is what you have said! By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, we know nothing of him except good.'

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was silent. While he was in that state, he saw a man in white [[al-Mubayyad (with a kasra on the ya'): one clothed in white. And al-sarab: what appears in the midday heat in the open desert as if it were water. And yazul: moves.]] whom the mirage moved, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

(Be Abu Khaythamah!)

It was Abu Khaythamah al-Ansari, and he was the one who had given a sa' of dates in charity, until the hypocrites mocked him.

Ka'b ibn Malik said: 'When it reached me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had turned back from Tabuk on his return, my anxiety overwhelmed me, and I began to think of lies, saying: "With what can I escape his displeasure tomorrow?" and I sought help in this from every man of judgment among my family. When it was said to me: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has drawn near, arriving," falsehood departed from me, until I knew that I would never be saved from him by anything at all. So I resolved to be truthful, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived in the morning. When he returned from a journey, he would begin at the mosque, pray two rak'ahs in it, and then sit down for the people. When he did that, those who had stayed behind came to him, began offering excuses to him and swearing oaths to him. They were some eighty men. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) accepted their outward profession, gave them allegiance, asked forgiveness for them, and left their inner states to Allah. Then I came, and when I greeted him, he smiled the smile of one who is angry. Then he said:

(Come here!)

So I came walking until I sat before him. He said to me:

(What held you back? Had you not purchased your mount?)

He said: I said: "O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, if I were sitting before anyone other than you of the people of this world, I would have thought that I could escape his displeasure with an excuse. I have indeed been given eloquence [[i.e., fluency and strength of speech, by which one may extricate oneself from what is attributed to him in a way that is accepted and not rejected.]], but by Allah, I know that if I tell you a lie today that pleases you with regard to me, Allah will soon make you angry with me. And if I tell you the truth that makes you angry with me, I hope for the outcome from Allah. By Allah, I had no excuse. By Allah, I had never been stronger or more affluent than when I stayed behind from you."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

(As for this, he has spoken the truth. Stand up until Allah decides concerning you.)

So I stood up, and men from Banu Salamah rose up against me [[i.e., they rushed upon me]] and followed me, saying to me: 'By Allah, we did not know you to have committed a sin before this! You were certainly incapable of not offering an excuse to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as those who stayed behind offered him excuses. Your sin would have been sufficient for you had the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked forgiveness for you!'

He said: 'By Allah, they continued to rebuke me until I wanted to return to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and call myself a liar.'

He said: 'Then I said to them: "Has anyone else met with what I have met?"'

They said: 'Yes! Two men met with you, and they said the same as you said, and it was said to them what was said to you.'

He said: I said: 'Who are they?'

They said: 'Murarah ibn Rabi'ah al-'Amiri and Hilal ibn Umayyah al-Waqifi.'

He said: 'They mentioned to me two righteous men who had witnessed Badr, in whom there is an example.' He said: 'So I went on when they mentioned them to me.'

He said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade the Muslims from speaking to us, O you three, from among all those who had stayed behind.'

He said: 'So the people avoided us, and they changed toward us, until the earth seemed unfamiliar to me within myself; it was not the earth that I knew. We remained in that state for fifty nights. As for my two companions, they grew weak and remained in their houses weeping. As for me, I was the youngest of the people and the strongest of them, so I would go out and attend the prayer and walk in the markets, but no one would speak to me. I would come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and greet him while he was in his gathering after the prayer, and I would say to myself: "Did he move his lips to return the greeting or not?" Then I would pray near him and steal glances at him. When I turned toward my prayer, he would look at me, and when I turned toward him, he would turn away from me. When this had become long for me because of the Muslims' estrangement, I walked until I climbed over the wall of the orchard of Abu Qatadah, who was my cousin and the dearest of people to me. I greeted him, but by Allah, he did not return my greeting. I said to him: "O Abu Qatadah, I adjure you by Allah! Do you know that I love Allah and His Messenger?"

He was silent. I returned and adjured him again, and he was silent. I returned and adjured him, and he said: "Allah and His Messenger know best!"

My eyes overflowed, and I turned away until I climbed back over the wall. While I was walking in the market of Madinah, behold, a Nabatean [[Nabatī: one of the Nabateans of the people of Syria, who had come with food to sell in Madinah]] said: "Who will guide me to Ka'b ibn Malik?"

He said: The people began pointing to me until he came to me and handed me a letter from the king of Ghassan. I was a writer, so I read it, and in it was:

"To proceed. It has reached us that your companion has treated you harshly, but Allah has not made you a place of humiliation or neglect. So join us, and we will console you."

He said: I said when I had read it: "This too is among the trials!"

So I took the letter to the oven and set it alight in it [[i.e., I kindled it with the letter.]], until when forty of the fifty days had passed and revelation was delayed, behold, the messenger of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) [[al-Waqidi said: this messenger was Khuzaymah ibn Thabit.]] came to me and said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commands you to keep away from your wife."

He said: I said: "Should I divorce her, or what should I do?"

He said: "No, rather keep away from her and do not approach her."

He said: He sent to my two companions with the same.

He said: I said to my wife: "Go to your family and stay with them until Allah decides this matter."

He said: The wife of Hilal ibn Umayyah came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, Hilal ibn Umayyah is a lost old man with no servant. Would you dislike it if I served him?"

He said: (No, but let him not approach you.)

She said: "By Allah, he has no inclination toward anything! By Allah, he has not ceased weeping since his affair began until this day of his."

He said: Some of my family said to me: "If only you had asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about your wife, for he permitted the wife of Hilal ibn Umayyah to serve him."

He said: I said: "I will not ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about her, and what do I know of what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) might say if I asked him about her, while I am a young man!"

He said: So I remained in that state for ten nights, and the fifty nights were completed for us from the time we were forbidden to speak.

He said: Then on the morning of the fiftieth night, I prayed the dawn prayer on the roof of one of our houses. While I was sitting in the state that Allah mentioned concerning us, my soul had become constricted within me and the earth had become confining for me despite its vastness, I heard the voice of a crier who had climbed up onto Sal' [[i.e., had ascended the mountain Sal'. al-Waqidi said: he was Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him.]], calling with his loudest voice: "O Ka'b ibn Malik, rejoice!"

He said: I fell down in prostration and knew that relief had come.

He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) announced to the people the acceptance of Allah's repentance upon us when he had prayed the dawn prayer, so the people went out to give us good news. Heralds went toward my two companions, a man rode a horse toward me, and a runner from Aslam hurried toward me and climbed the mountain. The voice was faster than the horse. When the one whose voice I had heard, bringing me good news, came to me, I took off my two garments and clothed him with them in return for his good news. By Allah, I did not own anything other than them that day. I borrowed two garments and put them on, and I set out to go to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The people met me in groups, congratulating me on the repentance and saying:"

Let your repentance be accepted by Allah and His pardon upon you, until I entered the mosque and there was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sitting in the mosque with people around him. Talhah ibn Ubayd Allah got up, hastening, until he shook my hand and congratulated me. By Allah, no man of the Muhajirun stood up except him.

He said:
So Ka'b would never forget it for Talhah.

Ka'b said:
When I greeted the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said, while his face was shining with joy and he was saying:
("Rejoice in the best day that has passed over you since your mother bore you.")

He said:
I said, "Is it from Allah, O Messenger of Allah, or from you?"
He said:
("No, rather it is from Allah.")
And when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was pleased, his face would light up until it seemed like a piece of the moon. 

He said:
And we used to recognize that.

He said:
When I sat before him, I said:
"O Messenger of Allah, part of the repentance of Allah toward me is that I withdraw from my wealth as charity to Allah and to His Messenger." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:
("Keep some of your wealth for yourself, for it is better for you.")

He said: I said:
"Then I will keep my share that is at Khaybar."

He said: And I said:
"O Messenger of Allah, indeed Allah saved me only through truthfulness, and part of my repentance is that I will not speak except the truth as long as I live."

He said:
By Allah, I know of no Muslim whom Allah has tested in truthfulness of speech since I mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) until this day, with a better test than the one Allah has given me. By Allah, I have not intentionally told a lie since I said that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) until this day, and I hope that Allah will protect me in what remains. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed:

"Allah has certainly turned in forgiveness to the Prophet and the Muhajirun and the Ansar who followed him in the hour of difficulty"... until His saying... "Indeed, He is Kind and Merciful to them. And [He turned in forgiveness] to the three who were left behind, until when the earth was constricted for them despite its vastness and their souls were confined to them"... until His saying... "O you who believe, fear Allah and be with the truthful."

Ka'b said:
By Allah, Allah has never bestowed upon me any blessing after guiding me to Islam greater in my soul than my truthfulness to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), lest I should have lied to him and then been destroyed as those who lied were destroyed. Indeed Allah spoke of those who lied, when He revealed the revelation, with the worst of words He used toward anyone, and Allah the Exalted said:
﴿They will swear by Allah to you when you return to them, that you may leave them alone. So leave them alone; indeed, they are impure, and their refuge is Hell as recompense for what they used to earn. They swear to you that you may be pleased with them. But if you are pleased with them, indeed Allah is not pleased with a defiantly disobedient people.﴾ [At-Tawbah: 95–96].

Ka'b said:
We, the three of us, were left behind from the matter of those who swore to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he accepted from them, and he gave them allegiance and asked forgiveness for them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) deferred our matter until Allah decided concerning it. Therefore Allah, mighty and majestic, said: "and the three," and what Allah mentioned of our being left behind is not our staying behind from the expedition, but rather His leaving us aside and deferring our matter, in contrast to those who swore to him and made excuses to him, and he accepted from them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Constricted for them the earth despite its vastness﴾, meaning, despite what had become spacious. It is said: a dwelling that is *rahb*, *rahib*, and *ruhab* (spacious). And "*ma*" here is a verbal (masdariyyah) particle, meaning the earth was constricted for them in its vastness, because they were shunned, not dealt with and not spoken to. And in this is evidence for the shunning of people of sin until they repent.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And their souls were confined to them﴾, meaning their hearts were constricted with worry and loneliness, and with what they encountered of coldness from the Companions.

("And they thought that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him"), meaning they were certain that there was no refuge they could turn to for pardon of them and acceptance of their repentance except Him.

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: Sincere repentance is that the earth becomes constricted for the penitent despite its vastness, and his own soul becomes constricted for him, as with the repentance of Ka'b and his two companions.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then He turned to them that they might repent. Indeed, Allah is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾. He began with repentance from Him. Abu Zayd said: I erred in four things: in the beginning with Allah the Exalted, I thought that I love Him, but He loves me, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He loves them and they love Him﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 54]. And I thought that I am pleased with Him, but He is pleased with me, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 119]. And I thought that I remember Him, but He remembers me, as Allah the Exalted said: "And the remembrance of Allah is greater." And I thought that I repent, but He had already turned to me in repentance, as Allah the Exalted said: "Then He turned to them that they might repent." It was also said: the meaning is, "Then He turned to them that they might remain steadfast in repentance," as the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, believe﴾ [An-Nisa: 136]. And it was said: meaning He granted them latitude and did not hasten their punishment as He did with others. The Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them﴾ [An-Nisa: 160].

**Question One:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And be with the truthful.﴾ This command to be with the people of truthfulness is fitting after the story of the three (who stayed behind), when truthfulness benefited them and carried them away from the abodes of the hypocrites. Mutarrif said: I heard Malik ibn Anas say: "Rarely is there a man who is truthful and does not lie but he is granted [long life with] his intellect, and he is not afflicted with what afflicts others of decrepitude and senility."

Scholars differed about who is meant here by "the believers" and "the truthful," giving several opinions. It was said: it is an address to those among the People of the Book who believed. It was said: it is an address to all believers, meaning, "Beware of opposing the command of Allah." "And be with the truthful," meaning: with those who went out with the Prophet ﷺ, not with the hypocrites. That is, follow the way and path of the truthful. It was said: they are the prophets, meaning, "Be with them through righteous deeds in Paradise." It was said: they are the ones intended by His saying: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces [toward east or west]﴾ [[See vol. 2, p. 237.]] up to His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who have been true﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:177]. It was said: they are "those who fulfilled what they covenanted," because of His saying: ﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they covenanted Allah﴾ [[See vol. 14.]] [Al-Ahzab 33:23]. It was said: they are the emigrants, because of the statement of Abu Bakr on the day of Saqifah: "Allah named us 'the truthful' when He said: ﴿For the poor emigrants﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 19.]] [Al-Hashr 59:8], up to the end of the verse. Then He named you 'the successful' when He said: ﴿And those who had settled the abode and the faith﴾ [Al-Hashr 59:9], up to the end of the verse." It was said: they are those whose outward and inward states are equal. Ibn al-Arabi said: this opinion is the reality and the ultimate goal to which one arrives, for by this quality hypocrisy in belief and opposition in action are lifted, and its possessor is called a *siddiq* (one exceedingly truthful), like Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and those below them, according to their ranks and times. As for the one who said they are the ones intended by the verse of al-Baqarah, that is the greatest truthfulness, and the lesser follows it, and that is the meaning of the verse of al-Ahzab. As for the interpretation of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, it is the one that encompasses all the statements, for all the qualities are present in them.

**Question Two:** Whoever understands from Allah and comprehends from Him has a duty to hold fast to truthfulness in speech, sincerity in deeds, and purity in states. Whoever is so, joins the righteous and reaches the pleasure of the All-Forgiving. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Hold to truthfulness, for truthfulness leads to righteousness, and righteousness leads to Paradise. A man continues to speak the truth and seek it out until he is recorded with Allah as a *siddiq*." Lying is the opposite of this. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Beware of lying, for lying leads to wickedness, and wickedness leads to the Fire. A man continues to lie and seek out lying until he is recorded with Allah as a *kadhdhab* (a great liar)." Muslim transmitted it. So lying is a disgrace, and its practitioners are stripped of [the right to] testimony. The Prophet ﷺ rejected the testimony of a man because of a single lie he told. Ma'mar said: "I do not know whether he lied about Allah, or lied about His Messenger, or lied about someone among the people."

Shurayk ibn Abdullah was asked: "O Abu Abdullah, a man whom we heard lying deliberately, should we pray behind him?" He said: "No." It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Lying is not proper, whether in earnest or in jest, nor that one of you promises something and then does not fulfill it. Recite, if you wish: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and be with the truthful﴾. Do you see any license in lying?"

Malik said: "The report of a liar is not accepted in matters concerning people, even if he is truthful in relating the words of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." Others said: "His narration is accepted." The sound position is that the testimony and report of a liar are not accepted, for what we have mentioned. Acceptance is a great rank and a noble office that is held only by one whose qualities are complete, and there is no quality worse than lying, for it removes offices and nullifies testimonies.

**Question 1:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿It was not for the people of Madinah and the Bedouins around them to remain behind from the Messenger of Allah﴾. Its outward form is a report, but its meaning is a command, like His saying: ﴿It is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 35], which has been discussed before [see vol. 14, p.]. "An yatakhallafu" (that they should remain behind) is in the position of the subject of *kana* (was). This is a rebuke to the believers of Yathrib and the Arab tribes around it, such as Muzaynah, Juhaynah, Ash'ja', Ghifar and Aslam, for remaining behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the expedition of Tabuk. The meaning is: it was not right for these mentioned people to remain behind, since the call to march forth (nafir) was directed at them. Others not called to march forth were not included, according to some scholars. It is possible that the call to march forth was addressed to every Muslim, and these were singled out for rebuke because of their proximity and neighbourhood, and because they had a stronger claim to this than others.

**Question 2:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and that they should not prefer themselves over his self﴾, meaning they should not be content for themselves with ease and comfort while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is in hardship. It is said: "raghibtu 'an kadhā" (I held myself aloof from such a thing), meaning I raised myself above it.

**Question 3:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿That is because they will not be afflicted by thirst﴾, i.e. thirst (*zama'*). 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read *zama'* with a long vowel (*maddah*). Both are dialectal forms, like *khata'* and *khata'* (error).

"Wa la nasab" (nor fatigue) is conjoined (*'atf*) to the preceding item, i.e. weariness. "Wa la" (nor) here is an extra particle (*za'idah*) used for emphasis. Likewise "wa la makhmasah" (nor hunger), i.e. famine. Its root meaning is the shrinking of the belly; from it come "rajul khamis" (a lean man) and "imra'ah khamsanah" (a lean woman). This has been mentioned before [see vol. 6, p. 64].

﴿in the way of Allah﴾ means in His obedience.

﴿nor do they tread a path﴾ means a land.

﴿that enrages the disbelievers﴾ means by treading upon it. This phrase is in the accusative position because it is a qualifier (*na't*) of "mawti'" (path), meaning "enraging" (*ghaziyan*).

﴿nor do they gain anything from an enemy, a gain﴾ means killing and defeat. Its origin is from "niltu al-shay' analu", meaning I attained the thing. Al-Kisa'i said: it comes from their saying "amr manil minhu" (a matter from which one can gain), and it is not from *tanawul* (taking hold of); *tanawul* comes from "nultuhu al-'atiyyah" (I gave him the gift).[[In b, 'a, k and h: "bi-l-'atiyyah" (with the gift). Both are dialectal forms.]] Another said: "nultu anulu" (I give) is from the wāw root in the sense of gift, while *nayl* (attainment) is from the yā' root; you say "niltuhu fa-ana na'il", meaning I reached it.

﴿nor do they cross a valley﴾. The Arabs say "wad" and "awdiyah" (valleys), which is not by regular analogy. Al-Nahhas said: as far as I know, there is no other *fa'l* / *af'ilah* pattern like this, and the analogical plural would be *wiyidān*, but they found the combination of two wāws heavy, though they sometimes find even one heavy, to the extent that they say *uqqitat* for *wuqqitat*. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh transmitted the diminutive of the name of a man, "Wasil" or "Yasil", and they say nothing else. Al-Farra' transmitted the plural of *wad* as *awda'* or *da'*. I say: its plural *awda'* has indeed been used. Jarir said:

*I recognized at Burqat al-Awda' traces,*
*effaced, your absence long from its remnants.*[[In his Diwan and in Yaqut's Mu'jam al-Buldan: "bi-Burqat al-Wada'" (at Burqat al-Wada'). Al-Wada' is a valley whose upper part belongs to Banu al-'Adawiyyah and al-Taym, and whose lower part belongs to Banu Kulayb and Dabbah.]]

﴿except that a righteous deed is recorded for them thereby﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: for every fright they suffer in the way of Allah, seventy thousand good deeds are recorded. In the Sahih it is reported: "Horses are of three kinds..." — and in it: "As for the one that is a reward for him: a man who tethered it in the way of Allah for the people of Islam in a pasture (*marj*)[[*Marj*: grazing ground for animals.]] or a meadow, so whatever it eats from that pasture or meadow, a number of good deeds is recorded for him equal to what it eats, and a number of good deeds is recorded for him equal to its dung and urine..." — the hadith. This is in its proper place, so how much more when they enter the land of the enemy[[*Adraba*: they entered the land of the enemy.]].

**Question 4:** Some scholars used this verse to argue that booty (*ghanimah*) is earned by entering the enemy's territory and remaining there; if he dies after that, he receives his share. This is the view of Ashhab, 'Abd al-Malik, and one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. Malik and Ibn al-Qasim said: he receives nothing, because Allah the Mighty and Majestic in this verse mentioned only the reward and did not mention a share.

I say: the first view is more correct, because Allah the Exalted made treading the abodes of the disbelievers equivalent to attaining gain from their wealth and expelling them from their homes. This is what enrages them and brings humiliation upon them. It is therefore equivalent to attaining booty, killing and taking captives. Since this is so, booty is earned by entering enemy territory, not by mere possession. For this reason 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "No people have been trodden in the heart of their homeland without being humiliated." And Allah knows best.

**Question 5:** This verse is abrogated by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And it is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122]. Its ruling applied when the Muslims were few; when they became numerous, it was abrogated, and Allah permitted remaining behind for whoever wished. This was said by Ibn Zayd. Mujahid said: the Prophet (ﷺ) sent some people to the desert dwellers to teach the people, and when this verse was revealed they were afraid and returned, so Allah revealed: ﴿And it is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾. Qatadah said: this was specific to the Prophet (ﷺ) when he went on campaign himself; so no one was permitted to remain behind him except with an excuse. As for other leaders and governors, whoever wished among the Muslims could remain behind them when the people had no need of him and no necessity. A third view is that it is *muhkam* (not abrogated). Al-Walid ibn Muslim said: I heard al-Awza'i, Ibn al-Mubarak, al-Fazari, al-Sab'i and Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz say about this verse that it applies to the first and last of this community.

I say: Qatadah's view is good, based on the expedition of Tabuk. And Allah knows best.

**Question 6:** Abu Dawud related from Anas ibn Malik that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You have left behind in Madinah people who, whenever you traveled a journey, spent any expense, or crossed a valley, were with you in it." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, how could they be with us when they are in Madinah?" He said: "The excuse has held them back." Muslim transmitted it from the hadith of Jabir, who said: We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on a campaign, and he said: "Indeed in Madinah there are men who, whenever you traveled a journey or crossed a valley, were with you; sickness has held them back." So he (ﷺ) gave the excused person the same reward as he gave to the strong one who acted.

Some people said: the reward for the excused person is not multiplied, while it is multiplied for the one who acts directly. Ibn al-'Arabi said: this is an imposition upon Allah the Exalted and a narrowing of the vastness of His mercy. Some people objected, saying: they are certainly given multiplied reward, and we cannot be certain of multiplication in any case, since it depends on the measure of intentions, and this is something unseen. What is certain is that there is multiplication, and your Lord knows best who deserves it.

I say: the apparent meaning of the hadiths and verses is equality in reward. Among them is his (ﷺ) saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever guides to good has a reward like that of the one who does it." And his saying: "Whoever performs ablution and goes out to prayer, and finds the people have already prayed, Allah gives him a reward like that of one who prayed it and attended it." This is also the apparent meaning of Allah's saying: ﴿And whoever leaves his home emigrating to Allah and His Messenger, then death overtakes him, his reward has indeed fallen upon Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 100]. And it is evidence that sincere intention is the essence of deeds. If it is sound in performing an act of obedience, but its doer is unable to perform it due to a barrier that prevented him, then there is nothing strange in the reward of that incapable one being equal to the reward of the able one who acts, and it may even exceed it, based on his (ﷺ) saying, peace be upon him: "The intention of the believer is better than his deed." And Allah knows best.
