**Issue 1:** The words ﴿وَمَا كَانَ الْمُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ indicate that jihad is not an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) but a collective obligation (fard kifaya), as has already been mentioned. If everyone went forth, those left behind among their dependents would be lost. So a group should go forth for jihad, and another group should remain to gain understanding of the religion and to guard the sacred territory. When those who went forth return, those who stayed behind inform them of what they have learned of the rulings of the Shari'ah and of what new revelation has come down to the Prophet (ﷺ). This verse abrogates (naskh) the verse ﴿إِلَّا تَنْفِرُوا﴾ [al-Tawbah: 39] and the verse preceding it, according to the view of Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

**Issue 2:** This verse is a basis for the obligation of seeking knowledge. The meaning is: "The believers should not all go forth together while the Prophet (ﷺ) remains and does not go forth, so that he is left alone." ﴿فَلَوْلَا نَفَرَ﴾ means: after they knew that going forth could not include all of them, ﴿مِنْ كُلِّ فِرْقَةٍ مِنْهُمْ طَائِفَةٌ﴾ (a group from every section of them), and the rest remain with the Prophet (ﷺ) so that they may bear the religion on his behalf and gain understanding. When those who went forth return to them, they inform them of what they heard and learned. In this there is an obligation to gain understanding of the Book and the Sunnah, and that this obligation is a collective one, not an individual one. The words of Allah ﴿فَسْئَلُوا أَهْلَ الذِّكْرِ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ [al-Nahl: 43] also indicate this. Thus it includes whoever does not know the Book and the Sunnah.

**Issue 3:** Concerning ﴿فَلَوْلَا نَفَرَ﴾, al-Akhfash said: that is, "fa-hallā nafara" (why did they not go forth?). ﴿مِنْ كُلِّ فِرْقَةٍ مِنْهُمْ طَائِفَةٌ﴾: the word ṭā'ifah (group) linguistically means a company, and it may apply to fewer than that, down to two men. It may also be used for one person, in the sense of "the very self of a group." It has already been mentioned that the intended meaning of Allah's words ﴿إِنْ نَعْفُ عَنْ طَائِفَةٍ مِنْكُمْ نُعَذِّبْ طَائِفَةً﴾ [al-Tawbah: 66] is one man. There is no doubt that what is intended here is a company, for two reasons: one rational and the other linguistic. The rational reason is that knowledge is generally not acquired by one person alone. The linguistic reason is His words ﴿لِيَتَفَقَّهُوا فِي الدِّينِ وَلِيُنْذِرُوا قَوْمَهُمْ﴾, where He uses the plural pronoun.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: Al-Qadi Abu Bakr and Shaykh Abu al-Hasan before him held that ṭā'ifah here means one person, and they support this with evidence for the obligation of acting upon a single-narrator report (khabar al-wahid), which is a sound view, not because ṭā'ifah applies to one person, but because the report of one person or of a few persons is a single-narrator report, and its opposite, mass-transmitted reports (tawatur), is not limited in number.

I say: The clearest proof that a single person may be called ṭā'ifah is His words ﴿وَإِنْ طَائِفَتَانِ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ اقْتَتَلُوا﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9], meaning two persons. The evidence for this is His words ﴿فَأَصْلِحُوا بَيْنَ أَخَوَيْكُمْ﴾ [al-Hujurat: 10], where He uses the dual form. And the pronoun in "اقْتَتَلُوا" (they fought), though it is a plural pronoun, the minimum plural is two according to one of the two opinions of the scholars.

**Issue 4:** Concerning His words ﴿لِيَتَفَقَّهُوا﴾, the pronoun in "لِيَتَفَقَّهُوا" and "وَلِيُنْذِرُوا" refers to those who remained with the Prophet (ﷺ). This was said by Qatadah and Mujahid. Al-Hasan said that they refer to the group that went forth, and al-Tabari chose this view. The meaning of ﴿لِيَتَفَقَّهُوا فِي الدِّينِ﴾ is that they may gain insight and certainty through what Allah shows them of victory over the polytheists and of the support of the religion.

﴿وَلِيُنْذِرُوا قَوْمَهُمْ﴾ means: from the disbelievers.

﴿إِذَا رَجَعُوا إِلَيْهِمْ﴾ means: from jihad. They inform them that Allah has given victory to His Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers, and that they have no power (yad, i.e., strength) to fight them or the Prophet (ﷺ), so that what befell their disbelieving companions will befall them. [Editor's note: "maa li-Fulan yadan" means "I have no strength against so-and-so."]

I say: The view of Mujahid and Qatadah is clearer, meaning that the group remaining behind should gain understanding with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while the others are away on expeditions (sarayah). This implies urging the seeking of knowledge and encouraging it, not obligation and compulsion, since that is not the force of the wording. The obligation of seeking knowledge arises only from its own proofs, said Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi.

**Issue 5:** Seeking knowledge is divided into two kinds: an obligation upon individuals (fard 'ayn), like prayer, zakat and fasting.

I say: A hadith to this effect has been related: "Seeking knowledge is an obligation." 'Abd al-Quddus ibn Habib, Abu Sa'id al-Wuhazi, related from Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman, from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, who said: "I heard Anas ibn Malik say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim.'" Ibrahim said: "I did not hear from Anas except this hadith."

And it is a collective obligation (fard kifaya), like obtaining rights, establishing the prescribed penalties (hudud), judging between disputants, and similar matters, since it is not suitable for all people to learn it, for then their affairs and their expeditions (the text variant reads "sawāhum," "others") would be neglected, and their livelihoods would decrease or be ruined. So between the two situations, it is necessary that some of them undertake it without specification, according to what Allah made easy for His servants and apportioned among them by His mercy and wisdom, through His preceding power and word.

**Issue 6:** Seeking knowledge is a great virtue and a noble rank that no other deed can equal. Al-Tirmidhi related from the hadith of Abu al-Darda', who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Whoever travels a path seeking knowledge, Allah will make for him a path to Paradise. The angels lower their wings out of pleasure for the seeker of knowledge. The one who has knowledge is asked forgiveness by those in the heavens and those on the earth, and even the fish in the depths of the water. The virtue of the scholar over the worshipper is like the virtue of the full moon over the rest of the stars. The scholars are the heirs of the Prophets. The Prophets did not bequeath dinars or dirhams; they bequeathed only knowledge, so whoever takes it has taken a great share.'"

Al-Darimi, Abu Muhammad, related in his Musnad: "Abu al-Mughirah related to us, al-Awza'i related to us, from al-Hasan, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about two men among the Children of Israel, one of whom was a scholar who prayed the obligatory prayers and then sat to teach people good, and the other who fasted by day and stood in prayer by night. Which of them is more excellent? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The virtue of this scholar who prays the obligatory prayers and then sits to teach people good over the worshipper who fasts by day and stands in prayer by night is like my virtue over the least of you.'"

Abu 'Umar related it in his book Bayan al-'Ilm from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The virtue of the scholar over the worshipper is like my virtue over my community."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "The best jihad is one who builds a mosque in which he teaches the Qur'an, fiqh and the Sunnah." This was related by Sharik from Layth ibn Abi Sulaym, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, from 'Ali al-Azdi, who said: "I wished to go for jihad, and Ibn 'Abbas said to me: 'Shall I not direct you to what is better for you than jihad? You come to a mosque and recite the Qur'an in it, and teach fiqh in it [in one text: the Sunnah].'"

Al-Rabi' said: "I heard al-Shafi'i say: Seeking knowledge is more obligatory than voluntary prayer."

The Prophet's words (peace be upon him), "the angels lower their wings..." etc., may have two interpretations. The first is that they incline toward him and show mercy to him, just as Allah said regarding the good treatment children should show their parents: ﴿وَاخْفِضْ لَهُمَا جَنَاحَ الذُّلِّ مِنَ الرَّحْمَةِ﴾ [al-Isra': 24], that is, "be humble toward them." The other interpretation is that the meaning of "lowering the wings" is "spreading them out," because in some narrations it reads: "the angels spread out their wings." That is, when the angels see the seeker of knowledge seeking it sincerely for the sake of Allah's pleasure, and all his other conditions are in harmony with the seeking of knowledge, they spread their wings for him on his journey and carry him upon them. From this he is protected: if he is walking he does not tire, and the long road is made easy for him, and he does not suffer the kinds of harm that a traveller suffers, such as illness, loss of wealth, and losing his way. Some of this meaning has already passed in Al 'Imran, at Allah's words ﴿شَهِدَ اللَّهُ﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18]. [Editor's note: see vol. 4, p. 40.]

'Imran ibn Husayn related: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A group of my community will continue to prevail upon the truth until the Hour comes." Yazid ibn Harun said: "If they are not the people of hadith, I do not know who they are."

I say: This is the view of 'Abd al-Razzaq in the interpretation of the verse, that they are the people of hadith, as mentioned by al-Tha'labi. I heard our shaykh, the master, the reciter, grammarian and narrator Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Qaysi al-Qurtubi, known as Ibn Abi Hajjah, may God have mercy on him, say concerning the interpretation of the Prophet's words (peace be upon him): "The people of the gharb will continue to prevail upon the truth until the Hour comes," that they are the scholars. He said: This is because gharb is a shared word, applied to a large bucket, to the west (maghrib of the sun), and to a flow of tears. So the meaning of "the people of the gharb" is the people of the flow of tears out of fear of Allah, with knowledge of Him and His rulings, continuing to prevail... [the hadith]. Allah said: ﴿إِنَّمَا يَخْشَى اللَّهَ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ الْعُلَمَاءُ﴾ [Fatir: 28].

I say: This interpretation is supported by the Prophet's words (peace be upon him) in Sahih Muslim: "Whomever Allah intends good for, He gives him understanding of the religion, and a company of Muslims will continue to fight for the truth, prevailing over those who oppose them until the Day of Resurrection." The apparent context indicates that its beginning is connected to its end. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 123:

There is one issue here: that Allah, glorified is He, taught them the manner of jihad, and that one should begin with the nearest of the enemy, then the nearest after them. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began with the Arabs, and when he had finished with them he turned to the Romans, who were in al-Sham (Greater Syria). Al-Hasan said: it was revealed before the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to fight the polytheists, so it belongs to the gradual stages that preceded Islam. Ibn Zayd said: what is meant by this verse at the time of its revelation is the Arabs; when he had finished with them, it was revealed concerning the Romans and others: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29].[[See p. 109 of this part.]] It has been narrated from Ibn 'Umar that what is meant by this is the Daylam. It was also narrated from him that he was asked, "With whom should one begin, the Romans or the Daylam?" He said, "With the Romans." Al-Hasan said: it is the fighting of the Daylam, the Turks and the Romans. Qatadah said: the verse is general concerning fighting the nearest and then the nearest, and the lower and then the lower.

I say: Qatadah's view is the apparent meaning of the verse. Ibn al-'Arabi preferred that the Romans be begun with before the Daylam, in accordance with what Ibn 'Umar said, for three reasons. The first: they are People of the Book, so the proof against them is greater and more binding. The second: they are nearer to us, I mean the people of Madinah. The third: the lands of the prophets are more in their lands, so reclaiming them from them is more obligatory. And Allah knows best.

(Wa-liyajidu fihim ghilzah) meaning harshness, strength and zeal. Al-Fadl narrated from al-A'mash and 'Asim "ghalzah" with a fatha on the ghayn and a sukun on the lam. Al-Farra' said: the dialect of the people of the Hijaz and Banu Asad is with a kasra on the ghayn (ghilzah), and the dialect of Banu Tamim is "ghulzah" with a damma on the ghayn.

"Mā" is an extra particle (ṣilah), and what is meant is the hypocrites. "Which of you has this increased in faith?" The discussion of the increase and decrease of faith has already been presented in the commentary on Surah Āl ʿImrān [see vol. 4, p. 280]. The meaning of the surah has also already been discussed in the introduction to the book [see vol. 1, p. 65], so there is no point in repeating it.

Al-Ḥasan wrote to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz [the text in al-Bukhārī reads: "ʿUmar ibn al-ʿAzīz wrote to ʿAdī ibn ʿAdī..." etc.; refer to it in the Book of Faith]: "Indeed, faith has sunnahs (practices) and obligations (farāʾid). Whoever completes them has completed faith, and whoever does not complete them has not completed faith."

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: "If I live, I will explain them to you; and if I die, I am not eager to remain in your company."

This was related by al-Bukhārī.

Ibn al-Mubārak said: "I found no alternative but to say that faith increases, or else I would have rejected the Qur'an."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 125:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But as for those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ means doubt, uncertainty, and hypocrisy. It has been mentioned previously [[See vol. 1, p. 197.]].

(﴿It adds to their uncertainty, added to their uncertainty﴾) meaning: doubt added to their doubt, and disbelief added to their disbelief. Muqatil said: sin added to their sin, and the meaning is close.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 9, verse 126:

His saying, exalted is He:

(Do they not see that they are tested once or twice every year?) The recitation of the majority (al-'ammah) is with the yā' (they), as a report about the hypocrites. Hamzah and Ya'qub recited it with the tā' (you), as a report about them and as an address to the believers. al-A'mash recited, "Aw lam yarawu" (Or did they not see). Talhah ibn Musarrif recited, "Awa-la tara" (Do you not see), and this is the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, as an address to the Messenger (ﷺ). As for "yuftanun" (are tested), al-Tabari said: they are examined (yukhtabarun). Mujahid said: with famine and hardship. 'Atiyyah said: with illnesses and pains, and these are the precursors of death. Qatadah, al-Hasan and Mujahid said: with raiding and fighting alongside the Prophet (ﷺ), and they see what Allah promised of victory. "Then they do not repent" from that, "nor do they take heed" (wa-la hum yadhdhakkarun).

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And when a surah is sent down, some of them look at others﴾. "Ma" is a *silah* (a filler particle that adds no meaning of its own). The intended people are the hypocrites. That is, when they were in the presence of the Messenger while he was reciting a Qur'an in which their disgrace, or the disgrace of one of them, was revealed, they began to look at one another with a frightened glance, as if asking one another: "Can anyone see you if you speak of this, so that he carries it to Muhammad?" This was out of ignorance of his prophethood, peace be upon him, and of the fact that Allah informs him of whatever part of the unseen He wills. It has also been said that *nazara* in this verse means *anba'a* (informed). Al-Tabari reported from some scholars that *nazara* in this verse is in the place of *qala* (said).

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then they turned away﴾, meaning they turned away from the path of guidance. When their secrets were exposed to them and they were informed of the hidden matters of their affairs, they inevitably felt amazement, hesitation and reflection. Had they been guided, that moment would have been a likely occasion for their faith. Instead, they persisted in disbelief and became entangled [[*irtabaka fi al-amr* means he fell into a matter and became stuck in it without escaping.]] in it, as if they had turned away from that situation, which was the likely occasion for sound reflection and guidance. They did not listen to the recitation of the Prophet ﷺ as one who contemplates it and reflects upon its signs. ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah are the deaf and dumb who do not reason﴾ [Al-Anfal: 22]. ﴿Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ [Muhammad: 24]. [[See vol. 7, p. 388.]] [[See vol. 16, p. 245.]]

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Allah has turned their hearts away﴾. There are three issues concerning this.

The first: The words ﴿Allah has turned their hearts away﴾ are a supplication against them, meaning: say this to them. It is also permissible that it be a report about Him turning their hearts away from good as a recompense for their deeds. It is a phrase by which one invokes (a curse), like His words: ﴿May Allah destroy them﴾ [At-Tawbah: 30]. The *ba'* in His words "bi-annahum" is a *silah* attached to *sarafa* (turned away).

The second: Ibn Abbas said: It is disliked to say "we turned away from the prayer" (*insarafna min al-salah*), because a people turned away and so Allah turned their hearts away; rather, say "we have completed the prayer" (*qadayna al-salah*). Al-Tabari traced this to him by a chain. Ibn al-Arabi said: There is a point to consider in this, and I do not think it is correct. The proper structure of the statement is: no one should say "we turned away from the prayer," because a people about whom it was said, "Then they turned away; Allah turned their hearts away," [were condemned]. Al-Qaysi, the preacher Muhammad ibn Abd al-Malik, informed us, from Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari, who said, hearing it from him: We were at a funeral, and al-Mundhir said during it: "Turn away, may Allah have mercy on you!" He said: No one should say "turn away," for Allah, the Exalted, said about a people He censured: "Then they turned away; Allah turned their hearts away." Rather, say: "Return, may Allah have mercy on you," for Allah, the Exalted, said about a people He praised: ﴿So they returned with a blessing from Allah and grace, and no harm touched them﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 174]. [[See vol. 4, p. 282.]]

The third: In this verse Allah, glory be to Him, informs that He is the one who turns hearts, directs them, causes them to turn, and alters them. This refutes the Qadariyya (the school that denies divine predestination), who hold that the hearts of creatures are in their own hands and their limbs under their own command, so that they act by their own will and judge by their own decision and choice. For this reason Malik said, in what Ashhab related from him: "How clear this is in refuting the Qadariyya!" ﴿Their building which they have built will not cease to be a source of doubt in their hearts, unless their hearts are cut to pieces﴾ [At-Tawbah: 110]. And the words of the Mighty and Majestic to Noah: ﴿That none of your people will believe except those who have already believed﴾ [Hud: 36]. This never happens, does not return, and does not cease.

These two verses are, according to Ubayy, the most recent of the Qur'an in terms of descent from the heavens. According to Sa'id ibn Jubayr, the last thing revealed of the Qur'an was ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 281], as has preceded [[See vol. 3, p. 350.]]. So it is possible that the statement of Ubayy, "the most recent of the Qur'an in descent from the heavens," refers to what came after his saying "And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah." And Allah knows best. The address is to the Arabs according to the majority opinion, and this is in the sense of enumerating the blessing upon them in this matter, since it came in their tongue and in what they understand, and they were honoured by it for all time. Al-Zajjaj said: it is an address to the entire world, and the meaning is: "There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among mankind." The first view is more correct. Ibn 'Abbas said: there is no tribe of the Arabs except that the Prophet (ﷺ) was born to it, so it is as if He said: "O assembly of the Arabs, there has certainly come to you a Messenger from the sons of Isma'il." The second view is stronger as proof, i.e., he is a human like you, so that you may understand from him and follow him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from among yourselves﴾ implies praise of the lineage of the Prophet (ﷺ), and that he is of the pure and select Arabs. In Sahih Muslim, from Wathilah ibn al-Asqa' who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed Allah chose Kinanah from the offspring of Isma'il, and chose Quraysh from Kinanah, and chose from Quraysh the Banu Hashim, and chose me from the Banu Hashim." And it is narrated from him (ﷺ) that he said: "I am from a lawful marriage and not from fornication." The meaning is that his lineage (ﷺ) back to Adam, peace be upon him, had no offspring except from lawful marriage, and there was no fornication in it. 'Abd Allah ibn Qusayt al-Makki read "min anfusikum" with a fatha on the fa', from "nafasah" (preciousness), and it was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) and from Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her, meaning: there has come to you a Messenger from the most noble and most excellent among you, from your saying: "a precious thing" when it is desired. It was also said: "from among yourselves" means the most obedient of you.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿distressing to him is your suffering﴾ means: your hardship is grievous to him. Al-'Anat is hardship, from their saying: "a hill ('akamah) 'anut" when it is difficult and destructive. Ibn al-Anbari said: the root of ta'annut is tashdid (severity). So when the Arabs say: "so-and-so causes so-and-so hardship (yata'annatu) and makes him suffer (yu'nituhu)," they mean he presses him severely and obliges him with what is hard for him to perform. This has been discussed earlier in [al-Baqarah] [[See vol. 3, p. 66.]]. The "ma" in "ma 'anittum" is verbal-masdar (infinitive), and it is the subject (mubtada'), and "'azeez" is the predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam). It is permissible for "ma 'anittum" to be the agent of "'azeez," and "'azeez" is then an attribute of the Messenger, and this is more correct. Likewise "ḥarīṣun 'alaykum" and likewise "ra'ūfun raḥīm," which is in the nominative as an attribute. Al-Farra' said: if it were read as "'azeezan 'alayhi ma 'anittum, ḥareesan, ra'ufan, raheeman" in the accusative as a state (ḥāl), it would be permissible. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: the best of what has been said about its meaning, in accordance with the speech of the Arabs, is what Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Azdi narrated to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad al-Khuza'i narrated to us, saying: I heard 'Amr ibn 'Ali say: I heard 'Abd Allah ibn Dawud al-Khuraybi say concerning His saying, mighty and majestic is He: "There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves; distressing to him is your suffering" — he said: "that you enter the Fire"; "ḥarīṣun 'alaykum" — he said: "that you enter Paradise." It was also said: "ḥarīṣun 'alaykum" means: that you believe. Al-Farra' said: "shaḥīḥun" meaning: he is miserly (desirous to keep) that you enter the Fire. And "al-ḥirṣ 'ala al-shay'" is the stinginess over it, that it be lost or destroyed.

(towards the believers he is ra'ūfun raḥīm) Al-Ra'ūf is one who exceeds in compassion and tenderness. The meaning of "ra'ūfun raḥīm" has been fully discussed earlier in [al-Baqarah] [[See vol. 1, p. 103; vol. 2, pp. 153, 158.]]. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: Allah did not combine two of His names for any of the prophets except for the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), for He said: "towards the believers he is ra'ūfun raḥīm," and said: ﴿Indeed Allah is to mankind Ra'ūf, Raḥīm﴾ [al-Hajj: 65]. And 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Yahya said: the arrangement of the verse is: "There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves, 'azīz, ḥarīṣ over you, towards the believers ra'ūfun raḥīm. Distressing to him is your suffering: nothing concerns him but your affair, and he is the one who stands as intercessor for you. So do not worry about what you suffer, as long as you hold to his sunnah, for nothing pleases him but your entering Paradise."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if they turn away, say: Allah is sufficient for me﴾ means: if the disbelievers turn away, O Muhammad, after these blessings with which Allah has favoured them, then say: "Allah is sufficient for me," i.e., Allah the Exalted is my sufficiency.

(There is no god but Him; upon Him I have relied) i.e., I have depended upon Him, and to Him I have entrusted all my affairs.

(And He is the Lord of the Mighty Throne) The Throne is singled out because it is the greatest of created things, so whatever is beneath it is included when it is mentioned. The reading of the majority is with the genitive "al-'azīm" as an attribute of "al-'arsh" (the Throne). It was also read with the nominative as an attribute of the Lord, narrated from Ibn Kathir, and it is the reading of Ibn Muhaysin. In the Book of Abu Dawud, from Abu al-Darda', he said: whoever says, when he enters the morning and when he enters the evening, "Allah is sufficient for me; there is no god but Him; upon Him I have relied, and He is the Lord of the Mighty Throne," seven times, Allah will suffice him for whatever concerns him, whether he says it truthfully or falsely. And in Nawadir al-Usul, from Buraydah, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says ten words after the end of every prayer, he will find Allah sufficient for him and rewarding him: five for this world and five for the Hereafter: 'Allah is sufficient for my religion; Allah is sufficient for my world; Allah is sufficient for what concerns me; Allah is sufficient against whoever oppresses me; Allah is sufficient against whoever envies me; Allah is sufficient against whoever plots evil against me; Allah is sufficient at death; Allah is sufficient at the questioning in the grave; Allah is sufficient at the Scale; Allah is sufficient at the Bridge; Allah is sufficient: there is no god but Him; upon Him I have relied, and to Him I turn in repentance.'" Al-Naqqash related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he said: the most recent of the Qur'an in terms of descent from Allah, exalted is He, are these two verses, "There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves" to the end of the surah, and we have explained this. Yusuf ibn Mihran narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the last thing revealed of the Qur'an was "There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves" and this verse; al-Mawardi mentioned it. We have mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas a difference of opinion to this, as we mentioned in [al-Baqarah], and it is more sound. Muqatil said: its descent occurred earlier in Mecca. This is far-fetched, because the surah is Medinan, and Allah knows best. Yahya ibn Ja'dah said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, would not confirm a verse in the Mushaf until two men testified to it. A man from the Ansar came to him with the two verses at the end of Surat Bara'ah: "There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves." 'Umar said: "By Allah, I will not ask you for a witness for them." Thus was the Prophet (ﷺ), and he confirmed them. Our scholars said: the man was Khuzaymah ibn Thabit, and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, confirmed them by his testimony alone, because the evidence for their authenticity in the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) was established, so it is an indicator that suffices without seeking another witness, unlike the verse of al-Ahzab: ﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they covenanted with Allah﴾ [[See vol. 14, verse 23.]] [al-Ahzab: 23], for that was confirmed by the testimony of Zayd and Khuzaymah, since they both heard it from the Prophet (ﷺ). This meaning has already been mentioned in the introduction of the book. And praise be to Allah.
